title: 2  Coancestry, and the two matrices
section: 2.4 f is not an ad hoc substitute
text:
2.4 f is not an ad hoc substitute
Two published lines of work use this matrix, or an affine function of it, to manage diversity. This section reports what each says, and what each says against it, because it is otherwise easy to read \(\mathbf{f}\) as “the thing we used because \(\mathbf{G}\) broke”.
Nejati-Javaremi et al. (1997) proposed the allelic-similarity method, \(f_{ij} = \tfrac{1}{4}\sum_{k=1}^{2}\sum_{l=1}^{2}\delta_{kl}\) with \(\delta_{kl} = 1\) when the \(k\)-th allele of \(i\) equals the \(l\)-th of \(j\) (the formula as reproduced by Gómez-Romano et al. (2016), p. 3). At a biallelic locus that is the term in brackets of Equation 2.5, so the genome-wide mean over loci is the identity-by-state average of Equation 2.5.
Gómez-Romano et al. (2016), in their discussion, compare this matrix with matrices built from the cross-product of centred genotype scores, normalised or not by the allele frequency. They report that the values of such relationship estimates “range from -1 to x, where x can be substantially larger than 1”, so that they can lie outside the interval \([0, 1]\) valid for a coefficient of coancestry, and in the next sentence that “estimates of the average coancestry across the whole genome tend to be within the valid range” but that this may not hold for a small region with few genotyped single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). They add two objections: the cross-product of centred scores gives a pair homozygous for the minor allele a higher relationship than a pair homozygous for the most frequent allele, so carriers of rare alleles would be penalised in the optimisation, and centring makes the matrix non-invertible. For the allelic-similarity method they say that it has a “natural” interpretation in relation to the definition of coancestry, and that positive definiteness should hold. The guarantee of staying in \([0, 1]\) for \(\mathbf{f}\) is the present book’s inference from Equation 2.5, whose terms are probabilities, not a statement of the paper. The zero total of Equation 2.4 is not a range violation. It comes from centring on the sample frequencies and it implies \(\mathbf{G}\mathbf{1} = \mathbf{Z}(\mathbf{Z}'\mathbf{1})/(2\sum_k p_k(1-p_k))
= \mathbf{0}\), so \(\mathbf{G}\) is singular, which is the non-invertibility the authors name.
The same matrix arrives, up to a fixed affine map, from a second direction. Meuwissen et al. (2020) (p. 3), citing Toro et al. (2014), state that using 0.5 as the base frequency for all loci, instead of the base-generation frequency \(p_{0,k}\), gives a relationship matrix – written there \(\mathbf{G}_{VR0.5}\) and here \(\mathbf{G}_{0.5}\) – that is “proportional to homozygosity and molecular coancestry”. The paper gives no formula or normalisation for it: the map below is derived in this chapter. With the 0/1/2 coding of Equation 2.1, \(2\sum_k p_k(1-p_k) = m/2\) at \(p_k = 0.5\) and
\[
\mathbf{G}_{0.5} \;=\; \frac{(\mathbf{M}^{H} - \mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}')
(\mathbf{M}^{H} - \mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}')'}{m/2}
\;=\; 4\,\mathbf{f} - 2\,\mathbf{J},
\tag{2.7}\]
with \(\mathbf{J}\) as in Equation 2.6. \(\mathbf{G}_{0.5}\) is therefore an affine function of \(\mathbf{f}\), not \(\mathbf{f}\) itself: its entries lie in \([-2, 2]\), negative exactly where \(f_{ij} < 0.5\); on the book data every \(f_{ij}\) exceeds \(0.5\), so the range in Table 2.7 is positive. For a vector of contributions \(\mathbf{c}\) with \(\mathbf{1}'\mathbf{c} = 1\), \(\mathbf{c}'\mathbf{J}\mathbf{c} =
1\) and \(\mathbf{c}'\mathbf{G}_{0.5}\mathbf{c} = 4\,\mathbf{c}'\mathbf{f}\mathbf{c}
- 2\), so under that normalisation the two matrices order selections identically. Replacing \(2p_k\) with \(1\) removes the population-dependent term that forced \(\mathbf{1}'\mathbf{G}\mathbf{1} = 0\).
The constant that Equation 2.7 removes is \(\mathbf{G}_{0.5} = 4(\mathbf{f} -
\tfrac12\mathbf{J})\): one half is the base-population floor of Equation 1.3 for a base at \(p_{b,k} = 0.5\) at every marker, since then \(p_{b,k}^2 + q_{b,k}^2 = 1/2\). It is a convention fixed in advance, not an estimate from the set being measured, and that is why \(\mathbf{1}'\mathbf{G}_{0.5}\mathbf{1}\) does not vanish. It is not the panel floor of the marker panel at hand, which is at least \(1/2\) and is generally larger, so \(\mathbf{G}_{0.5}\) is not zero for unrelated individuals either.


Show code
G05 <- tcrossprod(2 * X - 1) / (m / 2)         # M^H - 11' = 2X - 1
set.seed(2)
c_vec <- runif(N); c_vec <- c_vec / sum(c_vec)
stopifnot(min(f) > 0.5, all(abs(G05) <= 2),
          isTRUE(all.equal(G05, 4 * f - 2, tolerance = 1e-12)),
          isTRUE(all.equal(drop(crossprod(c_vec, G05 %*% c_vec)),
                           4 * drop(crossprod(c_vec, f %*% c_vec)) - 2,
                           tolerance = 1e-12)))
g05_tab <- fmt(c(minimum = min(G05), maximum = max(G05)))
knitr::kable(data.frame(Quantity = names(g05_tab), Value = unname(g05_tab)),
             row.names = FALSE, align = "lr")




Table 2.7: Smallest and largest entry of \(\mathbf{G}_{0.5}\) on the book data.






Quantity
Value




minimum
0.579


maximum
1.327








So, under normalised contributions, \(\mathbf{f}\) orders selections exactly as \(\mathbf{G}_{0.5}\), the VanRaden matrix centred at the fixed frequency \(0.5\). The two derivations of this section, the allelic-similarity route and the fixed-base route, are independent, and both land on the same matrix up to Equation 2.7. That is a consistency between two published treatments and this chapter’s algebra; it is not a proof that \(\mathbf{f}\) is the right matrix to constrain.
A limit of constraining this matrix. The sources of this section state one. Meuwissen et al. (2020) classify the molecular kinship matrix as homozygosity-based and report, in their abstract, that managing inbreeding with a homozygosity-based relationship “resulted in allele frequency changes toward 0.5 giving a low rate of increase in homozygosity for the panel used for management, but not for unmanaged neutral loci, at the expense of a high genetic drift”. In their Methods they state that with \(\mathbf{G}_{0.5}\) in optimal contributions “there will be pressure to move allele-frequencies toward 0.5”, with the covariance between the allele-frequency change and the base frequency negative (their Supplementary Information 1). Gómez-Romano et al. (2016) reach the same direction by intuition, not by a measurement, for allelic-similarity matrices, and say that the choice between matrices depends on the objective. A constraint on \(\theta_S\) computed from \(\mathbf{f}\) pins the homozygosity lens only; it does not pin \(F_{drift}\), which is computed from the allele frequencies against the frozen base (Section 1.2.3 for the scope, Chapter 10 for \(F_{hom}\), \(F_{drift}\) and their gap). The consequence of that gap for this book’s selections is measured where those metrics are reported, not here.

This split is the convention throughout hybdiv: the coancestry-based diversity metrics (theta_group() and those built on it, gene_diversity() and status_number()) take ctx[["f"]], and ctx[["G"]] appears only where traits are predicted. The frequency-based metrics (theta_from_freq(), he_nei() and the He, alleles_lost, F_hom and F_drift of freq_metrics()) are computed from colMeans(ctx[["X"]][idx, ]) and the frozen base frequencies ctx[["p0"]]; they never read ctx[["f"]], so a substitution of \(\mathbf{G}\) for \(\mathbf{f}\) cannot reach them (Section 1.2.3). tests/testthat/test-metrics.R asserts that every element of ctx[["f"]] lies in \([0, 1]\), which fails if a centered matrix is stored in its place; that \(|\sum \mathbf{G}| < 10^{-6} N^2\), the centering identity of Equation 2.4 up to floating-point tolerance; and that theta_group() over the whole population returns the mean of \(\mathbf{f}\), a value well away from the zero that \(\mathbf{G}\) would give, so a switch to \(\mathbf{G}\) inside theta_group(), and hence in the metrics built on it, fails the suite. Metrics that read ctx[["f"]] directly, without going through theta_group(), are not covered by that assertion.
Chapter 3 takes \(\mathbf{f}\) and asks what happens when the population it describes is not one population, but several.

title: 3  Diversity in a subdivided population
text:
3.1 Notation
A breeding programme is never one population. It is heterotic groups, or accessions, or landraces, or cycles – and the diversity of the whole is not the average of the diversity of the parts. Caballero and Toro (2002) give the partition that makes this precise, and it is the analytical backbone of everything that follows: the diversity-loss constraint \(\alpha\) (Equation 11.14, used in Chapter 15) bounds its total (Table 3.6), and the within/between asymmetry that makes plant hybrid breeding different from animal breeding is a statement about which term of it you are allowed to minimise (the second of the three departures of Section 1.3).
This chapter follows Chapter 2. There the molecular coancestry \(\mathbf{f}\) is defined between single individuals; here the same quantity is averaged over the individuals of subpopulations, and the partition of Caballero and Toro (2002) is stated in those terms. Chapter 1 states the partition for a set of hybrids (Equation 1.2); the step from subpopulations of individuals to hybrids partitioned over their parent lines is made in Section 3.11 below.
The paper’s central claim is uncomfortable and worth stating first: a method that ranks accessions by distance alone can invert the correct conclusion. In the paper’s own imaginary example, an accession can be the most distant while having so high an internal coancestry that removing it raises the diversity of the pool. Section 3.7.1 reproduces that result numerically.
crumbs: 3  Diversity in a subdivided population

title: 3  Diversity in a subdivided population
text:
A metapopulation of \(n\) subpopulations; subpopulation \(i\) has \(N_i\) individuals, \(N_T = \sum_i N_i\). In this chapter \(n\) and \(N\) count subpopulations and individuals, not the selected and candidate hybrids of



A tilde, \(\tilde{x}\), is a weighted mean within subpopulations: \(\tilde{f} = \sum_i f_{ii} N_i / N_T\), \(\tilde{F} = \sum_i F_i N_i / N_T\), \(\tilde{s} = \sum_i s_i N_i / N_T\). On an allele frequency, \(\tilde{p}_{k,i}\) is the frequency of allele \(k\) in subpopulation \(i\) (the mean over its individuals).
A bar, \(\bar{x}\), is a mean over all pairs in the metapopulation, between-subpopulation pairs included: \(\bar{f} = \sum_{i,j} f_{ij} N_i N_j / N_T^2\).
Always \(\bar{f} \le \tilde{f} \le \tilde{s}\). The differences between those three numbers are the partition of diversity. \(\bar{D} = \sum_{i,j} D_{ij} N_i N_j / N_T^2\), the mean over all pairs of the Nei distance \(D_{ij}\) of Equation 3.5, equals \(\tilde f - \bar f\) and enters Equation 3.7.
Sums and means (\(f_{ij}\), \(s_i\), \(\bar f\), \(\tilde f\), \(\tilde s\), the gene diversity (\(GD\)) terms) are computed per locus and then averaged over loci; never average frequencies first. The ratios (\(\alpha_i\), \(G_i\), \(G\), \(F_{IS}\), \(F_{ST}\), \(F_{IT}\)) are formed from those locus-averaged numerators and denominators (a ratio of means), not averaged locus by locus; the identities of Equation 3.10 hold in that form and not for the mean of per-locus ratios.
Quantities with the subscript \(i\) or \(ij\) (\(f_{ii}\), \(f_{ij}\), \(s_i\), \(F_i\)) refer to subpopulations: \(f_{ij}\) is the mean of the individual coancestry matrix of Chapter 2 over the block of an individual of \(i\) with an individual of \(j\), and \(s_i\) the mean self-coancestry of the individuals of \(i\). A single individual is the case \(N_i = 1\), which is the meaning these symbols have in Chapter 2 and Section 1.2.3. \(\mathbf{f}\) in bold is, in the worked example, the \(n \times n\) matrix of subpopulations.
\(k\) indexes the alleles of one locus in the formulas below (they are written for a multiallelic locus; at a biallelic locus the sum has two terms). The first bullet of Section 3.7.2 uses \(k\) for a biallelic locus instead, as Chapter 2 does for a marker.







WarningThe subtle point, and the one most often got wrong



Every coancestry here includes the pairs of an individual with itself – group coancestry in the sense of Cockerham (1967). That is what makes \(1 - f_{ii}\) exactly Nei’s gene diversity \(1 - \sum_k \tilde p_{k,i}^2\) (Nei 1973) – the plug-in form, without the small-sample correction \(2N_i/(2N_i - 1)\) (the factor that removes the bias derived under Equation 3.3) – and it is what makes the algebra close. The identity \(1 - f_{ii} = H_e\) for a set is Equation 1.2, derived in Section 11.2. Drop the diagonal and none of the identities of this chapter hold.
crumbs: 3  Diversity in a subdivided population

title: 3  Diversity in a subdivided population
text:
3.2 The three coancestry blocks

3.2.1 \(f_{ij}\), between subpopulations
The probability that two alleles, one sampled at random in subpopulation \(i\) and one in \(j\), are identical. From markers, \(f_{ij} = \sum_k \tilde p_{k,i}
\tilde p_{k,j}\).
Read it as redundancy between two materials. If you cross plants of \(i\) with plants of \(j\), the progeny has expected inbreeding \(F = f_{ij}\). It answers: what do I gain by recombining these two accessions?
On this molecular scale no fixed level of \(f_{ij}\) marks two materials as redundant. \(f_{ij}\) is identity in state, and it equals the pedigree coancestry only if the base population has all its alleles different (Caballero and Toro 2002, 292), which a biallelic panel cannot satisfy: for unrelated lines the expected \(f_{ij}\) is the base-population floor of the panel, \(m^{-1}\sum_k (p_{b,k}^2 + q_{b,k}^2) \ge 1/2\), and the observed level of a set is the panel floor of its own frequencies, which moves with the markers retained (Section 2.3, Table 2.5). The book’s simulated pools (book_cfg, Chapter 2) show a level well above zero for lines of different pools:


Show code
ctx <- simulate_data(book_cfg)
fL  <- ctx[["fL"]]
inA <- ctx[["pool"]] == "A"
fAB <- fL[inA, !inA]
fWI <- c(fL[inA, inA][upper.tri(fL[inA, inA])],
         fL[!inA, !inA][upper.tri(fL[!inA, !inA])])
fl_rng <- c(between_min = min(fAB), between_max = max(fAB),
            between_mean = mean(fAB), within_min = min(fWI),
            within_max = max(fWI), within_mean = mean(fWI))


The coancestry between two inbred lines from opposite heterotic pools ranges from 0.608 to 0.663 (mean 0.638), and between two lines of the same pool from 0.668 to 0.719 (mean 0.693). What separates complementary from redundant material is therefore the contrast between the two distributions, measured on one panel, and not a threshold carried over from another panel. The ranges above come from one simulated draw at the teaching scale and are not a property of maize pools.


3.2.2 \(f_{ii}\), within a subpopulation
The case \(i = j\). From markers \(f_{ii} = \sum_k \tilde p_{k,i}^2\), the expected homozygosity, so
\[1 - f_{ii} \;=\; H_{e,i} \;=\; \text{Nei's gene diversity of accession } i. \tag{3.1}\]
A landrace accession regenerated twenty times with forty ears per cycle accumulates coancestry and watches \(f_{ii}\) rise silently. It is the cheapest alarm for genetic erosion inside a genebank – and it is precisely what a distance tree cannot see.


3.2.3 \(s_i\) and \(F_i\), self-coancestry and molecular inbreeding
\[s_i = \sum_k \sum_l \frac{p_{k,l,i}^2}{N_i}, \qquad
  F_i = 2 s_i - 1, \qquad 2(1 - s_i) = 1 - F_i = H_{o,i} \tag{3.2}\]
with \(p_{k,l,i}\) the frequency of allele \(k\) within individual \(l\) of subpopulation \(i\): 0, 0.5 or 1 for a diploid, that is, the 0/1/2 dosage divided by 2 (ct_partition() does exactly this). For a biallelic marker and the reference allele, \(p_{k,l,i}\) is the within-individual frequency that 1 writes \(x\); there \(x_{ik}\) indexes an individual and a marker, here \(k\) indexes an allele. On the 0/1/2 scale itself \(s_i\) would leave \([0.5, 1]\) and \(F_i\) would leave \([0, 1]\). \(H_{o,i}\) is the observed heterozygosity, the mean over individuals of the fraction of loci at which the individual is heterozygous. A heterozygote has self-coancestry 0.5 at the locus, so \(1 - s_i\) is half the observed heterozygosity, not all of it.






Warning\(F_i\) here is molecular, and is not \(F_{IS}\)



By Equation 3.2 \(F_i = 1 - H_{o,i}\) is the observed fraction of homozygous loci of the individuals of \(i\), a function of their genotypes alone; it is not measured against a base. It is therefore not an inbreeding coefficient relative to a pedigree base, which would need the base to have all its alleles different (Section 3.2.1), and its level depends on the allele frequencies of the marker panel (the \(H_o\) of an outbred individual does), so it is not comparable across studies using different marker panels. For the question “is this population mating at random?”, use \(\alpha_i\) of Equation 3.3, read against its baseline (Equation 3.4).


In soybean, rice and wheat, pure lines have \(s_i \to 1\), so \(F_i \to 1\) and \(H_o \to 0\). That is expected, not a symptom. It changes only where the diversity resides.
crumbs: 3  Diversity in a subdivided population

title: 3  Diversity in a subdivided population
text:
3.3 Two per-subpopulation metrics
\[\alpha_i = \frac{F_i - f_{ii}}{1 - f_{ii}}, \qquad
  G_i = \frac{s_i - f_{ii}}{1 - f_{ii}} = \frac{1 + \alpha_i}{2} \tag{3.3}\]
\(\alpha_i\) is the subpopulation’s analogue of \(F_{IS}\), not the diversity-loss constraint \(\alpha\) of Chapter 15, and \(G_i\) is not a genomic relationship matrix \(\mathbf{G}\). A positive \(\alpha_i\) means an excess of homozygotes (selfing, mating among relatives, a Wahlund effect from internal substructure, null alleles); negative means an excess of heterozygotes (dioecy, self-incompatibility, selection, or a freshly formed F1 or synthetic) – but both are read against the baseline of the plug-in form, which is not zero.
The baseline under random mating. Take \(N_i\) diploid individuals whose genotypes are drawn independently at Hardy-Weinberg proportions from a population with allele frequencies \(p_k\) at a locus, and let \(\tilde p_k\) be the sample frequency, over the \(2N_i\) alleles. Then \(\mathbb{E}[F_i] = \sum_k p_k^2\) (the Hardy-Weinberg homozygosity) and \(\mathbb{E}[f_{ii}] = \mathbb{E}\sum_k \tilde p_k^2 = \sum_k p_k^2 +
(1 - \sum_k p_k^2)/(2N_i)\), because \(\mathrm{Var}(\tilde p_k) = p_k(1 - p_k)/(2N_i)\). So \(\mathbb{E}[F_i - f_{ii}] = -(1 - \sum_k p_k^2)/(2N_i)\), \(\mathbb{E}[1 - f_{ii}] = (1 - \sum_k p_k^2)(2N_i - 1)/(2N_i)\), and the ratio of these locus-averaged expectations (the form in which the chapter computes \(\alpha_i\), Section 3.1) is \[\mathbb{E}[F_i - f_{ii}] \,/\, \mathbb{E}[1 - f_{ii}] \;=\; -\frac{1}{2N_i - 1},
\qquad\text{so}\quad G_i = \frac{1 + \alpha_i}{2} \;\to\; \frac{N_i - 1}{2N_i - 1} < \tfrac12 . \tag{3.4}\] This is exact for the ratio of expectations and a first-order statement for the expectation of the ratio. Under exact random mating a negative \(\alpha_i\) and a \(G_i\) below \(1/2\) are therefore the null for a small accession, not evidence of an excess of heterozygotes: \(\alpha_i = -1/7\) for \(N_i = 4\) plants and \(-1/23\) for \(N_i = 12\), vanishing only as \(N_i\) grows. The same \(2N_i/(2N_i - 1)\) that multiplies \(1 - f_{ii}\) in the unbiased gene diversity removes this bias. Only the departure of \(\alpha_i\) from \(-1/(2N_i - 1)\) is read in the mating column of Table 3.1. Two limits of the derivation: it assumes independent sampling of individuals from a Hardy-Weinberg population (no subdivision inside the sample, no linkage effect on the expectation). It is algebra, so the chunk alpha-baseline-check checks it twice: by exact enumeration of the Hardy-Weinberg samples, and by simulating random-mating samples and passing them through ct_partition().


Show code
# (1) Exact. One biallelic locus, N diploids at Hardy-Weinberg: enumerate every
#     genotype count (n0, n1, n2) with its multinomial probability. Per count,
#     F = homozygous fraction and f_ii = pt^2 + (1 - pt)^2, pt = (n1 + 2 n2)/(2N).
enum_alpha <- function(N, p) {
  n <- as.matrix(expand.grid(n0 = 0:N, n1 = 0:N))
  n <- cbind(n, n2 = N - rowSums(n))
  n <- n[n[, "n2"] >= 0, , drop = FALSE]
  pr <- exp(lfactorial(N) - rowSums(lfactorial(n)) +
            drop(n %*% log(c((1 - p)^2, 2 * p * (1 - p), p^2))))
  pt <- (n[, "n1"] + 2 * n[, "n2"]) / (2 * N)
  c(total = sum(pr), EF = sum(pr * (n[, "n0"] + n[, "n2"]) / N),
    Ef = sum(pr * (pt^2 + (1 - pt)^2)))
}
N_chk  <- c(4, 12, 50)
p_grid <- c(0.05, 0.2, 0.5, 0.7, 0.95)
enum_dev <- vapply(N_chk, function(N) {
  e <- vapply(p_grid, function(p) enum_alpha(N, p), numeric(3))
  stopifnot(all.equal(e["total", ], rep(1, length(p_grid)), tolerance = 1e-12))
  a_loc <- (e["EF", ] - e["Ef", ]) / (1 - e["Ef", ])         # every locus
  a_avg <- mean(e["EF", ] - e["Ef", ]) / mean(1 - e["Ef", ]) # ratio of locus means
  c(max(abs(a_loc + 1 / (2 * N - 1))), abs(a_avg + 1 / (2 * N - 1)),
    abs((1 + a_avg) / 2 - (N - 1) / (2 * N - 1)))
}, numeric(3))
stopifnot(all(enum_dev < 1e-12))

# (2) Simulation: 60 random-mating samples of N = 4, 12, 50 plants at 3000 loci
#     through ct_partition(); mean over samples against the baseline, with the
#     Monte Carlo s.e. (samples are independent). Tolerance: 4 s.e.
m_sim <- 3000; R_sim <- 60
pop_sim <- rep(sprintf("N%02d", N_chk), N_chk)
set.seed(5)
p_sim <- stats::runif(m_sim, 0.05, 0.95)
sim <- vapply(seq_len(R_sim), function(r) {
  g <- do.call(rbind, lapply(N_chk, function(N)
         matrix(stats::rbinom(N * m_sim, 2, rep(p_sim, each = N)), N)))
  bs <- ct_partition(g, pop_sim)[["by_subpop"]]
  c(bs[["alpha_i"]], bs[["G_i"]])
}, numeric(6))
sim_mean <- rowMeans(sim); sim_se <- apply(sim, 1, stats::sd) / sqrt(R_sim)
sim_th   <- c(-1 / (2 * N_chk - 1), (N_chk - 1) / (2 * N_chk - 1))
sim_z    <- (sim_mean - sim_th) / sim_se
stopifnot(all(abs(sim_z) < 4))


The enumeration reproduces \(-1/(2N_i - 1)\) and \((N_i - 1)/(2N_i - 1)\) to \(4 \times 10^{-15}\) (machine precision), at every locus and for the locus-averaged ratio. The simulation gives a mean \(\alpha_i\) of -0.142, -0.043 and -0.01 for \(N_i = 4, 12, 50\) (baseline -0.143, -0.043, -0.01; largest deviation 1.0 Monte Carlo standard errors) and a mean \(G_i\) of 0.429, 0.478, 0.495, which is the baseline \((N_i - 1)/(2N_i - 1)\) and not \(0.5\).
\(G_i\) is the proportion of the accession’s diversity that sits between individuals rather than inside them, and it is probably the most underused quantity in the paper. It is a mating-system meter (Table 3.1):




Table 3.1: \(G_i\) (Equation 3.3), the share of an accession’s gene diversity that lies between individuals rather than within them, read as a mating-system meter: its value under each mating situation and the material in which that situation is typical. \(G_i\) tends to 0.5 under random mating only as \(N_i\) grows (Equation 3.4); \(N_i\) is the number of plants sampled.











\(G_i\)
Situation
Typical material




\(\approx (N_i - 1)/(2N_i - 1)\), below 0.5
random mating (plug-in baseline)
maize, sunflower, open populations


below that baseline
excess of heterozygotes
F1 synthetics, heterozygous clones, self-incompatibles


\(\to 1\)
all homozygous
inbred lines, doubled haploids, selfing species








Operationally, \(1 - G_i\) is the fraction of the diversity of the sample stored inside each plant. This is a qualitative guide to the sampling design, not a sample-size calculation (none is made here). With \(G_i \to 1\) (selfers), the diversity lies between plants, one plant carries almost none of it and many plants per accession are needed. With \(G_i\) near its random-mating baseline (maize), about half of the sample’s diversity lies inside each plant, so fewer plants are needed.

title: 3  Diversity in a subdivided population
section: 3.4 Distances, and what they actually are
text:
3.4 Distances, and what they actually are
Nei’s minimum distance between subpopulations (Toro and Caballero 2005, sec. 3a) is
\[D_{ij} = \frac{f_{ii} + f_{jj}}{2} - f_{ij}
                  = \sum_k \tfrac{1}{2}(\tilde p_{k,i} - \tilde p_{k,j})^2 . \tag{3.5}\]
Note what that is: half the sum of squared allele-frequency differences – a variance component, not an evolutionary distance calibrated in time. It is the piece that enters \(F_{ST}\), and it is legitimate. The error in a distance-only method is not using \(D_{ij}\); it is using only \(D_{ij}\).






TipNo double sum over individuals is needed



Between individuals \(l\) and \(l'\) the distance is \(d_{ll'} = (s_l + s_{l'})/2 - f_{ll'}\), with \(s_l\) and \(f_{ll'}\) the self-coancestry and coancestry of single individuals (Equation 3.2 with \(N_i = 1\)); at a biallelic locus it equals \((p_l - p_{l'})^2\), \(p_l\) the within-individual frequency, and over loci it is averaged. The mean of \(d_{ll'}\) over all pairs of an individual of \(i\) and an individual of \(j\), \(\bar d_{ij}\), computed literally as a double sum over all pairs of individuals, costs \(O(N_i N_j m)\). The identity \(\bar d_{ij} = (s_i + s_j)/2 - f_{ij}\) is exact and needs only the subpopulation frequencies and self-coancestries, at cost \(O(N_T m + n^2 m)\). \(\bar d_{ij}\) is not the \(D_{ij}\) of Equation 3.5: its diagonal \(\bar d_{ii} = s_i - f_{ii}\) is not zero, and Nei’s distance is recovered as \(D_{ij} = \bar d_{ij} - (\bar d_{ii} + \bar d_{jj})/2\). Both identities follow by substituting the definitions of \(d_{ll'}\), \(s_i\) (Equation 3.2) and \(f_{ij}\). No timing at genebank scale was run for this chapter.

title: 3  Diversity in a subdivided population
section: 3.5 The equation that matters most in practice
text:
3.5 The equation that matters most in practice
\[\bar{f} = \sum_{i} \frac{N_i}{N_T}
  \Big[\, \underbrace{f_{ii}}_{\text{internal coancestry}}
        - \underbrace{\textstyle\sum_j D_{ij} N_j / N_T}_{\text{mean distance to the others}} \Big] \tag{3.6}\]
In Equation 3.6, each accession’s contribution to global coancestry – that is, to the loss of diversity in the pool – has two terms of opposite sign:

Term 1 (+). The more internally fixed an accession is, the more it raises global coancestry: it dilutes the pool with copies of the same allele.
Term 2 (−). The more distant it is from the others, the more it reduces global coancestry.

A distance-only method sees term 2 alone. That is the whole mechanism of the inverted conclusions.

title: 3  Diversity in a subdivided population
text:
3.6 F statistics and the partition
\[F_{IS} = \frac{\tilde F - \tilde f}{1 - \tilde f}, \qquad
  F_{ST} = \frac{\tilde f - \bar f}{1 - \bar f} = \frac{\bar D}{1 - \bar f}, \qquad
  F_{IT} = \frac{\tilde F - \bar f}{1 - \bar f} \tag{3.7}\]
with \((1 - F_{IT}) = (1 - F_{IS})(1 - F_{ST})\). \(\tilde F\) is the \(N_i\)-weighted mean of the \(F_i\) of Equation 3.2; the subscripts follow the usual reading, I for individual, S for subpopulation, T for the whole metapopulation. Eq. 6 of Caballero and Toro (2002) writes these formulas, which they call Wright’s (1969) F-statistics (Evolution and the Genetics of Populations, vol. 2, as cited there); Toro and Caballero (2005, sec. 3a) credit the form \(F_{ST} = \bar D/(1 - \bar f)\) to Cockerham (1969). Those are the attributions this chapter reports; the original papers were not read for it.
What this \(F_{ST}\) is, in heterozygosity terms. With the plug-in form of Section 3.1, \(1 - \bar f = H_T\) (\(= GD_T\), Equation 3.9 below) is the gene diversity of the pooled sample’s frequencies \(\bar p_k\), \(1 - \tilde f = H_S\) (\(= GD_{WS}\)) is the \(N_i\)-weighted mean of the \(H_{e,i}\) of Equation 3.1, and \(\tilde F = 1 - H_o\) with \(H_o\) the \(N_i\)-weighted observed heterozygosity. Hence \[F_{ST} = \frac{H_T - H_S}{H_T}, \qquad F_{IS} = 1 - \frac{H_o}{H_S},
  \qquad F_{IT} = 1 - \frac{H_o}{H_T}, \tag{3.8}\] each \(H\) averaged over loci first, so that \(F_{ST}\) is a ratio of locus-averaged numerator and denominator (Section 3.1). It is also \(GD_{BS}/GD_T\) (Equation 3.10).


Show code
# The same 30 random hybrids as `tbl-keystone-check` (same seed, same draw).
set.seed(7)
idx_f <- sample(ctx[["N"]], 30)
tp    <- theta_pools(idx_f, ctx)
ft    <- (tp[["theta_A"]] + tp[["theta_B"]]) / 2                 # f-tilde
fb    <- (tp[["theta_A"]] + 2 * tp[["theta_AB"]] + tp[["theta_B"]]) / 4  # f-bar
fst_this    <- (ft - fb) / (1 - fb)                              # @eq-f-stats
fst_between <- (ft - tp[["theta_AB"]]) / (1 - tp[["theta_AB"]])  # between-referenced
stopifnot(all.equal(gd_partition(idx_f, ctx, tp)[["F_ST"]], fst_this, tolerance = 1e-12))
fst_cmp <- c(this = fst_this, between = fst_between, ratio = fst_between / fst_this)

# One biallelic locus, two populations of equal weight, from the coancestries:
# the closed forms of the prose, over 200 random (p_A, p_B), and the worked case.
one_locus <- function(pA, pB) {
  f1  <- function(p) p^2 + (1 - p)^2                    # f_ii at a biallelic locus
  fAB <- pA * pB + (1 - pA) * (1 - pB)
  tw  <- (f1(pA) + f1(pB)) / 2
  fb1 <- (f1(pA) + f1(pB) + 2 * fAB) / 4
  pb  <- (pA + pB) / 2; dp <- pA - pB
  this <- (tw - fb1) / (1 - fb1); btw <- (tw - fAB) / (1 - fAB)
  stopifnot(all.equal(this, dp^2 / (4 * pb * (1 - pb)), tolerance = 1e-12),
            all.equal(btw, dp^2 / (2 * pb * (1 - pb) + dp^2 / 2), tolerance = 1e-12),
            all.equal(btw / this, 4 * pb * (1 - pb) / (2 * pb * (1 - pb) + dp^2 / 2),
                      tolerance = 1e-12),
            all(btw / this >= 1 - 1e-12), all(btw / this <= 2))
  rbind(this = this, between = btw)
}
set.seed(11)
invisible(one_locus(stats::runif(200), stats::runif(200)))
stopifnot(all.equal(unname(one_locus(0.2, 0.6)[, 1]), c(1 / 6, 2 / 7), tolerance = 1e-12))


It is not the only statistic written \(F_{ST}\). A statistic referenced to the coancestry between populations, \((\theta_w - \theta_{AB})/(1 - \theta_{AB})\) with \(\theta_w\) the mean coancestry within populations and \(\theta_{AB}\) between populations, is also written \(F_{ST}\); Section 1.2.4 records that the book computes both and that they differ. This chapter cites no external source for that usage and does not use the statistic. The two take different values on the same data. At one biallelic locus with allele frequency \(p_A\) in one population and \(p_B\) in the other, equal weights, \(\bar p = (p_A + p_B)/2\) and \(\Delta p = p_A - p_B\), the statistic of Equation 3.7 is \(\Delta p^2 / (4\bar p \bar q)\) and the between-referenced one is \(\Delta p^2 / (2\bar p \bar q + \Delta p^2/2)\); their ratio, \(4\bar p \bar q / (2\bar p \bar q + \Delta p^2/2)\), lies in \([1, 2]\) and tends to 2 as \(\Delta p \to 0\). For \(p_A = 0.2\), \(p_B = 0.6\) the two are \(1/6\) and \(2/7\). On the 30 random hybrids of the book’s simulated pools used in Section 3.11, the between-referenced statistic, computed from locus-averaged coancestries, is 0.224 against 0.126 for the statistic of Equation 3.7, a ratio of 1.78 (one draw, seed 7). A value of \(F_{ST}\) must therefore be read with its reference stated; in this chapter it is always Equation 3.7.
The partition itself, of gene diversity (\(GD\)) into the terms named in Table 3.2, is the heart of Caballero and Toro (2002):
\[(1 - \bar f) = \underbrace{(1 - \tilde s)}_{GD_{WI}}
              + \underbrace{(\tilde s - \tilde f)}_{GD_{BI}}
              + \underbrace{(\tilde f - \bar f)}_{GD_{BS}} \tag{3.9}\]




Table 3.2: The partition of gene diversity of Caballero and Toro (2002) (Equation 3.9): each component, its definition in coancestries and its biological reading. \(\bar f\): mean coancestry over all pairs; \(\tilde f\), \(\tilde s\): within-subpopulation weighted means of coancestry and self-coancestry; \(H_e\), \(H_o\): expected and observed heterozygosity.











Component, defined in coancestries
Name
Biological reading




\(GD_T = 1 - \bar f\)
total diversity
\(H_e\) of the whole pool if everything were recombined


\(GD_{WI} = 1 - \tilde s\)
within individuals
half the observed heterozygosity inside each plant, \(H_o/2\)


\(GD_{BI} = \tilde s - \tilde f\)
between individuals, within accession
segregating variation available to within-population selection


\(GD_{WS} = 1 - \tilde f\)
within subpopulations
\(GD_{WI} + GD_{BI}\)


\(GD_{BS} = \tilde f - \bar f\)
between subpopulations
divergence; the only component a distance method sees








The four components satisfy the identities
\[\frac{GD_{WI}}{GD_T} = (1-G)(1-F_{ST}), \quad
  \frac{GD_{BI}}{GD_T} = G(1-F_{ST}), \quad
  \frac{GD_{WS}}{GD_T} = 1-F_{ST}, \quad
  \frac{GD_{BS}}{GD_T} = F_{ST}, \tag{3.10}\]
where \(G = (\tilde s - \tilde f)/(1 - \tilde f)\) is the metapopulation analogue of \(G_i\) (Equation 3.3). Since \(s_i - f_{ii} = G_i (1 - f_{ii})\), \(G = \sum_i N_i (1 - f_{ii}) G_i / \sum_i N_i (1 - f_{ii})\): a mean of the \(G_i\) weighted by \(N_i (1 - f_{ii})\), not the census mean \(\sum_i (N_i/N_T)\, G_i\). The two coincide when all \(G_i\) are equal or all \(f_{ii}\) are equal, and the first two identities then hold with either; when both the \(G_i\) and the \(f_{ii}\) differ the two means generally differ, and the first two identities fail with the census mean (the chunk of Table 3.3 exhibits one such case). They follow from \(1 - F_{ST} = (1 - \tilde f)/(1 - \bar f)\).
Every identity of this chapter so far needs individual genotypes, so the chunk below draws a toy metapopulation – two random-mating subpopulations and one of inbred lines, 400 biallelic loci – runs ct_partition() on it, and asserts each identity, the distance identities against a literal double sum over pairs of individuals; the resulting partition is printed in Table 3.3:


Show code
tol   <- 1e-12                                        # exact identities: machine precision
m_toy <- 400
N_toy <- c(10, 6, 8)
pop   <- rep(c("a_out", "b_out", "c_inbred"), N_toy)
set.seed(1)
p_toy <- matrix(stats::runif(3 * m_toy), 3)          # subpopulation frequencies
geno  <- rbind(                                       # 0/1/2 dosage
  matrix(stats::rbinom(N_toy[1] * m_toy, 2, rep(p_toy[1, ], each = N_toy[1])), N_toy[1]),
  matrix(stats::rbinom(N_toy[2] * m_toy, 2, rep(p_toy[2, ], each = N_toy[2])), N_toy[2]),
  matrix(2 * stats::rbinom(N_toy[3] * m_toy, 1, rep(p_toy[3, ], each = N_toy[3])), N_toy[3]))

ct  <- ct_partition(geno, pop)
gl  <- ct[["global"]]; GD <- ct[["diversity"]]; bs <- ct[["by_subpop"]]
s_i <- bs[["s_i"]]; f_ct <- unname(ct[["f"]])

# 2(1 - s_i) = 1 - F_i = H_o, with H_o counted from the genotypes
H_o <- as.vector(tapply(rowMeans(geno == 1), factor(pop), mean))
stopifnot(all.equal(2 * (1 - s_i), H_o, tolerance = tol),
          all.equal(1 - bs[["F_i"]], H_o, tolerance = tol),
          identical(s_i[3], 1))                       # inbred lines: 1 - s_i = 0
stopifnot(mean(geno^2 + (1 - geno)^2) > 1)            # 0/1/2 used as p: s leaves [0.5, 1]
stopifnot(all.equal(bs[["G_i"]], (1 + bs[["alpha_i"]]) / 2, tolerance = tol))

# f_bar <= f_til <= s_til, and f_bar = sum_i w_i [f_ii - sum_j D_ij w_j]
stopifnot(gl[["f_bar"]] <= gl[["f_til"]], gl[["f_til"]] <= gl[["s_til"]],
          all.equal(sum(bs[["contrib_fbar"]]), gl[["f_bar"]], tolerance = tol))

# census weights: f_bar is the mean of the individual coancestry matrix over all
# pairs, diagonal included (the group coancestry of the whole set)
stopifnot(all.equal(mean(molecular_coancestry(geno / 2)), gl[["f_bar"]], tolerance = tol))

# F statistics
stopifnot(all.equal(gl[["F_ST"]], (gl[["f_til"]] - gl[["f_bar"]]) / (1 - gl[["f_bar"]]),
                    tolerance = tol),
          all.equal(1 - gl[["F_IT"]], (1 - gl[["F_IS"]]) * (1 - gl[["F_ST"]]), tolerance = tol))

# @eq-f-stats-het: the same statistics from heterozygosities. Pooled frequencies
# (census weights) give H_T; H_S is the N_i-weighted mean of 2 p_i q_i; H_o is
# counted from the genotypes. Everything averaged over loci first.
p_i   <- t(vapply(split(seq_len(nrow(geno)), factor(pop)),
                  function(ix) colMeans(geno[ix, , drop = FALSE]) / 2, numeric(m_toy)))
p_all <- colMeans(geno) / 2
H_T_l <- 2 * p_all * (1 - p_all)                      # per locus
H_S_l <- colSums(ct[["w"]] * 2 * p_i * (1 - p_i))
H_T   <- mean(H_T_l); H_S <- mean(H_S_l); H_o_all <- mean(rowMeans(geno == 1))
stopifnot(all.equal(1 - gl[["f_bar"]], H_T, tolerance = tol),
          all.equal(1 - gl[["f_til"]], H_S, tolerance = tol),
          all.equal(gl[["F_ST"]], (H_T - H_S) / H_T, tolerance = tol),
          all.equal(gl[["F_IS"]], 1 - H_o_all / H_S, tolerance = tol),
          all.equal(gl[["F_IT"]], 1 - H_o_all / H_T, tolerance = tol))

# ratio of locus means (the chapter's F_ST) against the mean of per-locus ratios
stopifnot(all(H_T_l > 0))
fst_means <- c(ratio_of_means = (H_T - H_S) / H_T,
               mean_of_ratios = mean((H_T_l - H_S_l) / H_T_l))
stopifnot(!isTRUE(all.equal(fst_means[["ratio_of_means"]], fst_means[["mean_of_ratios"]])))

# the partition and the ratio identities, with the metapopulation G
stopifnot(all.equal(GD[["GD_T"]], GD[["GD_WI"]] + GD[["GD_BI"]] + GD[["GD_BS"]], tolerance = tol),
          all.equal(GD[["GD_WS"]], GD[["GD_WI"]] + GD[["GD_BI"]], tolerance = tol))
G_meta  <- (gl[["s_til"]] - gl[["f_til"]]) / (1 - gl[["f_til"]])
G_wmean <- sum(ct[["w"]] * bs[["G_i"]])
w_he    <- ct[["w"]] * (1 - diag(f_ct))                # G is the (1 - f_ii)-weighted mean
stopifnot(all.equal(G_meta, sum(w_he * bs[["G_i"]]) / sum(w_he), tolerance = tol))
F_ST    <- gl[["F_ST"]]
stopifnot(all.equal(GD[["GD_WI"]] / GD[["GD_T"]], (1 - G_meta) * (1 - F_ST), tolerance = tol),
          all.equal(GD[["GD_BI"]] / GD[["GD_T"]], G_meta * (1 - F_ST), tolerance = tol),
          all.equal(GD[["GD_WS"]] / GD[["GD_T"]], 1 - F_ST, tolerance = tol),
          all.equal(GD[["GD_BS"]] / GD[["GD_T"]], F_ST, tolerance = tol),
          # negative control, at the default tolerance 1.5e-8: the census mean fails
          !isTRUE(all.equal(GD[["GD_WI"]] / GD[["GD_T"]], (1 - G_wmean) * (1 - F_ST))))

# d_bar_ij = (s_i + s_j)/2 - f_ij against the literal double sum; per locus the
# distance between individuals l, l' is (s_l + s_l')/2 - f_ll' = (p_l - p_l')^2
P     <- geno / 2
idv   <- split(seq_len(nrow(P)), factor(pop))
d_lit <- matrix(0, 3, 3)
for (i in seq_along(idv)) for (j in seq_along(idv)) {
  for (l in idv[[i]]) for (l2 in idv[[j]])
    d_lit[i, j] <- d_lit[i, j] + mean((P[l, ] - P[l2, ])^2)
  d_lit[i, j] <- d_lit[i, j] / (length(idv[[i]]) * length(idv[[j]]))
}
d_bar <- outer(s_i, s_i, "+") / 2 - f_ct
stopifnot(all.equal(d_lit, d_bar, tolerance = tol),
          all.equal(unname(ct[["D_nei"]]),
                    d_bar - outer(diag(d_bar), diag(d_bar), "+") / 2, tolerance = tol))

toy_tab <- fmt(c(G_meta = G_meta, G_wmean = G_wmean, GD))
toy_lab <- c(G_meta = "$G$, weighted by $N_i(1 - f_{ii})$", G_wmean = "$G$, census mean",
             GD_T = "$GD_T$", GD_WI = "$GD_{WI}$", GD_BI = "$GD_{BI}$",
             GD_WS = "$GD_{WS}$", GD_BS = "$GD_{BS}$")
knitr::kable(data.frame(Quantity = unname(toy_lab[names(toy_tab)]),
                        Value = unname(toy_tab)), row.names = FALSE, align = "lr")

The identities of Equation 3.8 and the mean of the individual coancestry matrix hold to machine precision in the chunk. The ratio of locus means and the mean of the per-locus ratios are not the same number: for \(F_{ST}\) on this toy they are 0.2836 and 0.2715, and only the first obeys Equation 3.10.

3.6.1 Why the partition changes the strategy by species
The three bullets below are this book’s reading of what the partition implies for different reproductive systems, not results of Caballero and Toro (2002), whose examples are livestock breeds and a diploid, randomly mating setting. The first two follow from the definitions (\(\tilde s = 1\) for inbred lines gives \(GD_{WI} = 0\), which the chunk of Table 3.3 exhibits); the third and the regeneration advice are judgement.

Outcrossers (maize, sunflower, forages, forest trees): \(GD_{WI}\) is large. The diversity is literally inside the plants. Conserving means maintaining heterozygosity – regenerate with many individuals and balanced contributions.
Selfers (soybean, wheat, rice, beans) and doubled-haploid or line collections: \(GD_{WI} \approx 0\). All diversity is \(GD_{BI} + GD_{BS}\). Conserving means maintaining the number of distinct lines; heterozygosity is not a target. Regenerating with few plants per line is acceptable; losing lines is not.
Clonal crops (potato, sugarcane, fruit trees): \(GD_{WI}\) is high and frozen – it does not decay by drift while the clone exists. The \(N_e\) algebra does not apply without adaptation.

This is the reason a hybrid maize programme cannot manage diversity with a single pool-wide number: it needs \(GD_{WS}\) and \(GD_{BS}\) reported separately. Under drift alone in two closed pools of equal weight (\(f_{AA}\), \(f_{BB}\), \(f_{AB}\) in the notation of this chapter, \(\theta_A\), \(\theta_B\), \(\theta_{AB}\) in the code (theta_pools(), chunk fst-two-forms) and in 1, equal when the usage weights equal the census weights), \(f_{AB}\) is unchanged in expectation while \(f_{AA}\) and \(f_{BB}\) rise, so an expected rise \(\Delta\) in \(\tilde f\) raises \(\bar f\) by \(\Delta/2\): \(GD_{WS}\) falls by \(\Delta\), \(GD_{BS}\) rises by \(\Delta/2\), and \(GD_T\) falls by only \(\Delta/2\). A single total understates the within-pool loss; Section 5.8 shows what the between-pool gain is worth. The argument is for neutral drift in closed pools; selection is not covered by it, and the pools are closed, so it is not the asymptotic regime of Equation 3.11.

title: 3  Diversity in a subdivided population
text:
3.7 The worked example, reproduced
The metapopulation of Caballero and Toro (2002, 292, Tables 1 and 2): four subpopulations of \(N\) = 12, 4, 8, 6, three loci with 5, 3 and 3 alleles. The authors describe it as “an imaginary example based on allele frequencies of neutral genetic markers that could resemble allozyme data”; it is a teaching matrix, not a measured population, and the multiallelic loci put it outside the biallelic setting of the rest of the book. Its coancestry matrix, typed from Table 2a of the paper (the ten distinct entries compared with the printed table; the genotypes of its Table 1 are not reproduced here, so nothing below recomputes \(\mathbf{f}\) from genotypes):


Show code
f <- matrix(c(0.3391, 0.3021, 0.2535, 0.3229,
              0.3021, 0.8750, 0.3073, 0.3889,
              0.2535, 0.3073, 0.4766, 0.2483,
              0.3229, 0.3889, 0.2483, 0.3704), 4, 4, byrow = TRUE,
            dimnames = list(paste0("Sub", 1:4), paste0("Sub", 1:4)))
N <- c(12, 4, 8, 6)
w <- N / sum(N)


Note subpopulation 2: \(f_{22} = 0.875\), so \(H_e = 0.125\). It is nearly fixed internally. Now the global quantities, with the paper’s published values beside them (Table 3.4):


Show code
f_bar <- drop(w %*% f %*% w)
f_til <- sum(w * diag(f))
s_til <- 0.7056                       # published; needs individual genotypes

computed  <- c(f_bar = f_bar, f_til = f_til, GD_T = 1 - f_bar,
               GD_WI = 1 - s_til, GD_BI = s_til - f_til, GD_BS = f_til - f_bar,
               F_ST = (f_til - f_bar) / (1 - f_bar))
published <- c(f_bar = 0.3256, f_til = 0.4535, GD_T = 0.6744, GD_WI = 0.2944,
               GD_BI = 0.2521, GD_BS = 0.1279, F_ST = 0.1897)
# rows computed from f alone must match to half a unit of the 4th decimal
from_f <- c("f_bar", "f_til", "GD_T", "GD_BS", "F_ST")
stopifnot(max(abs(computed[from_f] - published[from_f])) < 5e-5)
# the published partition must close: three 4-dp roundings, at most 1.5e-4
stopifnot(abs(sum(published[c("GD_WI", "GD_BI", "GD_BS")]) -
              published[["GD_T"]]) < 1.5e-4)
# the prose: GD_BS is less than a fifth of the total (F_ST = GD_BS / GD_T)
stopifnot(computed[["F_ST"]] < 0.2)
ct_glob <- data.frame(quantity = names(computed),
                      computed = round(unname(computed), 4),
                      published = unname(published))

The chunk also asserts that the published \(GD_{WI}\), \(GD_{BI}\) and \(GD_{BS}\) sum to the published \(GD_T\), a check of the paper’s internal consistency. 3.7.1 Removing an accession can increase diversity
Table 3.5 gives the effect on \(GD_T\) of removing each subpopulation in turn.


Show code
res <- list(f = f, by_subpop = data.frame(N = N))
lg  <- cbind(ct_loss_gain(res),
             delta_pct_equal = ct_loss_gain(res, "equal")$delta_pct)
D_nei   <- outer(diag(f), diag(f), "+") / 2 - f
lg$dist <- drop(D_nei %*% w)               # mean distance to the pool
# the prose: f_22 is the largest diagonal entry, subpopulation 2 is the most
# distant, and removing it raises GD_T (census and equal weights) while removing
# any other lowers it
stopifnot(which.max(diag(f)) == 2, which.max(lg$dist) == 2,
          lg$delta_pct[2] > 0, all(lg$delta_pct[-2] < 0),
          lg$delta_pct_equal[2] > 0, all(lg$delta_pct_equal[-2] < 0))

The change is relative to \(GD_T\) of all four subpopulations, with census weights \(N_i/N_T\) or equal weights; a positive change means removal raises diversity. The last column is the mean Nei minimum distance to the pool, \(\sum_j D_{ij} N_j/N_T\) (Equation 3.5).

The number to look at is subpopulation 2. Its mean distance to the pool, \(\sum_j D_{2j} N_j/N_T\) (last column of Table 3.5), is the largest of the four, so a method that ranks accessions by distance alone would rank it first. The Weitzman approach discussed by Toro and Caballero (2005, sec. 3d) is such a method; the paper’s own Weitzman analysis uses Reynolds’ distance, not the Nei distance of this table, and gives subpopulation 2 the largest loss (\(-65.5\) %) with subpopulation 3 close behind (\(-63.3\) %) (Caballero and Toro 2002, Table 3, column 5); the authors report that Nei’s minimum and standard distances gave very similar results, not shown. The ranking by mean Nei distance in Table 3.5 is the book’s. The coancestry analysis says removing it raises pool diversity by 1.8 % (census weights) or 6.5 % (equal weights).
The arithmetic is in Equation 3.5: \(D_{2j}\) contains \(f_{22}/2\), and \(f_{22} = 0.875\) is far above the other diagonal entries, so the subpopulation is distant from the others in part because it is internally nearly fixed, and the same \(f_{22}\) is what raises global coancestry in the first term of Equation 3.6. What produced the near-fixation (a small sample of \(N_2 = 4\) plants, a founder effect, drift in the source population, selection) cannot be inferred from a coancestry matrix, and the example is imaginary; the chapter does not claim a cause. The same pattern is reported for the reanalysis of eleven European pig breeds of Laval et al. (2000) in Caballero and Toro (2002, Table 5, column 3): FRBA (Basque, France; the breed codes are defined in the footnote to Table 4 of Caballero and Toro (2002)), the breed with the largest Weitzman loss (-15.2 %), shows +0.67 % when removed, the value also given in the corrected form of Toro and Caballero (2005, Table 4). These values are quoted from the tables, not recomputed. In that column the subpopulations are not weighted by their effective sizes; in the column that is (column 6), FRBA is \(-0.0\) %, and the authors argue that weighting by size is desirable (Caballero and Toro 2002, 295). The +0.67 % is therefore the result without effective-size weighting, and not the only one the paper reports.






NoteWhat this does and does not license



For a genebank: a rare accession with few plants and high homozygosity – the archetypal “unique” accession on a distance tree – may be contributing negatively to the pool. That does not mean discard it. It means the correct priority may be to regenerate it at larger \(N\), not to replicate it into a core collection. Storing seed is cheap; extinction is irreversible.




3.7.2 Optimal contributions
Maximising \(GD_T = 1 - \sum_{i,j} f_{ij} c_i c_j\) subject to \(c_i \ge 0\) and \(\sum_i c_i = 1\) is a quadratic programme:


Show code
oc <- optimal_contributions(f)
stopifnot(identical(unname(round(oc[["c_i"]], 3)), c(0.522, 0, 0.270, 0.208)),
          oc[["c_i"]][2] == 0)


Subpopulation 2 receives weight zero (computed \(\mathbf{c} = (0.522,\, 0.000,\, 0.270,\, 0.208)\)), and total diversity rises from 0.6744 to 0.6874, a gain of 1.9 %. Rounded to three decimals the solution equals the published \(\mathbf{c} = (0.522,\, 0,\, 0.270,\, 0.208)\) of Caballero and Toro (2002); the chunk asserts it.
Three direct uses in plant breeding:

Base population for recurrent selection. \(c_i\) gives the seed proportion from each source that maximises the neutral-marker \(GD_T\) of the base. (In this bullet \(k\) indexes biallelic loci.) With \(f_{ij}\) built from population frequencies as above, \(GD_T = 1 - \sum_{i,j}
f_{ij} c_i c_j\) is the mean over loci of \(2\bar p_k \bar q_k\), where \(\bar p_k
= \sum_i c_i p_{ik}\) is the frequency of the mixture and \(\bar q_k = 1 - \bar
p_k\); it keeps the between-source term in full. If the mixture is intermated to Hardy-Weinberg proportions, the variance of the 0/0.5/1 genotype at locus \(k\) is \(\bar p_k \bar q_k / 2\), so the genic variance of the base (Equation 4.2, additive action; the variance is that of the mean of two alleles, each Bernoulli(\(\bar p_k\))) is \(\sum_k \beta_k^2 \bar p_k \bar q_k / 2\). With effects of equal size \(\beta\) at every one of the \(m\) loci and markers whose frequencies represent those of the quantitative trait loci, that is \(m \beta^2 GD_T / 4\): maximising \(GD_T\) maximises genic variance; with unequal effects the two differ by the squared-effect weighting. The case is different when the candidates are A \(\times\) B hybrids of two pools that are never intermated: Chapter 4, which derives the hybrid case and restates the case above as its limit with equal pool frequencies, shows that their genic variance contains only the within-pool part of gene diversity, not the between-pool term. In both cases neither \(GD_T\) nor the genic variance, being functions of allele frequencies and not of haplotypes, sees linkage disequilibrium.
Core collection. Instead of clustering heuristics plus proportional sampling, solve the quadratic programme directly with operational constraints (\(c_i \le\) multiplication capacity, \(c_i \ge\) a policy minimum for accessions of cultural importance).
Optimal contribution selection. Here \(\mathbf{c}\) and \(\mathbf{f}\) change object: \(\mathbf{c}\) is the vector of contributions of the \(N\) candidates and \(\mathbf{f}\) their \(N \times N\) coancestry matrix, not the contributions and the \(n \times n\) matrix of subpopulations above. Meuwissen (1997) maximises \(\mathbf{c}'\mathbf{u}\) subject to a bound on the group coancestry \(\mathbf{c}'\mathbf{f}\mathbf{c}\), with \(\mathbf{u}\) the vector of the candidates’ selection-criterion values (estimated breeding values in Meuwissen (1997), the multi-trait index \(u_i\) in Chapter 15); its Lagrangian form is \(\max \mathbf{c}'\mathbf{u} - \lambda\,\mathbf{c}'\mathbf{f}\mathbf{c}\), \(\lambda \ge 0\). This chapter is the case \(\lambda \to \infty\), pure diversity. A breeder operates in the middle of the curve – which is Chapter 15.

title: 3  Diversity in a subdivided population
text:
3.8 Equal contributions and effective size
Minimising \(\bar f\) maximises the status number \(N_s = 1/(2\bar f)\) (Lindgren et al. 1997) by definition. With census weights \(N_i/N_T\), \(\bar f\) is the mean of the individual coancestry matrix over all pairs, diagonal included, which is the group coancestry \(\theta_S\) of the whole set \(S\) (Chapter 2) whatever the subdivision; this \(N_s\) is then the \(1/(2\theta_S)\) of that chapter, and Table 3.6 writes \(GD_T = 1 - \bar f\) as \(1 - \theta_S\) (asserted in tbl-keystone-check). That chapter’s range \(N_s \in [1/2, 1]\) is a property of biallelic markers (\(\theta_S \ge 1/2\)); the multiallelic worked example of this chapter is not on it: \(N_s = 1/(2\bar f) =
1.54\) for its 30 individuals, and in neither case is \(N_s\) a head count. \(N_s\) is a static function of the current coancestry; the effective size \(N_e\) is defined from the rate at which inbreeding or coancestry rises across generations, so the two are not the same quantity, and lowering \(\bar f\) today does not by itself fix \(N_e\).
What links contributions to \(N_e\) is the asymptotic metapopulation effective size of Caballero and Toro (2002, Eq. 14), in the form restated by Toro and Caballero (2005, sec. 5a):
\[N_e \approx \frac{2Nn}{(V_W + V_B + 1)(1 - F_{ST})}, \tag{3.11}\]
with \(n\) subpopulations of equal size \(N\), and \(V_W\) and \(V_B\) the variances of the long-term contributions of individuals within and between subpopulations. Eq. 14 of Caballero and Toro (2002) has \((1 - F_{IT})\) in place of \((1 - F_{ST})\), and \((1 - F_{IT}) = (1 - F_{IS})(1 - F_{ST})\): Equation 3.11 is the case \(F_{IS} = 0\), random mating within subpopulations, which is its stated assumption. The model is a metapopulation of \(n\) subpopulations of constant size \(N\) with “any constant degree of migration” among them, discrete generations, and the formula holds only after enough generations for \(N_e\) and \(F_{ST}\) to reach their asymptotes. Two consequences. First, \(F_{ST}\) here is the asymptotic value of that metapopulation; it depends itself on the contribution variances and on migration, and for closed pools (the drift paragraph of Section 3.6.1) it tends to 1 and Equation 3.11 has no meaning. Second, the statement below holds the same \(F_{ST}\) on both sides. It does not apply as written to pools of inbred or doubled-haploid lines, where \(F_{IS} \ne 0\) and where the sampling unit is one allele copy per line rather than two per plant (Section 1.2). With random (Poisson) contributions within subpopulations and equal contributions of the subpopulations (\(V_W = 1\), \(V_B = 0\)) Equation 3.11 gives \(Nn/(1 - F_{ST})\); equalising contributions within subpopulations (\(V_W = 0\), \(V_B = 0\)) gives \(2Nn/(1 - F_{ST})\), double at the same \(F_{ST}\).


Show code
ne_fm  <- function(N, Vk) 4 * N / (2 + Vk)           # Falconer & Mackay, ch. 4
ne_ct  <- function(N, VW) 2 * N / (VW + 1)            # @eq-ne-meta, n = 1, F_ST = 0
N0     <- 100
V_k    <- c(random = 2, mother_once = 1, both_once = 0)  # variance of gametes per plant
ne_th  <- ne_ct(N0, V_k / 2)
# the two forms agree: algebra with V_W = V_k / 2, not evidence about N_e
stopifnot(all.equal(ne_fm(N0, V_k), ne_th, tolerance = 1e-12))
ne_gain <- c(seed_only = ne_th[["mother_once"]] / ne_th[["random"]],
             both      = ne_th[["both_once"]]   / ne_th[["random"]])
stopifnot(all.equal(ne_gain[["seed_only"]], 4 / 3, tolerance = 1e-12),
          all.equal(ne_gain[["both"]], 2, tolerance = 1e-12))


The chunk ne-equal-seed is the formula. The chunk ne-gene-dropping is the oracle: literal gene dropping in \(N = 100\) monoecious diploids with \(L = 500\) unlinked biallelic loci starting at \(p = 1/2\), and \(T = 25\) generations. In each generation every offspring takes one gamete (a random one of the two alleles at each locus, independently across loci) from its mother and one from its father; the schemes differ only in how mothers and fathers are chosen (selfing is possible in all three): independently at random (\(V_k = 2\)), every plant mother of exactly one offspring and the father at random (\(V_k = 1\)), every plant mother of exactly one offspring and father of exactly one (\(V_k = 0\)). The gene diversity \(H_t\) (the mean of \(2pq\) over loci) decays as \((1 - 1/(2N_e))^t\), so \(N_e\) is read from the slope of \(\log H_t\), one slope per independent pedigree (\(R = 30\) per scheme), inverted exactly: \(N_e = 1/(2(1 - e^{\text{slope}}))\). The comparison is made on the slope, against its Monte Carlo standard error over the 30 pedigrees, with tolerance 3 standard errors.


Show code
drop_genes <- function(N, L, T, scheme) {
  Z <- apply(matrix(rep(0:1, each = N), 2 * N, L), 2, sample)   # p = 1/2 at every locus
  A <- Z[seq_len(N), , drop = FALSE]; B <- Z[N + seq_len(N), , drop = FALSE]
  het    <- function() { p <- (colSums(A) + colSums(B)) / (2 * N); mean(2 * p * (1 - p)) }
  gamete <- function(par) {
    u <- matrix(stats::runif(N * L) < 0.5, N, L)
    ifelse(u, A[par, , drop = FALSE], B[par, , drop = FALSE])
  }
  H <- numeric(T + 1); H[1] <- het()
  for (t in seq_len(T)) {
    mo <- if (scheme == "random") sample.int(N, N, replace = TRUE) else sample.int(N)
    fa <- if (scheme == "both_once") sample.int(N) else sample.int(N, N, replace = TRUE)
    nA <- gamete(mo); nB <- gamete(fa); A <- nA; B <- nB
    H[t + 1] <- het()
  }
  H
}
R_ne <- 30; T_ne <- 25; L_ne <- 500
ne_of_slope <- function(s) 1 / (2 * (1 - exp(s)))
ne_obs <- vapply(names(V_k), function(sc) {
  set.seed(100 + match(sc, names(V_k)))                   # one seed per scheme
  slope <- vapply(seq_len(R_ne), function(r)
    stats::cov(0:T_ne, log(drop_genes(N0, L_ne, T_ne, sc))) / stats::var(0:T_ne), 0)
  s_hat <- mean(slope); s_se <- stats::sd(slope) / sqrt(R_ne)
  s_th  <- log(1 - 1 / (2 * ne_th[[sc]]))                 # slope implied by the formula
  c(Ne = ne_of_slope(s_hat),
    se = abs(ne_of_slope(s_hat - s_se) - ne_of_slope(s_hat + s_se)) / 2,
    z  = (s_hat - s_th) / s_se)
}, numeric(3))
stopifnot(all(abs(ne_obs["z", ]) < 3))


The measured \(N_e\) is 98.2 (\(\pm\) 1.6) for random contributions, 133.9 (\(\pm\) 1.7) when each plant is mother once and 199.0 (\(\pm\) 2.5) when it is mother once and father once, against 100.0, 133.3 and 200.0 from the formula; the largest deviation of the slope is 1.1 standard errors. That is the single-population case (\(n = 1\), \(F_{IS} = 0\)) of Equation 3.11, and nothing more.
The doubling assumes that each individual’s contribution is equalised as both female and male parent, which needs controlled pollination. In the single-population case Equation 3.11 reduces to \(2N/(V_W + 1)\), which is \(N_e = 4N/(2 + V_k)\) (Falconer and Mackay 1996) with \(V_W = V_k/2\), \(V_k\) the variance of the number of gametes an individual contributes. Harvesting the same number of seeds from every plant of an open-pollinated population equalises only the maternal contribution; with a maternal variance of 0 and a Poisson paternal variance of 1, \(V_k = 1\) and \(N_e = 4N/3\), a gain of 1.333 over Poisson contributions, not 2.






TipEqual contributions of both parents double \(N_e\)



Under controlled pollination, equal numbers of seeds from every plant as female and as male parent, and the same number of plants from every family, double the effective size (\(V_W = 0\) against \(V_W = 1\)). Equal seed numbers from open-pollinated plants alone give a factor of 4/3. Neither needs genotyping.


It is an intervention in germplasm management. The opposite – bulk harvest from a plot, which in practice samples the most productive plants disproportionately – inflates \(V_W\) and collapses \(N_e\).

title: 3  Diversity in a subdivided population
text:
3.9 The honest caveats
A breeder should take these seriously.
Criteria based on within-population variation favour the largest populations, which are often the commercial and least endangered ones (Toro and Caballero 2005, sec. 3e). A \(\bar f\) criterion can push a genebank toward abundant elite material – the opposite of the conservation objective. Beyond that:

Neutral markers do not measure adaptive value, disease resistance, stress adaptation or cultural value. A fixed accession may carry the only resistance allele to an emerging rust.
Allelic richness (which Caballero and Toro (2002, 297) call allelic diversity) is, they write, more sensitive to bottlenecks than average heterozygosity, and is often the more relevant criterion for pre-breeding. The argument that minimising \(\bar f\) maximises allelic richness in the long run (via the effective number of alleles being, by definition, the inverse of mean coancestry; (Toro and Caballero 2005, sec. 2)) is valid asymptotically but does not protect rare alleles in the short term. This is why allelic richness survives the redundancy analysis in Chapter 12 as the one genuinely independent axis.
Weighting between-group variation more heavily is arbitrary. A more defensible fix is to optimise \(\mathbf{c}\) with per-accession minimum constraints, as Toro and Caballero (2005, sec. 3e, Table 5) do for five Iberian pig strains.

Rule of thumb: use \(\bar f\) to decide proportions and regeneration effort; never use \(\bar f\) alone to decide discard.

section: 3.10 A correction published by the authors
text:
3.10 A correction published by the authors
Toro and Caballero (2005, Table 4, footnote a) republish the pig-breed reanalysis of Caballero and Toro (2002) and mark one entry (breed DESH, Schwäbisch-Hällisches, Germany) as correcting a mistake in the 2002 paper. Any value from that reanalysis should be read from the 2005 table; the 0.67 % of FRBA quoted in Section 3.7.1 is the same in the 2002 paper (Table 5, column 3) and in the 2005 table. The same review restates the effective-size result of Equation 3.11: equalising contributions within subpopulations doubles \(N_e\) (Toro and Caballero 2005, sec. 5a; Caballero and Toro 2002, Eq. 14).
What was compared with what, for this chapter. The full text of Caballero and Toro (2002) was read: the matrix of Table 2a, \(\tilde s\), \(\tilde f\), \(\bar f\), \(\bar D\), the \(F\) statistics and the \(GD\) components of Table 2b, the removal analysis and the contributions of Table 3, Eq. 6, 7, 8 and 14, and the pig-breed Table 5 were checked against the chapter, and the typed values agree. One difference is open: the chapter’s equal-weights column of Table 3.5 gives \(-6.92\) and \(-6.94\) % for subpopulations 1 and 3 where the paper’s unweighted column (Table 3, column 4) prints \(-6.8\) and \(-7.0\) %; the other two entries agree to the printed digit, the cause of the difference was not established, and the chapter does not rest on it. The 2005 review was consulted in excerpts (its section headings, Table 4 and the passages cited), not in full. Not read for this chapter, and therefore reported only as the secondary sources above attribute them: Wright (1969), Cockerham (1969), Cockerham (1967), Nei (1973) beyond its abstract, Lindgren et al. (1997), Falconer and Mackay (1996), and Meuwissen (1997) beyond its abstract.

title: 3  Diversity in a subdivided population
section: 3.11 What manages this quantity, and where
text:
3.11 What manages this quantity, and where
This chapter is the book’s keystone, and it is easy to read it as a self-contained treatment of Caballero and Toro (2002). The partition it derives (Equation 3.9) is not background: it is the object every later chapter operates on. Stated once, so the rest of the book can refer back rather than re-introduce it (Table 3.6):



Table 3.6: The three terms of the gene-diversity partition (Equation 3.9), what each measures, and the chapter of this book in which each is managed. \(\tilde s\), \(\tilde H_o\): within-pool means of self-coancestry and observed heterozygosity; \(\theta_S\): mean coancestry of the selected hybrids (the set \(S\)); \(\alpha\): the diversity-loss constraint.










Term
What it is
Where it is managed




\(GD_{WI}\)
diversity within individuals, \(1 - \tilde s = \tilde H_o/2\)
exactly zero with inbred parents (Chapter 11); the hybrid-level \(GD_{WI\text{-}hyb}\), half the mean heterozygosity of the selected hybrids, is what carries signal


\(GD_{BI}\)
between individuals, within pool
eroded by drift (Section 3.6.1); within-pool diversity also falls in the simulated cycles of Chapter 23, where drift and selection act together and are not separated; with inbred parents \(\alpha\) (Chapter 15) budgets \(GD_T = 1 - \theta_S = GD_{BI} + GD_{BS}\), not \(GD_{BI}\) alone


\(GD_{BS}\)
between pools
with flat dominance (\(d_k \equiv 1\)), inbred parents and the complete A \(\times\) B factorial, expected F1 heterozygosity per locus is exactly \(GD_T + GD_{BS}\) (Equation 5.5, Table 5.4): there \(GD_{BS}\) is the divergence term of heterosis, to be preserved not minimised; outside those conditions it is not an identity






For a set of hybrids the partition is taken over their parent lines. The “individuals” of Equation 3.9 are then the parent-line slots of the hybrids (one line of pool A and one of pool B per hybrid), the two pools are the subpopulations, and the weights are the usage weights of the lines, equal across the two pools by construction (Equation 1.2 and the identity \(F_{(ab)} = f^L_{ab}\) of Section 1.2.4; gd_partition() implements it). Within a pool the weights are the usage of each line, which is unequal in a random sample of hybrids (the chunk of Table 3.7 asserts it for its sample): a line used twice counts twice, so the individuals are the 30 line slots of each pool and not its 25 distinct lines. \(GD_{WI}\) (lines) and \(GD_{WI\text{-}hyb}\) (hybrids) are the same expression, \(1 - \tilde s\), over different individuals. The statements of the first row, and the identity \(GD_T = 1 - \theta_S = GD_{BI} + GD_{BS}\) of the second, are checked on 30 random hybrids of the book’s simulated pools with gd_partition() (Table 3.7):


Show code
set.seed(7)
idx_h <- sample(ctx[["N"]], 30)
gp    <- gd_partition(idx_h, ctx)
theta_S <- mean(ctx[["f"]][idx_h, idx_h])
H_hyb <- mean(rowMeans(ctx[["X"]][idx_h, , drop = FALSE] == 0.5))
use_A <- tabulate(ctx[["ped"]][["a"]][idx_h], nbins = ctx[["n_lines"]])
stopifnot(identical(idx_h, idx_f),                    # the draw of `fst-two-forms`
          length(unique(use_A[use_A > 0])) > 1,        # usage of the lines drawn is unequal
          abs(gp[["GD_WI"]]) < 1e-12,                 # inbred parents
          all.equal(gp[["GD_WI_hyb"]], H_hyb / 2, tolerance = 1e-12),  # half the F1 heterozygosity
          all.equal(1 - theta_S, gp[["GD_T"]], tolerance = 1e-12),
          all.equal(gp[["GD_T"]], gp[["GD_BI"]] + gp[["GD_BS"]], tolerance = 1e-12))
kt <- fmt(gp)
kt_lab <- c(GD_WI_hyb = "$GD_{WI\\text{-}hyb}$", GD_T = "$GD_T$", GD_WI = "$GD_{WI}$",
            GD_BI = "$GD_{BI}$", GD_BS = "$GD_{BS}$", F_ST = "$F_{ST}$")

Three consequences follow, and each is a chapter.
A single pool-wide statistic cannot express “conserve within, hold between”. That is why Chapter 11 reports the partition rather than only \(GD_T\), and why Chapter 13 makes stage S1 (conserving the heterotic groups, Table 1.1) a separate monitoring stage instead of folding pool conservation into the hybrid-selection constraint.
The between term is not a bonus to be maximised. Under the conditions of the \(GD_{BS}\) row (flat dominance, inbred parents, complete factorial, equal pool weights) expected F1 heterozygosity per locus is \(2\bar p\bar q + y^2/2\) (Equation 5.5), with \(2\bar p \bar q\) the “shared” term, which is \(GD_T\), and \(y^2/2\) the divergence term, which is \(GD_{BS}\). When the pools are redrawn further apart by neutral divergence from the same ancestral frequencies (Balding-Nichols draws, Section 5.8), the expectation of the sum does not change, so in expectation every unit of \(GD_{BS}\) gained is paid for, unit for unit, by \(GD_T\), and pushing the pools apart buys no heterosis. This is a statement about \(GD_T\) and \(GD_{BS}\), not about \(GD_{WS}\): by the drift accounting of Section 3.6.1 \(GD_{WS}\) falls by twice what \(GD_{BS}\) gains. It does not hold for non-flat dominance or for divergence that is aligned with the dominance effects, which Section 5.9 treats. The partition tells you where diversity is, not which direction to move it.
The within term is the one with a future. \(GD_{BI}\) is the raw material of next cycle’s response, which Chapter 4 makes precise: among A \(\times\) B hybrids genic variance is a sum over loci of the within-pool part of gene diversity, weighted by squared effect, while \(GD_T\) also carries the between-pool term that genic variance does not contain. Gene diversity is therefore a proxy for genic variance only through its within-pool part, only if effect sizes are unrelated to which loci lose diversity, and blind to disequilibrium; Chapter 24 is where the proxy is pushed until it breaks.

title: 4  Response to selection: the other half of the objective
text:
4.1 The breeder’s equation, and how well it does here
The preceding chapters define what a selection programme spends: coancestry (Chapter 2) and its partition over the two heterotic pools (Chapter 3), within the programme of Chapter 1. None of them writes down what selection buys. This chapter follows Chapter 3 because that chapter leaves two things to it: it names the component \(GD_{BI}\) of gene diversity (\(GD\)) as the raw material of the next cycle’s response without saying how response depends on it, and it defers the genic-variance argument for a mixture base. Section 4.2 carries both, and item 3 of the Preface (the diversity that protects response is the within-pool part) is what that section establishes.
The asymmetry is not cosmetic. Chapter 23 will report a constrained programme overtaking an unconstrained one after several cycles, at a crossover cycle that varies with the simulation seed. The book can report that because it simulated it, not because anything in the preceding chapters predicts it, and this chapter does not predict it either: a reader who wants to know when a crossover arrives in their programme still has to re-run the simulation with their own parameters. What this chapter installs are the pieces a prediction would be built from: the variance selection acts on, the equation that turns that variance into response, and the restricted selection index, which is set beside the book’s \(\alpha\) constraint at the end of the chapter (as a comparison, not as its proof).
The data come from simulate_pools(), the generator that Chapter 6 sets beside its own simulate_lines() and simulate_data(): it uses the same pool allele frequencies, drawn under the Balding-Nichols model (Balding and Nichols 1995) with parameter fst from ancestral frequencies, the same homozygous lines GL (0/1) and the same complete A \(\times\) B factorial of hybrids X (0/0.5/1), but a different trait. Its trait has n_qtl markers taken at random as quantitative trait loci (QTL) with independent standard-normal effects beta (zero elsewhere), and an index equal to the standardised true genetic value plus independent normal noise of variance \(1/h^2 - 1\), then standardised: before that last step the genetic value has unit variance, so \(h^2\) is the share of the index variance it contributes in expectation. Table 4.1 gives the size of the draw used in the rest of the chapter.
Response to one round of truncation selection is
\[R \;=\; i \, r \, \sigma_A \tag{4.1}\]
with \(i\) the selection intensity (a property of the selected fraction alone), \(r\) the accuracy of the criterion as a predictor of genetic value, and \(\sigma_A\) the additive standard deviation (Falconer and Mackay 1996).1 The equation is used here in the accuracy form \(i\,r\,\sigma_A\), which for \(r = h\) is the familiar \(i\,h\,\sigma_A\). Here the genetic value of the hybrids is the vector \(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta\) (gv), purely additive in the marker coding by construction of simulate_pools() (no dominance, \(d_k \equiv 0\)), so the genotypic value of a hybrid equals its additive value and \(\sigma_A\) is estimated by sd(gv). sel_intensity() returns \(i\); later chapters use it inside the usefulness criterion (Chapter 13) and, in Chapter 9, in a replicated check of an equation of this form on a different object. Table 4.2 sets the predicted response of Equation 4.1 beside the realised one for the top 60 hybrids on the index.
What “response” means in this chapter. The realised response is the mean genetic value of the selected hybrids minus the mean over all candidates: the genetic selection differential on the hybrids that were selected, not the change transmitted to a next generation. In the programme of Chapter 1 the hybrids are not recycled, lines are (assumption A3 there), so what a cycle transmits is a line’s value against a tester pool, a different object from the differential measured here. The comparison of Table 4.2 therefore asks one thing: whether Equation 4.1 reproduces the genetic selection differential of truncation selection on this generator. It is not a test of the response transmitted across cycles.
Show code
n_sel <- cfg$n_sel
N     <- nrow(X)
i_norm <- sel_intensity(n_sel / N)
r      <- cor(I, gv)
sel    <- order(I, decreasing = TRUE)[seq_len(n_sel)]

fmt(data.frame(
  quantity = c("intensity i", "accuracy r", "additive s.d. (sim. units)",
               "predicted response (sim. units)", "realised response (sim. units)"),
  value    = c(i_norm, r, sd(gv), i_norm * r * sd(gv), mean(gv[sel]) - mean(gv))), 3)

Intensities: normal-theory value of the selected fraction and realised standardised selection differential on the index. Two identities can be read off it. (1) The response from regression and the response with realised intensity are the same quantity written twice, since \(b\,S_I = i_{\text{real}}\,r\,\sigma_A\) identically (with \(b = \operatorname{Cov}(\mathrm{gv}, I)/\operatorname{Var}(I)\), \(S_I\) the selection differential on the index, \(i_{\text{real}} = S_I/\operatorname{sd}(I)\), \(r = \operatorname{Cov}(\mathrm{gv}, I)/(\operatorname{sd}(\mathrm{gv})\operatorname{sd}(I))\) and \(\sigma_A = \operatorname{sd}(\mathrm{gv})\), all on the \(N - 1\) scale, which cancels). (2) The regression residual \(e = \mathrm{gv} - \overline{\mathrm{gv}} - b\,(I - \bar I)\) has mean zero over the candidates, so the realised response minus the response from regression is exactly the mean residual over the selected set, \(\bar e_{\text{sel}}\): the part of the gap that is not an intensity effect is the selected hybrids’ average departure from the linear regression of genetic value on the index. The chunk below asserts both, to the relative tolerance \(1 \times 10^{-12}\) of the setup.
Show code
S_I  <- mean(I[sel]) - mean(I)
e    <- (gv - mean(gv)) - b * (I - mean(I))
dev1 <- dev_rel(b * S_I, i_real * r * sd(gv))
dev2 <- dev_rel((mean(gv[sel]) - mean(gv)) - b * S_I, mean(e[sel]))
stopifnot(dev1 < tol_exact, dev2 < tol_exact, abs(mean(e)) < tol_exact)
Deviations: identity (1) exactly 0, identity (2) \(1.1 \times 10^{-16}\); the mean residual over the selected hybrids is -0.546 simulation units.
With \(N =\) 625 candidates and \(n =\) 60 selected, \(i = \varphi(z)/(n/N)\), with \(z\) the standard-normal truncation point that leaves a fraction \(n/N\) above it and \(\varphi\) the standard-normal density, is the intensity of an infinitely large normal population (Falconer and Mackay 1996). At this finite \(N\) the expected standardised mean of the top \(n\) of \(N\) independent normal draws is smaller. A single draw cannot tell whether the remaining gap is structural or sampling, so Table 4.4 repeats the same simulate_pools() call over 30 seeds, and the finite-\(N\) intensity is estimated from 4000 normal samples.
Show code
one_seed <- function(s) {
  sm <- simulate_pools(n_A = book_cfg$n_pool_A, n_B = book_cfg$n_pool_B,
                       m = book_cfg$m, fst = cfg$fst, n_qtl = cfg$n_qtl,
                       h2 = cfg$h2, seed = s)
  g  <- drop(sm$X %*% sm$beta)
  Ix <- sm$index
  top <- order(Ix, decreasing = TRUE)[seq_len(n_sel)]
  pred <- sel_intensity(n_sel / length(Ix)) * cor(Ix, g) * sd(g)
  c(rel_gap = 1 - (mean(g[top]) - mean(g)) / pred,
    i_real  = (mean(Ix[top]) - mean(Ix)) / sd(Ix),
    skew    = mean(scale(Ix)^3))
}
rep_seeds <- t(vapply(seq_len(cfg$n_seeds), one_seed, numeric(3)))
n_rep  <- nrow(rep_seeds)
gap_se <- sd(rep_seeds[, "rel_gap"]) / sqrt(n_rep)
stopifnot(abs(mean(rep_seeds[, "rel_gap"])) < 2 * gap_se)   # the claim below

set.seed(cfg$seed_mc)
i_finite <- replicate(cfg$n_mc, {
  z <- rnorm(N)
  (mean(sort(z, decreasing = TRUE)[seq_len(n_sel)]) - mean(z)) / sd(z)
})

fmt(data.frame(
  quantity = c("relative gap 1 - realised/predicted", "realised intensity",
               "index skewness"),
  `mean over seeds` = colMeans(rep_seeds),
  `s.e.`            = apply(rep_seeds, 2, sd) / sqrt(n_rep),
  minimum           = apply(rep_seeds, 2, min),
  maximum           = apply(rep_seeds, 2, max),
  row.names = NULL, check.names = FALSE), 3)

Per quantity: mean over seeds, standard error of that mean (s.d./\(\sqrt{30}\)), minimum and maximum.
