The stopifnot() in that chunk asserts the chapter’s own claim, not an identity, so its error rates are computed, not assumed. The rule is \(|\bar g| < 2\,\mathrm{s.e.}\) with the s.e. estimated from the same \(n =\) 30 seeds. If the true mean gap is zero and the per-seed gaps are normal, \(\bar g/\mathrm{s.e.}\) follows a \(t\) distribution with \(n - 1\) degrees of freedom, and the rule fails to hold (a false alarm that stops the render under a different seed set) with probability \(P(|t_{n-1}| > 2)\). Against a true bias \(\delta\) the ratio is non-central \(t\) with parameter \(\delta\sqrt{n}/s\), \(s\) the per-seed s.d. of the gap.
Show code
s_gap    <- sd(rep_seeds[, "rel_gap"])
p_accept <- function(delta) {          # P(rule holds) at a true mean gap delta
  ncp <- delta * sqrt(n_rep) / s_gap
  pt(2, n_rep - 1, ncp = ncp) - pt(-2, n_rep - 1, ncp = ncp)
}
false_alarm <- 1 - p_accept(0)
delta80     <- uniroot(function(d) (1 - p_accept(d)) - 0.8, c(0, 10 * s_gap))$root
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(false_alarm, 2 * pt(-2, n_rep - 1))))
That is a false-alarm rate of 5.5 percent, about one seed set in 18. The assertion fails (flags a bias) with probability 0.8 only when the true mean gap is 0.046 in relative gap (4.6 percent of the predicted response), using this sample’s per-seed s.d. of 0.088; smaller true biases are flagged less often. A passing assertion therefore excludes biases of about that size and above, not smaller ones.
Over the 30 seeds the mean relative gap is 0.006 (standard error 0.016), the prediction exceeds the realised response in 19 of 30 seeds, and the mean realised intensity is 1.776 against a finite-\(N\) normal expectation of 1.771 (s.d. 0.044) and the infinite-population value 1.774.
The replicated mean gap is within two standard errors of zero, so at this scale the seed-1 overprediction is consistent with sampling variation. What 30 seeds can resolve is limited: two standard errors of the mean gap are 0.032, so a mean relative gap smaller than about that cannot be excluded, and the result is the absence of a detectable gap above that size, not a proof that the gap is zero. The two sizes, 0.046 and 0.032, answer different questions and are not two estimates of one bound: the first is the true mean gap that the rule above flags with probability 0.8 (its power, at this sample’s per-seed s.d.), the second is two standard errors of the observed mean gap, the threshold of the rule itself. In a normal approximation the first is the threshold plus 0.84 standard errors, that is 1.42 times the second; the non-central \(t\) computation above gives 1.43 times. (The seed-1 draw is one of the 30 seeds, not an independent replicate.) Limits of scope: only the teaching scale (25 + 25 lines, 2000 markers, 300 QTL, \(h^2 = 0.5\), Balding-Nichols fst = 0.15) was measured, so nothing here says how the gap behaves at production scale or under selection across cycles; the object is the genetic selection differential of the selected hybrids on an additive trait (see the definition of response before Table 4.2), not a transmitted response. The replicated sweep of Chapter 9 tests the equation on a different object, the change in the progeny mean, with \(r\) taken against the breeding value because that trait has dominance, so it is not a replication of this check and its numbers are not reproduced here.

title: 4  Response to selection: the other half of the objective
section: 4.2 Genic variance, and what it has to do with gene diversity
text:
4.2 Genic variance, and what it has to do with gene diversity
The additive variance in Equation 4.1 is not a fixed property of the population. Split it in two.
Genic variance is what the loci would contribute if they were independent:
\[V_{\text{genic}} \;=\; \sum_k \beta_k^2 \operatorname{Var}(x_k) \tag{4.2}\]
with \(\beta_k\) the effect of marker \(k\) and \(x_k\) its hybrid genotype. This is a definition of the chapter, not a result attributed to a source.
Realised variance is what the population actually has, \(\operatorname{Var}
(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta)\), which is the sum of the whole covariance matrix rather than only its diagonal. The difference is exactly the covariance term of Equation 4.3, an identity of the covariance matrix that needs no source:
\[\operatorname{Var}(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta) - V_{\text{genic}}
\;=\; 2\sum_{k<l}\beta_k\beta_l \operatorname{Cov}(x_k, x_l) \tag{4.3}\]
Bulmer (1971) is the reference for the mechanism by which selection makes this term negative (negative gametic-phase disequilibrium among trait loci, which lowers the additive variance below its genic value); the primary text was not read for this book, and the statement is reported, not checked. The term that Table 4.5 evaluates for the seed-1 draw is a different thing, and three assumptions decide what it is. (i) In simulate_pools() the genotypes of the lines are drawn independently across loci given the pool frequencies. (ii) No selection precedes the evaluation. (iii) Each pool has finitely many lines (25 + 25 here). Over the complete A \(\times\) B factorial, an identity of the design, \(\operatorname{Cov}(x_k, x_l) = [\operatorname{Cov}_A(u_k, u_l) +
\operatorname{Cov}_B(v_k, v_l)]/4\), with \(\operatorname{Cov}_A\) and \(\operatorname{Cov}_B\) the covariances across the lines of each pool (up to the \(N\) against \(N - 1\) divisor), so no between-pool term enters. Under (i) and (ii) each of the two pool covariances has expectation zero, so the term of the table is the sampling covariance among loci of 25 + 25 founder lines, with expectation zero; by (iii) it is not zero in a draw, and its sign and size change with the seed. The seed-1 value therefore cannot be read as the size or the sign of a Bulmer effect. Measuring a selection-induced term needs a control in which the same founders are selected at random, which is what Chapter 24 does.


Show code
Cx  <- cov(X)
ld  <- sum(outer(sim$beta, sim$beta) * Cx) - sum(sim$beta^2 * diag(Cx))
V_genic <- genic_var(X, sim$beta)
dev_ld     <- dev_rel(var(gv) - V_genic, ld)
dev_oracle <- dev_rel(V_genic, ref_genic_var(X, sim$beta))
stopifnot(dev_ld < tol_exact, dev_oracle < tol_exact)
fmt(data.frame(
  quantity = c("realised variance", "genic variance", "covariance term"),
  `value (sim. units squared)` = c(var(gv), V_genic, var(gv) - V_genic),
  check.names = FALSE), 4)




Table 4.5: Realised variance \(\operatorname{Var}(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta)\), genic variance (Equation 4.2, genic_var()) and their difference, the covariance term of Equation 4.3 (here the sampling covariance among loci of the 25 + 25 founder lines, expectation zero), over the 625 hybrids of the seed-1 draw (25 + 25 lines, 2000 markers, 300 QTL). Variances in squared simulation units.







quantity
value (sim. units squared)




realised variance
22.4837


genic variance
25.2051


covariance term

Deviations, relative to the larger of 1 and the quantity (tolerance \(1 \times 10^{-12}\)): of the covariance term from the sum of the off-diagonal covariance matrix (Equation 4.3) \(1.4 \times 10^{-14}\); of genic_var() from the literal oracle ref_genic_var() \(4.2 \times 10^{-16}\).
The design identity for \(\operatorname{Cov}(x_k, x_l)\) is asserted next in population-divisor form on the seed-1 draw, and the distribution of the term is computed over the 30 seeds of Table 4.4 and over a disjoint block of 200 seeds, so that the reading of the seed-1 value does not rest on a block that contains it.


Show code
U <- sim$GL[sim$pool == "A", ]
V <- sim$GL[sim$pool == "B", ]
pop_cov <- function(M) cov(M) * (nrow(M) - 1) / nrow(M)       # divisor n
dev_fact <- dev_rel(Cx * (N - 1) / N, (pop_cov(U) + pop_cov(V)) / 4)
stopifnot(dev_fact < tol_exact)

ld_seeds <- seq_len(cfg$n_seeds + n_blk)
ld_by_seed <- t(vapply(ld_seeds, function(s) {
  sm <- simulate_pools(n_A = book_cfg$n_pool_A, n_B = book_cfg$n_pool_B,
                       m = book_cfg$m, fst = cfg$fst, n_qtl = cfg$n_qtl,
                       h2 = cfg$h2, seed = s)
  g  <- drop(sm$X %*% sm$beta)
  vg <- genic_var(sm$X, sm$beta)
  c(term = var(g) - vg, share = (var(g) - vg) / vg)
}, numeric(2)))
blk1 <- ld_by_seed[seq_len(cfg$n_seeds), , drop = FALSE]
blk2 <- ld_by_seed[cfg$n_seeds + seq_len(n_blk), , drop = FALSE]
term_se  <- sd(blk2[, "term"]) / sqrt(n_blk)
z_term   <- mean(blk2[, "term"]) / term_se
# Claim "expectation zero": |z| < 3, false alarm P(|z| > 3) ~ 0.003 per seed set.
stopifnot(abs(z_term) < 3)
stopifnot(dev_rel(ld_by_seed[cfg$seed, "term"], var(gv) - V_genic) < tol_exact)


On the pool covariances, the factorial identity holds to a relative deviation of \(1.5 \times 10^{-15}\) (tolerance \(1 \times 10^{-12}\)). Over seeds 1 to 30 the term has mean -0.138 (s.e. 0.835) and is negative in 18 of them. Over the disjoint seeds 31 to 230 its mean is -0.212 (s.e. 0.326, so \(z =\) -0.65, inside the \(\pm 3\) the chunk asserts; false alarm 0.3 percent per seed set), and its share of the genic variance has mean -0.009 and s.d. 0.205. The seed-1 value, a share of -0.108, lies 0.53 s.d. from zero: it is the spread of the sampling covariance among loci, not an effect.
How does \(V_{\text{genic}}\) relate to gene diversity? Let \(p_{Ak}\) and \(p_{Bk}\) be the frequencies of the allele coded 1 at locus \(k\) among the inbred lines of pools A and B, \(q = 1 - p\) (so \(\bar q_k = 1 - \bar p_k\)), and \(\bar p_k = (p_{Ak} + p_{Bk})/2\) the hybrid-pool frequency. A hybrid of the complete A \(\times\) B factorial carries \(x_k = (u_k + v_k)/2\), with \(u_k \in \{0, 1\}\) the allele of its pool-A parent and \(v_k \in \{0, 1\}\) that of its pool-B parent (the \(u_{ik}\), \(v_{jk}\) of Section 5.11 without the line index), drawn independently from the two pools, so over the factorial (population-variance scale)
\[\operatorname{Var}(x_k) \;=\; \frac{p_{Ak}q_{Ak} + p_{Bk}q_{Bk}}{4}
\;=\; \frac{\bar p_k \bar q_k}{2} - \frac{(p_{Ak} - p_{Bk})^2}{8}. \tag{4.4}\]


Show code
pA <- colMeans(U)
pB <- colMeans(V)
pH <- (pA + pB) / 2
v_pop <- colMeans(X^2) - colMeans(X)^2                    # population scale (divisor N)
dev_var1 <- dev_rel(v_pop, (pA * (1 - pA) + pB * (1 - pB)) / 4)
dev_var2 <- dev_rel(v_pop, pH * (1 - pH) / 2 - (pA - pB)^2 / 8)
# scale: genic_var() and var(gv) use the divisor N - 1
dev_scale <- dev_rel(V_genic, N / (N - 1) * sum(sim$beta^2 * v_pop))
# equal effects (beta = 1 at all m loci): sum(v_pop) = m * GD_WS / 4, GD_T = GD_WS + GD_BS
m_loc <- ncol(X)
GD_WS <- mean(pA * (1 - pA) + pB * (1 - pB))
GD_BS <- mean((pA - pB)^2 / 2)
GD_T  <- mean(2 * pH * (1 - pH))
dev_eq1 <- dev_rel(sum(v_pop), m_loc * GD_WS / 4)
dev_eq2 <- dev_rel(GD_T, GD_WS + GD_BS)
stopifnot(c(dev_var1, dev_var2, dev_scale, dev_eq1, dev_eq2) < tol_exact)
# special case (a), pA = pB = pbar: Var(x_k) = pbar qbar / 2, equal effects m GD_T / 4
dev_mix <- dev_rel(sum(pH * (1 - pH) / 2), m_loc * GD_T / 4)
stopifnot(dev_mix < tol_exact)
ok <- pH > 0 & pH < 1
ratio <- v_pop[ok] / (pH * (1 - pH))[ok]


Deviations (tolerance \(1 \times 10^{-12}\), relative to the larger of 1 and the quantity): the two forms of Equation 4.4 against the empirical population variance of the hybrids, \(1.8 \times 10^{-16}\) and \(1.8 \times 10^{-16}\); the scale factor below, \(5.6 \times 10^{-16}\); the two equal-effect statements below, \(2.5 \times 10^{-15}\) and \(5.6 \times 10^{-17}\); and the mixture-base limit, \(3.1 \times 10^{-15}\).
The formula is on the population-variance scale (divisor \(N\)); genic_var() and var(gv) use the divisor \(N - 1\), so for this factorial genic_var(X, beta) equals \(N/(N-1)\sum_k \beta_k^2\,(p_{Ak}q_{Ak} +
p_{Bk}q_{Bk})/4\) exactly (the factor \(N/(N-1)\) on the population-scale genic variance): here 25.1648 on the population scale and 25.2051 from genic_var(), a ratio of 1.0016 against \(N/(N-1) =\) 1.0016. The per-locus variance entering \(V_{\text{genic}}\) (Equation 4.2) is therefore not proportional to \(\bar p_k \bar q_k\): the ratio \(\operatorname{Var}(x_k)/(\bar p_k \bar q_k)\) ranges from 0.107 to 0.5 across these loci. Gene diversity of the hybrid pool, \(\frac{1}{m}\sum_k 2 \bar p_k \bar q_k\), is \(GD_T\) of Equation 1.2 for the complete factorial of inbred lines with equal pool weights (Chapter 3, Table 3.6). It contains the between-pool term \(GD_{BS} =
\frac{1}{m}\sum_k (p_{Ak} - p_{Bk})^2/2\) that Equation 4.4 removes (since \(2\bar p_k\bar q_k = p_{Ak}q_{Ak} + p_{Bk}q_{Bk} + (p_{Ak} - p_{Bk})^2/2\)), while \(V_{\text{genic}}\) among hybrids sees only the within-pool part \(GD_{WS} = \frac{1}{m}\sum_k (p_{Ak}q_{Ak} + p_{Bk}q_{Bk})\), weighted by squared effect. \(GD_{WS} = GD_{WI} + GD_{BI}\) (Equation 3.9), so with inbred parents (\(GD_{WI} = 0\)) it is the \(GD_{BI}\) that Chapter 3 names: the two symbols are one number here, and this chapter writes \(GD_{WS}\) because the sum over the two pools is what enters \(V_{\text{genic}}\). The inference is that gene diversity is a proxy for genic variance only through \(GD_{WS}\), and only if effect sizes are unrelated to which loci lose diversity; this chapter does not test the second condition.
Two special cases of the same formula fix the scope, each under stated conditions. (a) A mixture base: with \(p_{Ak} = p_{Bk} = \bar p_k\) (equivalently, a mixture of sources intermated to Hardy-Weinberg proportions, \(x_k\) the mean of two independent alleles each Bernoulli(\(\bar p_k\))), \(\operatorname{Var}(x_k) =
\bar p_k\bar q_k/2\) and \(V_{\text{genic}} = \sum_k \beta_k^2 \bar p_k\bar q_k/2\). With effects of equal size \(\beta\) at all \(m\) loci, and markers whose frequencies represent those of the trait loci, that is \(m\beta^2 GD_T/4\), so maximising \(GD_T\) then maximises \(V_{\text{genic}}\); with unequal effects the two differ by the squared-effect weighting. This is the statement that Chapter 3 uses for a base population and defers here. (b) Hybrids of two pools never intermated, equal effects: \(V_{\text{genic}} = m\beta^2 GD_{WS}/4\), which equals \(m\beta^2 GD_T/4\) only when \(GD_{BS} = 0\), the case (a). The trait of this chapter (300 loci, \(N(0,1)\) effects) satisfies neither equal-effects condition, so (a) and (b) are statements about the proxy, not about the gv above. Neither \(GD_T\) nor \(V_{\text{genic}}\), being functions of allele frequencies and not of haplotypes, sees linkage disequilibrium.
The proxy is incomplete in two further ways. Gene diversity weights every locus equally, so it cannot distinguish a marker carrying half the genetic variance from one carrying none. And – more seriously – no frequency-based metric sees the covariance term, as the next box sets out.






WarningThe frequency-based metrics cannot see the covariance term



\(\theta_S\), \(GD_S\) (and \(GD_T\)), \(N_s\), allelic richness, \(F_{hom}\) and \(F_{drift}\) – including \(\theta_S\), the only metric the differential evolution (DE) selector constrains – are all functions of allele frequencies one locus at a time. The covariance term of Equation 4.3 does not move a single allele frequency. eff_dim() is the exception: it is computed from the spectrum of the double-centred \(f\), a multilocus quantity, so it does respond to disequilibrium, but it weights loci by nothing, not by effect. A flat gene diversity trajectory therefore does not imply flat additive variance, for two separate reasons. First, \(GD_T = GD_{WS} + GD_{BS}\) and only \(GD_{WS}\) enters \(V_{\text{genic}}\) among hybrids, so a flat \(GD_T\) can accompany a falling \(GD_{WS}\) whenever \(GD_{BS}\) rises (Chapter 3 gives the drift case). Second, the covariance term of Equation 4.3 is invisible to every one-locus metric, and enters \(\sigma_A^2\) and from there the predicted \(R\) of Equation 4.1. Chapter 24 tests the second reason only: it measures, against a random-selection control, whether selection builds this term and how quickly it decays, and does not compare a gene-diversity trajectory with a variance trajectory.

title: 4  Response to selection: the other half of the objective
section: 4.3 Combining ability against a tester pool
text:
4.3 Combining ability against a tester pool
Additive variance is the variance of breeding values, not of genotypic values. Two statements about combining ability separate the chapter’s additive trait from the dominance case, and the dominance assumption is declared where each is made. The model of Equation 1.1 splits a hybrid value into general combining ability (GCA) of the two parent lines and specific combining ability (SCA) of the pair; the concepts are those of Sprague and Tatum (1942), and the exact orthogonal split used here is the book’s own, derived in Section 5.11.
Without dominance (\(d_k \equiv 0\), the case of gv): the effect on the hybrid value of substituting one allele at locus \(k\) is \(\beta_k/2\) whatever the pool it is substituted into (a parental allele fixes one half of the hybrid coding \(x_k \in \{0, 1/2, 1\}\), so one substitution moves \(x_k\) by \(1/2\) and \(\mathrm{gv}\) by \(\beta_k/2\); this is the additive effect \(a_k\) of Chapter 1 and Chapter 5 for \(d_k \equiv 0\), since the two homozygotes, worth \(\pm a_k\) there, differ by \(2a_k = \beta_k\) here), a line’s GCA does not depend on the tester set (Chapter 1), the value of a hybrid is \(\mathrm{gv}_{ij} = a_i + b_j\) with \(a_i = \sum_k \beta_k u_{ik}/2\) and \(b_j = \sum_k \beta_k v_{jk}/2\); the GCAs are \(a_i\) and \(b_j\) centred on their means and the SCA is zero up to rounding. Over the complete factorial \(a_i\) and \(b_j\) are uncorrelated, so \(\operatorname{Var}(\mathrm{gv}) = \operatorname{Var}(\mathrm{GCA}_A) +
\operatorname{Var}(\mathrm{GCA}_B)\): the whole \(\sigma_A^2\) of Equation 4.1 is GCA variance, with no interaction part. The chunk below computes the split from the factorial table of gv itself (row and column means, the interaction as the residual), asserts these statements, and also estimates the GCA of the pool-A lines against only five of the pool-B lines as testers.


Show code
nA <- nrow(U); nB <- nrow(V)
GV <- matrix(gv, nA, nB)                       # ped varies pool A fastest
a_i <- drop(U %*% sim$beta) / 2                # a_i = sum_k beta_k u_ik / 2
b_j <- drop(V %*% sim$beta) / 2
gca_A_add <- rowMeans(GV) - mean(GV)           # GCA of A lines against all of pool B
gca_B_add <- colMeans(GV) - mean(GV)
sca_add   <- GV - mean(GV) - outer(gca_A_add, gca_B_add, "+")
tester    <- seq_len(5)                        # a five-line tester set from pool B
gca_A_sub <- rowMeans(GV[, tester]) - mean(GV[, tester])
dev_a_b   <- dev_rel(GV, outer(a_i, b_j, "+"))
dev_gca   <- dev_rel(c(gca_A_add, gca_B_add), c(a_i - mean(a_i), b_j - mean(b_j)))
dev_sca0  <- dev_rel(sca_add, 0)
dev_vadd  <- dev_rel(var(gv), var(rep(gca_A_add, times = nB)) +
                              var(rep(gca_B_add, each  = nA)))
dev_tstr  <- dev_rel(gca_A_sub, gca_A_add)
stopifnot(c(dev_a_b, dev_gca, dev_sca0, dev_vadd, dev_tstr) < tol_exact)


Deviations (tolerance \(1 \times 10^{-12}\)): \(\mathrm{gv}_{ij} = a_i + b_j\), \(7.8 \times 10^{-16}\); GCAs equal to the centred \(a_i\), \(b_j\), \(5.9 \times 10^{-16}\); largest SCA, \(1.1 \times 10^{-14}\); \(\operatorname{Var}(\mathrm{gv}) = \operatorname{Var}(\mathrm{GCA}_A) +
\operatorname{Var}(\mathrm{GCA}_B)\), \(7.9 \times 10^{-16}\), both sides being 22.4837; GCA of the pool-A lines against 5 testers instead of all 25, \(4.9 \times 10^{-16}\).
With dominance (\(d_k \not\equiv 0\)): the dominance part of a line’s GCA is an average effect evaluated at the opposite pool’s allele frequencies (Chapter 1), so combining ability is then a property of a line against a tester pool, never of the line alone, and an SCA component appears. The chunk below applies the split to an illustrative, dominance-only value \(H\) = heterosis_value(X, d), with dominance effects \(d_k \sim N(0.3, 0.1^2)\) drawn here and unrelated to \(\boldsymbol\beta\). The draw is not the one of Chapter 5 (a gamma-distributed \(d_k\), seed 4); that chapter owns the decomposition and its tests, and the shares below depend on the draw of \(d\). They are shares of that illustrative heterosis, not of the genetic variance of gv. The GCA and SCA of this half are those of \(H\) (Equation 5.14), not those of the cross mean gv of the paragraph above.


Show code
set.seed(cfg$seed_d)
d  <- rnorm(ncol(X), cfg$d_mean, cfg$d_sd)      # dominance effects
gs <- heterosis_gca_sca(U, V, d)
H  <- heterosis_value(X, d)

gA <- rep(gs$gca_A, times = nB)                 # ped varies pool A fastest
gB <- rep(gs$gca_B, each  = nA)
sc <- as.vector(gs$sca)

cc <- cor(cbind(gA, gB, sc))
dev_recon <- dev_rel(H, gs$mu + gA + gB + sc)
dev_vsum  <- dev_rel(var(H), var(gA) + var(gB) + var(sc))
dev_orth  <- max(abs(cc[upper.tri(cc)]))        # correlations, scale free
stopifnot(c(dev_recon, dev_vsum, dev_orth) < tol_exact)


The three components are orthogonal, so their variances add exactly. Deviations (tolerance \(1 \times 10^{-12}\)): reconstruction \(H = \mu + \mathrm{GCA}_A + \mathrm{GCA}_B + \mathrm{SCA}\), \(2.2 \times 10^{-15}\); \(\operatorname{Var}(H)\) against the sum of the three variances (both 38.1131), \(2.4 \times 10^{-15}\); largest absolute correlation between two components, \(3.1 \times 10^{-17}\). Table 4.6 gives the shares.


Show code
p <- c(gca_A = var(gA), gca_B = var(gB), sca = var(sc))
fmt(data.frame(component = names(p),
               `variance (sim. units squared)` = p,
               share = p / sum(p), row.names = NULL, check.names = FALSE), 3)




Table 4.6: Variance of the illustrative dominance-only value \(H\) = heterosis_value(X, d) (dominance effects \(d_k \sim N(0.3, 0.1^2)\), seed 7; one draw, 25 \(\times\) 25 factorial of the seed-1 pools) split into the general combining ability of pool A and pool B lines and the specific combining ability of their crosses. Variance in squared simulation units; share: fraction of the summed variance. These are shares of the illustrative heterosis, not of the genetic variance of the selected trait.

title: 4  Response to selection: the other half of the objective
text:
4.4 What weights = NULL is assuming
stage2_select() defaults (weights = NULL) to equal weight on every trait, and every chapter of this book including Chapter 25 takes that default. The criteria it weights are not phenotypes but the predicted trait values \(\hat{\mathbf{g}}\) of the hybrids (hybrids columns, passed to build_ctx() as traits). build_ctx() standardises each column before weighting, so the default index is \(\sum_j \hat g_j / \operatorname{sd}(\hat g_j)\), up to a positive affine transformation that does not change the ranking. In trait units that is the index \(\mathbf{a}'\hat{\mathbf{g}}\) with economic weights \(a_j = 1/\operatorname{sd}(\hat g_j)\). What the default assumes is therefore an economic statement: one standard deviation of predicted value is worth the same in every trait. It is a choice, not a neutral one.
Whether \(\mathbf{a}'\hat{\mathbf{g}}\) is the best index for those \(\mathbf{a}\) is a separate question, and the answer depends on what \(\hat{\mathbf{g}}\) is. Let \(W = \mathbf{a}'\mathbf{g}\) be the aggregate genotype (the breeding objective), with \(\mathbf{g}\) the vector of the traits’ genetic values (one entry per trait; not a vector over individuals). The weights \(\mathbf{b}\) on a vector of criteria \(\boldsymbol\xi\) that maximise the correlation between \(\mathbf{b}'\boldsymbol\xi\) and \(W\) are \(\operatorname{Var}(\boldsymbol\xi)^{-1}\operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol\xi, \mathbf{g}')\,\mathbf{a}\). When \(\boldsymbol\xi = \hat{\mathbf{g}}\) is the multi-trait best linear unbiased predictor (BLUP) of \(\mathbf{g}\), \(\operatorname{Cov}(\hat{\mathbf{g}},
\mathbf{g}') = \operatorname{Var}(\hat{\mathbf{g}})\) (a standard property of BLUP, used here without a citation and verified for the example below), so \(\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{a}\): weighting the predictions by the economic weights is then the optimum, not a departure from it. The condition fails in general for predictions that are not BLUP of \(\mathbf{g}\), single-trait BLUPs of genetically correlated traits included.
When \(\boldsymbol\xi\) is instead the vector of phenotypic records \(\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{g} + \mathbf{e}\), \(\mathbf{e}\) independent of \(\mathbf{g}\), with \(\operatorname{Var}(\mathbf{y}) = \boldsymbol\Sigma_P\) and \(\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{g}') = \boldsymbol\Sigma_G\), the same expression is the Smith-Hazel index (Smith 1936; Hazel 1943) (the two papers were not read for this book: the expression is checked here by algebra and by the BLUP chunk below, not against them, and the matrix notation is modern, not theirs), displayed in Equation 4.5:
\[\mathbf{b} \;=\; \boldsymbol\Sigma_P^{-1}\boldsymbol\Sigma_G\mathbf{a}, \tag{4.5}\]
with \(\boldsymbol\Sigma_P\) and \(\boldsymbol\Sigma_G\) the phenotypic and genetic covariance matrices of the traits (P and G in the code; \(\boldsymbol\Sigma_G\) is not the relationship matrix \(\mathbf{G}\)) and \(\mathbf{a}\) the economic weights. Table 4.7 evaluates Equation 4.5 for a two-trait example.


Show code
P <- matrix(c(4.0, 1.2, 1.2, 1.0), 2)      # phenotypic covariance
G <- matrix(c(2.0, 0.3, 0.3, 0.3), 2)      # genetic covariance
a <- c(1, 1)                               # equal economic weight
stopifnot(all(eigen(G, only.values = TRUE)$values > 0),      # G is a covariance
          all(eigen(P - G, only.values = TRUE)$values > 0))  # so is P - G




Show code
fmt(data.frame(trait = c("yield", "moisture"),
               `economic weight` = a,
               `Smith-Hazel weight` = index_smith_hazel(P, G, a),
               check.names = FALSE), 3)




Table 4.7: Smith-Hazel index weights (Equation 4.5) for an illustrative two-trait example with equal economic weights. Phenotypic covariance \(\boldsymbol\Sigma_P\): variances 4.0 and 1.0, covariance 1.2; genetic covariance \(\boldsymbol\Sigma_G\): variances 2.0 and 0.3, covariance 0.3. Values are invented for illustration, not estimated.

Equal economic weights do not give equal index weights on phenotypes here. \(\mathbf{b}\) is proportional to \(\mathbf{a}\) if and only if \(\mathbf{a}\) is an eigenvector of \(\boldsymbol\Sigma_P^{-1}\boldsymbol\Sigma_G\). A sufficient condition is \(\boldsymbol\Sigma_G = c\,\boldsymbol\Sigma_P\) – every trait with heritability \(c\) and genetic correlations equal to the phenotypic ones – which requires neither equal variances nor uncorrelated traits.


Show code
b_sh <- index_smith_hazel(P, G, a)
dev_prop <- dev_rel(index_smith_hazel(P, 0.5 * P, a), 0.5 * a)
# BLUP of g from one record per trait (known means): ghat = G P^-1 y.
K <- G %*% solve(P)
dev_blup1 <- dev_rel(drop(solve(K %*% P %*% t(K), K %*% G) %*% a), a)
dev_blup2 <- dev_rel(drop(t(K) %*% a), b_sh)
stopifnot(c(dev_prop, dev_blup1, dev_blup2) < tol_exact)


The first statement is the sufficient condition, checked for \(\boldsymbol\Sigma_G = 0.5\,\boldsymbol\Sigma_P\) (deviation of \(\mathbf{b}\) from \(0.5\,\mathbf{a}\): \(2.2 \times 10^{-16}\); tolerance \(1 \times 10^{-12}\)). The chunk also checks the two statements that tie the phenotypic and the predicted index together, for the BLUP from one record per trait with known means, \(\hat{\mathbf{g}} = \boldsymbol\Sigma_G\boldsymbol\Sigma_P^{-1}\mathbf{y}\): \(\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\mathbf{g}})^{-1}\operatorname{Cov}(\hat{\mathbf{g}},
\mathbf{g}')\,\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{a}\), and \(\mathbf{a}'\hat{\mathbf{g}}\) is the Smith-Hazel index \(\mathbf{b}'\mathbf{y}\) of Table 4.7. So the gap between \(\mathbf{b}\) and \(\mathbf{a}\) in that table is a property of an index on phenotypes; it is not a defect of weights = NULL, whose criteria are predictions. What the default does assume is the economic weighting \(a_j = 1/\operatorname{sd}(\hat g_j)\), and that the predictions behave as multi-trait BLUP; this chapter tests neither against a real breeding objective. The deviations of the two BLUP statements are \(2.2 \times 10^{-16}\) and \(1.1 \times 10^{-16}\).

title: 4  Response to selection: the other half of the objective
section: 4.5 The \(\alpha\) constraint beside the restricted index
text:
4.5 The \(\alpha\) constraint beside the restricted index
Chapter 15 argues that a diversity budget is approvable where a weighted sum is not: a breeding committee can approve a statement that the loss of diversity will be no more than a stated fraction, and cannot approve a price of \(\lambda\) index units per unit of diversity.
That argument is usually presented as a point about human decision-making. The constrained form has two earlier lineages, reported here with what was and was not read.
Restricted selection indices. Kempthorne and Nordskog (1959) is the reference the book cites for the index that maximises aggregate gain subject to zero expected change in specified traits. The paper is not open access and was not read for this book, so what it contains, and whether it solves the problem in the form below, is not verified here. The matrix form is the book’s own statement, in the \(\mathbf{C} = \boldsymbol\Sigma_G\mathbf{R}\) form used by index_restricted() (not claimed to be their notation), with \(\mathbf{R}\) the \(n_t \times n_r\) matrix of restricted directions for \(n_t\) traits and \(n_r\) restrictions and \(\boldsymbol\Sigma_P\), \(\boldsymbol\Sigma_G\), \(\mathbf{a}\) as in Equation 4.5:
\[\mathbf{b} \;=\; \boldsymbol\Sigma_P^{-1}\left[\boldsymbol\Sigma_G\mathbf{a} - \mathbf{C}
(\mathbf{C}'\boldsymbol\Sigma_P^{-1}\mathbf{C})^{-1}\mathbf{C}'\boldsymbol\Sigma_P^{-1}
\boldsymbol\Sigma_G\mathbf{a}\right], \qquad \mathbf{C} = \boldsymbol\Sigma_G\mathbf{R} \tag{4.6}\]
By direct substitution \(\mathbf{C}'\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{0}\), that is \(\mathbf{R}'\boldsymbol\Sigma_G\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{0}\). The chunk below checks it for a two-trait example, and that is all that is checked: the derivation of Equation 4.6 as the maximiser is not given here.
Constraining a group coancestry while maximising gain. In optimum contribution selection, as set out in the Methods of Meuwissen et al. (2020), the genetic level of the selected parents \(\bar g = \mathbf{c}'\hat{\mathbf{g}}\) is maximised over the vector of contributions \(\mathbf{c}\), with the rate of inbreeding constrained through the group coancestry of the selected parents, \(K = \tfrac12\mathbf{c}'\mathbf{G}\mathbf{c}\), where \(\mathbf{G}\) is the relationship matrix chosen for managing diversity; that paper compares several, among them molecular ones (\(\mathbf{G}_{0.5}\) and VanRaden’s). Its Introduction credits Meuwissen (1997) with optimum contribution selection that maximises gain for a given rate of inbreeding; the 1997 paper itself was not read for this book. The paper gives no formula for \(\mathbf{G}_{0.5}\); Chapter 2 derives one (Equation 2.7), from which, for contributions summing to one, the group coancestry of the molecular matrix \(\mathbf{f}\) behind \(\theta_S\) is an affine function of the \(\mathbf{G}_{0.5}\) group coancestry, so the two order selections identically. So restricting a group coancestry while maximising gain is not new to this book, and the restricted direction is not its contribution. What the book adds, as far as the sources read here go, is stated in the text of Section 11.9 and Chapter 15 (a budget measured against random subsets of the same size, applied to hybrids of two pools); this chapter has not checked that against the wider literature.
Table 4.8 compares the restricted index with the unrestricted index of Table 4.7 when moisture is held at zero.


Show code
R  <- cbind(c(0, 1))                       # hold moisture at zero gain
b_r <- index_restricted(P, G, a, R)
b_u <- index_smith_hazel(P, G, a)
cov_m <- c(drop(crossprod(R, G %*% b_u)), drop(crossprod(R, G %*% b_r)))
sd_I  <- sqrt(c(drop(b_u %*% P %*% b_u), drop(b_r %*% P %*% b_r)))   # sd of b'y
gain_m <- i_norm * cov_m / sd_I           # expected gain in moisture per round
# restricted: zero in expectation, to the tolerance; Smith-Hazel: clearly not
stopifnot(abs(cov_m[2]) < tol_exact, abs(gain_m[2]) < tol_exact, gain_m[1] > 0)

fmt(data.frame(
  quantity = c("weight on yield", "weight on moisture",
               "covariance of index with moisture",
               "expected gain in moisture per round"),
  `Smith-Hazel` = c(b_u, cov_m[1], gain_m[1]),
  restricted    = c(b_r, cov_m[2], gain_m[2]),
  check.names = FALSE), 4)

Covariance row: \(\mathbf{R}'\boldsymbol\Sigma_G\mathbf{b}\), the covariance of the index \(\mathbf{b}'\mathbf{y}\) with moisture; it depends on the scale of \(\mathbf{b}\) and is not a gain. Last row: the expected gain in moisture per round, \(i,\mathbf{R}'\boldsymbol\Sigma_G\mathbf{b}/\sqrt{\mathbf{b}'\boldsymbol\Sigma_P\mathbf{b}}\), at the normal-theory intensity \(i = 1.774\) of the top 60 of 625 (the selected fraction of Table 4.2), in trait units.

Zero here is exact to the tolerance of the setup: the restricted index has covariance \(2.6 \times 10^{-17}\) and expected gain \(4.4 \times 10^{-17}\) (tolerance \(1 \times 10^{-12}\)), against 0.22 for the Smith-Hazel index. As an independent check of the formula, a literal Monte Carlo selection on traits drawn from the two covariance matrices (\(\mathbf{g} \sim N(\mathbf{0}, \boldsymbol\Sigma_G)\), \(\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{g} + \mathbf{e}\), \(\mathbf{e} \sim N(\mathbf{0}, \boldsymbol\Sigma_P - \boldsymbol\Sigma_G)\)) selects the top fraction on each index.


Show code
set.seed(cfg$seed_gain)
n_mc_gain <- 4e5
gm <- matrix(rnorm(2 * n_mc_gain), ncol = 2) %*% chol(G)
ym <- gm + matrix(rnorm(2 * n_mc_gain), ncol = 2) %*% chol(P - G)
mc_gain <- mc_se <- numeric(2)
for (k in 1:2) {
  Ik  <- drop(ym %*% list(b_u, b_r)[[k]])
  top <- Ik >= quantile(Ik, 1 - cfg$n_sel / N_hyb)
  mc_gain[k] <- mean(gm[top, 2])
  mc_se[k]   <- sd(gm[top, 2]) / sqrt(sum(top))
}
# 4 s.e.: false-alarm probability 6e-5 per index
stopifnot(abs(mc_gain - gain_m) < 4 * mc_se)


Monte Carlo against formula, in trait units (400000 draws; the Monte Carlo s.e. is the s.d. of the selected moisture values over the square root of their count): Smith-Hazel 0.217 (s.e. 0.003) against 0.22; restricted -0.002 (s.e. 0.003) against zero. Both lie within the 4 s.e. the chunk asserts.
For the restricted index the covariance with moisture is zero, and for the Smith-Hazel index it is not. The expected gain in moisture per round of selection with intensity \(i\) is \(i\,\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf{b}'\mathbf{y},
\text{moisture})/\sqrt{\mathbf{b}'\boldsymbol\Sigma_P\mathbf{b}}\) (the slope of the regression of the genetic value on the index times the selection differential \(i\,\operatorname{sd}(\mathbf{b}'\mathbf{y})\)), so it is zero exactly when the covariance is. That is a statement about an expectation: it holds for known \(\boldsymbol\Sigma_P\) and \(\boldsymbol\Sigma_G\) and a linear regression of genetic value on the index, and the realised change of the restricted trait in a finite selected sample, or with estimated covariance matrices, is not zero.
Four differences keep the restricted index from being the \(\alpha\) constraint, or a proof of it.

Form. The restriction is an equality, linear in the index weights, with a closed form under the assumptions above. The \(\alpha\) constraint is an inequality, \(\alpha(S) \le \alpha_{\max}\), on the loss of gene diversity of a selected set \(S\) relative to the mean over random subsets of the same size (Section 11.9); \(\theta_S\) is a quadratic form in the contributions of a discrete selection, which the book solves by search (Chapter 15), not by a closed form.
Expectation against realisation. The restricted index fixes an expected gain. \(\alpha(S)\) is a deterministic function of the selected set, so the bound holds on the realised set itself, given the reference value it is measured against.
Which quantity is restricted. The budget acts on \(GD_T = 1 - \theta_S\), which contains the between-pool term \(GD_{BS}\) that Section 4.2 showed does not enter \(V_{\text{genic}}\) among hybrids. The restricted direction is therefore not the one that carries response, as item 3 of the Preface also notes; it protects variance only through \(GD_{WS}\).
Equality against inequality. What changes when the equality becomes an inequality is not worked out in this chapter, and Chapter 15 does not work it out either: it states the constraint as \(\alpha \le \alpha_{\max}\) (bounded relative to a resampling baseline, not held at zero) and notes that a budget above the attainable maximum restricts nothing.







NoteWhat the lineage does and does not show



Constraining rather than pricing is not specific to this book: the restricted selection index (for a trait, reported from Kempthorne and Nordskog (1959), not read) and optimum contribution selection with a bound on a group coancestry (Meuwissen et al. (2020), whose optimum-contribution paragraph and Introduction were read; Meuwissen (1997) reported through it) both have that form. The \(\alpha\) constraint is closest to the second, and the four differences above are why neither is a proof that it is the right constraint; whether to prefer a budget to a price remains the argument of Chapter 15.

title: 4  Response to selection: the other half of the objective
text:
4.6 Where this connects
Chapter 10 and Chapter 11 report the frequency-based metrics whose link to variance this chapter limited to the within-pool part (Equation 4.4); neither computes \(V_{\text{genic}}\). Chapter 14 measures a prediction accuracy for a different object from the \(r\) here, which this chapter constructs as the correlation between the index and the true genetic value, set by \(h^2 =\) 0.5; Finding 5 of Chapter 12 shows what happens when accuracy is assumed rather than measured. Chapter 15 states the \(\alpha\) constraint as an inequality and sets the budget; it does not derive the constraint from the restricted index, and nothing here does. Chapter 24 tests whether selection builds the covariance term of Equation 4.3, against a random-selection control: it finds a term that is significant against that control, largest in early cycles and decaying with recombination, and it argues from the decay that constraining allele frequencies and ignoring this term is justified. It ranks that cost below the permanent cost of changed allele frequencies, on the condition that the decay is fast. Chapter 5 completes the Foundations part with the dominance side of the hybrid value; the Simulation part then opens with Chapter 6, which builds step by step the generators, one of which (simulate_pools()) drew the data here in one call.

title: 5  Heterosis, dominance, and what divergence buys
text:
5.1 Three premises
Since Chapter 3 this book has repeated a claim without proving it: that the divergence between the heterotic pools is the engine of heterosis, and is therefore to be maintained rather than minimised. Chapter 11 will decompose diversity on that basis and Chapter 13 will build a monitoring panel around it. The claim has carried a lot of weight for an assertion.
The chapters before this one announce what it supplies. Chapter 1 states the identity numerically and hands its derivation here (Section 5.4) together with the dominance part of the combining-ability model of Equation 1.1 (Section 5.11); Chapter 2 introduces the dominance effects \(d_k\) and the heterosis \(H_i\) of Equation 5.3, derived below; Chapter 3 gives the partition the identity is stated in (Table 3.6); and Chapter 4 states two facts about combining ability – without dominance a line’s GCA is the same against any tester set, with dominance it is evaluated at the other pool’s frequencies – and refers the derivation to Section 5.11.
This chapter derives the claim, and then corrects it. The derivation is short and the identity is exact, under the conditions stated at each use: flat dominance, inbred parents and the complete \(A \times B\) factorial. It has two halves. At a given \(GD_T\) (total gene diversity) – the quantity the \(\alpha\) budget constrains (Table 3.6) – expected heterosis is \(GD_T + GD_{BS}\) (Equation 5.6), so a loss of \(GD_{BS}\) (the between-pool component) is a loss of expected heterosis, one for one: that is the sense in which the divergence is maintained. The correction concerns the other half: the reading of the identity that this chapter corrects is push the pools apart and you will get more heterosis. It is put here as the natural reading; it is not attributed to any author and no source is cited for it. That reading is false. Under neutral divergence expected heterosis does not move, in expectation over the draw of the pools (Equation 5.10), and the sweep of Section 5.8, one draw per row, is consistent with it.
The chapter then goes one step past the mean. Expected heterosis is what a pool pair is worth on average; what a breeder selects on is how heterosis is distributed across the crosses of the factorial. Those are different questions with different answers, and the second one is where general and specific combining ability (GCA, SCA) come from.
The derivations come first and Section 5.13 turns them into the eight steps that compute them on a real programme’s data, with the check and the failure mode of each one. Read that section first if the question is what to run rather than why it holds.
The data come from simulate_lines() and simulate_data(), drawn with the generator Chapter 6 builds (in the Simulation part that follows), and the fst sweep of Section 5.8 redraws the pools from it; pool_complementarity() supplies the three complementarity columns of the S1 panel (s1_monitor(); S1 is defined in Table 1.1 and the panel in Chapter 13).
Three premises carry everything below. They are stated here once, because every result in the chapter uses all three and two of them are restrictive.
Parents are fully inbred. Every parent line is homozygous at every locus, so an F1’s marker row is the average of its two parents’ rows and a locus is heterozygous in the F1 exactly when the parents differ. This is what makes the additive effects cancel from the mid-parent difference and what makes GD_WI zero. Note that this is a property of the programme, not of the mating system: the programme modelled here is that of an allogamous, maize-type crop with two heterotic pools under reciprocal recurrent selection (a modelling choice; no source for the heterotic-group system is cited in this chapter). Doubled-haploid (DH) induction or selfing to fixation is what delivers homozygous parents from it. Nothing here transfers to a programme crossing non-inbred parents (an inter-population cross, a synthetic, parents selfed once) without re-derivation, and Section 5.13.1 measures how large the error is if the formulae below are applied anyway: a multiple of the true gain, not a few per cent.
The genotypic model is dominance within loci and additivity between them. There is no epistatic term anywhere below: the genotypic value is a sum over loci, \(H_i\) is a sum of per-locus indicators, and the combining-ability expansion of Section 5.11 is bilinear only because no term couples two loci. Labroo et al. (2021) review epistasis alongside dominance as a proposed mechanism for heterosis; this model excludes it, and no result below should be read as evidence about it. What \(d_k\) does absorb is every within-locus story, as Section 5.2.2 sets out.
The marker panel is the set of dominance loci. \(d_k\) is indexed by the same \(k\) as the markers, so every locus carrying dominance is genotyped and the frequency statistics are computed on exactly the loci that generate heterosis. This is the strongest assumption of the three, and it is the one that carries the distance results of Section 5.7. A real panel tags causal loci through linkage disequilibrium rather than containing them, which weakens every statement below about markers predicting heterosis but does not change the algebra, since the algebra is written over whatever set \(k\) indexes. A related choice: every number below that depends on \(d\) (the correlation with marker distance, the alignment factor, the SCA shares) uses one draw of \(d_k\) from a gamma distribution (shape 2, rate 4, seed 4), positive at every locus and the same at every pool pair and scale, which is an illustrative assumption and not an estimate. The chapter does not vary it; the algebra holds for any \(d\), the magnitudes do not.

title: 5  Heterosis, dominance, and what divergence buys
text:
5.2 The dominance model, minimally

5.2.1 The one-locus scale
The classical parameterisation puts the origin at the midpoint of the two homozygotes: one homozygote is worth \(+a\), the other \(-a\), and the heterozygote \(d\). Under random mating at frequency \(p\), with \(q = 1 - p\), the population mean is (Falconer and Mackay 1996, Ch. 7)
\[M = a\,(p - q) + 2pq\,d \tag{5.1}\]
The first term is the additive contribution, and the mid-parent of any cross already carries it. The second is the dominance contribution. It is the only part of \(M\) that depends on how many heterozygotes there are, and therefore the only part a cross can add over its own mid-parent.






Note\(a\) is a scale, not a quantity this chapter computes



The symbols in Equation 5.1 are the textbook ones. This book’s additive marker effects are \(\beta_k\) (estimated in Chapter 14, later), and its \(\alpha\) is the diversity-loss statistic of Chapter 11, not the classical average effect of a substitution. The per-locus \(a_k\) reappears below and never as a result: in the genotypic-value model (Equation 5.2) used to show that it cancels, in the additive part of the GCA of the cross mean (Section 5.11) and of the two-way layout of Section 5.13, and, written without the index, in the definition of overdominance as \(|d| > |a|\) and in the average effect of a substitution \(a + d(q - p)\) (Section 5.11.1). No quantity this chapter reports depends on it.




5.2.2 What \(d_k\) is, and what it is not
\(d_k\) is the dominance effect at locus \(k\): the functional dominance, the departure of the heterozygote from the homozygote midpoint (the heterozygote value on the \(a\), \(d\), \(-a\) scale of Equation 5.1). It is a property of the locus. It does not move when allele frequencies move. This chapter, Chapter 1, Chapter 2, Chapter 3 and Chapter 4 call \(d_k\) the dominance effect and nothing else; the phrase dominance deviation is kept for the object that follows. Other chapters (Chapter 10 among them) still use the older name for \(d_k\); it is a difference of wording and not a different quantity.
Fisher’s statistical dominance deviation (Fisher 1918; Falconer and Mackay 1996, Ch. 7) is a different object: the residual left after projecting genotypic values onto the best additive model in a particular population. It is a property of the population as much as of the locus, and it changes when frequencies change.
Both appear in this chapter, and keeping them apart is the whole trick. \(d_k\) is the input. The specific combining ability of Section 5.11 is the statistical dominance deviation that a given \(d_k\) induces over a given pair of pools. One is a constant; the other is an answer that depends on where the pools happen to sit.
The distinction also buys the model what generality it has, and marks where that generality stops. Dominance, overdominance (a heterozygote outside both homozygotes, \(|d| > |a|\)) and pseudo-overdominance (two dominant favourable alleles in repulsion phase, too close for any marker to separate) are three different biological stories, and Labroo et al. (2021) review the evidence for each. At marker resolution they are the same arithmetic: a locus at which the F1 gains something the mid-parent does not. A single \(d_k\) absorbs all three, and nothing below can distinguish them – nor needs to. Epistasis is the fourth story on Labroo et al. (2021)’s list and \(d_k\) does not absorb it, because a single per-locus number cannot represent a term that depends on two loci at once. That is the second premise of Section 5.1 (dominance within loci, additivity between), and it is an exclusion rather than an approximation.


5.2.3 The mid-parent difference
Code a genotype by \(x_k \in \{0, 0.5, 1\}\), the frequency of the reference allele within the individual, and take the genotypic value to be the additive part plus the dominance effect at every heterozygous locus:
\[G(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_k a_k\,(2x_k - 1) + \sum_k d_k\,\mathbb{1}\{x_k = 0.5\} \tag{5.2}\]
The parents are fully inbred, so each is homozygous at every locus and the F1’s row is the average of its two parents’ rows. The additive part is linear in \(\mathbf{x}\), so the two parents’ additive values average exactly to the F1’s own and cancel from the mid-parent difference. What survives is the dominance effect at the loci where the F1 is heterozygous:
\[H_i = \sum_k d_k \, \mathbb{1}\{x_{ik} = 0.5\} \tag{5.3}\]
The additive effects never appear. That is the result, not an omission, and it is why heterosis_value() takes no additive-effect argument:


Show code
cat(deparse(heterosis_value), sep = "\n")
#> function (X, d) 
#> {
#>     stopifnot(length(d) == ncol(X))
#>     drop((X == 0.5) %*% d)
#> }


Against the literal oracle of Appendix C, which loops over loci and compares the two parents’ genotypes one at a time, on 25 hybrids drawn at random from the factorial (so that both pools’ line indexing is exercised; Table 5.1):


Show code
set.seed(12)                        # 25 random hybrids, not the first 25 rows
i25 <- sample(ctx$N, 25)
# ref_heterosis() takes the 0/2 line matrix L; the line-level functions of the
# package take 0/1 (see the protocol section)
oracle_gap <- max(abs(heterosis_value(ctx$X[i25, , drop = FALSE], d) -
                      ref_heterosis(L, ctx$ped[i25, ], d)))
stopifnot(oracle_gap < 1e-9)
kv(c(max_abs_difference = oracle_gap), sig = TRUE)

title: 5  Heterosis, dominance, and what divergence buys
section: 5.3 Expected heterosis over a pool pair
text:
5.3 Expected heterosis over a pool pair
Write \(p_{Ak}\) and \(p_{Bk}\) for the reference-allele frequencies at locus \(k\) in the two pools, each computed over that pool’s lines. A locus is heterozygous in the F1 when the two gametes carry different alleles, which for a cross drawn at random between the pools happens with probability \(p_A(1 - p_B) + (1 - p_A)p_B\). The expected heterosis over all \(A \times B\) crosses therefore follows from the pool frequencies alone:
\[\mathbb{E}[H] = \sum_k d_k \left[\, p_{A k} + p_{B k} - 2 p_{A k} p_{B k} \right] \tag{5.4}\]
The candidate set here is the full factorial, every \(A \times B\) pairing exactly once, and the frequencies are the means of those same lines. The closed form is then the mean of the realised values as an identity rather than an approximation, and the residual is at machine precision (Table 5.3):


Show code
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(heterosis_expected(pA, pB, d),
                           mean(heterosis_value(ctx$X, d)))))
kv(c(abs_difference = abs(heterosis_expected(pA, pB, d) - mean(heterosis_value(ctx$X, d)))),
   sig = TRUE)




Table 5.3: Absolute difference between the closed form heterosis_expected() (Equation 5.4) and the mean of heterosis_value() over the 625 crosses of the full factorial, in units of \(d\).







quantity
value




abs_difference
1.137e-13









That is a mean over \(N =\) 625 crosses, and a mean is not a ranking. Hold on to the question of how the individual crosses are spread around it; Section 5.11 answers it exactly.

title: 5  Heterosis, dominance, and what divergence buys
text:
5.4 The identity
Now split the bracket. Writing \(\bar p = (p_A + p_B)/2\) and \(y = p_A - p_B\), the per-locus F1 heterozygosity separates exactly:
\[p_A + p_B - 2 p_A p_B \;=\; \underbrace{2 \bar p (1 - \bar p)}_{\text{shared}}
                            \;+\; \underbrace{y^2 / 2}_{\text{divergence}} \tag{5.5}\]
The first term is the heterozygosity a single merged pool at frequency \(\bar p\) would produce under random mating. The second is what keeping the pools apart adds on top of it. Average both over loci with \(d_k \equiv 1\), so that the weighting does not obscure the algebra, and they are exactly the \(GD_T\) and \(GD_{BS}\) of the partition of Caballero and Toro (2002) that Chapter 3 derived and gd_partition() computes (Table 5.4):


Show code
hp <- heterosis_partition(pA, pB, rep(1, ctx$m)) / ctx$m
gp <- gd_partition(seq_len(ctx$N), ctx)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(hp[["shared"]],     gp[["GD_T"]],  tolerance = 1e-12)),
          isTRUE(all.equal(hp[["divergence"]], gp[["GD_BS"]], tolerance = 1e-12)))
fmt(data.frame(term       = c("shared", "divergence"),
               heterosis  = c(hp[["shared"]], hp[["divergence"]]),
               partition  = c(gp[["GD_T"]],   gp[["GD_BS"]]),
               residual   = c(abs(hp[["shared"]]     - gp[["GD_T"]]),
                              abs(hp[["divergence"]] - gp[["GD_BS"]]))), 12)




Table 5.4: Expected heterosis per locus under flat dominance (\(d_k \equiv 1\)), split into its shared and divergence terms by heterosis_partition() (Equation 5.5), beside \(GD_T\) and \(GD_{BS}\) of gd_partition() on the full A x B factorial of the book’s teaching scale (25 + 25 inbred lines, 2000 markers). Residual: absolute difference between the two columns.

NoteThe divergence term and \(GD_{BS}\)



The divergence term, \(\sum_k d_k\,y_k^2/2\), is the divergence half of expected heterosis, and with flat dominance (\(d_k \equiv 1\)), inbred parents and the complete factorial it is \(GD_{BS}\) itself. Under those conditions “between-pool divergence is the heterosis engine” is an identity, not a slogan; with a \(d_k\) that varies across loci \(GD_{BS}\) is its unweighted version and the identity holds for the weighted term only.


One thing to be clear about before reading on. \(GD_T\) is the gene diversity of the merged population, and by Chapter 3 it already contains \(GD_{BS}\): with inbred lines, \(GD_T = GD_{BI} + GD_{BS}\). Expected F1 heterozygosity is therefore \(GD_{BI} + 2\,GD_{BS}\), the between-pool component counted twice – once inside the shared term, once as the divergence term. That factor of two is where the classical result sits. The heterosis of a cross between two random-mating populations is \(\sum_k d_k y_k^2\) (Falconer and Mackay 1996, Ch. 14), exactly twice the divergence term of Equation 5.5. The two do not conflict; they use different mid-parents. Theirs is two random-mating populations, each carrying its own within-pool heterozygosity, so their \(H\) is the total above \(\sum_k d_k (p_{Ak}q_{Ak} + p_{Bk}q_{Bk})\). Ours is two inbred lines carrying none, so the whole F1 heterozygosity is heterosis, and the shared term is the mean of the two pools’ random-mating heterozygosities plus the half of \(\sum_k d_k y_k^2\) that \(GD_T\) already holds.
That paragraph is an algebraic claim and it can be checked rather than asserted. Subtract the random-mating mid-parent from the F1’s total dominance value and what is left is \(\sum_k d_k y_k^2\), exactly twice this chapter’s divergence term (Table 5.5):


Show code
hpd  <- heterosis_partition(pA, pB, d)
mid_random_mating <- sum(d * (pA * (1 - pA) + pB * (1 - pB)))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(hpd[["total"]] - mid_random_mating,
                           2 * hpd[["divergence"]])),
          isTRUE(all.equal(2 * hpd[["divergence"]], sum(d * (pA - pB)^2))))
kv(c(F1_total          = hpd[["total"]],
     mid_random_mating = mid_random_mating,
     difference        = hpd[["total"]] - mid_random_mating,
     twice_divergence  = 2 * hpd[["divergence"]],
     sum_d_y2          = sum(d * (pA - pB)^2)), 3)

The first number is what an F1 between two inbred lines gains over its mid-parent of zero; the third is what the same F1 gains over a mid-parent of two random-mating pools. They differ by 289.8 units of dominance value that the random-mating parents already carry themselves. Which mid-parent is the right one is not a matter of convention: it is whichever one the programme actually plants. Section 5.13.1 measures the consequence of getting it wrong.

5.4.1 A third form: one minus the between-pool coancestry
The sum of the two components has a name of its own. \(\theta_{AB} = \mathbf{w}_A'
\mathbf{f}^L \mathbf{w}_B\) is the between-pool coancestry, written \(f_{AB}\) in Chapter 3 and \(\theta_{AB}\) in Chapter 11 (later), and \(\bar f^{L}_{AB}\) in Chapter 2, where its complement is the heterozygous fraction of the F1s: on the full factorial, where the line weights are uniform, it is the probability that an allele drawn from a pool-A line and an allele drawn from a pool-B line are identical in state. Its complement is the whole bracket (checked on the book’s data in Table 5.6):
\[GD_T + GD_{BS} \;=\; 1 - \theta_{AB} \tag{5.6}\]


Show code
tp <- theta_pools(seq_len(ctx$N), ctx)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(gp[["GD_T"]] + gp[["GD_BS"]], 1 - tp[["theta_AB"]],

     one_minus_theta_AB     = 1 - tp[["theta_AB"]]), 8)

This one is algebra rather than simulation. gd_partition() defines \(GD_T = 1 - \bar f\) and \(GD_{BS} = \tilde f - \bar f\) with \(\bar f = (\theta_A + 2\theta_{AB} + \theta_B)/4\) and \(\tilde f = (\theta_A + \theta_B)/2\), and the sum collapses to \(1 - \theta_{AB}\). Which is the shortest statement the chapter has to make: expected F1 heterozygosity is one minus between-pool coancestry. Everything else here is a weighting of that quantity, or a way of splitting it. The same identity is stated numerically for the book’s data in Section 1.2, appears as the diagonal of the coancestry matrix in Chapter 2 (Table 2.6) and as the heterosis row of Table 3.6; this section is where it is derived.

section: 5.5 A second identity, at the hybrid level
text:
5.5 A second identity, at the hybrid level
Chapter 3 reports GD_WI_hyb (Table 3.7), the within-individual gene diversity actually carried by the F1s, separately from the line-level partition, because with inbred parents GD_WI is zero by construction and carries no signal. A hybrid’s self-coancestry is \(1 - h_i/2\), with \(h_i\) its heterozygous fraction, so GD_WI_hyb is half the mean F1 heterozygosity, that is, half the observed heterozygosity \(H_o\) of the F1s in Chapter 1, and the two levels are linked by Equation 5.7, checked in Table 5.7:
\[2 \cdot GD_{WI\text{-}hyb} = GD_T + GD_{BS} \tag{5.7}\]


Show code
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(2 * gp[["GD_WI_hyb"]], gp[["GD_T"]] + gp[["GD_BS"]],
                           tolerance = 1e-12)),
          abs(gp[["GD_WI"]]) < 1e-12)
kv(c(lhs = 2 * gp[["GD_WI_hyb"]], rhs = gp[["GD_T"]] + gp[["GD_BS"]],
     GD_WI = gp[["GD_WI"]]), sig = TRUE)




Table 5.7: Both sides of Equation 5.7 on the full A x B factorial (25 + 25 inbred lines, 2000 markers), and the line-level \(GD_{WI}\), which is zero with inbred parents.

Exact on the full factorial, because every \(A \times B\) pairing is present exactly once. On a selected subset it holds only approximately. There \(GD_T\) and \(GD_{BS}\) are computed from the line-usage weights, which is what a random re-pairing of the selected parents would give, while GD_WI_hyb scores the pairs actually chosen. The gap is the pairing structure of the subset. tests/testthat/test-dominance.R asserts the identity to 1e-12 on the full factorial and, on a random 40-hybrid subset at one scale (12 lines per pool, 800 markers; tests/testthat/setup.R), bounds the gap with expect_equal(tolerance = 5e-3) (test-dominance.R). That tolerance is relative, not absolute: on a gene-diversity value of order 0.4 the absolute bound it enforces is of order 2e-3. A subset chosen by an optimiser, which concentrates line usage deliberately, is not covered by that bound. Section 10.3.2, in the Metrics and prediction part, measures the gap on four 60-hybrid selections at this book’s scale, of which three are distinct – one random draw, one max-diversity greedy and truncation on the index (the index-weighted greedy returns the truncation set) – none of them an optimiser’s output, and reports the largest departure of the four.

title: 5  Heterosis, dominance, and what divergence buys
section: 5.6 Inbreeding depression, and why it does not price \(\alpha\)
text:
5.6 Inbreeding depression, and why it does not price \(\alpha\)
The same model run backwards gives inbreeding depression (\(ID\)). A locus at frequency \(p\) in a population with inbreeding coefficient \(F\) is heterozygous with probability \(2pq(1-F)\), so the mean declines linearly in \(F\) (Falconer and Mackay 1996, Ch. 14):
\[ID \;=\; 2F\sum_k d_k \, p_k q_k \tag{5.8}\]
At \(F = 1\) that is exactly the shared term of heterosis_partition() evaluated at \(p_A = p_B = p\). So the depression of a pool driven to complete homozygosity and the expected heterosis of a cross made within that same pool are one quantity seen from two sides. Mackay et al. (2021) treat heterosis and inbreeding depression together on that basis, alongside transgressive segregation, which this chapter does not take up. The identity needs no new machinery (Table 5.8):


Show code
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(inbreeding_depression(pA, d),
                           heterosis_partition(pA, pA, d)[["shared"]],
                           tolerance = 1e-12)))
kv(c(inbreeding_depression = inbreeding_depression(pA, d),
     shared_term           = heterosis_partition(pA, pA, d)[["shared"]],
     deviation             = abs(inbreeding_depression(pA, d) -
                                   heterosis_partition(pA, pA, d)[["shared"]])), sig = TRUE)




Table 5.8: Inbreeding depression at \(F = 1\) (inbreeding_depression(), Equation 5.8) beside the shared term of heterosis_partition() at \(p_A = p_B\) (pool A of the chapter), and their absolute difference; sums over loci, in units of \(d\).

The closed form is checked against simulated genotypes rather than against its own algebra, which is what ref_inbreeding_depression() exists for: it draws each genotype as identical by descent with probability \(F\) and as two independent alleles otherwise, so the two should agree to Monte Carlo error. Table 5.9 gives the closed form, the mean of the eight simulated runs with different seeds, the standard deviation of one run, and the standardised difference \(z\):

k <- seq_len(300)
n_id <- 8
id_sim <- vapply(seq_len(n_id), function(s)
  ref_inbreeding_depression(pA[k], d[k], 0.6, n = 20000, seed = s), numeric(1))
id_closed <- inbreeding_depression(pA[k], d[k], 0.6)
id_se <- sd(id_sim) / sqrt(n_id)

Result. The standard deviation of one simulated run over the 8 seeds is 0.026; the mean of the 8 runs differs from the closed form by -0.011, which is -1.2 standard errors of that mean. The closed form and the simulation agree within the Monte Carlo error of this run (300 loci of one pool, \(F = 0.6\)).
Now the part that matters, because the obvious next step is wrong.
It is tempting to argue: \(\alpha\) budgets a loss of gene diversity; with inbred parents the quantity it budgets is \(GD_T = GD_{BI} + GD_{BS}\) of the merged candidate set, the mean over loci of \(2\bar p_k\bar q_k\) (Table 3.6), and not \(GD_{BI}\) alone; inbreeding depression is \(2F\sum_k d_k\,p_kq_k\); therefore spending \(\alpha\) costs yield in the current cycle, and that is the price of the budget. The algebra does not support it (Table 5.10).


Show code
stopifnot(max(abs(heterosis_value(rbind(U, V), d))) == 0)
kv(c(max_dominance_contribution_of_an_inbred_line = max(abs(heterosis_value(U, d)))))




Table 5.10: Largest absolute dominance contribution, heterosis_value(), of any pool-A line of the book’s teaching scale (coded 0/1), in units of \(d\).







quantity
value




max_dominance_contribution_of_an_inbred_line

Zero, exactly. A fully inbred line has no heterozygous loci, so its dominance contribution is zero whatever the pool’s allele frequencies are. (On the simulated lines, coded 0/1, this holds for any matrix: no entry can equal 0.5, so the check illustrates the algebra and tests nothing about the pool; it is informative only on real genotypes, where the matrix can carry 0.5.) In a programme whose parents are inbred lines the depression was paid in full when the lines were made; it is a constant, and it does not move when the pool subsequently loses diversity. Equation 5.8 describes the gap between a hypothetical random-mating pool and its inbred derivatives, and that gap shrinks as \(p_kq_k\) shrinks – but nothing in the programme stands at the random-mating end of it.






WarningInbreeding depression is not the current-cycle price of the diversity budget



This is the same fact that makes \(GD_{WI}\) exactly zero in the partition of Chapter 3 (Table 3.6), and it has the same cause: with inbred parents there is no within-individual variation left to lose. Two consequences.
The cost of \(\alpha\) in this system is not a yield loss booked this season. Whether it is paid later, as lost response, is a different question. Section 4.2 states the condition under which gene diversity stands in for genic variance – only through \(GD_{WS}\), which is not what \(\alpha\) budgets, and only if effect sizes are unrelated to which loci lose diversity – and does not test it; this chapter does not either, and so does not say that the cost of \(\alpha\) arrives in the additive variance. Chapter 23 runs selection under the budget on an additive index.
And inbreeding depression is the live quantity wherever the population is only partially inbred (\(0 < F < 1\): the F2, F3 and F4 generations that Chapter 7 sizes, where \(F\) is still climbing). This book does not model it there. Chapter 7 lists phenotypic inbreeding depression among what it does not model (its SA9), and the only place the book applies the quantity to a population is at \(F = 1\) (Chapter 9), where it is the shared term above. The one other evaluation, at \(F = 0.6\) in Table 5.9, checks the formula against simulation on 300 loci of one pool and is not a partially inbred generation of the programme. Equation 5.8 gives the expected depression at inbreeding coefficient \(F\) relative to random mating; Chapter 10 writes the same formula for the crossing block without computing it, and the book computes it for no partially inbred generation.


Note also what this does not say. Expected heterosis in the product is a separate question. Section 5.8 answers it for the neutral case: under drift the shared term lost and the divergence term gained cancel in expectation (Equation 5.11), so expected hybrid heterosis is invariant for a \(d\) drawn independently of the frequencies. Under selection the frequencies move directionally, and what happens to expected heterosis is then the alignment question of Section 5.9, which can go either way. In neither case is the diversity loss itself an immediate dominance cost. Whether it is a cost later, in the variance available to select on, is the conditional question of Section 4.2, not a result of this chapter.

section: 5.7 When genetic distance predicts heterosis exactly
text:
5.7 When genetic distance predicts heterosis exactly
Before the corrections start, one special case is worth having, because it is the only case in which marker distance and heterosis are the same number.
Set \(d_k \equiv d\), constant across loci. Then \(H\) stops being a weighted count and becomes a plain one: \(d\) times the number of loci at which the two parents differ. For inbred lines that count is exactly what the coancestry kernel of Chapter 2 measures, so for a cross between pool-A line \(i\) and pool-B line \(j\)
\[H_{ij} \;=\; d\,m\,(1 - f^L_{ij}) \;=\; d\,m\,\mathrm{MRD}_{ij}^2 \tag{5.9}\]
where \(\mathrm{MRD}_{ij}\) is the modified Rogers distance between the two lines. Table 5.11 checks both equalities on the full factorial.


Show code
h1 <- heterosis_value(ctx$X, rep(1, ctx$m))
fL <- molecular_coancestry(L / 2)
ab <- cbind(ctx$ped$a, ctx$ped$b)
stopifnot(max(abs(h1 - ctx$m * (1 - fL[ab]))) < 1e-9,
          max(abs(h1 - ctx$m * mrd_matrix(L / 2)[ab]^2)) < 1e-9)
kv(c(vs_coancestry = max(abs(h1 - ctx$m * (1 - fL[ab]))),
     vs_mrd        = max(abs(h1 - ctx$m * mrd_matrix(L / 2)[ab]^2))), sig = TRUE)




Table 5.11: Largest absolute difference over the full A x B factorial between the heterosis under flat dominance (\(d_k \equiv 1\)) and \(m(1 - f^L_{ij})\), and between it and \(m,\mathrm{MRD}_{ij}^2\) (Equation 5.9), in units of \(d\).

Both residuals are at machine precision. Under flat dominance, heterosis and molecular coancestry are one statistic seen twice – the identity of the modified Rogers distance with coancestry is Trap 1 of Chapter 13, met later; the link to heterosis is made here – and the diversity kernel this whole book runs on turns out to be the right object for the heterosis question as well.
Flat \(d\) is also precisely the condition under which \(H\) is a function of marker distance alone. It is a strong condition, and it fails as soon as \(d\) varies: two crosses at the same distance then differ by which loci they differ at. With the gamma-distributed dominance effects used everywhere else in this chapter the relationship survives but stops being an identity (Table 5.12):


Show code

     cor_real_d    = cor(heterosis_value(ctx$X, d), 1 - fL[ab])), 3)

A correlation of 0.78 is a useful predictor and a poor identity. Two things move it, and both are properties of the germplasm rather than of the statistic: how \(d\) is spread over the loci at which the parents differ, which is what Section 5.9 is about, and – once the premise that the marker panel is the set of dominance loci (Section 5.1) is relaxed – how well the panel tags the causal loci. Under flat \(d\) on a panel that is the causal set the correlation is 1 by Equation 5.9. Departing from either condition generally lowers it – not always, since a \(d\) that varies only across loci at which no pair of parents differs changes no \(H_i\) at all – and by how much is something this chapter does not attempt to predict.

title: 5  Heterosis, dominance, and what divergence buys
text:
5.8 Divergence is not a bonus
Read divergence as free money and you will reach for \(F_{ST}\). Do not.
Draw the pools further apart and watch all three terms (Table 5.13). Nothing here is selected. The claim to be tested is an expectation (Equation 5.10, Equation 5.11); the sweep has one draw per row, so it can show that the totals stay close to the expected level and that the two changes are of the same size, not that they are equal. Each point re-draws both pools from the same ancestral frequencies – the ancestral vector is fixed by seed = 5 and shared across the sweep, while the two pool-frequency vectors are fresh Balding-Nichols draws (Balding and Nichols 1995) at each fst (Appendix A) – so what varies along the sweep is how far the draw scatters and nothing else.
Two quantities are kept apart in this chapter, each with its own symbol (Section 1.2.4, Appendix A). \(F_{BN}\) is the Balding-Nichols parameter of the simulation, fst in the code: the variance of a pool’s allele frequency around the ancestral one \(p^{*}\) (Equation 6.1, stated later, in Chapter 6; a quantity of the draw, never observed; \(q^{*} = 1 - p^{*}\)), in units of \(p^{*}(1-p^{*})\). Every expectation below is a function of \(F_{BN}\). \(F_{ST}\) is the statistic \(GD_{BS}/GD_T\) computed on the pools’ frequencies (Caballero and Toro 2002, Eq. 8), which under Balding-Nichols estimates approximately \(F_{BN}/(2 - F_{BN})\) rather than \(F_{BN}\) (Appendix A) and is larger again on finite pools. Where the text says that \(F_{ST}\) “is a function of the frequencies only” (Section 5.9, Section 5.13.8) it means the statistic. No conclusion here depends on the difference between the two: both are functions of the frequencies, and \(d\) enters neither.


Show code
sweep_het <- function(fst) {
  cf <- modifyList(book_cfg, list(fst = fst, seed = 5))
  Lf <- simulate_lines(cf)
  pl <- rep(c("A", "B"), c(cf$n_pool_A, cf$n_pool_B))
  Pf <- pool_freqs(Lf / 2, pl)
  hp <- heterosis_partition(Pf["A", ], Pf["B", ], rep(1, cf$m)) / cf$m
  cm <- pool_complementarity(Lf / 2, pl)
  data.frame(fst = fst, shared = hp[["shared"]], divergence = hp[["divergence"]],
             total = hp[["total"]],
             frac_opposite_fixed = cm[["frac_opposite_fixed"]],
             mean_abs_delta_p = cm[["mean_abs_delta_p"]],
             mean_sq_delta_p = cm[["mean_sq_delta_p"]])
}
sw <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(0.02, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.45), sweep_het))
# Read again in @sec-heterosis-step5: no marker is fixed for opposite alleles

# more than doubled between fst = 0.02 and 0.10.
stopifnot(all(sw$frac_opposite_fixed[sw$fst <= 0.10] == 0))
fmt(sw, 4)

Across the sweep the divergence term rises by a factor of 7.9. The comparison that matters is in absolute units, not in ratios: divergence gains 0.0739 per locus and the shared term loses 0.0756. The two changes are not equal in this draw, because each row is one sample of both pools; the expectation says they are equal, and the sweep shows them within 2 % of each other, with no replicate to say how far apart two draws can be. The total does not move in expectation, and in this draw the six totals lie between 0.362 and 0.3664 (the total column of Table 5.13).

5.8.1 The two terms, term by term
The algebra is one line. Pool A and pool B are drawn independently around a common ancestral frequency \(p^{*}\), so \(\mathbb{E}[p_A] = \mathbb{E}[p_B] = p^{*}\) and \(\mathbb{E}[p_A p_B] = p^{*2}\). Therefore
\[\mathbb{E}\!\left[p_A + p_B - 2 p_A p_B\right] = 2p^{*}(1-p^{*}), \tag{5.10}\]
which contains no \(F_{BN}\) at all. With ancestral frequencies drawn uniformly on \([0.05, 0.95]\) the predicted level is \(\mathbb{E}[2p^{*}(1-p^{*})] =\) 0.365, against a simulated mean of 0.3646 across the whole sweep (the six rows range from 0.362 to 0.3664).
That the sum is flat is the headline, but the Balding-Nichols model predicts each half separately, which is the sharper statement. Under it \(\mathrm{Var}(p_A) = \mathrm{Var}(p_B) = F_{BN}\,p^{*}(1-p^{*})\), so \(\mathrm{Var}(\bar p) = F_{BN}\,p^{*}(1-p^{*})/2\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(y) = 2F_{BN}\,p^{*}(1-p^{*})\). Substituting:
\[\mathbb{E}\!\left[2\bar p(1 - \bar p)\right] = 2p^{*}(1-p^{*})\left(1 - \tfrac{F_{BN}}{2}\right),
\qquad
\mathbb{E}\!\left[y^2/2\right] = F_{BN}\,p^{*}(1-p^{*}) \tag{5.11}\]
The shared term loses \(F_{BN}\,p^{*}(1-p^{*})\) and the divergence term gains \(F_{BN}\,p^{*}(1-p^{*})\) in expectation over the draw of the pools: the same expression with opposite signs, exactly and at every value of \(F_{BN}\), not approximately. Both predictions are parameter-free once the ancestral distribution is fixed, so they can be laid straight on top of the sweep (Table 5.14, Figure 5.1):

sw$pred_divergence <- Ep * sw$fst / 2

Figure 5.1: Expected heterosis per locus at \(d_k \equiv 1\) (total, black filled circles) and its shared (grey triangles) and divergence (black open squares) components (Equation 5.5) as the pools are driven apart by drift alone, against the target Balding-Nichols fst (\(F_{BN}\)). Each point is one draw of both pools from one fixed ancestral frequency vector (seed 5) at the book’s teaching scale (25 + 25 inbred lines, 2000 markers), with no replication. Dashed lines are the Balding-Nichols predictions for the shared (grey) and divergence (black) components separately (Equation 5.11), with no fitted parameter; the dotted line is the mean total over the sweep. Nothing is selected.





The measured divergence sits above its prediction at every fst, and the measured shared term about the same distance below it. That is not drift, it is estimation. The pool frequencies are estimated from 25 and 25 sampled lines, and a frequency estimated from \(n\) lines carries sampling variance \(\mathrm{Var}(\hat p) = pq/n\). Conditional on the true pool frequencies, \(\mathbb{E}[\hat y^2/2] = y^2/2 + [\mathrm{Var}(\hat p_A) + \mathrm{Var}(\hat p_B)]/2\) and \(\mathbb{E}[2\hat{\bar p}(1 - \hat{\bar p})] = 2\bar p(1 - \bar p) - [\mathrm{Var}(\hat p_A) + \mathrm{Var}(\hat p_B)]/2\): equal and opposite, so the total estimated from sample frequencies is unbiased while each half is not.
The offset is not constant along the sweep. It is proportional to \(\mathbb{E}[p_Aq_A + p_Bq_B]\), which the pools themselves erode as they diverge, so it shrinks with \((1 - F_{BN})\): about 0.0072 per locus at fst = 0.02, down to 0.004 at fst = 0.45, against measured gaps of 0.007 and 0.0025.
Those two pairs do not agree equally well. At fst = 0.02 prediction and measurement are within 2 % of each other; at fst = 0.45 the measured gap is 38 % below the predicted offset. The formula gives an expectation; each row of the sweep is one draw of 2000 loci at one seed, and the scatter of that draw is not constant either. \(\mathrm{Var}(y)\) is \(2F_{BN}\,p^{*}(1-p^{*})\), so the per-locus divergence \(y^2/2\) has a variance that grows with \(F_{BN}\) while the number of loci averaging it stays fixed – the high-fst rows are the noisy ones, and the agreement at the bottom of the sweep is the more informative of the two. The offset is the right order and the right sign at both ends; it is not a per-point prediction, and nothing below rests on it being one.
What changes by an order of magnitude along the sweep is not the offset but the signal it sits on: at fst = 0.02 the offset exceeds the predicted divergence of 0.0036, and by fst = 0.45 it is a small fraction of it. A pool pair’s apparent divergence overstates its true divergence, most severely when the true divergence is small and the pools are few.






WarningEvery unit of divergence is paid for out of the shared term, \(GD_T\)



Under neutral divergence the trade is one for one in expectation. Drifting the pools apart does not create expected heterosis; it relocates it from the shared term to the divergence term. A programme that maximises \(F_{ST}\) by drift has bought no expected heterosis and has spent gene diversity to do it.


The term that pays unit for unit is the shared term, \(GD_T\), which contains \(GD_{BS}\); it is not the within-pool term \(GD_{WS}\) (the \(GD_{BI}\) of the budget paragraph above, since \(GD_{WS} = GD_{WI} + GD_{BI}\) and \(GD_{WI} = 0\) with inbred parents). With inbred parents and the complete factorial \(GD_T = GD_{WS} + GD_{BS}\) per locus (the identity \(2\bar p\bar q = p_Aq_A + p_Bq_B + y^2/2\) of Section 4.2), so by Equation 5.11 \(GD_{WS}\) falls by \(F_{BN}\,p^{*}(1-p^{*})\) (the shared term’s loss) plus the \(F_{BN}\,p^{*}(1-p^{*})\) that \(GD_{BS}\) gains: twice what \(GD_{BS}\) gains, the accounting of Section 3.11. Both statements are expectations over the draw of the pools, under the conditions above, and the chapter does not measure \(GD_{WS}\) along the sweep. This is the mechanism behind Chapter 13 Trap 3, in the Metrics and prediction part. That section states the symptom – “\(F_{ST}\) keeps rising as pools drift apart at loci that are already divergent, which buys no additional heterosis” – and points here for the reason. Table 5.13 and Figure 5.1 are that reason.
