title: 5  Heterosis, dominance, and what divergence buys
text:
5.9 What actually buys heterosis
If divergence per se is worth nothing, why do heterotic groups work?
Because real pools are not diverged at random with respect to \(d\). The divergence term is \(\sum_k d_k y_k^2 / 2\), a weighted sum. It grows when the loci that diverge are the loci that carry dominance; under drift the two are independent, which is exactly why the total was flat.

5.9.1 Alignment is a covariance
That sentence can be a number rather than a word. A sum of products is \(m\) times a mean times a mean, plus \(m\) times a covariance – the population covariance with divisor \(m\), which is why the chunk rescales cov():
\[\sum_k d_k\,y_k^2 / 2 \;=\; \frac{m}{2}\Big[\, \bar d \; \overline{y^2}
  \;+\; \mathrm{cov}(d,\, y^2) \,\Big] \tag{5.12}\]


Show code
y2 <- (pA - pB)^2
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(sum(d * y2 / 2),
  ctx$m / 2 * (mean(d) * mean(y2) + cov(d, y2) * (ctx$m - 1) / ctx$m))))
c(divergence = sum(d * y2 / 2),
  from_parts = ctx$m / 2 * (mean(d) * mean(y2) + cov(d, y2) * (ctx$m - 1) / ctx$m))
#> divergence from_parts 
#>   32.94521   32.94521


The first bracketed term is what \(F_{ST}\) can see: average divergence times average dominance. The second is what it cannot. Alignment is \(\mathrm{cov}(d, y^2)\), and no statistic computed from allele frequencies alone can contain it, because \(d\) does not appear in one.


5.9.2 The scenarios
Hold the pools fixed, hold \(F_{ST}\) fixed, hold the multiset of dominance effects fixed, and change only which locus gets which \(d_k\). aligned gives the largest \(d_k\) to the largest \(y_k^2\), anti-aligned does the reverse, and independent is the draw as made (Table 5.15, Figure 5.2):


Show code
mk <- function(dec) { v <- numeric(ctx$m); v[order(y2)] <- sort(d, decreasing = dec); v }
scen <- list(`anti-aligned` = mk(TRUE), `independent` = d, `aligned` = mk(FALSE))
al <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(scen), function(n) {
  h <- heterosis_partition(pA, pB, scen[[n]])
  data.frame(scenario = n, cor_d_y2 = cor(scen[[n]], y2),
             shared = h[["shared"]], divergence = h[["divergence"]], total = h[["total"]])
}))
al$relative <- al$total / al$total[al$scenario == "independent"]
fmt(al, 3)

5.9.3 Isolating the divergence channel
One honest qualification. Sorting \(d\) against \(y^2\) moves the shared term as well, because \(y^2\) is not independent of \(2\bar p(1 - \bar p)\): a locus with a large frequency difference tends to sit at an intermediate mean frequency. Part of the effect above therefore arrives through the shared half, not the divergence half.
The channel can be separated. Permute \(d\) only within groups of loci that share a value of the shared weight \(2\bar p(1 - \bar p)\). The shared term is then invariant by construction – exactly, not approximately – and whatever moves is the divergence channel alone (Table 5.16):


Show code
hz  <- 2 * ((pA + pB) / 2) * (1 - (pA + pB) / 2)
grp <- split(seq_len(ctx$m), round(hz, 9))
strat <- function(dec) {
  v <- numeric(ctx$m)
  for (i in grp) v[i[order(y2[i])]] <- sort(d[i], decreasing = dec)
  v
}
st <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(aligned = FALSE, `anti-aligned` = TRUE), function(dec)
  as.data.frame(as.list(heterosis_partition(pA, pB, strat(dec))))))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(st$shared[1], st$shared[2])))
fmt(st, 4)

5.10 Reading the S1 panel
Chapter 13 will log frac_opposite_fixed and mean_abs_delta_p every cycle as stand-ins for heterosis potential. The sweep of Section 5.8 says how good they are.
mean_sq_delta_p is not a proxy at all. It is \(\overline{y^2}\), so half of it is the unweighted divergence term \(GD_{BS}\), exactly (Table 5.17):


Show code
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(sw$mean_sq_delta_p / 2, sw$divergence)))
kv(c(half_mean_sq = mean(sw$mean_sq_delta_p) / 2,
     divergence   = mean(sw$divergence)), 6)

What it cannot carry is the weighting by \(d\), which is the point of Section 5.9; the frequency half of the divergence term it reports without loss.
frac_opposite_fixed is a different matter (its column in Table 5.13).
Up to fst = 0.10 it is exactly zero – not one marker in 2000 qualifies – and it first exceeds 1 % of markers at fst = 0.3, near the top of the sweep. It counts near-fixed opposite loci, and the divergence lives at intermediate frequency differences, which the threshold discards.
Log mean_sq_delta_p. It is exact, it is monotone across the whole sweep, and it costs one squaring more than the statistic already being logged. pool_complementarity() and s1_monitor() return it.

title: 5  Heterosis, dominance, and what divergence buys
text:
5.11 General and specific combining ability
Everything so far has been about \(\mathbb{E}[H]\). Now the spread.
The same expansion that produced the shared/divergence split produces the combining-ability decomposition, with no new machinery and no model fitting. Let \(u_{ik} \in \{0, 1\}\) be the genotype of pool-A line \(i\) at locus \(k\) and \(v_{jk}\) that of pool-B line \(j\), and write each as its pool frequency plus a deviation, \(u = p_A + \delta u\) and \(v = p_B + \delta v\). The per-locus heterozygosity of the cross, \(u + v - 2uv\), expands to
\[u + v - 2uv \;=\; \underbrace{p_A + p_B - 2p_Ap_B}_{\text{mean}}
  \;+\; \underbrace{(1 - 2p_B)\,\delta u}_{\text{parent A}}
  \;+\; \underbrace{(1 - 2p_A)\,\delta v}_{\text{parent B}}
  \;-\; \underbrace{2\,\delta u\, \delta v}_{\text{both}} \tag{5.13}\]
Four terms: one constant, one linear in each parent, one bilinear. Weight by \(d_k\), sum over loci, and a decomposition of the form of the classical one into general and specific combining ability (Sprague and Tatum 1942; Griffing 1956) falls out,
\[H_{ij} = \mu + g^A_i + g^B_j + s_{ij} \tag{5.14}\]
with
\[g^A_i = \sum_k d_k (1 - 2p_{Bk})\,\delta u_{ik}, \qquad
  s_{ij} = -2 \sum_k d_k\, \delta u_{ik}\, \delta v_{jk} \tag{5.15}\]
and \(g^B_j\) symmetrically.
What these symbols denote. \(\mu\), \(g^A_i\), \(g^B_j\) and \(s_{ij}\) are used here for the decomposition of the mid-parent heterosis \(H_{ij}\) (Equation 5.3), not of the cross mean \(\bar y_{ij}\) of Equation 1.1 (the model for a factorial between two sets of lines, the North Carolina Design II of Comstock and Robinson (1948), as in Chapter 1). For the cross mean, with additive effects \(a_k\) and no epistasis, the GCA of pool-A line \(i\) is \(\sum_k [a_k + d_k(1 - 2p_{Bk})]\,\delta u_{ik}\) (Section 18.2). The \(g^A_i\) of Equation 5.15 is the dominance part of that GCA, with the additive part \(\sum_k a_k\,\delta u_{ik}\) – which cancels from \(H_{ij}\) – removed; \(s_{ij}\) is the same object in both. Where the two have to be told apart, this book writes GCA for heterosis for the term of this section and GCA, unqualified, for the term of Equation 1.1. The exact orthogonal split is the book’s own; the concept of combining ability is that of the sources cited above.
What is linear in one parent is general combining ability: it is carried into every cross that parent enters. What is bilinear depends on which two lines met, and is specific combining ability. Because the deviations are taken from each pool’s own line frequencies they sum to zero over that pool’s lines, which is what makes the three components mean zero and mutually orthogonal. heterosis_gca_sca() is Equation 5.13 weighted by \(d_k\) and nothing more:


Show code
cat(deparse(heterosis_gca_sca), sep = "\n")
#> function (U, V, d) 
#> {
#>     stopifnot(ncol(U) == ncol(V), length(d) == ncol(U))
#>     pA <- colMeans(U)
#>     pB <- colMeans(V)
#>     cU <- sweep(U, 2, pA)
#>     cV <- sweep(V, 2, pB)
#>     list(mu = heterosis_expected(pA, pB, d), gca_A = drop(cU %*% 
#>         (d * (1 - 2 * pB))), gca_B = drop(cV %*% (d * (1 - 2 * 
#>         pA))), sca = -2 * (cU * rep(d, each = nrow(U))) %*% t(cV))
#> }


It reconstructs every hybrid in the factorial exactly, and all three components are mean zero (Table 5.18):


Show code
cs <- heterosis_gca_sca(U, V, d)
H  <- heterosis_value(ctx$X, d)
ia <- ctx$ped$a
ib <- ctx$ped$b - nA
tol_H <- 1e-9 * max(abs(H))                  # relative to the scale of H
recon_gap <- max(abs(H - (cs$mu + cs$gca_A[ia] + cs$gca_B[ib] + cs$sca[cbind(ia, ib)])))
stopifnot(recon_gap < tol_H, abs(cs$mu - mean(H)) < tol_H,
          abs(mean(cs$gca_A)) < tol_H, abs(mean(cs$gca_B)) < tol_H,
          abs(mean(cs$sca)) < tol_H)
kv(c(max_residual = max(abs(H - (cs$mu + cs$gca_A[ia] + cs$gca_B[ib] +
                                 cs$sca[cbind(ia, ib)]))),
     mu_vs_mean   = abs(cs$mu - mean(H)),
     mean_gca_A   = mean(cs$gca_A), mean_sca = mean(cs$sca)), sig = TRUE)

This is not a decomposition that resembles the two-way analysis of variance. It is the two-way analysis of variance: \(\mu\), \(g^A\) and \(g^B\) are the grand mean and the row and column effects of the \(H_{ij}\) table, and \(s_{ij}\) is the interaction residual of the additive fit, to machine precision (Table 5.19):

lm_gap <- max(abs(resid(lm(H ~ factor(ia) + factor(ib))) - cs$sca[cbind(ia, ib)]))
stopifnot(lm_gap < tol_H)

Both are asserted: the reconstruction residual is \(8.0 \times 10^{-13}\) and the lm() gap \(7.0 \times 10^{-12}\), against a tolerance of \(3.9 \times 10^{-7}\) (1e-9 times the largest \(|H_{ij}|\), 391.4).
The tester-based schemes of the book (Section 1.1) evaluate candidates by their cross performance against a sample of the other pool. Comstock et al. (1949) is the procedure the book cites for them; the paper’s title states that it was designed “to make maximum use of both general and specific combining ability”, and this chapter reports nothing of that paper beyond its title. The algebra above says what each component is made of, and Section 5.11.1 works out, as the book’s own derivation, what a tester-based mean of \(H\) carries.

5.11.1 GCA is an average effect in the other pool’s background
Look at the weight on \(\delta u\): it is \(d_k(1 - 2p_{Bk})\), and \(1 - 2p_B\) is \(q_B - p_B\). That is the frequency factor of the classical average effect of a gene substitution, \(a + d\,(q - p)\) (Falconer and Mackay 1996, Ch. 7), with two differences: the additive part \(a\) is absent, because it belongs to the parental mean and not to \(H\), and the frequencies are pool B’s, not pool A’s.
This is the whole reason combining ability is not a property of a line. A pool-A line’s alleles are always substituted into a pool-B background, so its general combining ability for heterosis is a dominance effect evaluated at the tester pool’s frequencies. Change the tester pool and every number changes. Two limits follow immediately:

A locus at which the tester pool sits at \(p_B = 0.5\) contributes exactly zero to \(g^A\), whatever \(\delta u_{ik}\) is. It still contributes to \(g^B\), through \((1 - 2p_A)\,\delta v_{jk}\), and to \(s_{ij}\); what it cannot do is discriminate between pool-A parents.
A locus at which the tester pool is fixed, \(p_B \in \{0, 1\}\), has \(\delta v \equiv 0\), so it contributes \(\pm d_k\,\delta u_{ik}\) to \(g^A\) and nothing to either \(g^B\) or \(s_{ij}\). The cross is then predictable from the pool-A parent by itself.

Between those two limits sits every real programme, and Section 5.12 is about which limit divergence pushes it towards.
What a tester-based mean of \(H\) carries (the book’s own derivation). The following is algebra in this chapter’s model – fully inbred candidates (the first premise of Section 5.1), \(H_{ij} = \mu + g^A_i + g^B_j + s_{ij}\) – and not a report of what any published scheme does or selects on; whether the procedure of Comstock et al. (1949) works on lines or on heterozygous plants, this chapter does not say, and the decomposition above is derived for lines only. Evaluate each pool-A candidate by the mean of its \(H_{ij}\) over a set \(T\) of \(k\) pool-B testers. Because the deviations sum to zero over the pool, that mean is, over all \(n_B\) testers, exactly \(\mu + g^A_i\): \(s_{ij}\) averages out and \(g^A_i\) is the whole of what distinguishes candidates. Over a sample of \(k < n_B\) testers it is \(\mu + g^A_i + \bar g^B_T + \bar s_{i\cdot T}\), where \(\bar g^B_T\) is the same for every candidate (it moves the level, not the ranking) and \(\bar s_{i\cdot T}\), the mean of \(k\) specific deviations, stays in the ranking: its expectation over random tester sets is zero but it is not zero in any one set. That remainder is what \(\rho_k\) of Equation 5.21 measures in Section 5.13.6, so “averaging over testers removes \(s_{ij}\)” is exact only for the complete tester set and in expectation otherwise.
Two further limits. First, cross performance is a genotypic value, not a mid-parent difference, so a testcross mean also carries the candidate’s own additive contribution – the part that cancelled out of \(H\) in the mid-parent derivation (Equation 5.3) and is not in this decomposition at all. The row effect of a testcross mean is therefore the sum of that additive part and the GCA for heterosis, and that sum is the GCA of Equation 1.1; what the algebra here delimits is its dominance part, the GCA for heterosis against the tester pool. Second, \(g^A_i\) is defined against the frequencies \(p_B\) of the tester pool. In a recurrent scheme the tester pool is itself changed by selection from one cycle to the next, so the \(g^A_i\) of a candidate in one cycle is not the quantity it has in the next, and the derivation above is per cycle.


5.11.2 SCA is minus twice a weighted parental inner product
The bilinear term is \(s_{ij} = -2\sum_k d_k\,\delta u_{ik}\,\delta v_{jk}\): minus twice the \(d\)-weighted inner product of the two parents’ centred genotypes, a covariance up to the factor \(1/m\). For \(d_k > 0\), two parents that deviate from their pools in the same direction have a positive inner product and therefore a negative SCA.
Read in words: two parents that resemble each other – after removing what is typical of each pool – cross badly, and the resemblance that counts is weighted by \(d\), not by marker count. Similarity enters negatively throughout this chapter – \(1 - \theta_{AB}\), \(d\,m\,(1 - f^L_{ij})\) – but everywhere else it is similarity measured against a fixed base. Here it is measured against each pool’s own mean, which is what makes the term specific to a pair rather than a property either parent carries into all its crosses.
It is also Section 5.7 again. Since \(\mu\), \(g^A\) and \(g^B\) are the grand, row and column means of the \(H_{ij}\) table, \(s_{ij}\) is the double-centred \(H\) matrix. Under flat \(d\), \(H_{ij} = d\,m\,(1 - f^L_{ij})\), and double-centring annihilates the constant and flips the sign of what remains (Equation 5.16, checked in Table 5.20):
\[s_{ij} \;=\; -\,d\,m \cdot \mathrm{DC}\big(f^L\big)_{ij}, \tag{5.16}\]
with \(\mathrm{DC}(f^L)_{ij} = f^L_{ij} - \bar f^L_{i\cdot} - \bar f^L_{\cdot j} + \bar
f^L_{\cdot\cdot}\) over the \(A \times B\) block (row, column and grand means).


Show code
s_flat <- heterosis_gca_sca(U, V, rep(1, ctx$m))$sca
fAB    <- fL[seq_len(nA), nA + seq_len(book_cfg$n_pool_B)]
DC_fAB <- fAB - outer(rowMeans(fAB), colMeans(fAB), "+") + mean(fAB)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(s_flat, -ctx$m * DC_fAB, check.attributes = FALSE)))
kv(c(max_residual = max(abs(s_flat + ctx$m * DC_fAB))), sig = TRUE)

The factor \(-dm\) is not cosmetic: \(s_{ij}\) is on the trait scale and \(f^L\) is a probability, and the minus is the same minus as in \(-2\sum_k d_k \delta u\, \delta v\) – more coancestry than the two margins predict means less SCA. So the coancestry kernel determines SCA under exactly the condition it determines heterosis, up to that constant, and stops doing so under exactly the same condition: a \(d\) that varies across loci.


5.11.3 The variance components
Because the three components are orthogonal, the variance of heterosis over the factorial splits with them. Under the sampling model of the simulation – each line’s genotype an independent Bernoulli(\(p_{Ak}\)) draw at every locus, so unrelated lines and linkage equilibrium within each pool – each piece has a closed form in the pool frequencies, compared with the observed variances in Table 5.21:
\[\sigma^2_{GCA_A} = \sum_k d_k^2\,(1 - 2p_{Bk})^2\,p_{Ak}q_{Ak},
\qquad
\sigma^2_{SCA} = 4 \sum_k d_k^2\,p_{Ak}q_{Ak}\,p_{Bk}q_{Bk} \tag{5.17}\]


Show code

qb <- pB * (1 - pB)
pvar <- function(x) mean((x - mean(x))^2)   # divisor n, as in the closed forms

  component = c("GCA_A", "GCA_B", "SCA"),
  observed  = c(pvar(cs$gca_A), pvar(cs$gca_B), pvar(as.vector(cs$sca))),
  closed_form = c(sum(d^2 * (1 - 2 * pB)^2 * qa),
                  sum(d^2 * (1 - 2 * pA)^2 * qb),
                  4 * sum(d^2 * qa * qb))), 2)

GCA rows: over the 25 lines of a pool; SCA row: over the 625 crosses. One realisation of the pools (25 + 25 inbred lines, 2000 markers) and of \(d\) (seed 4).

The closed forms of Equation 5.17 take the sample frequencies as the pool frequencies; the observed column is one realisation of them, computed with divisor \(n\) (a population variance over the lines), which is the divisor the closed forms carry. The GCA rows are variances over 25 lines, whose relative standard deviation is about \(\sqrt{2/n} \approx\) 28 %: one standard deviation of the statistic, not a tolerance, and the deviations of the observed variances from the closed forms for these lines are in the last row of Table 5.30. That figure belongs to the independent-Bernoulli sampling model declared immediately above, not to the statistic: it is the sampling error of a variance over \(n\) independent observations, and a recycled pool has no such \(n\). Section 5.13.7 measures how the dispersion of that deviation changes once the lines are related.
Note what each one requires. \(\sigma^2_{SCA}\) carries \(p_Aq_A\,p_Bq_B\): it needs both pools to be polymorphic. Fix either pool at a locus and that locus contributes no specific combining ability at all, whatever its \(d_k\). Within-pool diversity is not merely something the diversity constraint defends; it is the raw material of SCA.

title: 5  Heterosis, dominance, and what divergence buys
section: 5.12 Divergence destroys SCA faster than it builds GCA
text:
5.12 Divergence destroys SCA faster than it builds GCA
Put the two closed forms of Equation 5.17 next to the drift argument of Section 5.8 and the variance tells a different story from the mean. The mean was flat; the variance is not, and it does not merely change shape.
Under Balding-Nichols, \(\mathbb{E}[p_Aq_A] = p^{*}(1-p^{*})(1 - F_{BN})\) and \(\mathbb{E}[(1 - 2p_B)^2] = (1-2p^{*})^2 + 4F_{BN}\,p^{*}(1-p^{*})\), and \(p_A\) and \(p_B\) are independent given the ancestral \(p^{*}\) (Equation 6.1, stated later, in Chapter 6). Per locus, in expectation over the draw,
\[\mathbb{E}\big[\sigma^2_{SCA,k}\big] = 4d_k^2\,p^{*2}(1-p^{*})^2\,(1 - F_{BN})^2,
\qquad
\mathbb{E}\big[\sigma^2_{GCA_A,k}\big] = d_k^2\,p^{*}(1-p^{*})\,(1 - F_{BN})
  \left[(1-2p^{*})^2 + 4F_{BN}\,p^{*}(1-p^{*})\right] \tag{5.18}\]
Read the two expressions before reading the sweep, because they already say what it will show.
Both carry the erosion factor \((1 - F_{BN})\), and both are zero at \(F_{BN} = 1\): a pool fixed at every locus has no two lines that differ, so it has no combining-ability variance of either kind. Divergence therefore cannot transfer variance from one component to the other indefinitely; it destroys both in the limit. SCA carries the factor twice, because it needs both pools polymorphic at the same locus. GCA carries it once, multiplied by the tester factor \((1 - 2p_B)^2\), whose expectation grows with \(F_{BN}\).
The two expressions therefore behave differently in \(F_{BN}\). The SCA expression is convex and decreasing on \([0, 1]\): it is a positive constant times \((1 - F_{BN})^2\), so it only ever falls. The GCA expression is a concave parabola, its \(F_{BN}^2\) coefficient being \(-4d_k^2p^{*2}_k(1-p^{*}_k)^2\), and differentiating it gives the only turnover in this section. GCA variance rises from \(F_{BN} = 0\) at a locus if and only if \(8p^{*}(1-p^{*}) > 1\), that is \(\tfrac12(1 - 1/\sqrt2) < p^{*} < \tfrac12(1 + 1/\sqrt2)\), and turns over at
\[F^\star_k = \frac{8p^{*}_k(1-p^{*}_k) - 1}{8p^{*}_k(1-p^{*}_k)}, \tag{5.19}\]
which is negative outside that interval – at such loci GCA variance falls from the start. A sum of concave parabolas is a concave parabola, and its maximum works out to the \(d_k^2\,(p^{*}_kq^{*}_k)^2\)-weighted mean of the \(F^\star_k\). Whether that mean lands inside \([0, 1]\) is a property of the ancestral frequency distribution, not a theorem: pools founded mostly at extreme frequencies would put it below zero and GCA variance would decline monotonically. Under the \(U(0.05, 0.95)\) ancestral draw used here enough loci sit in the interval to place it inside the range, which is why the expected GCA curve of the sweep of Table 5.23 has an interior peak. The weighted mean locates the peak; a grid of single draws can bracket it only roughly, because the curve is flat near the top (see below). With \(d\) drawn independently of \(p^{*}\) the weight reduces to \((p^{*}_kq^{*}_k)^2\) in expectation, and \((p^{*}q^{*})^2 F^\star = p^{*}q^{*}(8p^{*}q^{*} - 1)/8\) (Table 5.22):


Show code
pq <- function(p) p * (1 - p)
F_peak <- integrate(function(p) pq(p) * (8 * pq(p) - 1) / 8, 0.05, 0.95)$value /
          integrate(function(p) pq(p)^2, 0.05, 0.95)$value
# the sweep evaluates the closed form at sample frequencies of n inbred lines,
# whose divergence from the ancestral p is F_eff = F + (1 - F)/n; on the
# target-F_BN axis the peak therefore sits at (F_peak - 1/n)/(1 - 1/n)
stopifnot(book_cfg$n_pool_A == book_cfg$n_pool_B)
n_ln <- book_cfg$n_pool_A
F_peak_axis <- (F_peak - 1 / n_ln) / (1 - 1 / n_ln)
kv(c(expected_GCA_peak_fst = F_peak, on_target_axis = F_peak_axis), 3)




Table 5.22: Expected position of the peak of the GCA variance in divergence: \(\bar F^\star\) (expected_GCA_peak_fst; Equation 5.19 weighted by \((p^{*}_kq^{*}_k)^2\), ancestral \(p^{*}\) uniform on [0.05, 0.95]) and its position on the target-\(F_{BN}\) axis of the sweep after the sample-frequency offset (on_target_axis; 25 lines per pool). Dimensionless.







quantity
value




expected_GCA_peak_fst
0.383


on_target_axis
0.357









Call this weighted mean \(\bar F^\star\); here \(\bar F^\star =\) 0.383. It is the turnover in the divergence, from the ancestral frequencies, of whatever frequencies the closed form is evaluated at. The sweep of Table 5.23 evaluates it at frequencies estimated from \(n =\) 25 inbred lines per pool. Given the ancestral \(p^{*}\), such an estimate has variance \(p^{*}q^{*}F_{BN} + \mathbb{E}[p_{\mathrm{pool}}q_{\mathrm{pool}}]/n = p^{*}q^{*}\,[F_{BN} + (1 - F_{BN})/n]\), so its divergence is \(F_{\mathrm{eff}} = F_{BN} + (1 - F_{BN})/n\), not the target \(F_{BN}\) – the same sampling term sized for the mean in Section 5.8. On the target-\(F_{BN}\) axis of the sweep the expected peak is therefore \((\bar F^\star - 1/n)/(1 - 1/n) =\) 0.357.
What is monotone is the ratio (Equation 5.20),
\[\frac{\mathbb{E}[\sigma^2_{SCA,k}]}{\mathbb{E}[\sigma^2_{GCA_A,k}]}
  = \frac{4p^{*}(1-p^{*})\,(1 - F_{BN})}{(1-2p^{*})^2 + 4F_{BN}\,p^{*}(1-p^{*})}, \tag{5.20}\]
which falls in \(F_{BN}\) at every locus. So the defensible statement is about the share, not about a transfer. Expected heterosis, we already know, is flat in \(F_{BN}\). Sweeping the pools apart – same ancestral frequencies, fresh Balding-Nichols draws at each fst, as in Section 5.8 – and evaluating the closed forms on the realised frequencies (Table 5.23, Figure 5.3):


Show code
grid_fst <- c(0.02, 0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20, 0.30, 0.45)
reloc <- function(fst, seed = 5) {              # pool seed 5 is the chapter's draw
  cf <- modifyList(book_cfg, list(fst = fst, seed = seed))
  Pf <- pool_freqs(simulate_lines(cf) / 2,
                   rep(c("A", "B"), c(cf$n_pool_A, cf$n_pool_B)))
  a <- Pf["A", ]; b <- Pf["B", ]
  va <- sum(d^2 * (1 - 2 * b)^2 * a * (1 - a))
  vb <- sum(d^2 * (1 - 2 * a)^2 * b * (1 - b))
  vs <- 4 * sum(d^2 * a * (1 - a) * b * (1 - b))
  data.frame(fst = fst, var_GCA = va + vb, var_SCA = vs,
             frac_SCA = vs / (va + vb + vs))
}
rl <- do.call(rbind, lapply(grid_fst, reloc))
# Grid maximum of the GCA curve for pool seeds 1 to 20 (the position of the
# maximum is a property of the draw; the expected peak is not).
peak_by_seed <- vapply(1:20, function(sd_) {
  r <- do.call(rbind, lapply(grid_fst, reloc, seed = sd_))
  r$fst[which.max(r$var_GCA)]
}, numeric(1))
pk_tab   <- table(peak_by_seed)
peak_txt <- paste0(sprintf("%.2f", as.numeric(names(pk_tab))), " in ", pk_tab,
                   collapse = ", ")
stopifnot(F_peak_axis > min(grid_fst), F_peak_axis < max(grid_fst),
          F_peak_axis > min(peak_by_seed), F_peak_axis < max(peak_by_seed),
          identical(rl, do.call(rbind, lapply(grid_fst, reloc, seed = 5))))
fmt(rl, 3)

Figure 5.3: The same neutral divergence sweep, read through the combining-ability decomposition rather than through the mean: closed-form variances of heterosis over the factorial (Equation 5.17), evaluated at the realised pool frequencies of each draw, in squared units of \(d\), against the target Balding-Nichols fst (\(F_{BN}\)). GCA is the sum of both pools’ GCA variances. One draw per point (seed 5 for the pools, seed 4 for \(d\); 25 + 25 inbred lines, 2000 markers), no replication; values in Table 5.23.





Take the three columns in order, because the headline is in the arithmetic between them.
SCA variance falls by 70 % across the sweep, a drop of 64 units. GCA variance ends 30 % above where it started, a gain of 17.8 units, and has its largest value on this grid at an fst of 0.3. The position of the grid maximum is a property of this draw, not of the model: repeating the sweep for pool seeds 1 to 20 on the same grid and the same \(d\), the grid maximum fell at 0.20 in 1, 0.30 in 10, 0.45 in 9. The curve is flat near its top, so a grid of single draws locates the peak only to the range of those values. What the model gives is the expected peak on this axis, computed from Equation 5.19 with the sample-frequency offset above, 0.36, which lies inside that range. So the GCA gain recovers about 28 % of what SCA lost. The rest is gone: total variance in heterosis over the factorial falls from 151.9 to 105.7, a 30 % decline, while the mean stays fixed throughout.
Read those four percentages as one realisation, not as constants. They come from a single pair of seeds – seed = 5 for the pool frequencies, set.seed(4) for \(d\) – with no replication and no dispersion reported, and they will move if either changes. What does not depend on the seed is the direction, which is already in Equation 5.18: \(\sigma^2_{SCA}\) is a positive multiple of \((1 - F_{BN})^2\) and can only fall, and both components vanish at \(F_{BN} = 1\), so no amount of neutral divergence can hold the total up. The ordering of the columns is algebra; their magnitudes are this draw.
The share of that variance which is specific falls from 0.605 to 0.263. That statement – about the share – is the one the sweep supports; “the dominance expressed as SCA reappears as GCA” is not, and the two variance columns of Table 5.23 are why.
The share result itself is not new in direction. Reif et al. (2007) prove that the ratio of dominance to additive variance in a hybrid population falls as its two parent populations diverge, and conclude that superior hybrids then become predictable from general combining ability effects. The direction of this section’s share result is theirs; the quantity is not the same one. Their ratio is \(\sigma^2_D / \sigma^2_A\) over the hybrid population, whose denominator contains the additive variance contributed by the parents – the part that cancelled out of \(H\) in the mid-parent derivation (Equation 5.3) and is absent from everything computed here. The ratio in Table 5.23 (frac_SCA) is \(\sigma^2_{SCA}\) over \(\sigma^2_{GCA_A} + \sigma^2_{GCA_B} + \sigma^2_{SCA}\) within heterosis only. The two move the same way and are not interchangeable. What the sweep adds is the denominator, which a ratio hides: a ratio can fall because its numerator falls, because its denominator rises, or both, and the columns of Table 5.23 say which. Here the numerator collapses and the denominator recovers only part of it, so the share falls and the total falls with it.






WarningNeutral divergence shrinks the part of hybrid variation that only a cross can reveal



Neutral divergence – drift, the only kind on this sweep – does not buy expected heterosis, and it does not move heterosis from one combining-ability component into the other. It shrinks the part of hybrid variation that only a cross can reveal, destroying SCA variance faster than it builds GCA variance. An additive model looks better against diverged pools mainly because there is less left for it to miss. Divergence that is aligned with dominance is a different matter and Section 5.9 is where it is measured; the sweep here holds alignment at zero by construction.


This sharpens a question Chapter 14 will have to leave open. That chapter fits one additive effect per marker and notes that such a model cannot represent SCA at all. The sweep says how large the unrepresentable share is, and how it moves: against poorly separated pools most of the variance in heterosis is specific; against well separated ones a minority is. These are shares of the variance in heterosis, not of total hybrid value, whose parental-mean part is additive at every \(F_{BN}\). The nearest empirical statement this chapter can cite is that of Technow et al. (2014), for Dent and Flint heterotic groups: they report that the contribution of SCA variance to total genetic variance was comparatively small in their data, and high prediction accuracy from models that include GCA effects (their genomic best linear unbiased prediction (GBLUP) model fitted GCA and SCA terms and their BayesB model additive and dominance effects, so that accuracy is not that of an additive model). The sentence that follows from this chapter is that a small SCA share in well-separated groups is consistent with the mechanism of this section. The quantities differ – their share is of total genetic variance, this chapter’s is of the variance in heterosis – and a single observational study in one crop cannot test the mechanism.






WarningA smaller SCA share is not a better programme, and this is not a licence to maximise \(F_{ST}\)



Three things stay true at every point on that sweep, all of them in expectation over the draw of the pools (the sweep itself is one draw per point). Expected heterosis does not change. The gene diversity spent to buy the divergence is spent for good: \(GD_T\) falls by what \(GD_{BS}\) gains, and \(GD_{WS}\) by twice that (Section 5.8). And \(\sigma^2_{SCA} \to 0\) is the limit in which no cross is better than its parents predict – there is nothing left to find by testing combinations, which is the activity the whole factorial exists to support. Past the peak of the GCA curve in Figure 5.3 even the predictable part, the GCA variance, shrinks: at \(F_{BN} = 1\) there is no combining-ability variance of either kind, because no two lines in a pool differ.
The falling SCA share is therefore a fact about what a predictor can express, not a gain. A programme reading it as one would be congratulating itself on having less to predict.
So this is a second reason, independent of the diversity-side one, for the prescription Chapter 13 Trap 3 will make, to hold the statistic \(F_{ST}\) in a band rather than at a maximum. Section 5.8 gave the diversity-side reason. This is the prediction-side one, and it points the same way.



5.12.1 What this says about ranking crosses
The F1 of two fixed lines is genetically uniform, so the progeny-variance term that drives the usefulness criterion of stage S2 (Table 1.1; the criterion is set out in Chapter 13) is zero for the hybrid itself, and cross ranking reduces to ranking means. That is true, and it is why this book ranks hybrids on an index rather than on \(\mu + i h \sigma\).
It does not follow that the ranking is easy. The mean of an F1 contains an SCA term that an additive \(\mathbf{G}\) omits entirely, and Section 5.12 sized its share of the variance in heterosis: a majority of it against weakly separated pools, a minority against well separated ones, and zero only where, at every locus, at least one of the two pools is fixed – one pool fixed everywhere is a special case of that, not the condition. The progeny variance collapses; the specific combining ability in the mean does not.

section: 5.13 Running this on a real programme
text:
5.13 Running this on a real programme
Eight steps, in the order they have to be executed on a maize-type programme’s own data. Each one names the function to call, the quantity to check and what failure looks like. Steps 1-5 need only genotypes and pool labels. In every Call line GL is the line genotype matrix coded 0/1, the package convention for line-level functions; this chapter’s simulate_lines() returns 0/2, which is why its code passes L / 2. Data coded 0/1/2 must be halved once, before step 1, and never again.
Steps 6-8 need more, and the requirement is worth naming because it is the reason these steps are rarely run. \(H_{ij}\) is a mid-parent difference, so fitting the decomposition on real data needs the hybrid trial and per-se phenotypes of the parent lines, measured on the same scale as the hybrid trial: a separate inbred-level trial, in the same environments, with a common check set or an overlapping design to put the two on one scale. Very few programmes run one, because inbred per-se performance has no commercial value. Without it what the two-way layout of step 6 fits is hybrid performance, not heterosis, and its row effects are the GCA of Equation 1.1: the GCA for heterosis of Section 5.11 plus the parent’s own additive contribution \(\sum_k a_k\,\delta u_{ik}\), the term that is not in \(H\) at all. Both decompositions are legitimate; they are not the same decomposition, and the difference is exactly the parental additive part.

5.13.1 Step 1 – Verify the parents are inbred, and price it if they are not
Every formula in this chapter rests on the premise that the parents are fully inbred (Section 5.1). It is checkable in one line: an inbred line’s self-coancestry is exactly 1, and its heterozygous fraction exactly 0 (Table 5.24).


Show code
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(diag(molecular_coancestry(L / 2)), rep(1, nrow(L)),
                           check.attributes = FALSE)),
          max(abs(heterosis_value(rbind(U, V), d))) == 0)
kv(c(min_self_coancestry = min(diag(molecular_coancestry(L / 2))),
     max_het_fraction    = max(rowMeans(L / 2 == 0.5)),
     dominance_value_of_the_most_heterozygous_line =
       max(abs(heterosis_value(rbind(U, V), d)))))




Table 5.24: Check of the inbred premise on the simulated lines (25 + 25, coded 0/1): smallest self-coancestry, largest fraction of heterozygous loci in any line, and largest absolute dominance value, heterosis_value(), of any line (units of \(d\)).

If those numbers are not 1, 0 and 0, the parents are not fixed and the mid-parent already carries dominance of its own. On the simulated lines they are 1, 0 and 0 by construction, since the matrix is coded 0/1; the check is meaningful on real data. The size of the resulting error is not small. Build parents that are intra-pool F1s instead of inbred lines – one random cross within each pool, so each parent sits at its pool’s random-mating heterozygosity – then cross them across pools by drawing one gamete per parent per locus (Table 5.25):


Show code
intra_pool_f1 <- function(W, n, seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  (W[sample.int(nrow(W), n, TRUE), ] + W[sample.int(nrow(W), n, TRUE), ]) / 2
}
ZA  <- intra_pool_f1(U, nrow(U), 101)
ZB  <- intra_pool_f1(V, nrow(V), 102)
pd2 <- expand.grid(a = seq_len(nrow(ZA)), b = seq_len(nrow(ZB)))

# One gamete per parent per locus, five independent draws of the whole factorial.
draw <- t(vapply(seq_len(5), function(r) {
  set.seed(200 + r)
  gA <- matrix(rbinom(length(ZA), 1, ZA), nrow(ZA))[pd2$a, ]
  gB <- matrix(rbinom(length(ZB), 1, ZB), nrow(ZB))[pd2$b, ]
  H  <- heterosis_value((gA + gB) / 2, d)
  mp <- (heterosis_value(ZA, d)[pd2$a] + heterosis_value(ZB, d)[pd2$b]) / 2
  c(hybrid_value = mean(H), mid_parent_gain = mean(H - mp))
}, numeric(2)))

closed_form <- heterosis_expected(colMeans(ZA), colMeans(ZB), d)
fmt(data.frame(quantity = c("parent_het_fraction", "closed_form", "simulated_hybrid",
                            "simulated_gain", "sd_across_draws", "exact_sum_d_y2",
                            "overstatement"),
               value = c(mean(c(ZA, ZB) == 0.5), closed_form,
                         mean(draw[, "hybrid_value"]), mean(draw[, "mid_parent_gain"]),
                         # parental term fixed across draws: same s.d. for the gain
                         sd(draw[, "hybrid_value"]), sum(d * (pA - pB)^2),
                         closed_form / mean(draw[, "mid_parent_gain"])),
               unit = c("fraction", rep("sum over loci, in d", 5), "ratio")), 3)

Result. The parents carry 0.294 of their loci heterozygous. heterosis_expected() is still correct about the hybrid: it predicts 355.4 against a simulated 355.1 (s.d. 1.71 over five gamete draws), because that formula uses gamete frequencies only and does not care what the parents’ own genotypes are. What it is not correct about is the gain: the mid-parent difference is 67.2, the same 1.71 standard deviation shifted down by the parents’ own dominance value, so reading the closed form as heterosis overstates the gain by a factor of 5.29. The simulated gain agrees with the exact \(\sum_k d_k y_k^2\) of Section 5.4, 65.9, to within one standard deviation of the gamete draw.
Interpretation, with its limit. The correction is not a fudge factor: it is the parents’ own dominance contribution, 287.9 here, which heterosis_value() computes on the parent matrix directly and which is exactly zero under the inbred premise. Subtracting it recovers the mid-parent gain, and that gain matches the \(\sum_k d_k y_k^2\) of Section 5.4 in expectation only: the realised intra-pool F1 parents are one draw, not their own expectation, so each replicate’s mid-parent carries a sampling deviation of its own – which is why the agreement reported above is to within one standard deviation of the gamete draw and not exact. The factor of 5.29 itself is specific to this configuration – fst = 0.15, gamma-distributed \(d\), parents at full random-mating heterozygosity – and it shrinks toward 1 as the parents approach fixation. Five gamete draws at one seed family give the dispersion reported and no more.
Call. diag(molecular_coancestry(GL)); heterosis_value() on the parent matrix, not only on the hybrids. Check. Self-coancestry 1 and heterozygous fraction 0 for every parent. Warning sign. Any parent with a heterozygous fraction above the marker error rate. Partially inbred parents (one or two generations of selfing, clonal maintenance of a heterozygous plant) invalidate the mid-parent cancellation, not the hybrid prediction. Threshold. heterosis_value() on the parent set must return zero to machine precision. If it does not, subtract it: the mid-parent gain is the hybrid value minus the parents’ mean, always.


5.13.2 Step 2 – Compute pool frequencies, and keep them distinct from \(p_0\)
pool_freqs(GL, pool) returns one row per pool. These are the current cycle’s frequencies and they are supposed to move; they are not the frozen base \(p_0\) against which the two inbreeding lenses (defined in Section 1.2.4, measured in Chapter 10) are measured; \(p_0\) is defined in Section 1.2. Both objects are frequency vectors over the same markers and confusing them produces a heterosis prediction anchored to a population that no longer exists.
Call. pool_freqs(GL, pool) on the current cycle’s line matrix. Check. nrow() == 2 and the pool labels are the heterotic groups, not families or locations. Warning sign. A pool frequency vector computed over hybrids rather than lines. On the full factorial that gives \((p_A + p_B)/2\) for both pools – Section 10.7.1 checks the identity on selected sets – which sets \(y \equiv 0\) and reports the divergence term as zero. Threshold. None; this is a bookkeeping step, and the only failure is silent.


5.13.3 Step 3 – Decide what stands in for \(d_k\), and say so
Nothing below step 4 can be computed without a weight per locus. Three defensible choices, in decreasing order of what they require:

Estimated \(d_k\) from a dominance model fitted on hybrid data. This is what the premise that the marker panel is the set of dominance loci (Section 5.1) assumes exists, and it is the only option that lets \(\mathrm{cov}(d, y^2)\) be computed.
Flat \(d_k \equiv 1\), which makes \(H\) proportional to marker distance and the whole calculation a function of the coancestry kernel (Section 5.7). Everything in this chapter’s frequency algebra still holds; what is lost is alignment, which is exactly the term flat \(d\) sets to zero.
No \(d\) at all, reporting only \(GD_{BS}\) and mean_sq_delta_p, which is the frequency half of the divergence term and is exact (Section 5.9 says what is missing).

The cost of choice 2 is measurable, and it is the correlation already computed in Section 5.7: under flat \(d\) heterosis and marker distance are the same statistic, and under the gamma-distributed \(d\) used here the correlation between them is 0.78.
Call. heterosis_value(X, d) with whichever vector you have chosen, and record the choice next to the number. Check. length(d) == ncol(X) and \(d\) indexed in the same marker order. Warning sign. A report that gives expected heterosis without saying which of the three choices produced it. At the correlation just quoted the choices are not interchangeable for ranking crosses, and their absolute values are on different scales altogether. Threshold. If choice 2 is used, state that alignment is assumed zero, because that is what flat \(d\) asserts.


5.13.4 Step 4 – Partition, and cross-check against the diversity partition
heterosis_partition(pA, pB, d) returns shared, divergence and total. With \(d \equiv 1\) and divided by \(m\) the first two are the \(GD_T\) and \(GD_{BS}\) of gd_partition(), and the chunk in Section 5.4 asserts that to a relative tolerance of 1e-12. Running both is a consistency test worth the two lines it costs – but only if the two calls are given the same line weights, and by default they are not.
The algebra says why. For any weights \(\mathbf{w}_A\) over the lines of pool A summing to 1 within the pool (line_weights() rescales usage this way), with inbred lines, \(\theta_A = \overline{p_{A,w}^2 + q_{A,w}^2}\) where \(p_{A,w} = \sum_i w_{A,i} u_{ik}\) is the weighted pool frequency, and the same for \(B\) and for \(\theta_{AB}\). Substituting into gd_partition()’s definitions, \(GD_T = 1 - \bar f = \overline{2\bar p(1 - \bar p)}\) and \(GD_{BS} = \tilde f - \bar f = \overline{(p_{A,w} - p_{B,w})^2}/2\), which are exactly heterosis_partition()’s two terms evaluated at \(p_{A,w}\) and \(p_{B,w}\). So the identity holds for any weighting – as long as both sides use the same one. gd_partition(idx, ctx) weights each line by how often the selection uses it (line_weights()), while pool_freqs() is unweighted. On the full factorial usage is uniform and the two coincide; on a selected subset they do not, and the discrepancy is not small (Table 5.26; the usage of the selection is in Table 5.27):

Interpretation. The two functions are not inconsistent; they answer the same question on two different populations – a notional pool in which every line is equally represented, and the pool as the selection actually weights it. Which one a report wants depends on the question, and the only error is comparing one with the other and calling the difference a bug. The order of magnitude quoted here is one selection at one scale; a plan with a usage cap (max_use) sits between the two rows.
Call. heterosis_partition() on the pool frequencies and gd_partition(idx, ctx) on the hybrid set – with the pool frequencies weighted by line_weights(idx, ctx) if the two are to be compared at all. On the full factorial, or under any uniform usage, the unweighted pool_freqs() satisfies this too. Warning sign. A disagreement on a selected subset is almost always the weighting above, not a coding error: check line_weights() first, and only then whether the lines are coded 0/1 or the pool labels differ between the calls. A \(GD_{WI}\) that is not zero is the separate failure – with inbred parents it must be, and a non-zero value means the line matrix contains heterozygotes, back to step 1. Threshold. Machine precision when both sides carry the same weights. With unweighted pool frequencies against a selected subset, expect tens of per cent on the divergence term, of the size measured above, and do not treat it as a tolerance to tighten.


5.13.5 Step 5 – Log mean_sq_delta_p every cycle
s1_monitor(GL, pool, cycle) is the per-cycle panel. Of its three complementarity columns only mean_sq_delta_p is exact – it is \(\overline{y^2}\), so half of it is \(GD_{BS}\) – and frac_opposite_fixed is zero across most of the useful range, as the sweep in Section 5.8 shows.
Call. s1_monitor() once per cycle, appended to a single data frame. Check. mean_sq_delta_p / 2 against gd_partition()’s GD_BS, on the full factorial, where line usage is uniform. On a selected subset the two agree only if the pool frequencies are usage-weighted (Section 5.13.4); with the unweighted frequencies s1_monitor() uses, expect a gap of the size measured there. Warning sign. frac_opposite_fixed used as the divergence statistic. In the sweep of Section 5.8 it is exactly zero at every fst up to 0.10 – not one marker in 2000 – while over the same span the divergence term has already risen by a factor of 2.3 (0.0107 to 0.0246 per locus at \(d = 1\)). The first non-zero grid point is at fst = 0.2, by which point divergence has risen 4.1-fold. Threshold. A band on \(F_{ST}\), not a maximum. Section 5.8 gives the diversity-side reason and Section 5.12 the prediction-side one.


5.13.6 Step 6 – Check that the crossing layout identifies what you intend to fit
This is the step most often skipped, and it is arithmetic, not opinion. The general rule – a crossing plan as a bipartite graph, the rank of the GCA design matrix as lines minus connected components, and the accuracy of a testcross mean against the number of testers with plot error included – is developed in the Mating and testing design part, later, at Section 18.2.3 and Section 18.3. This step keeps only what the heterosis decomposition adds: the layout check on the chapter’s own factorial, and the finite-population correction for drawing testers from a pool of \(n_B\). In this step \(k\) is the number of testers, as in Section 18.3; everywhere else in the chapter it indexes loci. The decomposition \(H_{ij} = \mu + g^A_i + g^B_j + s_{ij}\) is the two-way layout with identified rows and columns. Count the degrees of freedom the layout actually provides (Table 5.28):


Show code
layout_df <- function(n_testers) {
  k <- which(ib <= n_testers)
  a <- factor(ia[k]); b <- factor(ib[k])
  X_add <- if (n_testers > 1) model.matrix(~ a + b) else model.matrix(~ a)
  X_sat <- if (n_testers > 1) model.matrix(~ a * b) else X_add
  data.frame(testers = n_testers, crosses = length(k),
             rank_mu_gca = qr(X_add)$rank, rank_with_sca = qr(X_sat)$rank,
             sca_df = qr(X_sat)$rank - qr(X_add)$rank,
             residual_df = length(k) - qr(X_sat)$rank)
}
fmt(do.call(rbind, lapply(c(1, 2, 5, book_cfg$n_pool_B), layout_df)))

Result. With a single tester the \(\mu + g^A\) model already has rank equal to the number of crosses, so sca_df is 0: specific combining ability is not estimable, not merely imprecise. From two testers onward sca_df is positive. residual_df is 0 in every row, because there is one observation per cross – SCA becomes identifiable from the layout at two testers and testable only when the trial adds replication.
How much a small tester set costs for general combining ability is a separate question with a closed-form answer. Averaging a pool-A line over \(k\) testers leaves it with \(g^A_i\) plus the mean of \(k\) specific deviations, so the correlation between the testcross mean and the true \(g^A\) is
\[\rho_k = \left[1 + \frac{\sigma^2_{SCA}}{\sigma^2_{GCA_A}}
        \cdot \frac{n_B - k}{k\,(n_B - 1)}\right]^{-1/2} \tag{5.21}\]
where the second factor is the finite-population correction for drawing \(k\) of the \(n_B\) available testers without replacement; at \(k = n_B\) it vanishes and \(\rho_k = 1\) exactly, because the row mean of the complete factorial is \(\mu + g^A_i\). This is the least-squares accuracy \(\rho\) of Section 18.3 with \(\sigma^2_g = \sigma^2_{GCA_A}\), \(\sigma^2_s = \sigma^2_{SCA}\), \(c = k\) and no plot error (\(\sigma^2_e = 0\), since \(H\) here is known exactly); as \(n_B \to \infty\) the correction tends to \(1/k\) and the two expressions coincide. Many random tester sets per \(k\) (Table 5.29):


Show code
Htab  <- matrix(H, nA, book_cfg$n_pool_B)   # rows = pool A, columns = pool B
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(Htab, cs$mu + outer(cs$gca_A, cs$gca_B, "+") + cs$sca)))
v_gca <- pvar(cs$gca_A)                     # divisor n, as rho_k assumes
v_sca <- pvar(as.vector(cs$sca))
nBt   <- book_cfg$n_pool_B
n_sets <- 4000
tester_scan <- function(k, reps = n_sets) {
  r <- vapply(seq_len(reps), function(i) {
    set.seed(55 + 100000 * k + i)               # 1000 * k would collide across k
    cor(rowMeans(Htab[, sample.int(nBt, k), drop = FALSE]), cs$gca_A)
  }, numeric(1))
  data.frame(testers = k, cor_mean = mean(r), cor_sd = sd(r),
             predicted = 1 / sqrt(1 + (v_sca / v_gca) * (nBt - k) / (k * (nBt - 1))))
}
ts <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(1, 2, 3, 5, 10, nBt), tester_scan))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(ts$cor_mean[ts$testers == nBt], 1)))
# The residual is only interpretable where the tester sets differ at all; at
# k = n_B there is one possible set, so cor_sd is a rounding residue and the
# ratio would be 0/0 dressed up as a number.
ts$resid_se <- ifelse(ts$cor_sd > 1e-12,
                      (ts$cor_mean - ts$predicted) / (ts$cor_sd / sqrt(n_sets)), NA)
fmt(ts, 4)

Result. A single tester ranks pool-A lines for general combining ability with a correlation of 0.55 (s.d. 0.12 over 4000 tester choices); five testers give 0.85 and ten give 0.94. The mean over tester sets and the closed form differ by at most 0.003 at any \(k\). At \(k = 1\) the difference is 0.02 standard errors of the mean; at \(k = 2, 3, 5, 10\) the mean lies above the closed form by 0.001 to 0.003, which is 1.6 to 4.5 standard errors. The closed form is therefore exact at \(k = 1\) within the noise of this scan and understates the mean correlation slightly, by a few thousandths, for \(k\) between 2 and 10.
Reading of the residuals, and its limit. The deviations are small against the quantity being predicted and the closed form is adequate to size a tester set; this section does not claim it is exact. Two possible reasons for the sign are not tested here: \(\rho_k\) is a function of an expected sampling variance, whereas Table 5.29 averages correlations, and \(x \mapsto (1 + x)^{-1/2}\) is convex, which by Jensen’s inequality would put the mean of the correlations above the function of the mean; and \(\mathrm{cov}_i(g^A_i, \overline{s}_{i\cdot})\) vanishes only when the mean runs over all \(n_B\) testers, not over a subset. The scan is a measurement on one realisation of the pools and of \(d\), with the dispersion over tester sets reported, not a validation of the formula at other pools.
Interpretation. The whole scan is driven by one ratio, \(\sigma^2_{SCA}/\sigma^2_{GCA_A} =\) 2.29 here. That ratio is what Section 5.12 shows falling as the pools diverge, so the number of testers a programme needs is not a constant of the crop: well separated pools need fewer. Two limits. This is heterosis only – the parental additive contribution to testcross performance is not in \(H\) and is not tested here – and it is one realisation of \(d\) and one pool pair, so the ratio, and with it every entry in Table 5.29, moves with the seed.
Call. qr(model.matrix(...))$rank on the layout you actually have, before fitting anything; heterosis_gca_sca() only once the layout supports it. Check. sca_df > 0 if SCA is to be estimated; residual_df > 0 if it is to be tested. Warning sign. A testcross file against one inbred tester per pool, analysed as though it estimated SCA. It estimates \(\mu + g^A_i + (\text{that tester's contribution})\) and nothing else. Threshold. Two testers to identify SCA. For ranking GCA, at this \(\sigma^2_{SCA}/\sigma^2_{GCA_A}\) ratio of 2.29 – one pool’s GCA variance in the denominator, not the two-pool sum of Section 5.12 – Equation 5.21 first exceeds \(\rho_k = 0.85\) at \(k =\) 5 testers. At five testers the scan’s mean is 0.8534, which is 4.9 standard errors of the mean of 4000 sets above 0.85, while the s.d. over tester sets at five testers is 0.044, so a single set of five testers can fall on either side of 0.85. The scan puts the mean correlation above 0.85 from five testers in this realisation, in agreement with the closed form; ten testers give 0.94. Recompute the requirement when the ratio changes.


5.13.7 Step 7 – Fit the decomposition and check it reconstructs
heterosis_gca_sca(U, V, d) is Equation 5.15, not a model fit: it needs no solver and returns \(\mu\), gca_A, gca_B and the sca matrix. On simulated \(d\) it must reconstruct every hybrid exactly, and the chunks in Section 5.11 assert that, together with the lm() interaction equivalence, to 1e-9 times the largest \(|H_{ij}|\) (the render stops if either fails). On real data \(d\) is unknown, so the route reverses: fit lm(H ~ factor(a) + factor(b)), take the row and column effects as \(g^A\) and \(g^B\) and the residual as \(s_{ij}\). The two routes coincide only on a complete, balanced factorial.
Call. heterosis_gca_sca() when \(d\) is known (simulation); lm() with both parent factors when it is not. Check. The reconstruction residual, and that all three components are mean zero. Warning sign. A non-zero mean for gca_A or sca. The deviations are taken from each pool’s own line frequencies, so they sum to zero over that pool by construction; a non-zero mean means the frequencies used were not the pool’s. Threshold. Machine precision for the reconstruction. For the variance components there is no threshold that transfers to a real pool, and the \(\sqrt{2/n}\) figure quoted in Section 5.11 is not one. It is one relative standard deviation of the variance of \(n\) independent observations, so even for independent lines about a third of the GCA components falls outside it by construction (band_ind in Table 5.32), and it is valid only because the closed forms are derived under the simulation’s sampling model – each line’s genotype an independent Bernoulli(\(p_k\)) draw at every locus, hence unrelated lines and linkage equilibrium within pool. A recycled heterotic pool satisfies neither: assumption A3 (Section 1.1; declared in Section 10.1) makes within-pool recycling the normal state of this system, so its lines share ancestors.
What a construction can measure is how the dispersion of the deviation of the observed variance from its closed form changes when the lines are related, for the part that founder sampling causes. Re-derive each pool as 25 doubled haploids drawn from crosses among six of its own members – one Bernoulli draw per locus, so loci recombine freely and there is no physical linkage, but the lines are related, and descent from six founders induces linkage disequilibrium among them all the same. Table 5.30 shows five such pairs of pools beside the independent lines, as an illustration of what the deviations look like. The comparison that carries the inference follows it (Table 5.31, Table 5.32).


Show code
rel_dev <- function(A, B) {                     # % deviation, observed vs closed form
  p1 <- colMeans(A); p2 <- colMeans(B)
  cc <- heterosis_gca_sca(A, B, d)
  obs <- c(pvar(cc$gca_A), pvar(cc$gca_B), pvar(as.vector(cc$sca)))
  cf  <- c(sum(d^2 * (1 - 2 * p2)^2 * p1 * (1 - p1)),
           sum(d^2 * (1 - 2 * p1)^2 * p2 * (1 - p2)),
           4 * sum(d^2 * p1 * (1 - p1) * p2 * (1 - p2)))
  100 * (obs / cf - 1)
}
recycle <- function(W, n_found) {               # DH lines from crosses among founders
  fo <- W[sample.int(nrow(W), n_found), , drop = FALSE]
  t(vapply(seq_len(nrow(W)), function(i) {
    pr <- sample.int(n_found, 2)
    rbinom(ncol(W), 1, (fo[pr[1], ] + fo[pr[2], ]) / 2)
  }, numeric(ncol(W))))
}
dev <- t(vapply(seq_len(5), function(r) {
  set.seed(500 + r)                             # seeded per draw, not once
  rel_dev(recycle(U, 6), recycle(V, 6))
}, numeric(3)))
dimnames(dev) <- list(paste0("draw", seq_len(5)), c("GCA_A", "GCA_B", "SCA"))
tab7 <- rbind(dev, `independent lines` = rel_dev(U, V))

Result 2. The comparison is 1000 recycled pairs of pools (seeds 7001 to 8000) against 1000 independent sets of 25 lines per pool drawn as Bernoulli at the pool frequencies of the original lines (seeds 8001 to 9000). Over those replicates the standard deviation of the deviation is larger for recycled pools than for independent lines in all three components: by a factor of 1.15 (95 % interval 1.07 to 1.22) for GCA_A, 1.22 (1.14 to 1.31) for GCA_B and 1.65 (1.54 to 1.77) for SCA. Independent lines already fall outside the \(\sqrt{2/n}\) band in 30 % and 32 % of replicates for the two GCA components, against 39 % and 42 % for recycled pools. Measured against the central 95 % range of the independent deviations, recycled pairs fall outside in 9 %, 13 % and 23 % of replicates (GCA_A, GCA_B, SCA), against the 5 % that independent lines give by construction. The mean deviation of the recycled GCA components is below that of the independent ones (-4.0 and -3.6 % against 1.1 and -0.4 %; the standard error of each mean is about 1.1 points).
Interpretation, and its limits. A tolerance calibrated on independent lines is too narrow for related lines in this construction, most of all for the specific component, whose dispersion is the one that grows most in relative terms (1.65-fold, against 1.15 and 1.22). Counting the components of the five-draw table that lie outside the \(\sqrt{2/n}\) band (5 of 15, 5 of them in the GCA columns) would suggest that the GCA components carry the failure and the SCA component does not. The count is not a measure, because the band is one standard deviation and the independent comparison is a single draw; the replicated comparison shows a larger dispersion in all three components. Why the dispersion grows is not tested. The closed forms, being sums of per-locus terms, contain neither the covariance between loci across lines (linkage disequilibrium, here induced by descent from few founders) nor the relatedness between lines; the construction changes both at once and does not separate them. A third candidate is the loss of segregating loci under six founders, which changes the effective number of loci that the statistic averages. Each is a candidate explanation, not a result. The inference is limited to this construction: six founders, one doubled haploid per F1, free recombination, 25 lines per pool, one \(d\) and one pool pair, and a comparison against independent Bernoulli lines at the pool frequencies, not against a programme’s own pedigree. A real recycled pool also carries disequilibrium that physical linkage maintains across cycles, and the size of that contribution is not measured anywhere in this book. The tolerance for a real pool must therefore be recalibrated empirically on the programme’s own pedigree; the closed forms remain exact statements about the sampling model they are derived under.


5.13.8 Step 8 – Decide the \(F_{ST}\) band on alignment, not on \(F_{ST}\)
The output of steps 4-7 answers one management question: should the pools be pushed further apart? The chapter’s answer is that \(F_{ST}\) cannot inform it (Section 5.8: the total does not move in expectation) and that the quantity that can is \(\mathrm{cov}(d, y^2)\) (Section 5.9: a factor of 1.55 at constant \(F_{ST}\), in the one generating model of that section).
Call. \(\mathrm{cov}(d, y^2)\) with the population divisor, alongside \(\bar d\,\overline{y^2}\); the two-term identity Equation 5.12 is the check. Check. The sign and magnitude of the covariance relative to \(\bar d\,\overline{y^2}\). Warning sign. A proposal to raise \(F_{ST}\) justified by the divergence term alone. Under neutral divergence the shared term pays for all of it, unit for unit in expectation, and \(\sigma^2_{SCA}\) falls at the same time. Threshold. No universal one exists, and this chapter does not supply it: the missing weight \(\lambda\) between within- and between-pool diversity needs the two covariances listed in Section 5.14.1, and this book estimates neither.

title: 5  Heterosis, dominance, and what divergence buys
text:
5.14 What this does not change






ImportantThe diversity constraint stays additive



Nothing in this chapter reopens the optimisation. \(\theta_S\), \(GD_T\) and \(\alpha\) are computed on molecular coancestry and are functions of the frequencies alone; no dominance term enters them, and Chapter 15, Chapter 16 and Chapter 17 are untouched. The combining-ability split of Section 5.11 sits outside the constraint for the same reason: it is a statement about the objective, not about the feasible set.
A dominance model changes the mean-performance ranking, not the diversity term. Chapter 25 states the same separation from the other side. Do not conflate them, and do not read this chapter as licence to put a heterosis term inside the constraint.


What it does change is the interpretation of the constraint’s output. By the two-term identity Equation 5.12, the divergence term of a plan’s selected lines is \(\tfrac{m}{2}[\bar d\,\overline{y^2} + \mathrm{cov}(d, y^2)]\), and \(GD_{BS}\) fixes only \(\overline{y^2}\). Two plans with the same \(\alpha\) and the same \(GD_{BS}\) therefore differ in that term by exactly \(m/2\) times the difference in their \(\mathrm{cov}(d, y^2)\) (both computed on usage-weighted frequencies, Section 5.13.4), a quantity the partition does not contain and only an estimate of \(d\) can supply. How large that difference can be between two attainable plans is not measured in this book. The scenario table, Table 5.15, a factor of 1.55 between its extremes, does not measure it: it holds one pool pair’s frequencies fixed and re-places \(d\) across loci, which compares genetic architectures, while a selection plan cannot move \(d\) and changes only the selected lines’ frequencies, within what the candidate set and the budget on \(\alpha\) allow.

5.14.1 What it would take to use \(d\)
Chapter 11, later, leaves a weight \(\lambda\) undetermined between within- and between-pool diversity and shows that, with expected heterosis as the objective, \(\lambda\) is \(1/2\) under flat dominance and otherwise \(\lambda_d\), a ratio of two weighted means of \(d\) (Equation 11.12). This chapter can now say what would have to be estimated to set it, and it is not much:

\(\lambda\) needs two covariances, not \(d\) itself. Each weighted mean of \(d\) in \(\lambda_d\) is \(\bar d\) plus a covariance divided by a mean, as in Equation 5.12, so \(\lambda_d\) needs \(\mathrm{cov}(d, y^2)\) and \(\mathrm{cov}(d, H_S)\), with \(H_{S,k} = p_{Ak}q_{Ak} + p_{Bk}q_{Bk}\) the within-pool heterozygosity of locus \(k\), each relative to \(\bar d\), on top of what the frequencies already give. A programme does not need per-locus dominance effects to weight the two diversity terms against each other; it needs to know whether its divergence is landing on its dominance loci.
Ranking crosses needs more. \(s_{ij}\) is a \(d\)-weighted inner product between two specific parents, so it needs the dominance effects locus by locus. This is the extension Chapter 25 names and the book does not attempt.
Fitting it needs a factorial, and a testcross file is not one. The decomposition is the two-way layout with identified rows and columns, and against a single common tester no SCA is identifiable (Section 5.13.6 counts the degrees of freedom; Section 18.2.3 gives the general rank rule). Programmes that already cross two pools in a partial factorial for hybrid evaluation have the layout; programmes that testcross against one inbred tester per pool do not.

title: 5  Heterosis, dominance, and what divergence buys
text:
5.15 Where this connects
Chapter 3 supplied the partition and Chapter 11 will use it; this chapter supplies the reason the \(GD_{BS}\) component is singled out for protection, and the reason protecting it is not the same as maximising it. Chapter 13 Trap 3, later, recommends holding \(F_{ST}\) in a band: Section 5.8 is why a band, and Section 5.9 is what to watch instead of the band. Section 5.7 closes the loop with the coancestry kernel of Chapter 2: under flat dominance, the diversity matrix and the heterosis prediction are the same object.
Chapter 14 is the chapter this one supplies a missing term to. It predicts breeding values with an additive model on a trait that is additive by construction, and lists specific combining ability first among what it does not model. Section 5.11 is where that term comes from and Section 5.12 is what share of the variance in heterosis it holds; both are derived here rather than fitted, because on a simulated \(d\) they can be.
It also gives a reason why a heterotic pattern – which pool crosses well onto which – is not recoverable from how far apart the pools have drifted: Section 5.9’s three scenarios share every frequency-based statistic and differ by a factor of 1.55 in expected heterosis in the generating model used here. White et al. (2020) describe both the diversity structure and the heterotic patterns of North American proprietary dent germplasm; this chapter’s reading is that the two cannot be recovered from one another.
Forward, the alignment result raises a question for the recurrent loop. Drift moves frequencies independently of \(d\), and selection on a line’s own performance cannot respond to \(d\) either, because an inbred line’s dominance contribution is exactly zero (Section 5.6). That leaves selection on cross performance as the only process of those considered here that can move frequencies in a way that depends on where the dominance is, and it suggests that the alignment between divergence and dominance is something each cycle either builds or erodes rather than a standing asset; this is an inference from the algebra of this chapter, not a result shown in it. A one-cycle constraint cannot see that, and neither can \(F_{ST}\). The loop on a dominance trait is run in Chapter 9, which is the pipeline this chapter’s algebra describes. Chapter 23 runs selection under the diversity budget on an additive index, with no dominance in the traits, and so does not test the inference.

title: 6  Simulating lines, pools and crosses
text:
6.1 What has to be produced
The Foundations part defined the quantities the book manages – coancestry (Chapter 2) and its partition over two pools (Chapter 3) – the response they are traded against (Chapter 4), and the heterosis that pool divergence is maintained for (Chapter 5). Chapter 4 drew its data from simulate_pools() and Chapter 5 from simulate_lines() and simulate_data(), both without deriving them. This chapter builds the generator step by step, with simulate_lines() and simulate_data().
simulate_pools() uses the same Balding-Nichols pool frequencies, homozygous lines and A x B factorial, but a different trait: n_qtl loci with independent effects plus noise, where the traits built here have correlated effects at every marker and no noise. Up to the lines the two generators consume R’s random stream in the same order, so called with book_cfg’s values (25 + 25 lines, \(m\) = 2000, fst = 0.15, seed 1) they return the same lines and the same hybrid marker matrix X (asserted in Section 6.2); only the traits differ.
The book_cfg values coincide with the arguments written in Chapter 4’s chunk, which asserts that its fst and seed equal book_cfg’s. simulate_pools() also clamps its pool frequencies to \([10^{-6}, 1 - 10^{-6}]\) and simulate_lines() does not, so the pool frequencies of the two functions agree to within \(10^{-6}\) and not exactly; at the arguments of Section 6.2 the lines are identical (asserted there).
Everything downstream of this chapter consumes three objects and knows nothing about where they came from. That is deliberate: it is the seam at which a simulation is swapped for real data, and it is the only place that has to change when it is.
This chapter builds those objects. It also builds the candidate set the rest of the book selects from, so the choices made here – how divergent the pools are (Section 6.2.2), how the index is constructed (Section 6.4) – determine what the later chapters have to work with.
Table 6.1 lists the three objects, and the optional fourth.

title: 6  Simulating lines, pools and crosses
text:
6.2 Simulating the lines
Two heterotic pools are generated with a Balding-Nichols-type model. From Balding and Nichols (1995) this chapter takes the name of the model and the idea of expressing the divergence of a population from a common ancestral one in a single parameter; the Beta densities of Equation 6.1 and the reading of \(F_{BN}\) given with it are this book’s own specification for a biallelic locus, implemented in simulate_lines(), and are not quoted from that paper; the book attributes to Balding and Nichols (1995) no particular parameterisation. Ancestral allele frequencies \(p^{*}_k\) are drawn uniform on \([0.05, 0.95]\), then pool A’s frequency at marker \(k\) is drawn as
\[p_{Ak} \sim \text{Beta}\!\left(p^{*}_k \frac{1 - F_{BN}}{F_{BN}},\;
                                (1 - p^{*}_k) \frac{1 - F_{BN}}{F_{BN}}\right), \tag{6.1}\]
and independently for pool B (\(p_{Bk}\)), where \(k = 1, \dots, m\) indexes markers, \(p^{*}_k \in [0.05, 0.95]\) is the ancestral frequency of the allele coded 1, \(p_{Ak}, p_{Bk} \in (0, 1)\) are the pool frequencies of that allele, and \(F_{BN} \in (0, 1)\) is the parameter fst of the configuration (Appendix A). The Beta of Equation 6.1 has mean \(p^{*}_k\) and variance \(F_{BN}\, p^{*}_k (1 - p^{*}_k)\) (from \(\mathrm{Var} = ab/[(a+b)^2(a+b+1)]\) with \(a + b = (1 - F_{BN})/F_{BN}\)): \(F_{BN}\) is the divergence of each pool from the ancestral frequency, measured as that variance in units of \(p^{*}_k(1 - p^{*}_k)\), not a divergence between the two pools. The ancestral frequency \(p^{*}_k\) belongs to the draw: it is a parameter of the simulation and is never observed in the data. It is neither a pool frequency \(p_{Ak}\), \(p_{Bk}\) nor the frozen base ctx$p0 of the candidate set, which is a sample quantity of the hybrids (defined at the end of Section 6.5). Between the pools, \(\mathrm{Var}(p_{Ak} - p_{Bk}) = 2 F_{BN}\, p^{*}_k (1 - p^{*}_k)\), and the \(F_{ST}\) statistic of Equation 3.7 computed on two pools of unbounded size estimates approximately \(F_{BN}/(2 - F_{BN})\) (Appendix A): at the book’s \(F_{BN}\) = 0.15 that is 0.081, not 0.15.
Genotypes are then drawn as \(2 \times \text{Bernoulli}(p)\), which makes every line fully homozygous, as an inbred line should be. Table 6.2 checks the result.

Only 0 and 2 appear: no residual heterozygotes. With real data those must be imputed or dropped before this point, because the hybrid-genotype identity in Chapter 2 assumes homozygous parents.

6.2.1 What the generator assumes
The data of this chapter are generated under the assumptions listed here, and the numbers it reports (the grid, the replicates, the expectations derived for the divergence knob) are conditional on them. The exact algebraic identities it checks do not need them all: the per-hybrid heterozygous fraction equals \(1 - f^L_{ab}\) for any inbred parents, the identity of \(f\) with tcrossprod(cbind(X, 1 - X)) / m holds for any marker matrix coded 0, 0.5, 1, and \(\sum G = 0\) holds for any panel centred on its own sample frequencies. Independence across loci enters the dispersion of the replicates, not the expectations, which are sums over loci.
In the labels A1–A8 (listed in Chapter 1; Chapter 8 maps all eight for its own operation) the generator meets A1, A2, A5, A7 and A8, and the frozen base of A6 is the p0 it stores once in ctx; A3 and A4 do not arise, because one generation of lines is drawn once, with no recycling and no cycles.

Biallelic, neutral, unlinked markers. The pools diverge by drift alone from one ancestral frequency vector (no selection, mutation or migration after the split), and the loci are independent of one another: \(p^{*}_k\), \(p_{Ak}\), \(p_{Bk}\) and every genotype are drawn independently across \(k\). There is no genetic map and no recombination, so no linkage disequilibrium arises beyond sampling noise. Chapter 7 (one cross, F1 to F4) and Chapter 8 (one conversion) are where a map and recombination first appear, in the simulators of the package; Chapter 9 relaxes this too, adding outbred founders, directional dominance and several generations of selection.
Unrelated lines, inbred by fiat. Given \(p_{Ak}\), the lines of pool A are independent draws of \(2 \times \text{Bernoulli}(p_{Ak})\) at each locus, and likewise for pool B: there is no pedigree and no shared descent among lines of a pool beyond what the pool frequency carries. Each line is drawn directly at fixation (0 or 2 at every marker); the generator does not model the doubled-haploid or selfing path that produces inbred lines in a programme (Section 1.1); Chapter 7 models the selfing path, F1 to F4, for one cross.
Equal pool sizes and the complete A x B factorial. \(n_A = n_B\) in the configuration, and every A x B combination is formed once, with equal weight (Section 6.3). This is an assumption, not a property of hybrid programmes: the identities of the grid of Table 6.3 that tie the heterozygous fraction to \(GD_T + GD_{BS}\) need it. Chapter 18 and Chapter 20 choose which crosses are made instead.
Additive traits, effects at every marker, known without error (section “Predicted traits”): no dominance and no prediction error. Dominance enters in Chapter 5 and Chapter 9, and prediction error in






6.2.2 The divergence knob
fst sets how much of the pools’ diversity sits between them rather than within; it is not compared here with the number of markers, the number of lines or the trait correlation, so nothing is claimed about its rank among the parameters. What the divergence buys is less obvious than it looks: Figure 6.1 plots the heterozygous fraction of the F1 over a grid of \(F_{BN}\), Table 6.3 gives the coancestries and diversity components behind it, and Table 6.4 the changes between the two ends of the grid. The grid uses the teaching configuration (25 + 25 lines, \(m\) = 2000) with fst replaced by the grid value, so its row at \(F_{BN}\) = 0.15 is the F1 of the lines L of Section 6.2 and the heterozygous fraction of Table 2.6 of Chapter 2 (asserted against L in the chunk).


Show code
# the two trade ratios and the heterozygous fraction over replicate grids at the
# two ends; simulate_lines() seeds from cfg$seed, so seed s is explicit
gd_ends <- function(fst, seed) {
  cfg <- modifyList(book_cfg, list(fst = fst, seed = seed))
  fL  <- molecular_coancestry(simulate_lines(cfg) / 2)
  A <- seq_len(cfg$n_pool_A); B <- cfg$n_pool_A + seq_len(cfg$n_pool_B)
  f_til <- mean(c(fL[A, A], fL[B, B])); f_bar <- mean(fL)
  c(GD_WS = 1 - f_til, GD_BS = f_til - f_bar, GD_T = 1 - f_bar,
    het = 1 - mean(fL[A, B]))
}
n_rep <- 200
rep_lo <- vapply(seq_len(n_rep), function(s) gd_ends(min(fst_grid), s), numeric(4))
rep_hi <- vapply(seq_len(n_rep), function(s) gd_ends(max(fst_grid), s), numeric(4))
rep_x  <- rep_hi - rep_lo                        # change, largest minus smallest
rep_ratio <- rbind(-rep_x["GD_BS", ] / rep_x["GD_T", ],
                   -rep_x["GD_WS", ] / rep_x["GD_BS", ])
rep_het_diff <- rep_x["het", ]                   # paired by seed

               (1 - mean(molecular_coancestry(L / 2)[a_L, b_L])))
stopifnot(dev_grid < tol_exact, length(i_cfg) == 1, dev_row < tol_exact)

     ylim = y_rng + c(-1, 1) * 0.25 * diff(y_rng),
