Across a 20-fold range of \(F_{BN}\) the heterozygous fraction stays between 0.3617 and 0.3663, against an expectation of 0.3650 that contains no \(F_{BN}\). Each point is one draw of a finite pair of pools. Over 200 replicate draws (seeds 1 to 200, the two ends of the grid only) the heterozygous fraction has mean 0.3651 (s.d. 0.0033) at \(F_{BN}\) = 0.02 and 0.3651 (s.d. 0.0059) at \(F_{BN}\) = 0.40; the mean change between the ends, paired by seed, is \(2.2 \times 10^{-6}\) with standard error \(4.0 \times 10^{-4}\), 0.01 standard errors from zero. A single draw per point therefore scatters by about 0.006, and the range of the six single draws (0.0046) is of that order: the figure by itself cannot separate a flat line from a small trend, and the replicate means and the expectation of Section 5.8 are what carry the flatness. Over the same range, in the terms of Chapter 3 with \(\tilde f\) the group coancestry within a pool (self-coancestry included, within_pool_f), the within-subpopulation gene diversity \(GD_{WS} = 1 - \tilde f = GD_{WI} + GD_{BI}\) of Equation 3.9 changes by $-$0.1323, the between-pool component \(GD_{BS}\) by 0.0674 and the total \(GD_T\) by $-$0.0649.
The \(GD_{BS}\) gain is 1.04 times the \(GD_T\) loss and the within-pool loss is 1.96 times the \(GD_{BS}\) gain; the expectations under drift in two equal pools are 1 and 2 (Chapter 3). Both ratios are single draws. Over the 200 replicate grids they have mean 1.005 and 2.003 with standard deviation 0.086 and 0.086, so the departure of this draw from 1 and 2 is within ordinary sampling variation.
The stopifnot() in the code of Figure 6.1 asserts the identity that ties the first trade to the flat line (deviation \(1.1 \times 10^{-16}\), tolerance \(1 \times 10^{-12}\)): with equal pool sizes the heterozygous fraction is exactly \(GD_T + GD_{BS}\), so a constant heterozygous fraction means that what \(GD_{BS}\) gains, \(GD_T\) loses.
That is not an artefact of this grid, under the assumptions of Section 6.2.1. For the F1 of inbred parents \(a\) and \(b\) the heterozygous fraction is exactly \(1 - f^{L}_{ab}\), hybrid by hybrid (asserted in the chunk of Table 6.8); its mean over the complete A x B factorial is \(1 - \bar f^{L}_{AB}\), with \(\bar f^{L}_{AB}\) (between_pool_f) the mean coancestry between a pool-A and a pool-B line (written \(f_{AB}\) in Chapter 3 and \(\theta_{AB}\) in Appendix A; Chapter 5 identifies them on the complete factorial). Section 5.8 derives, for pools of unbounded size (Equation 5.11), that the shared term \(2\bar p(1 - \bar p)\) (here \(GD_T\)) loses and the divergence term (here \(GD_{BS}\)) gains \(F_{BN}\,p^{*}(1-p^{*})\). Here \(GD_T\) and \(GD_{BS}\) are computed from the sample frequencies of \(n\) lines per pool, which add binomial variance \(p_{Ak}(1 - p_{Ak})/n\) to each pool frequency; then \(E[GD_{BS}] = F_{BN}\,p^{*}q^{*} + (1 - F_{BN})\,p^{*}q^{*}/n\) per marker, with \(q^{*} = 1 - p^{*}\), and the loss of \(GD_T\) and the gain of \(GD_{BS}\) are both \(F_{BN}\,p^{*}q^{*}(1 - 1/n)\) in expectation. The factor \((1 - 1/n)\) cancels in the ratios 1 and 2. With \(n\) = 25 and the \(F_{BN}\) range of the grid, the expected change is 0.0666, against 0.0693 for unbounded pools. Section 5.8 derives the same sample-frequency offset on a different grid (seed 5, \(m\) = 2000) as \(E[2p^{*}q^{*}](1 - F_{BN})(1/n_A + 1/n_B)/4\), which at \(n_A = n_B = n\) is the \((1 - F_{BN})\,p^{*}q^{*}/n\) above; the formulas agree, and the numbers here are a different draw of the generator.
What this chapter measures is the heterozygous fraction and its split into \(GD_T\) and \(GD_{BS}\). Its data carry no dominance (the traits of Section 6.4 are additive), so the heterozygous fraction is not heterosis here. It is the F1 heterosis per locus only for flat dominance, \(d_k = 1\) at every locus (Equation 5.3), and its identification with \(GD_T + GD_{BS}\) needs in addition inbred parents, the complete A x B factorial and equal pool weights, the conditions of the \(GD_{BS}\) row of Table 3.6. Under those conditions neutral divergence relocates diversity from \(GD_T\) to \(GD_{BS}\) and creates no expected heterosis. Outside them this chapter says nothing about heterosis. Whether \(GD_{BS}\) is to be preserved is not a consequence of the flat line: Table 3.6 in Chapter 3 states it for those conditions and defers the argument to Chapter 5, and Section 5.9 treats what has to be true of the divergence, namely its alignment with the dominance effects, for the divergence to be worth anything.

Every A x B combination is formed. With 25 lines per pool that is 625 candidates; at the production scale of 71 lines per pool it is 5041. Table 6.5 gives the size of the resulting dosage matrix M and Table 6.6 the first rows of the pedigree ped.

title: 6  Simulating lines, pools and crosses
text:
6.4 Predicted traits
Marker effects are drawn correlated across traits, through a Cholesky factor of a fixed correlation matrix, and the predicted values are the centered marker matrix times those effects. In this chapter R (the target correlation of the marker effects), B (the matrix of marker effects) and L (the line genotype matrix) are names of code objects, not the \(\mathbf R\), \(\mathbf B\) and \(L\) of Appendix A, and \(n_A\), \(n_B\) count the lines of pool A and pool B, not the female and male lines of Chapter 18.


Show code
set.seed(cfg$seed + 99)
R <- matrix(c(1, 0.3, -0.3,
              0.3, 1,  0.1,
             -0.3, 0.1, 1), 3, 3)
stopifnot(nrow(R) == cfg$n_traits)       # R is written for three traits
vr <- vanraden_G(M)
B <- matrix(rnorm(cfg$m * cfg$n_traits), cfg$m) %*% chol(R)
traits <- scale(vr$Z %*% B)
rank_Z <- qr(vr$Z)$rank
stopifnot(rank_Z == cfg$n_pool_A + cfg$n_pool_B - 2)


Table 6.7 sets the realised correlations of the predicted traits beside the target R.


Show code
ij <- which(upper.tri(R), arr.ind = TRUE)
fmt(data.frame(traits = paste(ij[, 1], "x", ij[, 2]),
               target_R = R[ij], realised = cor(traits)[ij]), 3)

The Cholesky step gives each row of B, the effects of one marker on the 3 traits, covariance R. It does not make the realised trait correlations equal R: they depart from it by up to 0.140 in absolute value. The hybrid values are linear combinations of the columns of the centred matrix Z, whose rank is 48 \(= (n_A - 1) + (n_B - 1)\) for an additive A x B factorial, so each realised correlation rests on one draw of effects projected onto 48 dimensions. The target is a property of the effect distribution, not of this draw; how closely the realised correlations approach it on average over draws was not measured here.






ImportantWhat this simulation deliberately does not model



These predicted values are constructed from known marker effects, so they carry no prediction error. Real genomic estimated breeding values (GEBVs) do. The book therefore treats ctx$index as given throughout.

The optimum. For a given candidate set and a given constraint on diversity, no selection made on estimated values can have a higher mean true index than the optimum computed on the known values, because the optimum maximises that index over every feasible selection. This is a statement about the optimum.
The heuristics. The gains this book reports come from greedy, differential-evolution and local-search selections, which at the teaching scale are not certified optima (Section 17.4; ocs_bound() gives a valid upper bound, and sel_exact() does not converge there). A feasible selection is not a bound: a selection made on estimates could exceed a heuristic’s index on the known values, so a gain in ctx$index does not bound the gain that a selection on estimates could achieve.
Scope. That statement about the optimum concerns the index only: it does not apply to the diversity metrics, which do not depend on the traits, nor to anything outside the additive model.
Additive only. The additive model also carries no dominance, so it cannot express specific combining ability (Section 5.11 models it; the caveats of Chapter 25 remain); the gap in prediction is closed in
crumbs: 6  Simulating lines, pools and crosses

6.5 The two matrices, both built


Show code
X <- M / 2
ctx <- build_ctx(X = X, f = molecular_coancestry(X), G = vr$G, traits = traits,
                 ped = ped, n_lines = nrow(L),
                 pool = rep(c("A", "B"), c(cfg$n_pool_A, cfg$n_pool_B)),
                 fL = molecular_coancestry(L / 2), cfg = cfg)

# the heterozygous fraction of hybrid (a, b) is 1 - fL[a, b] (inbred parents)
dev_G   <- abs(sum(ctx[["G"]])) / sum(abs(ctx[["G"]]))   # relative to sum |G|
dev_f   <- rel_dev(ctx[["f"]], tcrossprod(cbind(X, 1 - X)) / ncol(X))
dev_het <- rel_dev(rowMeans(ctx[["X"]] == 0.5),
                   1 - ctx[["fL"]][cbind(ped$a, ped$b)])
stopifnot(dev_G < tol_exact,
          min(ctx[["f"]]) >= 0, max(ctx[["f"]]) <= 1,
          dev_f < tol_exact, dev_het < tol_exact)

# simulate_data() builds the same ctx, apart from the column names of traits
ctx_sd <- simulate_data(book_cfg)
same <- setdiff(names(ctx), "traits")
stopifnot(identical(names(ctx_sd), names(ctx)),
          all(vapply(same, function(k)
            isTRUE(all.equal(ctx[[k]], ctx_sd[[k]], tolerance = tol_exact)),
            logical(1))),
          isTRUE(all.equal(unname(ctx[["traits"]]), unname(ctx_sd[["traits"]]),
                           tolerance = tol_exact, check.attributes = FALSE)))

Table 6.8 shows the result. sum(G) is zero up to floating-point rounding: it is \(-4.18 \times 10^{-11}\), \(1.5 \times 10^{-15}\) of \(\sum |G|\), and not exactly 0. It is zero because vanraden_G() centres the markers on the sample frequencies of this very panel, colMeans(M) / 2, so that the columns of \(\mathbf Z\) sum to zero and \(\mathbf 1'\mathbf G\mathbf 1 = 0\) (Equation 2.4); G here is the matrix of Equation 2.3, and the property belongs to this centring, not to the matrix at other reference frequencies, where the sum need not vanish. f is inside \([0, 1]\), the other property of Chapter 2, on this dataset. Two identities are asserted with it (tolerance \(1 \times 10^{-12}\)): f equals tcrossprod(cbind(X, 1 - X)) / m to exactly 0, and the heterozygous fraction of each hybrid equals 1 - fL[a, b] to \(5.6 \times 10^{-17}\). The range of f is nonetheless narrow and far from 0: f is identity in state, unrelated individuals are not at 0 and its level is set by the marker panel (Chapter 2), so the assertion min(f) >= 0 is the weak property and the informative one is the range printed in the table.
The context also stores three objects computed once, from the 625 hybrids, at construction, and not to be recomputed per scenario (Table 6.9):

               max = vapply(stored, max, numeric(1)),
               row.names = NULL))
# p0 is the mean of the two pools' sampled line frequencies (L is coded 0/2)
dev_p0 <- rel_dev(ctx[["p0"]], (colMeans(L[a_ids, ]) + colMeans(L[b_ids, ])) / 4)

p0 is the allele frequency vector of the candidate set, colMeans(X) over the 625 hybrids. It is the base against which F_hom and F_drift are measured in Chapter 10, and recomputing it per scenario would silently zero out the historical memory of erosion. It is a sample quantity of this draw: with equal pools and the complete factorial it is the mean of the two pools’ sampled line frequencies (asserted in the chunk of Table 6.9, deviation \(1.1 \times 10^{-16}\)). It is therefore a different object from the ancestral frequency \(p^{*}_k\) of Equation 6.1, which is never observed, and from the pool frequencies \(p_{Ak}\), \(p_{Bk}\). maf_pop is the minor-allele frequency of p0, pmin(p0, 1 - p0), and index is the multi-trait index of the hybrids, standardised once.

For real data the same function is called with your own matrices:


Show code
st1 <- stage1_build(
  X      = hybrid_markers,   # N x m, coded 0/1/2 or 0/0.5/1
  ped    = pedigree,         # data.frame with columns a, b
  traits = predicted_traits, # N x n_traits
  fL     = line_coancestry,  # optional
  coding = "012"             # or "0-0.5-1"; NULL (default) auto-detects
)


stage1_build() rescales 0/1/2 dosages to 0/0.5/1 before computing f. With coding = NULL it infers the coding from the values present, ignoring missing calls: any value above 1 means 0/1/2. That rule assumes a 0/1/2 matrix contains at least one dosage-2 call. A matrix holding only 0 and 1 is ambiguous – inbred lines coded 0/0.5/1, or 0/1/2 dosages with no homozygote for the allele coded 2 – and no rule applied to the values can resolve it; stage1_build() then assumes 0/0.5/1 and warns. Declaring coding removes the assumption. On the simulated hybrids, which contain dosage-2 calls, the two codings give the same f:


Show code
tr <- st1$hybrids[, grep("^trait", names(st1$hybrids))]
pd <- data.frame(a = st1$hybrids$line_A, b = st1$hybrids$line_B)
stopifnot(any(st1$X * 2 == 2),
          identical(stage1_build(st1$X, pd, tr)$f,
                    stage1_build(st1$X * 2, pd, tr)$f))


The ambiguous case: two hybrids at three markers, coded 0/1/2, with no dosage-2 call. Auto-detection reads each 1 as a homozygote, so it returns the coancestry of two inbred individuals that these hybrids are not; the declared coding returns the coancestry computed directly from the 0/0.5/1 matrix (Table 6.12).


Show code
X_amb   <- rbind(c(0, 1, 1),
                 c(1, 0, 1))                 # 0/1/2 dosages, no dosage 2

tr_amb  <- data.frame(trait1 = c(0, 0))
f_auto <- withCallingHandlers(
  stage1_build(X_amb, ped_amb, tr_amb)$f,
  warning = function(w) { message("warning: ", conditionMessage(w))
                          invokeRestart("muffleWarning") })
f_012  <- stage1_build(X_amb, ped_amb, tr_amb, coding = "012")$f
f_true <- molecular_coancestry(X_amb / 2)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(f_012, f_true)),
          !isTRUE(all.equal(f_auto, f_true)))

6.7 What the candidate set looks like
Figure 6.2 shows the two quantities every later chapter trades: the index of the candidates and the gene diversity of random subsets of them.


Show code
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.2, 4.2, 2.5, 1))
hist(ctx$index, breaks = 40, col = "grey85", border = "white",
     main = "multi-trait index", xlab = "index (s.d. units)")
set.seed(cfg$seed + 3)
gd_random <- replicate(n_subsets, gene_diversity(sample.int(ctx$N, n_sub), ctx))
hist(gd_random, breaks = 30, col = "grey85", border = "white",
     main = paste("GD of random subsets of", n_sub), xlab = "gene diversity")
abline(v = gene_diversity(seq_len(ctx$N), ctx), col = book_pal[["ink"]], lwd = 2)
par(op)








Figure 6.2: The candidate set at the teaching scale (25 + 25 lines, 625 A x B hybrids, 2000 markers). Left: histogram of the multi-trait selection index of the 625 hybrids: the equally weighted sum of the standardised predicted traits (default weights of build_ctx()), re-standardised to mean 0 and s.d. 1. Right: histogram of the gene diversity of 400 random subsets of 60 hybrids, the baseline every later chapter measures against; dark vertical line: gene diversity of the whole candidate set.





The dark vertical line is the gene diversity of the whole candidate set. It does not sit at the centre of the distribution of random subsets of 60 – it sits above it. That gap is pure sampling, it has nothing to do with selection, and mistaking it for a loss is the subject of Section 11.9. Table 6.13 gives the size of the gap, from one set of 400 random subsets, with the Monte Carlo standard error of their mean: the gap is 59 standard errors, so it is not sampling noise of the subsets. Section 11.9 measures the same gap on the same ctx with its own subsets and derives its expectation, and the percentages differ only by the draw of the subsets.


Show code
stopifnot(gd_whole > gd_mean)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  quantity = c("GD, whole candidate set", "GD, mean of random subsets",
               "Monte Carlo s.e. of that mean", "apparent loss (%)",

title: 7  Sizing a segregating population, F1 to F4
text:
7.1 The simulated space is ancestry, not alleles
Chapter 6 draws its parent lines “inbred by fiat” (every locus 0 or 2) and does not model the selfing path that produces inbred lines. This chapter models that path for one biparental cross, carried F1 -> F2 -> F3 -> F4 by selfing, and asks the question every programme has to answer before it plants anything – how many plants? What is sized is the panel of F4 lines the cross yields, a line-level object; it is not the hybrid candidate set, which is formed from lines afterwards (Chapter 6).
Where the cross sits in the programme. In the terms of Table 1.1, selfing to fixation is the alternative to doubled-haploid induction that A2 allows for deriving lines from a within-pool cross (S2); the simulation stops at F4, not at fixation, so the route is the one A2 licenses and the F4 panel is not yet A2’s product (its lines carry \(H = 0.125\), Section 7.7). The cross simulated here has its two inbred parents fixed for different alleles at every locus (SA2 below). If the two parents belong to different heterotic groups, the panel is a derived population of the kind A3 excludes from the programme’s recycling loop (Section 1.1, Section 10.1): a pre-breeding or donor cross, outside A1–A8 (Chapter 8 treats introgression from a donor on its own terms). Against the labels A1–A8 (listed in Chapter 1; Chapter 8 maps all eight), this chapter uses A2 for the parents (SA2), meets A3 only if the cross is within a pool, and departs from A5 (linked markers, SA4) and A8 (own scale); A1, A4, A6 and A7 are not used (no heterotic groups, cycles, frozen base or dominance in the simulator). Which of the two cases applies does not enter any number below, because the simulator labels ancestry (parent 1 or parent 2) and carries no heterotic-group identity; it decides only whether a panel of this kind belongs to the programme’s cycle.
In the grid of this chapter the objectives saturate at very different \(N\) (Table 7.12), so for this simulated cross there is no single optimal \(N\): it depends on what is sized for, and an \(N\) chosen for the objective that saturates earliest leaves the later ones unmet.
Each genome position is coded 0 (from parent P1) or 1 (from parent P2). The simulator carries only loci at which the two inbred parents are fixed for different alleles, one allele each, so ancestry identifies the allele. Loci at which the parents share an allele, and multiallelic loci, are not simulated. Throughout this chapter, “allele frequency” means “frequency of P1 ancestry”. The parents are written P1 and P2; the assumptions of the chapter are labelled SA1 to SA9 (“sizing assumption”) so that the two are not confused.

title: 7  Sizing a segregating population, F1 to F4
section: 7.2 The assumptions, one at a time
text:
7.2 The assumptions, one at a time
These are the assumptions the numbers rest on. Read them before trusting any of the numbers.
SA1. Ancestry, not alleles. As in Section 7.1: loci fixed for different alleles in the two parents, biallelic, coded by ancestry.
SA2. Parents fully homozygous and fixed for alternative alleles. Consequently every F1 plant is genetically identical, so the F1 carries one genotype whatever the number of plants. Sizing the F1 is a logistical decision, not a genetic one – unless the parents carry residual heterozygosity, which Section 7.5 handles.
SA3. The genetic map. Ten chromosomes whose lengths (maize_chr_len) total 1670 cM, i.e. \(L\) = 16.7 Morgans. The lengths are a model input chosen to approximate a composite maize map built without intermating; they are not taken from a single published map. Do not use map lengths estimated in intermated recombinant inbred lines (RILs) such as the intermated B73 x Mo17 (IBM) population: five generations of intermating B73 x Mo17 produced “nearly a four-fold increase in the genetic map distance” (Lee et al. 2002, abstract). The junction recursion of SA7, which is this chapter’s own, gives for \(g\) random-mating generations after the F2, followed by selfing to fixation, \((2 + g/2)L\) junctions per haplotype, i.e. \(4L\) at \(g = 4\) and \(4.5L\) at \(g = 5\), against \(L\) for an F2 haplotype and \(2L\) for selfing to fixation without intermating. A “four-fold increase” is therefore baseline dependent: against \(L\) the recursion gives 4 and 4.5, against \(2L\) it gives 2 and 2.25. Which baseline Lee et al. (2002) use, and whether the generation that produced the F2 is counted as an intermating, was not checked against the full text (UNVERIFIED); this chapter does not settle it. Winkler et al. (2003) treat the expected recombination fraction and the map expansion in intermated recombinant inbred populations (abstract only read); the formula \((2 + g/2)L\) is not taken from them. A map expanded in this way overstates the recombination the sized population actually undergoes.


Show code
map <- build_map(maize_chr_len, spacing_cM = 2)


The 2 cM map built from these lengths has 10 chromosomes, 846 markers and a total length of 1670 cM (16.7 Morgans).
SA4. Haldane recombination, no interference, identical in male and female. The probability of a haplotype switch between adjacent markers \(d\) cM apart is \(r = 0.5(1 - e^{-2d/100})\) (Haldane 1919); the first marker of each chromosome gets \(r = 0.5\), which produces independent segregation between chromosomes automatically.
Limitation: without interference the variance in crossover number is inflated (Poisson). Maize crossovers show positive interference: Falque et al. (2009) estimate that about 15% of crossovers (6% to 23% depending on the chromosome) come from a non-interfering pathway and the rest from an interfering one. The simulated block-length distribution may therefore have a longer tail than under interference. The map length fixes the mean number of crossovers per meiosis, hence the expected junction count of the recursion in SA7 when every crossover is observed. What interference would change is the joint distribution of crossovers: the junctions lost to double events inside one marker interval (the bias of SA9) and the extent of the region dragged around a distorter (SA5). The size of these effects was not measured here, so the statement that mean block length is unaffected holds for the expected crossover number, not for the marker-observed count or for the drag.
SA5. Segregation distortion by rejection sampling, therefore exact rather than approximate. Two mechanisms: gametophytic (of the Ga1 type, a unilateral cross-incompatibility system whose Ga1 gene acts through male function (Zhang et al. 2018)) acting only on the male gamete, and zygotic (hybrid lethality or subvitality) as genotype fitnesses. Because rejection acts on the whole gamete, the region linked to the distorter is dragged along – which is exactly the phenomenon of interest. Distortion is common in maize mapping populations: 17% of 1,820 markers across four populations, and 36% in B73/Mo17, with three known gametophytic factors as possible causes (Lu et al. 2002). The three distorters of Table 7.1, their positions and their strengths are model inputs. All three act against P2 ancestry (P1 transmission above 0.5 at the two gametic loci, a reduced P2P2 fitness at the zygotic one). The bin numbers in label are placeholders, not mapped positions of the named loci.


Show code
g <- f2_distorters$type == "gametic"
stopifnot(all(f2_distorters$k[g] > 0.5),
          all(f2_distorters$w11[!g] < f2_distorters$w00[!g]))

                           "$w_{00}$", "$w_{01}$", "$w_{11}$", "label"),
             row.names = FALSE)

In the grid of Section 7.4 this is the input whose effect on diversity more plants barely reduce inside the range tested (the distortion gap of Figure 7.1). No sensitivity to the strengths, positions or number of the distorters was run: every statement below about distortion – the gap, “more plants buy little distortion protection”, the recovery numbers – is a statement about this one configuration. Replace f2_distorters with your own F2 genotyping data before using any number here to decide field area.


SA6. Five schemes, all ending with \(H = 0.125\) so they are directly comparable: ssd (single-seed descent, SSD: one seed per plant per generation – the neutral reference, no selection, no drift beyond the meiotic), ssd_attr (SSD with a random loss of 15% of plants per generation, standing for vigour, partial sterility or flowering asynchrony; the rate is a scenario parameter, f2_opt$attrition, not an empirical estimate), bulk (differential seed contribution, a Wright-Fisher model with weights \(w_i = e^{\beta(z_i - \bar z)}\) where \(z_i\) is the share of plant \(i\)’s genome from P1, which the model takes as the adapted parent, and \(\beta\) = 6 (f2_opt$beta_bulk) is a model input not estimated from data – a phenomenological model of polygenic natural selection, not a model of adaptation loci; because \(w_i\) increases with \(z_i\), the bulk selects against P2 ancestry by construction), and syn1/syn2 (Syn1, Syn2: one or two random intercrossing cycles in the F2 before the two selfings).
SA7. The F4 panel is not a RIL panel. Residual heterozygosity is \(H = 0.125\), and that changes every theoretical expectation (Table 7.2). Here \(H\) is the observed heterozygosity \(H_o\) of Section 1.2 – the fraction of loci at which a plant is heterozygous – averaged over the plants of the panel and over loci; it is not the expected heterozygosity \(H_T\), \(H_S\) of Chapter 3, which is computed from allele frequencies. The last row of Table 7.2 counts junctions in the sense of Fisher (1954): \(A_t\) junctions per haplotype in generation \(t\), \(L\) the map length in Morgans, \(h_t\) the heterozygosity of the parent whose meiosis produces generation \(t + 1\) (the \(H_t\) of Equation 1.4 is a different quantity, the expected heterozygosity of a set at generation \(t\)).

The form \(0.5/\sqrt{N}\) for SE(\(\hat p\)) is the case \(H\) = 0 (fully inbred lines, F\(_\infty\)). The diversity row of Table 7.2 is the identity used throughout the chapter. Let \(p_j \in [0, 1]\) be the frequency of P1 ancestry at marker \(j = 1, \dots, m\) in a panel of \(N\) F4 lines, one per F2 plant, and \(D = m^{-1} \sum_j 2 p_j (1 - p_j) / 0.5 \in [0, 1]\) the diversity retained (diversity_retained()), with the frequency base the panel itself. Without distortion and without selection (ssd), \[
\mathrm{E}[D] = 1 - \frac{1 - H}{N},
\tag{7.1}\] with \(H\) = 0.125 the F4 heterozygosity of SA7 and the expectation taken over replicate populations. Section 7.3 checks it by simulation; it was not derived in full here, only by the following argument at \(p_0 = 1/2\). There \(\mathrm{E}[D] = 1 - 4\,\mathrm{Var}(\hat p)\) and, for \(N\) independent F4 lines, \(\mathrm{Var}(\hat p) = (1 - H)/(4N)\) (first row of Table 7.2). At \(H = 0\) this is the \(1/n\) loss of Equation 1.4 for a pool of \(n\) = \(N\) doubled haploid lines, each passing one gamete (Section 1.2), and the same sampling factor as the finite-set bias of Section 11.9. What the factor \((1 - H)\) adds is that the one-step loss \(1/n_{gam}\) of Equation 1.4 equals \((1 - H)/N\) when \(n_{gam} = N/(1 - H)\): a heterozygous line carries both ancestries at a locus, so \(n_{gam}\) rises from \(N\) at \(H = 0\) to \(2N\) at \(H = 1/2\). This is an equivalence of the sampling variance of \(\hat p\), not a Wright effective size.
SA8. The standard error is estimated between replicates, not between markers. This is essential: linked markers are strongly autocorrelated, so the spread across markers within one replicate is not an estimator of sampling error.
SA9. What is not modelled, and therefore cannot be answered here: deliberate artificial selection, quantitative trait locus (QTL) architecture, phenotypic inbreeding depression, mutation (irrelevant on this timescale), and structural variation. If you know there is a large inversion between your parents, zero the recombination rate over that interval in build_map().
Known bias: a junction is counted only as a change of ancestry between adjacent markers, so two junctions inside the same marker interval cancel and the simulated count is biased downward. Its size at the grid’s spacing and at 1 cM is measured in Section 7.3.

text:
7.3 Verifying the identities live
The theory of Section 7.2 is not decoration – it is checkable, and the simulator is only trustworthy if it reproduces it. The heterozygosity and diversity checks (Table 7.3, Table 7.4) run on a 10 cM map with distortion switched off, so the neutral expectations apply exactly. The junction checks do not share that setup: Table 7.6 uses the cached grid (2 cM map, distortion active), and Table 7.7 uses live neutral panels on 2 cM and 1 cM maps; each caption states its setup.


Show code
map10 <- build_map(maize_chr_len, spacing_cM = 10)
neutral <- make_distortion(map10, NULL, active = FALSE)

set.seed(4)  # one draw: a single F1 -> F4 lineage of 400 plants
F1 <- make_F1(map10, 400)
F2 <- cross_indices(F1, 1:400, 1:400, map10, neutral)
F3 <- cross_indices(F2, 1:400, 1:400, map10, neutral)
F4 <- cross_indices(F3, 1:400, 1:400, map10, neutral)

stopifnot(ncol(F4$H1) == 400)  # "400 plants" in the caption
het_chk <- do.call(rbind, lapply(list(F1, F2, F3, F4), function(P) {
  h <- colMeans(P$H1 != P$H2)          # per-plant heterozygosity
  c(H_observed = mean(h), se = stats::sd(h) / sqrt(length(h)))
}))
het_chk <- data.frame(generation = c("F1", "F2", "F3", "F4"), het_chk,
                      H_expected = c(1, 0.5, 0.25, 0.125))
# tolerance: 4 standard errors between plants (the F1 has none)
stopifnot(all(abs(het_chk$H_observed - het_chk$H_expected) <=
              pmax(4 * het_chk$se, 1e-12)))
knitr::kable(fmt(het_chk, 4),
             col.names = c("generation", "H_observed", "s.e.", "H_expected"))

Every scheme counts fewer junctions than predicted: -3.8% for SSD, -5.1% and -6.4% for one and two intercrossing cycles. This is the known bias of SA9, and it is larger than the single-meiosis Haldane deficit at 2 cM, \(r/d - 1\) = -2%. 7.4.4 The metrics saturate at different N
This is the central practical result of the chapter, for this simulated cross, and the reason the question “what is the optimal \(N\)?” has no single answer (Table 7.12). To make “saturates” checkable it is defined on the grid: for \(D\) and for the worst region \(\min(p, 1-p)\), \(N_{90}\) is the smallest grid \(N\) whose replicate mean has reached 90% of the gain from the smallest to the largest \(N\) tested. The definition is relative to the grid’s upper end (390), so a longer grid would move it. The replicate means carry sampling error, and so does the threshold, which is built from the two end means; Table 7.12 therefore also gives a two-standard-error bracket: the last grid \(N\) whose mean lies more than two standard errors below the threshold, and the first that lies more than two above it. For recovery of a P2 homozygote at \(k\) unlinked loci the target is absolute, \(P \geq 0.95\). Its distortion-free closed form, the classical number of plants needed to recover a genotype (Sedcole 1977), is
\[
N_{95}(k) = \frac{\log 0.05}{\log\left[1 - \left(\frac{1-H}{2}\right)^k\right]},
\tag{7.2}\]
with \((1 - H)/2\) the probability that an F4 line is P2P2 at one locus (SA7) and the \(k\) loci on different chromosomes. \(P\) is the probability that at least one of the \(N\) F4 lines of a panel is P2P2 at all \(k\) loci, for loci drawn at random on distinct chromosomes (multilocus_recovery(), 300 locus sets per population). The closed form takes the lines as independent and the loci as independent, which holds for \(N\) F2 plants of one uniform F1 and for loci on different chromosomes.
Recovery is measured on replicate populations. The cached grid holds one population per \(N\) for this objective, so its first-crossing \(N\) cannot be separated from between-population variance, and the first crossing of a noisy curve is biased low. The chunk below therefore replaces it by 20 live populations per grid \(N\) (SSD, 2 cM map, distortion active, the 20 sizes of the grid, seed 20261108 + \(N\)), with the same 300 locus sets per population (Figure 7.3 plots the replicate means). The design is the first one run, and was not changed after its results were seen (one earlier timing run used the same seeds and settings): \(N_{95}\) is the first grid \(N\) whose replicate mean reaches 0.95, reported with a two-standard-error bracket (last \(N\) whose mean + 2 s.e. is below 0.95, first \(N\) whose mean - 2 s.e. is at or above it), and the standard error is between populations, so it includes the locus-set sampling.


Show code
n90 <- function(N, y) {
  thr <- y[1] + 0.9 * (y[length(y)] - y[1])
  N[which(y >= thr)[1]]
}
# 2-s.e. bracket of the crossing; se = between-replicate sd / sqrt(n_rep)
n90_bracket <- function(N, y, se) {
  n   <- length(y)
  thr <- y[1] + 0.9 * (y[n] - y[1])
  z   <- (y - thr) / sqrt(se^2 + 0.01 * se[1]^2 + 0.81 * se[n]^2)
  below <- which(z < -2 & N < n90(N, y))
  above <- which(z > 2 & N >= n90(N, y))
  c(lo = if (length(below)) N[max(below)] else NA_real_,
    hi = if (length(above)) N[min(above)] else NA_real_)
}

title: 7  Sizing a segregating population, F1 to F4
text:
7.5 Sizing the F1
With fully homozygous parents the F1 is genetically uniform and the decision is logistical.
Suppose instead that each parent is still heterozygous at a fraction \(h_{res}\) of the \(n_{loc}\) loci that are polymorphic between the two parents and segregate independently. Here \(1 - h_{res}\) is the proportion of those loci at which a parent is homozygous, not an inbreeding coefficient relative to a base population, and \(h_{res}\) = 0.05, \(n_{loc}\) = 5000 are scenario values, not estimates for any germplasm. Heterozygosity is assumed to arise independently in the two parents, so there are \(2 h_{res} n_{loc}\) heterozygous (parent, locus) pairs in expectation. Each F1 plant receives one random gamete from each parent, so at a heterozygous (parent, locus) pair one of the parent’s two alleles is transmitted to no F1 plant when all \(n\) plants receive the same one, with probability \(2(1/2)^n\). The expected number of parental alleles lost is therefore \(2 h_{res} n_{loc} \cdot 2(1/2)^n\), the quantity f1_sizing() returns.
That is not the number of loci lost. Under the biallelic assumption of SA1, a parent heterozygous \(Aa\) at a locus where the other parent is \(aa\) loses polymorphism at that locus only if every F1 plant receives \(a\), with probability \((1/2)^n\); losing \(a\) leaves the other parent’s \(a\) in the F2. A locus heterozygous in both parents (probability \(h_{res}^2\)) becomes monomorphic only if all \(n\) F1 plants are \(AA\) or all are \(aa\), with probability \(2(1/4)^n\). The expected number of loci made monomorphic is \(n_{loc}\left[2 h_{res}(1 - h_{res})(1/2)^n + h_{res}^2 \cdot 2(1/4)^n\right]\) (Table 7.14).


Show code
s <- f1_sizing(n_F1 = 1:20, h_res = h_res, n_loci_eff = n_loc)
lost_col <- grep("lost", names(s), value = TRUE)   # alleles lost, per f1_sizing()
stopifnot(length(lost_col) == 1,
          isTRUE(all.equal(s[[lost_col]], 2 * h_res * n_loc * 2 * 0.5^s$n_F1)))
s$expected_loci_monomorphic <- n_loc * (2 * h_res * (1 - h_res) * 0.5^s$n_F1 +
                                        h_res^2 * 2 * 0.25^s$n_F1)
# oracle: enumeration of parental genotype classes. A gamete is allele 0 or 1;
# a heterozygous parent transmits (1/2, 1/2), a homozygous one allele 0, except
# in the homozygous x homozygous case, where the parents differ (SA1). The F2 is
# monomorphic iff all n F1 plants have the same dose and it is 0 or 2.
p_mono <- function(g1, g2, n) {
  d <- c(g1[1] * g2[1], g1[1] * g2[2] + g1[2] * g2[1], g1[2] * g2[2])
  d[1]^n + d[3]^n
}
het <- c(0.5, 0.5); hom0 <- c(1, 0); hom1 <- c(0, 1)
enum_mono <- n_loc * (h_res^2 * p_mono(het, het, s$n_F1) +
                      2 * h_res * (1 - h_res) * p_mono(het, hom0, s$n_F1) +
                      (1 - h_res)^2 * p_mono(hom0, hom1, s$n_F1))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(s$expected_loci_monomorphic, enum_mono)))
n_f1     <- min(s$n_F1[s[[lost_col]] < 1])
n_f1_loc <- min(s$n_F1[s$expected_loci_monomorphic < 1])
s_show <- s[s$n_F1 %in% sort(unique(c(4, n_f1_loc - 1, n_f1_loc, n_f1,
                                      12, 16, 20))), ]
s_show[-1] <- lapply(s_show[-1], formatC, digits = 3, format = "g")
knitr::kable(s_show, row.names = FALSE)

WarningOn the “equivalent N”



\(N_{eq} = (1 - H)/(1 - D)\) answers “how many F4 lines without distortion would give the diversity actually observed”. It is a communication device, not a Wright effective size: it converts a deterministic bias into a drift equivalent. Use it to compare scenarios; never substitute it into an \(N_e\) formula.

title: 7  Sizing a segregating population, F1 to F4
text:
7.7 Where this connects
The rest of the book works on one kernel: molecular coancestry \(f\) (Chapter 2) and gene diversity \(GD = 1 - \theta\) (Equation 1.2, derived in Section 11.2). An F4 panel can be put through it, and this section measures two things about the result: the identity between \(D\) and \(GD\), and what a selection of lines from the panel can and cannot do to \(GD\) (Table 7.16).
Scope of the bridge. The later chapters budget the \(GD\) of hybrids formed from lines of two pools, against a frozen base \(p_0\) and a random-subset reference, under A2 (inbred parents, so \(GD_{WI} = 0\)), A5 (independent loci) and A8 (the teaching scale), the assumptions declared in Section 10.1. The panel here departs from each: its lines carry \(H = 0.125\), so \(GD_{WI} > 0\) at the line level; its markers are linked (SA4); its frequency base is the panel itself and \(D\) divides by the cross’s own maximum 0.5, not by a frozen base. What is established below is the line-level quantity of one derived panel, not the quantity the later chapters budget.


Show code
map_br  <- build_map(spacing_cM = 10)
dist_br <- make_distortion(map_br, active = TRUE)
n_sub <- 10   # lines selected from each panel (scenario value)
stopifnot(n_sub == 10)  # "subsets of 10 lines" in the caption

bridge <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(30, 120, 480), function(n) {
  set.seed(3 + n)
  pop <- run_scheme("ssd", n, map_br, dist_br, opt = f2_opt)
  X   <- t((pop$H1 + pop$H2) / 2)          # lines x markers, 0/0.5/1
  f   <- molecular_coancestry(X)
  th  <- mean(f)                           # all pairs, self included
  p   <- panel_freq(pop)
  gd_of <- function(i) 1 - mean(f[i, i, drop = FALSE])
  sel <- integer(0)                        # greedy: add the line that lowers theta most
  for (j in seq_len(n_sub)) {
    cand <- setdiff(seq_len(n), sel)
    th_c <- vapply(cand, function(i) mean(f[c(sel, i), c(sel, i)]), numeric(1))
    sel  <- c(sel, cand[which.min(th_c)])
  }
  set.seed(100 + n)
  rnd <- replicate(200, gd_of(sample.int(n, n_sub)))
  data.frame(n_F2 = n, D = diversity_retained(p), theta = th, GD = 1 - th,
             Ns = 1 / (2 * th), fixed = mean(p == 0 | p == 1),
             GD_random = mean(rnd), GD_random_sd = stats::sd(rnd),
             GD_greedy = gd_of(sel), bound = (1 - mean(p == 0 | p == 1)) / 2)
}))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(bridge$GD, bridge$D / 2)),
          isTRUE(all.equal(bridge$Ns, 1 / (2 - bridge$D))),
          all(bridge$GD_greedy <= bridge$bound + 1e-12))
knitr::kable(fmt(bridge[c("n_F2", "D", "theta", "GD", "Ns", "fixed", "bound")], 4))

\(D\), the chapter’s own diversity-retained statistic, and \(GD\), the quantity the later chapters constrain, are the same quantity up to a factor: \(GD = D/2\) exactly, asserted in the chunk. With the 0/0.5/1 coding and \(\theta\) the mean of the molecular coancestry over all pairs of lines, self included (Caballero and Toro 2002), \(\theta\) averages \(p^2 + (1-p)^2\) over markers, so \(GD = 1 - \theta\) is the mean of \(2p(1-p)\), which is \(D/2\) because \(D\) divides the same mean by its maximum 0.5. The frequency base is the F4 panel itself.
What the panel’s \(GD\) limits. A locus fixed in the panel is fixed in every subset of its lines, so \(GD\) of any subset is at most \((1 - \text{fixed})/2\) (the bound column of Table 7.17, asserted in the chunk that builds Table 7.16). The fraction of markers fixed is 0 at most in these three panels (10 cM map, distortion active), so the bound is not the binding limit here. The measured statement is narrower: on each of the three panels the greedy choice of 10 lines reaches \(GD\) = 0.479 to 0.488, against 0.482 to 0.494 for the whole panel and 0.451 to 0.454 for random subsets of the same size. In these three panels the greedy subset did not exceed the \(GD\) of its panel. That is three panels, one subset size, one distorter configuration and a heuristic that is not an exact optimum, so it does not establish a ceiling. The book’s own results show that, on hybrids against a random-subset reference, a selection can have \(\alpha < 0\) (Section 11.9), so a subset can be more diverse than a random one; here the comparison is with the whole panel’s own \(GD\). What is certain is the conditional statement: no selection of lines restores an allele that the panel does not carry.






Note\(N_s\) on these panels



The status number is \(N_s = 1/(2\theta) = 1/(2 - D)\), between 0.966 and 0.988 in Table 7.16 whatever the sizing, and bounded above by 1 because \(D \leq 1\). On molecular coancestry at biallelic loci \(\theta \in [1/2, 1]\), so \(N_s \in [1/2, 1]\) for every set of lines, one cross or many (Section 11.3): \(N_s\) is a monotone rescaling of \(\theta\), not a head count, and no pooling of crosses would make it one. The values in Table 7.16 are correct rather than broken; \(N_s\) is a monotone function of \(D\) and carries no information that \(D\) does not, compressed into \([1/2, 1]\), so use \(D\) and \(GD\) to compare sizing scenarios.


Chapter 13 measures how the loss is distributed across stages S2 to S4 (Table 1.1); it does not vary the number of plants per cross, and this chapter measures no cost, so what “more plants” would cost against what it buys is not established here. Chapter 24 is where the same question is asked about the variance rather than the frequencies, and reaches a different conclusion about what is recoverable.

title: 8  Introgressing several genes by backcrossing
text:
8.1 The operation, in one diagram
Chapter 7 sized a segregating population for four objectives (Table 7.12): the diversity retained \(D\) (not the donor dosage \(D\) used from Section 8.2 on), the minor allele frequency, the standard error of \(\hat p\), and the recovery of a P2 homozygote at \(k\) unlinked loci (Equation 7.2). The first three ask how much of the cross is sampled. Section 8.7 asks the fourth kind of question (a homozygote at \(k\) unlinked loci, here from a BC3 and not from an F2 to F4 population), and the rest of the chapter is the mirror image of the first three. A donor line carries \(k\) genes worth having and an elite line carries everything else worth having, and the job is to move the \(k\) genes across while throwing the rest of the donor away. Here donor genome is contamination, and the only diversity that is wanted is the \(k\) target loci themselves.
Where this chapter stands. Chapter 7 placed donor introgression outside the programme of A1–A8 (Section 10.1, Section 1.1) and promised to treat it on its own terms; this is that treatment. Conversion is not one of the four stages S1–S4 of Table 1.1: it is a pre-breeding operation that produces one line, and the stages select among lines that already exist. Of the assumptions, A2 holds of the recurrent parent, which is fully inbred, and of the converted line, which is fixed at the end by doubled haploids (DH) or by selfing; the BC1–BC3 populations in between are not fixed, being heterozygous at the target loci. A3 does not: the donor is outside the recurrent pool, so a converted line is not germplasm recycled within its own pool; whether it enters the candidate set of the later chapters is a decision, taken in Section 8.10. A5 is dropped in the main body (the markers lie on a genetic map with linkage, which is the point of the chapter) and restored in Section 8.10, where markers are independent. A1, A4, A6, A7 and A8 are not used: the main body has no heterotic pools, cycles, frequency base, dominance or simulated panel, and Section 8.10 uses the book’s inbred 0/1 coding on independent markers (A7 holds there: no dominance enters \(\theta\)).
The operation is marker-assisted backcrossing (MABC). The numbers below come from a simulator of it: a marker grid at 5 cM on ten maize chromosomes (1670 cM), one selected plant advanced per generation, \(k = 1\) to \(4\) recessive targets from a single donor, on four different chromosomes, carried to the third backcross generation, BC3. The engine and the selection index are R/08_mabc.R; the experiment driver inst/scripts/run_mabc.R writes tables of the shape of the six cached mabc_*.csv files, but not every cached copy was written by its current version; Section 8.8 states which run produced each one and how to re-run it.
Before any sizing question can be asked, the crossing operations have to be unambiguous – which plant is pollinated by which, and what is genotyped at each step (Figure 8.1).
Figure 8.1: The marker-assisted backcrossing (MABC) operation for k target genes from one donor, schematic (no data). Left column: the cross made in each generation. Right column: what is genotyped and selected on, and the population size that criterion demands. The recurrent parent E re-enters at every backcross; the fork at the bottom is the fixation step, where doubled haploids and selfing differ by more than an order of magnitude in plants required at four genes. Selection at BC3 is shown as under the drag-priority index (rec_drag); the expected identity-by-descent (IBD) annotation is for s = 0.60.
Two features of that diagram do all the work in the rest of the chapter. The recurrent parent re-enters at every backcross, so donor content halves every generation whether or not anyone selects for it; and the fork at the bottom is where the plant numbers explode, because fixation asks for a homozygote and backcrossing never does.
crumbs: 8  Introgressing several genes by backcrossing

title: 8  Introgressing several genes by backcrossing
text:
8.2 The model
Two states, one haplotype. The recurrent parent is a fully homozygous inbred, so the gamete it contributes is invariant and only the donor-derived haplotype has to be tracked: a binary vector over 344 markers. Meiosis is a per-interval Bernoulli switch with the map function of Haldane (1919),
\[
r = \tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(1 - e^{-2d/100}\bigr),
\tag{8.1}\]
where \(d\) is the length in cM of the marker interval and \(r\) its recombination fraction. The formula is the standard Haldane map function, checked below against the package’s haldane_r(); the page-level attribution to Haldane (1919) (J. Genet. 8:299–309) was not verified here (the paper was not accessible). The chain of switches is exact for the marker chain precisely because Haldane is memoryless; it is not exact for the chromosome, for two reasons stated at the limit in Section 8.9. A switch is recorded only as a change between adjacent markers, so two crossovers inside one 5 cM interval cancel and are not counted (Section 7.3 measured the same bias in junction counts of simulated lines at 2 cM and 1 cM spacing, reduced but not removed at 1 cM; it was not measured here, at 5 cM, on drag, and its direction for drag is not shown). And linkage drag is measured in whole marker cells (drag_total() sums interval edges), so it has a floor of one cell, 5 cM, per target and takes values on a 5 cM lattice; the ceiling of 30 cM per gene is 6 cells.


Show code
d_chk <- c(1, 5, 20, 50)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(haldane_r(d_chk), 0.5 * (1 - exp(-2 * d_chk / 100)))),
          haldane_r(1e6) == 0.5)


Donor dosage and identity by descent (IBD) are different quantities. Donor and elite already share a fraction \(s\) of the genome by descent – they are both maize, and often both from the same heterotic group. Donor genome inside a shared tract costs nothing. So with \(D\) the donor dosage,
\[
\text{IBD}_E = 1 - (1 - s)\,D, \qquad \text{IBD}_E + \text{donor-specific} = 1 .
\tag{8.2}\]
The second identity of Equation 8.2 holds exactly in the simulator for every plant. The first holds in expectation only: the shared fraction is a realised draw of windows, not a per-plant rate, and the target windows are forced to be non-shared, so a plant’s realised IBD scatters around \(1 - (1-s)D\). The test battery asserts the second with exact equality and the first with tolerance 0.02 (tests/testthat/test-mabc.R). Everything below uses \(s = 0.6\).
Coupling phase. All \(k\) targets come from one donor, on the same haplotype. Two consequences, and the second is easy to get wrong. Linked targets travel together, so linkage drag is the union of the donor segments, not their sum. And conditional on both flanking targets being donor-derived, an even number of crossovers is forced in the interval between them, so the probability that they sit in one continuous donor segment is not \(e^{-L}\) but
\[
P_{\text{same}} = \frac{e^{-L}}{\bigl(1 + e^{-2L}\bigr)/2},
\qquad L = d/100 \text{ Morgans}.
\tag{8.3}\]

section: 8.3 Three criteria; at \(s = 0.60\) one of them binds
text:
8.3 Three criteria; at \(s = 0.60\) one of them binds
A conversion programme is usually written with three success conditions at BC3: do not lose the genes, recover the recurrent parent, and do not drag a chunk of donor chromosome along with each target. They are not equal in cost, and which one binds depends on \(s\): this section states the result at \(s = 0.6\), the value of the whole chapter, and measures the case \(s = 0\) at the end of it (Table 8.4).
Not losing the genes is exact and cheap. A backcross plant receives the donor allele at each target from its heterozygous parent with probability 1/2 (Mendelian segregation), independently across targets because the \(k\) targets sit on different chromosomes, so it is foreground-positive with probability \(q = (1/2)^k\) and \(n\) plants fail with probability \((1-q)^n\) (Table 8.2):


Show code

# smallest n with P(no foreground-positive plant) = (1 - q)^n <= 1 - 0.95
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(mb_sz$q_foreground, 0.5^mb_sz$genes)),
          (1 - mb_sz$q_foreground)^n_fg <= 0.05,
          (1 - mb_sz$q_foreground)^(n_fg - 1) > 0.05)
knitr::kable(data.frame(genes = mb_sz$genes, q = mb_sz$q_foreground, n_BC_per_gen = n_fg),
  row.names = FALSE)

At four genes the figure of Table 8.2 is 47 plants per generation, and a per-generation figure is not the programme’s. A lineage is lost when any one of the 3 backcrosses has no foreground-positive plant, so with 47 plants in every generation it survives with probability \((1 - (1-q)^{47})^{3} =
0.862\), and holding the whole lineage at \(0.95\) takes 64 plants per generation (each generation at \(0.95^{1/3}\)). The uniform scan under rec_drag at \(s = 0.6\) gives the same picture: the proportion of replicates that lost a target at four genes is 0.193 at 40 plants per generation (300 replicates) and 0.05 at 60 (200 replicates). These figures assume independent segregation of the targets (different chromosomes) and independent generations. Foreground failure is cheap to avoid, a few tens of plants per generation at four genes, and it is not zero.
Recovering the elite is free by BC3, at \(s = 0.6\). The F1 carries donor dosage 1/2, and each backcross to the recurrent parent halves the expected donor content of an unselected plant, so with no background selection at all the expected donor dosage after 3 backcrosses is \((1/2)^{4}
= 0.0625\), and
\[
\text{IBD}_E = 1 - (1 - s)\,(1/2)^{4} = 0.975
\]
at \(s = 0.6\). This is the expectation for a plant on which no selection has acted. Foreground selection conditions on the \(k\) targets being donor-derived, so the donor segments attached to them are retained and the realised dosage is higher: under the drag-priority index (rec_drag, defined in Section 8.4) the mean simulated IBD at BC3 with four genes, over the replicates that kept all targets, ranges from 0.946 to 0.964 across the population sizes of the scan (Table 8.3). The mean is conditional: at the smallest size, 20 plants, a proportion 0.603 of replicates lost a target and is not in it. At \(s = 0.6\) the mean is above a 90% target before a single background marker is scored.

WarningThe reframing



An index that spends its decisive stage on background recovery is spending it on a criterion that, at \(s = 0.6\), was already satisfied. 8.4 Which selection index
Four policies (Table 8.5), all applied to foreground-positive plants only:



Table 8.5: The four selection policies, by the key used in mabc_uniform.csv and in run_bc_program(strategy =). All are applied to foreground-positive plants only.









Key
Rule




bg
minimise background donor content


rec12
recombinant selection in BC1-BC2 only, then background


rec_bg
recombinant selection throughout, background decides among survivors


rec_drag
recombinant selection throughout, linkage drag decides, background breaks ties






rec_bg is the natural-looking two-stage rule: truncate on drag, then pick the cleanest background among the survivors. Stage 2 discards stage 1. The plant with the least drag survives the truncation and then loses to a sibling that happens to carry less donor genome somewhere irrelevant.

The two indices were compared at \(s = 0.6\) only; whether the wall is also an artefact at \(s = 0\), where recovery of the elite binds (Table 8.4), was not run.

Under the drag-priority index the higher of the two, 20/150/190, is separated from the next schedule, 200/120/40 (\(z = 3.86\)); under the background-priority index the higher of the two, 20/150/190 (0.632), is not separated from 200/120/40 (0.662, \(z = 1.4\)), so under that index the ranking rests on point estimates only. In the two 20-plant schedules a target was lost in 0.063 and 0.057 of replicates, against \((1 - (1/2)^{3})^{20} = 0.069\) for one generation of 20 plants with no other cause of loss; the schedules whose smallest generation has 40 plants lose a target in at most 0.005 of replicates (\((1 - (1/2)^{3})^{40} = 0.005\)).
Conditioning on the targets being kept (a replicate that lost one counts as a failure, so \(P(\text{both} \mid \text{kept}) = P(\text{both}) / (1 - P(\text{lost}))\)), the drag-priority success rate is 0.969 for 120/120/120, 0.931 for 20/150/190 and 0.722 for 300/40/20.
The inference is that the two extreme schedules fail for different reasons. The back-loaded 20/150/190 loses most of its deficit to foreground failure in its 20-plant BC1; the front-loaded 300/40/20 also loses targets, but most of its deficit remains after conditioning on keeping them, which is consistent with having only 20 BC3 plants among which to select on drag at the last meiosis. Neither pattern requires a difference in how efficiently a BC1 or a BC3 plant reduces drag. The comparison is limited to five schedules at one budget, one gene number and one value of \(s\), and it does not order the three schedules without a 20-plant generation beyond the intervals shown. For context only: Hospital (2001) concludes analytically that it is generally more profitable to allow three or more backcross generations than to favour recombination in early generations. That result concerns the number of generations for one introgressed gene (with flanking markers), not the allocation of a fixed number of plants among three generations for \(k\) genes, so it is a different problem and the comparison is not a test of either.

title: 8  Introgressing several genes by backcrossing
section: 8.7 Fixing the stack: selfing against doubled haploids
text:
8.7 Fixing the stack: selfing against doubled haploids
Backcrossing only ever asks for a heterozygote. Fixation asks for a homozygote at all \(k\) targets, and that is where the plant numbers move: the BC3F2 plants needed for 3 homozygotes are 4.6 times the backcross plants needed for one foreground-positive plant at one gene and 34.3 times at four (Figure 8.6). Selfing a BC3F1 heterozygous at \(k\) unlinked targets gives the recessive homozygote at each with probability 1/4, so \(q = (1/4)^k\); a doubled haploid (DH) derived from a BC3F1 gamete is homozygous everywhere, and the gamete carries the donor allele at each target with probability 1/2, so \(q = (1/2)^k\).
And the requirement is not one plant but 3, which is a cumulative binomial \(P(\text{Bin}(n, q) \ge 3) \ge 0.95\), not \(1 - (1-q)^n\) (Table 8.8; Figure 8.5 sets the binomial against simulation). Equation 7.2 of Chapter 7 is the same derivation for a different event (at least one F4 line homozygous at \(k\) loci, \(q = ((1-H)/2)^k\) with the heterozygosity \(H\) of the F2 to F4 scheme); here \(n_{keep} = 3\) homozygotes are required, from a BC3F1, with \(q = (1/4)^k\) or \((1/2)^k\). Both assume independent segregation of the targets and no segregation distortion; Chapter 7 found that its closed form understated what the simulated cross needed at \(k = 5\) once distortion was active, and the simulation checked here (mabc_bcnf2.csv) is distortion-free, so it cannot show whether the same holds for the BC3F2 binomial:

title: 8  Introgressing several genes by backcrossing
section: 8.9 Assumptions, and what is not modelled
text:
8.9 Assumptions, and what is not modelled
These matter more than usual here, because unlike the diversity chapters this one is used to decide field area.
No crossover interference (material, and it cuts against the results of this chapter). Meiosis is Haldane (Equation 8.1) (Haldane 1919), so crossovers are independent between intervals. Maize crossovers show positive interference: Falque et al. (2009) fit a two-pathway model in which most crossovers follow a gamma renewal process with shape \(4.2 < \nu < 6.2\) on most chromosomes and a minority do not interfere. For the event this simulation depends on most when both flanking crossovers arise in the same meiosis – a double recombinant in the two 5 cM intervals flanking a target, which is what turns a long donor segment into a short one – Haldane gives \(r^2 =\) \(2.3 \times 10^{-3}\). Positive interference makes a crossover in each of two adjacent short intervals rarer than the product of their recombination fractions, so the model over-produces tight recombinants, and every population size quoted for close-in trimming is expected to be a lower bound. By how much was not computed here. Note the direction: the index correction makes the problem easier, interference makes it harder, and they do not cancel in any principled way. The fix is a crossover-position sampler – chiasmata as a stationary gamma renewal process with shape \(\nu\), plus a non-interfering fraction as in Falque et al. (2009) – which reduces to Haldane exactly at \(\nu = 1\) and so is backward compatible.
One value of each criterion. The drag ceiling (30 cM per gene), the IBD target (0.9), the marker grid (5 cM) and, except in Table 8.4, \(s\) (0.6) were each run at one value. Every statement of the form “this criterion binds” or “that one is satisfied” is conditional on that set, and the sizes quoted for it are not transferred to another set. The marker-resolution limits of the grid (cancelled double crossovers within an interval, a drag floor of one cell) are stated in the model section (Section 8.2); their direction for drag was not measured here.
One plant advanced per generation. A programme that advances several plants per generation and crosses each to the recurrent parent is not modelled. Every probability in this chapter is therefore a single-lineage probability: it understates achievable progress and it removes lineage-level variance from every distribution shown.
Uniform recombination rate, no distortion, no genotyping error. The local meiotic recombination rate is far from uniform in maize. Rodgers-Melnick et al. (2015) state that it varies over 1000-fold across the genome (their Abstract and Significance statement, as background); what they measure is the breakpoints of about 136 000 recombination events in nested association mapping populations, with hotspots at crossover rates from threefold to over 100-fold the uniform expectation. A target in a cold region carries drag no feasible population will trim, and the model assigns the same rate everywhere. Segregation distortion is common in maize mapping populations, with gametophytic factors among the possible causes (Lu et al. 2002) (read at abstract level, as in Chapter 7); at a distorted locus the foreground frequency is not \(1/2\), so \(q = (1/2)^k\) and \(q = (1/4)^k\) are not exact there, and no distortion is modelled in the sizing of this chapter (the BC3F2 binomial was checked against a distortion-free simulation only, and Chapter 7 found that its closed form, Equation 7.2, understated what the simulated cross needed at \(k = 5\) once distortion was active). Map positions here are illustrative and not pinned to a named consensus map, and map lengths estimated in intermated populations of the B73 x Mo17 (IBM) type (Lee et al. 2002) are not to be used as they stand: Chapter 7 explains why a “four-fold” expansion depends on its baseline and leaves it UNVERIFIED for Lee et al. (2002); it gives no rescaling procedure, and none is applied here.
Triploid endosperm genetics is not modelled. The illustrative targets are endosperm genes. The endosperm is triploid, two maternal copies and one paternal. Assuming the donor allele is completely recessive in the endosperm, a kernel shows the phenotype only if all three copies are the donor allele: a backcross ear pollinated by the recurrent parent carries one dominant paternal copy in every kernel, so no kernel of a BC plant shows it, and the phenotype is read only on a selfed ear (BC3F2 kernels), one generation after the genotype. This is a deduction from Mendelian segregation under that assumption, not a cited result; no source was checked for it, and partial dominance or dosage effects in the endosperm would change it.
The gene set is illustrative, not a breeding recommendation. Whether all four targets are worth stacking is a breeding decision outside this model; dropping one turns the hard case (\(k = 4\)) into the comfortable one (\(k = 3\)). o2 alone gives opaque endosperm, not quality protein maize (QPM): QPM was created by selecting multiple, unlinked o2 modifier loci (Holding et al. 2008), which are unmodelled here and change the problem class from “stack \(k\) Mendelian genes” to “stack \(k\) genes plus a quantitative trait locus (QTL) background”.






WarningTwo statistical habits this chapter had to be repaired for



Select on the interval, not the point estimate. The first version of the sizing tables took the first grid point whose point estimate crossed 0.95. With few replicates per cell that is a winner’s curse: a success probability that is monotone in \(N\) reads as non-monotone through noise. The uniform scan still shows it at four genes under rec_drag: 0.989 at \(N = 320\) and 0.967 at \(N = 400\), on 90 replicates each. Selection is now on the Clopper-Pearson lower bound. Clopper-Pearson intervals are drawn in Figure 8.2 and Table 8.7 and the lower bound is tabulated in Table 8.6; Figure 8.4 gives a binomial standard error in its caption; Table 8.3, Figure 8.3 and Figure 8.5 show point estimates only, as their captions state.
Never type a number into the prose. Every figure in the original narrative was a string constant written against an earlier configuration; re-runs put the true values outside the reported confidence intervals, and the same document contradicted itself in three places. Results in this chapter’s prose and captions are computed at render time from the cached tables or from package functions; the only typed values are design inputs (the map spacing, the schedules, \(k\), \(s\) and the criteria in MB) and the replicate counts of the allocation scan and of the BC3F2 scan (MB_alloc, MB_f2), which their CSVs do not record; both are checked against the CSVs for consistency, not derived from them. Section 8.8 states where each table comes from.

title: 8  Introgressing several genes by backcrossing
text:
8.10 Where this connects
Chapter 7 sized a population for four objectives (Table 7.12), of which the diversity retained saturates earlier than recovery of a homozygote at several loci; this chapter sized one to discard donor genome everywhere except at \(k\) loci. The two share their machinery – the same ten-chromosome map and the same Haldane meiosis, at different marker spacings (2 cM there, 5 cM here, with the resolution limit stated in Section 8.9) and the same distinction between what is segregating and what is fixed – and the lesson that dominates both: size for the objective that binds. In Chapter 7 that meant not sizing for the diversity retained alone. Here it means that, at \(s = 0.6\), background recovery is already satisfied at BC3 and the plants go into linkage drag; at \(s = 0\) (Table 8.4) it is not satisfied, so the IBD criterion binds as well. Linkage drag does not stop binding at \(s = 0\): the table measures the IBD criterion alone, under rec_drag, and the joint drag-and-IBD criterion at \(s = 0\) was not run (stated above), so the second criterion is added to the first, not substituted for it.
The converted lines this chapter produces are candidates for the set the rest of the book selects from; they are not germplasm recycled within a heterotic pool (A3), and whether they enter a pool is a breeding decision outside this chapter. A conversion programme run for its own sake reduces diversity by construction: it makes an elite line into a near-copy of itself. If several conversions are run in parallel off the same recurrent parent, the resulting lines are close to each other.
Up to here that is an assertion, not a measurement; item 5 of the Preface’s chain of argument cites the measurement of Table 8.12. It is cheap to measure, and the size of it is the argument: a ratio of gene diversities, in expectation and over replicate draws. No optimiser is run or bounded here, so the measurement bears on how much gene diversity a set of conversions can contribute, not on what a selection rule could or could not recover from it. Eight BC3 conversions off one recurrent parent, against eight unrelated elite lines, are put through the kernel of Chapter 2 (Table 8.12). The lines are inbred, coded 0/1 at biallelic markers with allele frequency 1/2, drawn independently at each marker (no linkage; the markers are neutral and no dominance enters \(\theta\)).
The donor is one line, common to the eight conversions, and the chapter’s \(s\) is the fraction of markers at which donor and recurrent parent are identical by descent: at such a marker the donor allele is the recurrent parent’s, with probability \(s = 0.6\) per marker; elsewhere the donor is an unrelated line, which matches the recurrent parent only by state, at about half the markers (allele frequency 1/2). The two kinds of identity are not the same, and the state-matching of unrelated lines is the baseline on top of which \(s\) acts, not a substitute for it. A conversion carries the donor allele at a marker with probability \(D = (1/2)^{4}\), the expected donor dosage at BC3 without selection, and the recurrent-parent allele otherwise. Because \(\theta\) is a mean of per-marker identities, its expectation depends only on these per-marker probabilities; linkage would change its dispersion, not its expectation. The case \(s = 0\) (no sharing by descent) is computed beside it for comparison.


Show code
D <- expected_donor(MB$n_bc)
m_c <- 2000; n_conv <- 8
# Group coancestry (diagonal included) of the conversions and of the first
# n_conv unrelated lines; set.seed immediately before the draw
conv_theta <- function(s, seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  elite <- matrix(rbinom(40 * m_c, 1, 0.5), 40, m_c)   # unrelated elite lines
  rec   <- elite[1, ]                                   # one recurrent parent
  # donor: the recurrent parent's allele where shared by descent (prob. s),
  # an unrelated line's allele (elite[40, ]) elsewhere
  donor <- ifelse(rbinom(m_c, 1, s) == 1, rec, elite[40, ])
  conv  <- t(sapply(seq_len(n_conv), function(i)
    ifelse(rbinom(m_c, 1, D) == 1, donor, rec)))
  c(conv  = mean(molecular_coancestry(conv)),
    unrel = mean(molecular_coancestry(elite[seq_len(n_conv), ])))
}
th_s <- conv_theta(MB$s, 11); th_0 <- conv_theta(0, 11)
cost <- data.frame(
  panel = c(sprintf("8 BC3 conversions, one recurrent parent, s = %.2f", MB$s),
            "8 BC3 conversions, one recurrent parent, s = 0",
            "8 unrelated elite lines"),
  theta = c(th_s[["conv"]], th_0[["conv"]], th_s[["unrel"]]))
cost$GD <- 1 - cost$theta
stopifnot(th_s[["unrel"]] == th_0[["unrel"]])   # same elite draw in both calls

# Replicates: 200 seeds, ratio of gene diversities against its expectation
# 2 D (1 - D) (1 - s); a seed-free check of the claim of the text
rat <- function(s, seed) { th <- conv_theta(s, seed); unname((1 - th[1]) / (1 - th[2])) }
n_cc <- 200
rat_s <- vapply(seq_len(n_cc), function(i) rat(MB$s, i), numeric(1))
rat_0 <- vapply(seq_len(n_cc), function(i) rat(0, i), numeric(1))
exp_s <- 2 * D * (1 - D) * (1 - MB$s); exp_0 <- 2 * D * (1 - D)
stopifnot(abs(mean(rat_s) - exp_s) < 4 * sd(rat_s) / sqrt(n_cc),
          abs(mean(rat_0) - exp_0) < 4 * sd(rat_0) / sqrt(n_cc))
knitr::kable(cost, row.names = FALSE, digits = 4,
  caption = sprintf("Group coancestry theta (diagonal included) and gene diversity GD = 1 - theta of eight BC%d conversions off one recurrent parent, at s = %.2f (donor and recurrent parent identical by descent at a proportion s of markers) and at s = 0, and of eight unrelated elite lines: one draw (set.seed(11)) of %d unlinked markers, inbred lines coded 0/1, donor allele with probability 1/2^%d per marker and per conversion, no selection. The unrelated panel is the same draw in both calls.", MB$n_bc, MB$s, m_c, MB$n_bc + 1))




Table 8.12: Group coancestry theta (diagonal included) and gene diversity GD = 1 - theta of eight BC3 conversions off one recurrent parent, at s = 0.60 (donor and recurrent parent identical by descent at a proportion s of markers) and at s = 0, and of eight unrelated elite lines: one draw (set.seed(11)) of 2000 unlinked markers, inbred lines coded 0/1, donor allele with probability 1/2^4 per marker and per conversion, no selection. The unrelated panel is the same draw in both calls.






panel

0.9769
0.0231


8 BC3 conversions, one recurrent parent, s = 0
0.9452

8 unrelated elite lines

At \(s = 0.6\) the converted panel carries 0.053 times the gene diversity of the unrelated one in this draw; at \(s = 0\) it carries 0.125. Over 200 independent draws (seeds 1 to 200) the ratio has mean 0.047 and standard deviation 0.004 at \(s = 0.6\), and mean 0.117 (s.d. 0.006) at \(s = 0\). In expectation, two conversions differ at a marker only when exactly one carries the donor allele and the donor differs from the recurrent parent there, probability \(2D(1-D)\,(1-s)\,\tfrac12\) with \(D = (1/2)^{4}\) (the donor differs from the recurrent parent with probability \((1-s)/2\): not shared by descent, and unequal by state), against \(1/2\) for two unrelated lines, so the off-diagonal ratio is \(2D(1-D)(1-s) =
0.047\) at \(s = 0.6\) and \(2D(1-D) = 0.117\) at \(s = 0\) (asserted against the replicate means in the chunk). The diagonal of \(\theta\) is 1 in both panels and scales both gene diversities by the same factor, so this is also the expected ratio of the two. The inference is that conversion makes lines nearly identical everywhere except at the target, as designed, and that the amount of gene diversity a panel of conversions retains relative to unrelated lines is a small fraction of it, smaller the larger \(s\). What limits it: the ratio is an expectation under independent markers and a single donor, the replicate dispersion above is for that model, linkage and selection on the background are not in it, and the unrelated panel is drawn at allele frequency 1/2 with no sharing among its lines.
Two consequences for the rest of the book, limited to what was measured. First, \(\alpha\) in Chapter 15 is the shortfall of the selected set’s \(GD\) against the mean \(GD\) of random subsets of the same candidate set (Section 11.9), so conversions inside the candidate set lower the \(GD\) of the set and of that reference alike: the budget does not charge their cost, it changes the level of both. Second, \(\theta\) separates a panel of conversions from a single line entered eight times only by the small ratio above (eight copies of one line have \(GD = 0\) exactly), so the conversions should be recognised as near-copies when the candidate set is built; this recommendation is not tested here. The per-line usage cap max_use of Chapter 12 and Chapter 16 (Chapter 15 has the continuous upper cap, its analogue) caps how often a line is used, and capping the near-copies of one recurrent parent jointly requires them to be identified as a group first; whether it handles this was not run.






WarningDo not enter a converted panel as independent lines



The failure mode is administrative, not statistical. Conversions arrive with distinct line codes and distinct pedigree entries, so a pipeline that trusts the codes will treat them as eight parents. The coancestry matrix will not, and the argument for computing \(\theta\) on markers rather than on pedigree (Section 1.2.3, Chapter 2) is what protects against exactly this.

title: 8  Introgressing several genes by backcrossing
text:
Reproduce this chapter
All the code of this chapter, in order and with the explanation kept as comments, is one script: 04b-backcross-introgression.R. Download it, install hybdiv, and run it top to bottom in an empty directory; cached results are fetched on first use.
