title: 9  Simulating a hybrid breeding programme: AlphaSimR from the ground up
text:
9.1 Step 1 – Founder genomes: what a founder is, and which engine to use
Chapter 6 built the {X, f, hybrids, fL} contract with a deliberately fast simulator: Balding-Nichols allele frequencies, independent markers, no recombination, no dominance. That is enough to exercise the diversity and selection machinery, but it is not how a hybrid breeding programme is actually run, and it is not how anyone would build one from scratch. The two chapters between that one and this (Chapter 7, the size of a segregating population from F1 to F4, and Chapter 8, introgression by backcrossing) run on the package’s own map-and-meiosis simulators, not on AlphaSimR, and are not prerequisites for what follows; this chapter returns to the contract of Chapter 6 and replaces its generator.
This chapter builds one. The crop in mind is maize, the canonical allogamous hybrid crop: two heterotic pools, inbred lines (doubled haploids, DH) drawn from each, lines judged by their testcrosses onto the other pool rather than by themselves, pools improved by reciprocal recurrent selection (RRS; the paper the book cites for the name is Comstock et al. (1949), and its content is not reported here beyond its title, as in Chapter 5), and a commercial product that is a single cross between one line from each pool – the programme described in Chapter 1. Steps 1 to 7 are a step-by-step construction with AlphaSimR (Gaynor et al. 2021), written out in the primitive calls – runMacs(), SimParam, addTraitAD(), makeCross(), hybridCross(), makeDH(), setPheno(), selectInd() – with a plant breeder’s reading of each argument and a measurement at each step. Step 8 assembles those primitives into RRS, replicates it against a paired no-selection control, and shows that the same stage-1 contract comes out the other end, so stage2_select() runs on it exactly as it does on the book’s own simulated data.
Why this machinery, and why it has no counterpart in a self-pollinated programme. In an autogamous (self-pollinated) crop – wheat, rice, soybean, common bean – recombination happens once, in the F1, and the programme then narrows a segregating population toward homozygosity by selfing or single-seed descent, selecting throughout on a line’s own (per se) phenotype, because a self-pollinated genotype breeds true and its own performance is what a farmer will grow: the released variety is very often the same homozygous line the breeder selected. Chapter 22, later in the Evidence and practice part, builds exactly that programme with the same AlphaSimR primitives – makeDH(), setPheno(), selectInd() – and can be read against this one, step by step. None of Steps 2, 4 and 6 below would have a job there: there is no dominance for per se selection to be blind to (an inbred line’s value is its additive merit alone – Step 3 makes this an identity, varD = 0 on a homozygous panel, to rounding in the numbers), no tester to cross a candidate onto, no general or specific combining ability to estimate (Sprague and Tatum 1942), and no second, deliberately divergent population to keep apart, because there is only one gene pool, not two heterotic ones held apart on purpose. What follows instead is specific to an allogamous, hybrid-product crop: the inbred line is not the product, the F1 is (Step 5); a line’s breeding value depends on which pool it will be crossed to, not on itself alone (Step 6’s tester dependence); and the trait improvement a programme has made is realised only in a cross remade every season, never in either parental line by itself.
The pedagogical source is the AlphaSimR course of Gorjanc and colleagues (Gorjanc et al. 2022): its vignettes on simulating DNA, simulating traits, the DNA lottery, single- and multi-trait selection, and a plant breeding programme. The course has no hybrid programme of its own; the wheat programme it does build is the subject of Chapter 22. This chapter takes the course’s primitives and assembles them into the hybrid case.
The order matters. Everything in Step 8 is a wrapper in R/13_alphasimr_bridge.R – rrs_config, alphasimr_founder_pools(), alphasimr_rrs_cycle(), alphasimr_make_hybrids(), alphasimr_to_stage1(), alphasimr_pipeline() – and a wrapper is only readable once you know what it is wrapping. AlphaSimR is a Suggests dependency, guarded exactly like quadprog and highs elsewhere in the package; this chapter and Chapter 22 are the only ones that need it.
Every AlphaSimR simulation starts with founder haplotypes. Before choosing an engine, it is worth seeing what one produces, at a size small enough to read. inbred = TRUE makes every founder fully homozygous, which is what a panel of inbred lines is.
Show code
set.seed(1)
tiny <- quickHaplo(nInd = 3, nChr = 2, segSites = 4, inbred = TRUE)
SPt  <- SimParam$new(tiny)
tiny_pop <- newPop(tiny, simParam = SPt)
pullSegSiteHaplo(tiny_pop, simParam = SPt)
#>     1_1 1_2 1_3 1_4 2_1 2_2 2_3 2_4
#> 1_1   0   0   0   1   0   1   1   0
#> 1_2   0   0   0   1   0   1   1   0
#> 2_1   0   1   1   0   1   0   1   1
#> 2_2   0   1   1   0   1   0   1   1
#> 3_1   1   0   0   0   0   1   0   1
#> 3_2   1   0   0   0   0   1   0   1
One row per haplotype, two per diploid individual (1_1 and 1_2 are the two chromosome copies of individual 1), one column per segregating site across both chromosomes (1_3 is chromosome 1, site 3). Alleles are coded 0 and 1 – ancestral and derived under a coalescent engine, arbitrary labels under quickHaplo(). Because the founders are inbred, the two rows of each individual are identical. pullSegSiteGeno() sums the two rows into an allele dosage in {0, 1, 2}:
Show code
tiny_geno <- pullSegSiteGeno(tiny_pop, simParam = SPt)
tiny_geno
#>   1_1 1_2 1_3 1_4 2_1 2_2 2_3 2_4
#> 1   0   0   0   2   0   2   2   0
#> 2   0   2   2   0   2   0   2   2
#> 3   2   0   0   0   0   2   0   2
stopifnot(all(tiny_geno %in% c(0, 2)))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(diag(molecular_coancestry(tiny_geno / 2)),
                           rep(1, 3))))
The two assertions fix the coding for the rest of the book. AlphaSimR’s dosage is 0/1/2; the contract of Chapter 6 codes the same information as 0/0.5/1, the within-individual frequency of the reference allele (AlphaSimR’s derived allele plays that role), and every bridge function divides by two on the way across (stage1_build() also detects and rescales 0/1/2 on its own). On an inbred individual the molecular self-coancestry of Chapter 2 is exactly 1, which is the second assertion.
There are two engines, and the choice is not cosmetic. runMacs() runs a backward-in-time coalescent, the MaCS program (Chen et al. 2009), under a species-specific demography – species = "MAIZE", "WHEAT", "CATTLE" – so the founders carry a realistic allele-frequency spectrum and realistic linkage disequilibrium (LD). quickHaplo() samples 0s and 1s directly: instant, and with no history behind it. Table 9.1 compares the two.
Show code
tm <- function(expr) as.numeric(system.time(expr)["elapsed"])

# reproducibility: two calls from the same seed, and R's own stream after each
set.seed(7); qa <- quickHaplo(nInd = 20, nChr = 10, segSites = 50, inbred = TRUE)
rs_qa <- .Random.seed
set.seed(7); qb <- quickHaplo(nInd = 20, nChr = 10, segSites = 50, inbred = TRUE)
rs_qb <- .Random.seed
set.seed(7); ma <- runMacs(nInd = 20, nChr = 10, segSites = 50, inbred = TRUE,
                           species = "MAIZE")
rs_ma <- .Random.seed
set.seed(7); mb <- runMacs(nInd = 20, nChr = 10, segSites = 50, inbred = TRUE,
                           species = "MAIZE")
rs_mb <- .Random.seed
stopifnot(identical(rs_qa, rs_qb), identical(rs_ma, rs_mb),
          identical(qa@geno, qb@geno))
# no assertion on ma vs mb: whether two runMacs() draws differ is what the
# table reports (same_twice), not something a render may require

# timing: one runMacs() call; quickHaplo() over n_rep_q calls, because a
# single call is below the clock's resolution
n_rep_q <- 100
t_m <- tm(runMacs(nInd = 20, nChr = 10, segSites = 50, inbred = TRUE,
                  species = "MAIZE"))
t_q <- tm(for (k in seq_len(n_rep_q))
            quickHaplo(nInd = 20, nChr = 10, segSites = 50, inbred = TRUE)) / n_rep_q

fmt(data.frame(engine              = c("quickHaplo", "runMacs"),
               seconds_per_call    = c(t_q, t_m),
               same_twice          = c(identical(qa@geno, qb@geno),
                                       identical(ma@geno, mb@geno)),
               R_stream_same_after = c(identical(rs_qa, rs_qb),
                                       identical(rs_ma, rs_mb))), 4)




Table 9.1: The two founder engines on one founder set of 20 inbred individuals, 10 chromosomes and 50 segregating sites per chromosome (species = "MAIZE" for runMacs()). seconds_per_call: wall-clock seconds per call, machine-dependent (quickHaplo() averaged over 100 calls); same_twice: identical haplotypes from two calls after the same set.seed(7) (one pair of calls per engine, one render); R_stream_same_after: identical .Random.seed after those two calls.

Read the last two columns of Table 9.1 together. What was measured is one pair of calls per engine, each pair after the same set.seed(7), in this render. For quickHaplo() the two outputs are identical, as expected of pure R sampling. For runMacs() (species = "MAIZE", default threading) the two outputs differed, while R’s .Random.seed after the two calls was identical (asserted in the chunk). Because R’s stream is identical after both calls, every draw R makes afterwards is the same in both runs; what can differ between two calls is the haplotypes MaCS returns. What one pair does not show: how often runMacs() returns different haplotypes from the same seed (a pair is a count of one, and whether it repeats on another render is not recorded here); whether runMacs2() does, which this chunk never calls and Step 8 uses; and why. A hypothesis, untested in this chapter, is that the output of the multithreaded coalescent depends on thread scheduling (the nThreads argument of runMacs()); nothing below depends on it.
(The seconds_per_call column is wall clock and will differ on your machine and between renders. runMacs() takes seconds; quickHaplo(), timed over 100 calls because one call is below the clock’s resolution, takes about 0.45 ms per call.)
So what does quickHaplo() give up? Linkage disequilibrium among the founders. The honest way to measure that is against the sampling floor: with n individuals, two completely independent loci still show r^2 of about 1 / (n - 1) by chance alone. Table 9.2 sets each engine against that floor.
Show code
ldstat <- function(fg) {
  SPx <- SimParam$new(fg)
  g <- pullSegSiteGeno(newPop(fg, simParam = SPx), simParam = SPx)
  g <- g[, apply(g, 2, stats::sd) > 0, drop = FALSE]
  chr <- sub("_.*$", "", colnames(g))           # "chr_site" column names
  r <- stats::cor(g)
  adj <- diag(r[-nrow(r), -1])                  # consecutive columns ...
  adj <- adj[chr[-length(chr)] == chr[-1]]      # ... on the same chromosome
  c(adjacent = mean(adj^2),                     # neighbouring sites, same chromosome
    overall  = mean(r[upper.tri(r)]^2),         # all pairs, mostly distant
    noise    = 1 / (nrow(g) - 1))               # what pure chance gives
}
set.seed(3); lq <- ldstat(quickHaplo(nInd = 100, nChr = 5, segSites = 200,
                                     inbred = TRUE))
set.seed(3); lm_ <- ldstat(runMacs(nInd = 100, nChr = 5, segSites = 200,
                                   inbred = TRUE, species = "MAIZE"))
fmt(rbind(quickHaplo = lq, runMacs = lm_))




Table 9.2: Mean linkage disequilibrium (\(r^2\) between allele dosages) among 100 inbred founders, 5 chromosomes and 200 segregating sites per chromosome, one draw per engine (seed 3). adjacent: neighbouring sites on the same chromosome; overall: all pairs of polymorphic sites; noise: \(1/(n - 1)\), the \(r^2\) expected between independent loci in a sample of \(n\) individuals. The runMacs row is one draw; its repeatability from the seed was not tested (Table 9.1).

adjacent is the mean r^2 between neighbouring sites on the same chromosome (pairs that straddle a chromosome boundary are excluded); overall is over all pairs, most of them on different chromosomes. quickHaplo()’s adjacent-site r^2 sits on the noise floor: there is no founder LD at all, as designed. runMacs()’s is 13 times the floor in this render, and its overall r^2 is barely above it – so the LD it creates is local, decaying with map distance, which is what real LD does.
The runMacs row of Table 9.2 is one draw (seed 3); whether a second call from that seed returns the same row was not tested (Table 9.1 reports the one pair that was). The quickHaplo row is reproducible to the last digit.
What that does and does not imply for the rest of the chapter. In the pair measured, R’s random-number state was identical after the two MaCS calls (asserted in the chunk), so any step that draws its own quickHaplo() founders from a fresh set.seed() is exactly reproducible, and so would be a step that did not reseed. What may move between executions is anything computed from MaCS founders – the runMacs rows of Table 9.1 and Table 9.2, and all of Step 8, whose engine runMacs2() was not measured. The chapter still calls set.seed() immediately before each step’s own founder draw rather than once at the top, so that each step’s founders do not depend on what earlier steps drew. The draws that follow a founder draw are not all reseeded: in Steps 3 and 4 the phenotyping, the three rounds of random mating and the crosses of the DNA lottery take R’s stream from Step 2’s set.seed() through chunk order, so they are reproducible as part of this chapter’s execution order, not on their own. With that in place, two independent executions agree on every number in Steps 1 to 7 except the wall-clock seconds and the runMacs rows, whose repeatability is the open question above.
The policy this chapter follows does not need that question answered:
Founder LD does matter where the association between markers and quantitative trait loci (QTL) is the mechanism, which is genomic prediction. Chapter 14 does not model it: its traits are built on the markers themselves, so every causal locus is genotyped, there is no marker-QTL gap for founder LD to bridge, and its accuracies are a best case in that respect.

title: 9  Simulating a hybrid breeding programme: AlphaSimR from the ground up
text:
WarningFounders from MaCS: what is established here and what is not



Reproducibility from set.seed() is the first property to check in a simulation, because its failure is silent: the code looks reproducible, runs without complaint, and returns different numbers. Established in this chapter: one pair of runMacs() calls after the same seed returned different haplotypes in this render, with R’s stream identical after both calls (asserted in the chunk). Not established: a rate for runMacs(), anything for runMacs2() (the engine of Step 8, whose founders the help page of alphasimr_founder_pools(), Chapter 24 and Chapter 22 treat as not reproducible from cfg$seed; this chapter did not test that), and a mechanism. The chapter therefore assumes neither answer, and follows three rules that hold whichever is true:

Found once, then branch. Any experiment comparing two schemes must draw the founders a single time and start both arms from that one object. Draw them twice and, if founders can differ between calls, the two arms start from different founders and the comparison measures the founders as much as the schemes. Chapter 24’ linked arm is built this way, and so is Step 8’s paired control below.
Seed immediately before each founder draw, not once at the top, so that a founder draw does not inherit the stream of whatever ran before it.
Save what you cannot reseed. saveRDS(founderGenomes, ...) is the only way to get the same coalescent history back in a later session if a re-call does not return it.

The consequence for this book: the HTML and the PDF are produced by separate executions of the chapter (Quarto’s _freeze keeps html.json and typ.json apart), and each execution calls the founder draw again. Whether two such draws coincide is not established here for runMacs2(): the chapter measures one runMacs() pair per render and does not measure runMacs2(). If they do not coincide, every number that depends on the founders (the pooled gene-diversity \(t\) of Step 8, the \(GD_{BS}\) and \(F_{ST}\) \(t\), the sign of the stage-2 attainable-\(\alpha\) ceiling, the covariance term at each split of the sweep) may differ between the two formats, and no conclusion should rest on a statistic close to a critical value. The covariance term at one split time of the sweep is such a case (see the multiplicity paragraph there).
Everything after the founders – the crosses, the doubled haploids, the phenotyping error, the recombination – is drawn from R’s stream and is controlled by set.seed(), given the same founder object.









quickHaplo(inbred = TRUE) for Steps 2–7 and all of Chapter 22. They teach the arithmetic of dominance, heterosis and response, where founder LD is not the point, and in exchange every number printed is reproducible from a clean clone. AlphaSimR still applies a real genetic map and real meiosis to every descendant, so linkage and the Bulmer effect of Chapter 24 still operate – only the founders’ history is stylised.
runMacs2(split = ) in Step 8. There the divergence between two heterotic pools is the object of study, and no amount of speed compensates for not having it. Every Step 8 result is therefore replicated over founder draws, each drawn once and branched into both arms, and the verdicts that rest on a t near its critical value are written as conditional on the render.

title: 9  Simulating a hybrid breeding programme: AlphaSimR from the ground up
section: 9.2 Step 2 – SimParam, and defining a trait with dominance
text:
9.2 Step 2 – SimParam, and defining a trait with dominance
SimParam holds everything global: the genetic map, which sites are quantitative trait loci (QTL), the trait effects, the error variances. It is an R6 object, so its methods are called with $, and a variable named SP is picked up automatically by every AlphaSimR function that needs it.
A hybrid programme exists because of dominance: without it a line’s cross performance is its own breeding value and there is nothing a testcross can see that the line per se could not (Chapter 5). So the trait defined here, and used through Step 6, carries a dominance term from the start. This is exactly the reason an autogamous programme has no equivalent of this step: there, dominance is invisible by construction (a released, self-pollinated variety is homozygous, so no heterozygote is ever evaluated or sold) and SP$addTraitA() – additive effects only – is the whole model, the case Chapter 22 starts from, before adding genotype-by-environment with SP$addTraitAG().


Show code
# Seeded here, not once at the top of the chapter: Step 1 draws from R's random
# stream (each runMacs() call consumes a fixed amount of it), so everything
# downstream would move with any edit of Step 1 unless the seed
# is reset immediately before the draw that matters.
set.seed(101)
founders <- quickHaplo(nInd = 60, nChr = 10, segSites = 100, inbred = TRUE)
SP <- SimParam$new(founders)
SP$addTraitAD(nQtlPerChr = 100, mean = 10, var = 1,
              meanDD = rrs_cfg[["mean_dd"]], varDD = rrs_cfg[["var_dd"]])
SP$setVarE(h2 = 0.4)


AlphaSimR 2.1.0 has 8 trait constructors (addTraitA(), addTraitAD(), addTraitADE(), addTraitADEG(), addTraitADG(), addTraitAE(), addTraitAEG(), addTraitAG()): one per combination of additive effects with dominance (D), epistasis (E) and genotype-by-environment (G). Choosing between them is choosing a model of gene action; the four that bear on a plant programme are:








Method
Adds
When a plant programme needs it




SP$addTraitA()
additive only
line per se performance; the course’s teaching case (Gorjanc et al. 2022), and Step 7 here


SP$addTraitAD()
+ dominance
testcross and hybrid value. This is what Steps 2–6 and Step 8 use


SP$addTraitAG()
+ genotype-by-environment
multi-location yield trials, where the same genotype is scored in several places. Chapter 22 uses it


SP$addTraitADE()
+ epistasis
available; used nowhere in this book




9.2.1 The dominance model, as AlphaSimR writes it
For a diploid with QTL \(k = 1, \dots, m\), let \(x_{ik} \in \{0, 1, 2\}\) be the dosage of the derived allele of individual \(i\) at QTL \(k\) (the column of pullQtlGeno()). AlphaSimR’s TraitAD genetic value is
\[G_i \;=\; \mu_0 + \sum_{k=1}^{m} a_k\,(x_{ik} - 1) + \sum_{k=1}^{m} d_k\,\mathbb{1}[x_{ik} = 1] \tag{9.1}\]
with \(G_i\) the genetic value of individual \(i\) (the \(G(\mathbf{x})\) of Appendix A, written here on the 0/1/2 dosage rather than on the 0/0.5/1 row; not the Caballero-Toro statistic \(G_i\) of Chapter 3), \(x_{ik}\) in this chapter always the 0/1/2 dosage (an entry of \(\mathbf{M}^H\), not of \(\mathbf{X}\)), \(\mu_0\) an intercept, \(a_k \in \mathbb{R}\) the additive effect (half the difference between the two homozygotes, on the classical scale of Falconer and Mackay (1996) [ch. 7; the chapter locators given for this book in this chapter are not checked against a copy], which puts the origin at the midpoint of the two homozygotes and assigns them \(+a\) and \(-a\) and the heterozygote \(d\); no equation number is attributed here, the scale is stated in full) and \(d_k \in
\mathbb{R}\) the dominance effect, the departure of the heterozygote from that midpoint (a property of the locus, as in Section 5.2.2; not Fisher’s statistical dominance deviation, a property of a population, which is what varD and genicVarD below measure). Equation 9.1 is the model of Chapter 5 with AlphaSimR’s coding, and the chunk checks it rather than trusts it:


Show code
tr <- SP$traits[[1]]
a  <- tr@addEff
d  <- tr@domEff
pop0 <- newPop(founders, simParam = SP)
x0   <- pullQtlGeno(pop0, simParam = SP)
gv_by_hand <- as.numeric(tr@intercept + (x0 - 1) %*% a + (x0 == 1) %*% d)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(gv_by_hand, as.numeric(gv(pop0)))))


meanDD and varDD parameterise the dominance degree \(\delta_k = d_k / |a_k|\): AlphaSimR draws \(\delta_k \sim N(\texttt{meanDD},
\texttt{varDD})\) and sets \(d_k = \delta_k\,|a_k|\), so \(\delta_k = 0\) is additivity, \(\delta_k = 1\) complete dominance, \(\delta_k > 1\) overdominance, and a positive mean is directional dominance: on average the heterozygote sits above the homozygote midpoint, whichever allele is favourable. Directional dominance is what makes heterosis positive and inbreeding depression a loss on the trait scale; the presence of inbreeding depression is itself the evidence for it (Mackay et al. 2021), and maize grain yield is generally reported to show large inbreeding depression (Hallauer et al. (2010) is the maize reference; no page is cited, as the book was not available to check one). Table 9.3 compares the requested and the realised dominance degrees.


Show code
dd_k <- d / abs(a)
fmt(data.frame(statistic = c("mean", "variance"),
               requested = c(rrs_cfg[["mean_dd"]], rrs_cfg[["var_dd"]]),
               realised  = c(mean(dd_k), stats::var(dd_k))), 3)




Table 9.3: Dominance degree \(\delta_k = d_k / |a_k|\) of the trait of Step 2 over its 1000 QTL (seed 101): the meanDD and varDD passed to addTraitAD() (requested) against the mean and variance of \(\delta_k\) in the draw (realised).

nQtlPerChr sets how polygenic the trait is. Setting it equal to segSites makes every segregating site a QTL, which is what this chapter does throughout – convenient, because then the marker matrix and the causal loci are the same set and there is no marker-versus-QTL gap to reason about. Real programmes have that gap; this book does not measure it, and Chapter 10 (assumption A5) states the same collapse as a limit.
mean fixes the mean genetic value of the founders. var fixes their additive variance (useVarA = TRUE, the default), not their total genetic variance – with inbred founders the two coincide, for a reason Step 3 shows. corA (Step 7) sets the genetic correlation between traits.
The environmental variance has two routes, and plant breeders use the second:

SP$setVarE(h2 = 0.4) fixes an error variance once, from the founders’ genetic variance (here 1.5), and every later setPheno() reuses it.
setPheno(varE = , reps = ) sets it per call. reps is the plant idiom for locations: varE is the plot-level error, and a genotype scored in reps plots has its error variance divided by reps, so the phenotype is an entry mean. That is how a staged programme raises selection accuracy from one stage to the next without ever changing the trait’s heritability – the mechanism Chapter 22 is built on, and the one Step 6 uses for testers.

9.3 Step 3 – The base population, and where the variance components live
newPop() turns founder haplotypes into individuals and, because a trait is now defined, computes their genetic values immediately (Table 9.4).


Show code
pop <- setPheno(newPop(founders, simParam = SP), simParam = SP)
fmt(data.frame(n = pop@nInd, meanG = as.numeric(meanG(pop)),
               varG = as.numeric(varG(pop)), varP = as.numeric(varP(pop)),
               h2_realised = as.numeric(varG(pop) / varP(pop))), 3)

The realised heritability is near but not equal to the requested 0.4: setVarE() fixes a variance, and the ratio it produces in any finite sample is itself a random variable. This is a general and useful habit – check what the simulation realised, do not assume what you requested.
genParam() returns the full decomposition. Four of its fields are the ones a hybrid programme cares about, and they read differently on a panel of inbred lines and on a random-mating population made from them (Table 9.5):


Show code
mixed <- pop
for (k in 1:3) mixed <- randCross(mixed, nCrosses = 1000, simParam = SP)

vrow <- function(p, lab) {
  g <- genParam(p, simParam = SP)
  data.frame(population = lab,
             meanG     = as.numeric(g[["mu"]]),

             ratio     = as.numeric(g[["varA"]] / g[["genicVarA"]]),
             varD      = as.numeric(g[["varD"]]),
             genicVarD = as.numeric(g[["genicVarD"]]))
}
vtab <- rbind(vrow(pop,   "founders (fully inbred)"),
              vrow(mixed, "after 3 random matings"))
fmt(vtab)
stopifnot(vtab[["varD"]][1] < 1e-10)

Show code
# Among fully homozygous lines the locus value is a (x - 1), so at linkage
# equilibrium varA = sum 4 p q a^2, while genicVarA = sum 2 p q alpha^2 with
# alpha = a + d (q - p): under dominance the LE ratio is close to, not
# exactly, 2. What varA carries above varA_LE is disequilibrium.
p_f      <- colMeans(x0) / 2                        # founder allele frequencies
varA_f   <- vtab[["varA"]][1]
genic_f  <- vtab[["genicVarA"]][1]
varA_LE  <- sum(4 * p_f * (1 - p_f) * a^2)
ratio_LE <- varA_LE / genic_f
varA_LD  <- varA_f - varA_LE
ratio_LD <- varA_LD / genic_f
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(bv(pop, simParam = SP)[, 1]),
                           as.numeric(sweep(x0, 2, 2 * p_f) %*% a))))
# Verification echo, not a table: every value is cited in the text below.
c(varA = varA_f, varA_LE = varA_LE, ratio_LE = ratio_LE,
  varA_LD = varA_LD, ratio_LD = ratio_LD) |> fmt(4)
#>     varA  varA_LE ratio_LE  varA_LD ratio_LD 
#>   1.0000   0.8495   1.9875   0.1505   0.3522


varA is the realised additive variance; genicVarA is what it would be if the loci were independent and in Hardy-Weinberg proportions. Their ratio is the whole subject of Chapter 24. “Genic variance” has two definitions in the book, and they are not interchangeable. The package’s genic_var() (Equation 4.2, Section 4.2) is \(\sum_k \beta_k^2 \operatorname{Var}(x_k)\) with the observed per-locus variance of the genotype matrix it is given, so a ratio of the realised variance to it isolates the covariance between loci. AlphaSimR’s genicVarA is \(\sum_k 2 p_k q_k \alpha_k^2\) (below), the Hardy-Weinberg expectation with the average effect \(\alpha_k\), so a ratio to it carries the homozygosity of the population as well. The two coincide only for an additive trait in Hardy-Weinberg proportions; on the inbred panel below they differ by about the factor the next paragraph separates. This chapter uses AlphaSimR’s.
The founders’ ratio of 2.34 has two parts, and the chunk separates them. Among fully homozygous lines the value at QTL \(k\) is \(a_k (x_{ik} - 1)\) with \(x_{ik} \in \{0, 2\}\), and AlphaSimR’s bv() on these founders is exactly \(\sum_k a_k (x_{ik} - 2 p_k)\) (asserted in the chunk). At linkage equilibrium its variance is varA_LE \(= \sum_k 4 p_k q_k a_k^2 =\) 0.8495, against a genic value of 0.4274: a ratio of 1.99, exact given the effects and the frequencies. That part is inbreeding – a homozygous population has per-locus variance 4pq where a Hardy-Weinberg one has 2pq. It is close to 2 and not exactly 2 because genicVarA is written with the Hardy-Weinberg average effect \(\alpha_k = a_k + d_k (q_k - p_k)\) defined below, whereas the homozygous lines carry \(a_k\); twice the genic value equals varA_LE only where \(d_k (q_k - p_k) = 0\) at every locus. The remainder, varA_LD = varA - varA_LE \(=\) 0.1505, or 0.35 in ratio units, is sampling (gametic-phase) disequilibrium among only 60 founders’ worth of gametes. Three rounds of random mating restore Hardy-Weinberg and pull the ratio to 1.06; what remains is that same disequilibrium. A ratio away from 1 in an outbred population is the gametic-phase disequilibrium Chapter 4 defines and Chapter 24 measures; a ratio away from 1 in an inbred one is mostly the homozygosity.
The dominance columns carry the hybrid lesson. varD among the inbred founders is zero to rounding (\(9.6 \times 10^{-33}\), asserted below 1e-10 in the chunk above): a homozygous line has no heterozygous locus, so its dominance contribution is zero whatever \(d_k\) is, and no amount of per se evaluation of inbred lines can see dominance. This single identity is the operational reason an autogamous programme stops at per se selection and never needs a testcross: its released lines are exactly this “founders” row, varD = 0 for the whole life of the programme, so a line’s genetic value equals its breeding value up to a constant common to all lines (the bv() assertion above: \(G_i - \sum_k a_k (x_{ik} - 2p_k) = \mu_0 +
\sum_k a_k (2p_k - 1)\)), and its per se phenotype is that value plus error. After random mating varD appears. Two identities make that quantitative. With \(p_k\) the founders’ frequency of the derived allele at QTL \(k\) and \(q_k = 1 - p_k\), the population mean under Hardy-Weinberg proportions is the single-locus mean of Falconer and Mackay (1996, ch. 7), summed over loci (no equation number is attributed)
\[M_{HW} \;=\; \mu_0 + \sum_k \big[a_k\,(p_k - q_k) + 2\,p_k q_k\,d_k\big] \tag{9.2}\]
while the inbred panel at the same frequencies has only the first term of Equation 9.2. The difference, \(2\sum_k d_k p_k q_k\), is the inbreeding depression of Chapter 5 at \(F = 1\), which the package computes as inbreeding_depression(p, d, F_coef = 1). And the genic additive variance is \(\sum_k 2 p_k q_k \alpha_k^2\) with \(\alpha_k = a_k + d_k\,(q_k - p_k)\) the average effect of a gene substitution. Falconer and Mackay (1996) define \(\alpha\) in Ch. 7 and the single-locus additive variance \(2pq\alpha^2\) in Ch. 8; the equation numbers are not attributed here, so both identities are stated in this chapter’s notation: \(\alpha_k = a_k + d_k\,(q_k - p_k)\) and, summed over independent loci, \(\sum_k 2 p_k q_k \alpha_k^2\), which is the genic variance. (\(\alpha_k\) is the average effect throughout this chapter, not the diversity-loss budget \(\alpha\) of the rest of the book.) The chunk asserts both identities; Table 9.6 gives the two means.


Show code
gp  <- genParam(pop, simParam = SP)
alpha_f <- a + d * (1 - 2 * p_f)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(gp[["mu_HW"]] - gp[["mu"]]),
                           inbreeding_depression(p_f, d, F_coef = 1))))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(gp[["genicVarA"]]),
                           sum(2 * p_f * (1 - p_f) * alpha_f^2))))
fmt(data.frame(mean_inbred = as.numeric(gp[["mu"]]),
               mean_HW = as.numeric(gp[["mu_HW"]]),
               inbreeding_depression = inbreeding_depression(p_f, d, F_coef = 1)), 3)

The gap between the two means is the amount a random-mating population built from these lines would sit above the lines themselves – and, read in the other direction, the amount an open-pollinated population loses on being driven to homozygosity. It is the same \(d\) that Step 4 turns into heterosis.

text:
9.4 Step 4 – The DNA lottery, heterosis, and why an F1 is not a family
The course (Gorjanc et al. 2022) demonstrates Mendelian sampling by crossing outbred founders and showing that full sibs vary. With inbred parents the result is different (Table 9.7), and it is the fact hybrid breeding is organised around.


Show code
crosses <- list(c(1, 2), c(1, 3), c(2, 3))
n_lot   <- 200   # F1 plants and DH lines per cross
lottery <- do.call(rbind, lapply(crosses, function(ij) {
  plan <- matrix(ij, ncol = 2)
  f1 <- makeCross(pop, plan, nProgeny = n_lot, simParam = SP)
  dh <- makeDH(makeCross(pop, plan, nProgeny = 1, simParam = SP),
               nDH = n_lot, simParam = SP)
  better <- max(gv(pop)[ij])
  data.frame(cross         = paste(ij, collapse = " x "),
             parent_mean   = mean(gv(pop)[ij]),
             better_parent = better,
             f1_mean       = as.numeric(meanG(f1)),
             f1_sd         = as.numeric(sqrt(varG(f1))),
             dh_sd         = as.numeric(sqrt(varG(dh))),
             dh_best       = max(gv(dh)),
             transgressive = mean(gv(dh) > better),
             # how far the better parent sits above the DH mean, in DH s.d.
             gap_in_dh_sd  = (better - mean(gv(pop)[ij])) / as.numeric(sqrt(varG(dh))))
}))
fmt(lottery[, c("cross", "parent_mean", "better_parent", "f1_mean", "f1_sd")], 3)
fmt(lottery[, c("cross", "dh_sd", "dh_best", "transgressive", "gap_in_dh_sd")], 3)
stopifnot(all(lottery[["f1_sd"]] < 1e-8))
stopifnot(which.max(lottery[["transgressive"]]) == which.min(lottery[["gap_in_dh_sd"]]))

f1_sd is zero, asserted to machine precision. Two fully inbred parents are homozygous everywhere, so every gamete each one makes is identical, and every F1 is the same heterozygote. The 200 F1 plants from a cross of two inbred lines are 200 copies of one genotype. There is no lottery yet – and this uniformity is the first reason a single-cross hybrid is a saleable variety.
f1_mean sits well above better_parent. That is heterosis, and under the model of Equation 9.1 it has an exact value: for inbred parents \(i\) and \(j\) with allele indicators \(u_{ik}, u_{jk} \in \{0, 1\}\) (their dosage halved), the F1 is heterozygous exactly where they differ, so
\[H_{ij} \;=\; G_{ij} - \tfrac{1}{2}(G_i + G_j) \;=\; \sum_k d_k\,\mathbb{1}[u_{ik} \neq u_{jk}] \tag{9.3}\]
with \(G_{ij}\) the genetic value of the F1 between \(i\) and \(j\) (Equation 9.1 applied to its dosages). The additive terms cancel from the mid-parent difference because an inbred parent’s additive contribution is exactly half the F1’s. heterosis_value(X, d) is this sum, with X the F1’s 0/0.5/1 genotype; the chunk asserts it against AlphaSimR’s genetic values and Table 9.8 lists it per cross:


Show code
H <- vapply(seq_along(crosses), function(s) {
  ij <- crosses[[s]]
  f1 <- makeCross(pop, matrix(ij, ncol = 2), nProgeny = 1, simParam = SP)
  hv <- as.numeric(heterosis_value(pullQtlGeno(f1, simParam = SP) / 2, d))
  stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(gv(f1)) - mean(gv(pop)[ij]), hv)))
  hv
}, numeric(1))
names(H) <- lottery[["cross"]]
fmt(data.frame(cross = names(H), heterosis = unname(H)), 3)

Over a set of crosses the same identity has a closed form in the allele frequencies. Take the 60 founders as two arbitrary halves, “pool A” (lines 1–30) and “pool B” (lines 31–60) – arbitrary because quickHaplo() gave them a common history and no divergence, which Step 8 will add – and cross every A line to every B line. hybridCross(crossPlan = "testcross") is the full factorial. With \(p_{Ak}\) and \(p_{Bk}\) the derived-allele frequencies of the two pools at QTL \(k\), the mean of \(H_{ij}\) over the factorial is heterosis_expected(pA, pB, d), the identity of Chapter 5:
\[\bar H \;=\; \sum_k d_k\,\big(p_{Ak} + p_{Bk} - 2\,p_{Ak}\,p_{Bk}\big) \tag{9.4}\]
with \(\bar H\) the mean mid-parent heterosis over the factorial (the \(\mu\) of Appendix A, renamed because \(\mu_0\) is the intercept here; Table 9.9).


Show code
n_half <- pop@nInd / 2

B <- pop[n_half + seq_len(n_half)]
fact <- hybridCross(A, B, crossPlan = "testcross", simParam = SP)

V  <- pullQtlGeno(B, simParam = SP) / 2
pA <- colMeans(U)
pB <- colMeans(V)
H_bar_obs <- as.numeric(meanG(fact)) - (as.numeric(meanG(A)) + as.numeric(meanG(B))) / 2
H_bar_exp <- heterosis_expected(pA, pB, d)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(H_bar_obs, H_bar_exp)))
fact_tab <- c(n_hybrids = fact@nInd, mean_A = as.numeric(meanG(A)),
  mean_B = as.numeric(meanG(B)), mean_hybrids = as.numeric(meanG(fact)),
  heterosis_observed = H_bar_obs, heterosis_expected = H_bar_exp,
  pct_of_midparent = 100 * H_bar_obs / ((as.numeric(meanG(A)) + as.numeric(meanG(B))) / 2))
# one row per statistic: seven columns would not fit the page
fmt(data.frame(statistic = names(fact_tab), value = unname(fact_tab)), 3)

Exact, on the full factorial, because every A x B pairing is present once. The size – 44.3 percent of the mid-parent – follows from meanDD and from quickHaplo()’s frequencies near one half, where \(p_A + p_B - 2 p_A p_B\) is near its maximum; it is not calibrated to a crop. Falconer and Mackay (1996, ch. 14) derive the heterosis of the F1 between two random-mating populations as \(H_{F1} = \sum_k d_k y_k^2\) with \(y_k = p_{Ak} - p_{Bk}\) (stated here in this chapter’s notation rather than by their equation number; it is twice the divergence term of heterosis_partition()). The two do not conflict; they use different mid-parents. Theirs carries each population’s own random-mating heterozygosity; an inbred line carries none, so the whole F1 heterozygosity is heterosis and Equation 9.4 keeps the shared term as well – Chapter 5 works the reconciliation through.
The lottery starts one meiosis later. dh_sd is the standard deviation among doubled haploids drawn from that F1, and it is substantial – this is the segregation that F2, DH and recombinant inbred line (RIL) populations exist to sample. The number of DH lines you pull from a cross is the number of tickets you buy, and no downstream selection stage can recover a combination that was never sampled; Chapter 7 sizes that number for selfing-derived F4 lines, not for DH lines.
transgressive is the fraction of DH lines exceeding the better parent per se: 0.025, 0.01 and 0.32 for the three crosses. It depends strongly on the cross, and gap_in_dh_sd says why: the DH lines are centred on the mid-parent, so what matters is how far the better parent sits above it in units of the DH standard deviation – 1.95, 2.19 and 0.45. The cross with the smallest gap is the one with the most transgressive lines (asserted), 32 percent of them; the other two, whose better parent is 2.19 and 1.95 DH standard deviations above the mid-parent, give 1 and 2.5 percent. These are the values of this draw of 200 DH lines per cross; the ordering is asserted, the percentages are not a constant of the model. Crossing two parents whose favourable alleles sit at different loci produces progeny beyond either of them – transgressive segregation, which Mackay et al. (2021) treat, with heterosis and inbreeding depression, as consequences of one mechanism: favourable alleles dispersed between the parents, plus directional dominance – and how often depends on the gap between the parents relative to the segregation variance, not on a constant.

title: 9  Simulating a hybrid breeding programme: AlphaSimR from the ground up
section: 9.5 Step 5 – Selfing, doubled haploids, and why hybrid seed is remade every year
text:
9.5 Step 5 – Selfing, doubled haploids, and why hybrid seed is remade every year
A plant breeder has to get from a heterozygous F1 to a homozygous line. There are two routes, and AlphaSimR implements both. Following the same cross through selfing generations also answers a question every hybrid grower has asked: what happens if the F1 seed is saved and sown again.
This is the one step where the allogamous, hybrid case and the autogamous case use literally the same primitive – makeDH() is exactly what Chapter 22 calls to take its wheat F1s straight to a homozygous line, one generation instead of the six or seven selfing generations traced in Table 9.10 – and where they diverge again in what the resulting inbred line is for. In an autogamous programme that homozygous line is commonly the release: it breeds true, so what leaves the DH pipeline is what a farmer eventually grows. In this chapter’s programme the homozygous DH line is a parent, held inside a heterotic pool, testcrossed and recycled (Step 6, Step 8), and never sold on its own; the object a grower plants is the F1 these lines make together, which is the reason it cannot be saved.
Under selfing without selection, the fraction of the F1’s heterozygous loci still heterozygous in generation \(F_t\) is \((1/2)^{t-1}\) in expectation, so the expected mean of the selfed generation is
\[\mathbb{E}[M_{F_t}] \;=\; \tfrac{1}{2}(G_i + G_j) + H_{ij}\,(1/2)^{t-1} \tag{9.5}\]
with \(H_{ij}\) the F1 heterosis of Equation 9.3. The index \(t\) counts generations from the F1 (\(t = 1\)), so this is the halving of heterozygosity per selfing of Section 1.2.4 with its index shifted by one, and Section 7.3 checks the per-plant heterozygosity against it by simulation. At \(t = 2\) this is the classical result that the F2 retains half the F1 heterosis, \(H_{F2} = \tfrac{1}{2} H_{F1}\), which Falconer and Mackay (1996) derive in Ch. 14 for the F2 of a cross between two populations (stated here in this chapter’s notation rather than by their equation number); Equation 9.5 extends it to later selfed generations by the same argument, since the expected heterozygosity at every locus is halved each generation. Table 9.10 follows one cross through seven generations.


Show code
homozygosity <- function(p)
  mean(pullSegSiteGeno(p, simParam = SP) %in% c(0, 2))

# Seeded here so that the |z| < 4 check below does not inherit the RNG state
# of Step 4: this z-statistic is not exactly Gaussian at this sample size, so
# an unrelated upstream edit that reseeded Step 4 could otherwise flip the
# check and break the render even though it passes for the seed used here.
set.seed(55)
n_f1 <- 400   # F1 plants, each the root of one selfing lineage
ij <- c(1, 2)
midparent <- mean(gv(pop)[ij])
f1  <- makeCross(pop, matrix(ij, ncol = 2), nProgeny = n_f1, simParam = SP)
gen <- f1
traj <- data.frame(generation = "F1", homozygosity = homozygosity(f1),
                   meanG = as.numeric(meanG(f1)), sdG = as.numeric(sqrt(varG(f1))),
                   expected = midparent + H[["1 x 2"]])
for (t in 2:7) {
  gen  <- self(gen, nProgeny = 1, simParam = SP)
  traj <- rbind(traj, data.frame(generation = paste0("F", t),
                                 homozygosity = homozygosity(gen),
                                 meanG = as.numeric(meanG(gen)),
                                 sdG = as.numeric(sqrt(varG(gen))),
                                 expected = midparent + H[["1 x 2"]] * (1 / 2)^(t - 1)))
}
dh1 <- makeDH(f1, nDH = 1, simParam = SP)
traj <- rbind(traj, data.frame(generation = "DH", homozygosity = homozygosity(dh1),
                               meanG = as.numeric(meanG(dh1)),
                               sdG = as.numeric(sqrt(varG(dh1))),
                               expected = midparent))
traj[["z"]] <- (traj[["meanG"]] - traj[["expected"]]) / (traj[["sdG"]] / sqrt(n_f1))
traj[["z"]][1] <- 0   # F1: no variance, and the identity of Step 4 is exact
fmt(traj, 3)
stopifnot(all(abs(traj[["z"]]) < 4),
          traj[traj[["generation"]] == "DH", "homozygosity"] == 1)

Three columns, three lessons.
homozygosity: self() halves the remaining heterozygosity every generation – the familiar 1 - (1/2)^(t-1) approach to fixation, which never quite arrives. makeDH() gets there in one step, at 1.0 exactly, by doubling a haploid gamete.
meanG against expected: the F2 mean falls by half the heterosis, the F3 by three quarters, and the DH lines land on the mid-parent. Each row is 400 plants, one per F1 plant: self(nProgeny = 1) carries 400 parallel, independent selfing lineages forward, so within a row the 400 values are independent and sdG / sqrt(n_f1) is the standard error of the row’s mean. The check is statistical: z is the observed minus expected mean in units of that standard error, and the chunk asserts every |z| < 4. Across rows the same 400 lineages are followed – each \(F_t\) plant is the selfed progeny of one \(F_{t-1}\) plant – so successive rows are correlated, and the table is 400 lineages checked at seven generations, not seven independent samples. Nothing about the parents changed; the loss is the heterozygosity being halved, times \(d\). This is why hybrid seed is remade from the two inbred parents every season and why a maize F2 crop yields visibly less than the F1 it was saved from.
sdG: the F1 has none and the F2 has plenty. The F2 is not a variety; it is a segregating population, and a uniform, high-yielding one cannot be recovered from it by anything but selection and re-fixation – which is the line development a breeding programme does, not something a grower can do.
The saving DH buys is seasons, and seasons are the currency of a breeding programme: six or seven selfing generations against one DH cycle. Step 8’s scheme uses makeDH() for precisely this reason, and the cost that never shows up in the simulation is that DH production is a laboratory operation with its own failure rate and its own genotype-dependent response.
The other operations a scheme needs are all one call each: randCross() for random mating within a pool, makeCross() for a specified crossing plan, hybridCross() for a full factorial or a testcross between two groups, and mergePops() or c() to combine populations.

9.6 Step 6 – Phenotyping and selection: per se, then on the testcross
Selection needs a criterion. setPheno() supplies the noisy one; selectInd() acts on it. This step does it twice: first on a line’s own phenotype, as the course does (Gorjanc et al. 2022), to check the breeder’s equation; then on the testcross, which is how a hybrid programme actually ranks lines.

9.6.1 Per se selection and the breeder’s equation
Table 9.11 checks the breeder’s equation on per se selection.


Show code
n_prog <- 1000   # progeny of the selected parents, per draw
be_draw <- function(q, r) {
  set.seed(500 + r)
  mx    <- setPheno(mixed, simParam = SP)
  sel   <- selectInd(mx, nInd = round(q * mx@nInd), use = "pheno", simParam = SP)
  prog  <- randCross(sel, nCrosses = n_prog, simParam = SP)
  S     <- as.numeric(meanP(sel) - meanP(mx))
  vA    <- as.numeric(varA(mx, simParam = SP))
  i_emp <- S / sqrt(as.numeric(varP(mx)))
  r_emp <- stats::cor(bv(mx, simParam = SP)[, 1], pheno(mx)[, 1])
  c(i_empirical = i_emp,
    R_S_h2      = S * vA / as.numeric(varP(mx)),
    R_i_r_sdA   = i_emp * r_emp * sqrt(vA),
    R_observed  = as.numeric(meanG(prog) - meanG(mixed)))
}
n_be <- 20
sweep_q <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(0.05, 0.10, 0.20), function(q) {
  draws <- t(sapply(seq_len(n_be), function(r) be_draw(q, r)))
  gap   <- draws[, "R_observed"] - draws[, "R_S_h2"]
  data.frame(q = q, i_normal = sel_intensity(q),
             t(colMeans(draws)),
             R_observed_sd = stats::sd(draws[, "R_observed"]),
             gap_mean = mean(gap), gap_sd = stats::sd(gap))
}))
fmt(sweep_q[, c("q", "i_normal", "i_empirical", "R_S_h2", "R_i_r_sdA")], 3)
fmt(sweep_q[, c("q", "R_observed", "R_observed_sd", "gap_mean", "gap_sd")], 3)

Both forms of the breeder’s equation are here, each averaged over 20 independent draws of the phenotypes, the selection and the progeny (the population selected from is the same mixed every time, so varA is fixed and only S, the accuracy and the Mendelian sampling vary). R = S * h2 uses the selection differential directly, with h2 the narrow-sense heritability varA / varP of the population selected from; R = i * r * sigma_A decomposes it into intensity, accuracy and available variation – the form Chapter 4 builds the book’s objective side on. Because the trait has dominance, the accuracy r is the correlation of the phenotype with the breeding value (bv()), not with the total genetic value: only the additive part is transmitted. This is not the \(r\) of Equation 4.1 in Chapter 4, which is the accuracy as a predictor of genetic value for a purely additive trait (\(d_k \equiv 0\), \(\sigma_A\) estimated by sd(gv)); the two coincide only if \(d = 0\). And R_observed is not the object Chapter 4 checks: there the response is the genetic selection differential of the selected hybrids, not a transmitted change, whereas here R_observed is the realised change in genetic mean between the selected parents’ random-mated progeny and the starting population, which is what the prediction is a prediction of. The letter \(r\) also names the number of locations in the next subsection; it is the accuracy only in this subsection.
gap_mean is the paired difference between the observed response and R_S_h2, with gap_sd its standard deviation over the draws. The mean gap is -0.5 percent of the prediction at q = 0.05 and 2.5 percent at q = 0.20; its standard error over the 20 draws is gap_sd / sqrt(20), and the largest gap in units of that standard error is 1.1. A single draw is another matter: R_observed_sd says that one realisation of the response scatters by around 11 percent of the prediction at q = 0.05, which is why the course’s one-off comparison (Gorjanc et al. 2022) “did not match perfectly” and why this one is replicated. The equation predicts the additive response to first order in the allele-frequency change; what it leaves out is second order in that change and the dominance contribution of the progeny’s departure from Hardy-Weinberg proportions, both small with 1000 progeny from 50 or more parents. The empirical intensity agrees with the normal-theory value to within 0.2 percent: with 1000 candidates and a criterion that is a sum over 1000 loci plus normal error, the two assumptions of sel_intensity() – an infinite population and a normal criterion – are nearly met.
The book exports its own selection intensity, and AlphaSimR exports one too. They are independent implementations of phi(z) / q:


Show code
q <- 0.05
d_int <- abs(sel_intensity(q) - selInt(q))
stopifnot(d_int < 1e-10)          # two implementations of phi(z) / q
c(hybdiv = sel_intensity(q), AlphaSimR = selInt(q)) |> fmt(10)
#>    hybdiv AlphaSimR 
#>  2.062713  2.062713
cat("absolute difference:", format(d_int, digits = 2), "(asserted < 1e-10)\n")
#> absolute difference: 0 (asserted < 1e-10)


selectInd() takes use = "pheno", "gv" or "ebv". Selecting on "gv" is selecting with perfect accuracy – impossible in a real programme, and the correct way to compute the ceiling a scheme is being measured against. use = "ebv" selects on whatever has been written into the population’s ebv slot, which is how genomic selection enters a simulation (Chapter 22). selectTop = FALSE selects downwards, for traits where less is better.
selectWithinFam() is the plant-specific one. A programme that truncates globally on a set of families concentrates its selections in the best crosses, by an amount that depends on the number and size of the families and on the heritability (none of which is measured here); capping the number retained per family holds the programme’s genetic base open at some cost in immediate gain. It is the same trade-off as the max_use parental cap of Chapter 16, applied one stage earlier.


9.6.2 Selection on the testcross: general combining ability
A maize breeder does not rank inbred lines on their own yield. A line is crossed to a tester from the opposite pool, the testcross hybrids are grown in yield trials, and the line is ranked on the mean of its testcrosses. This subsection is the one with no autogamous counterpart at all: a self-pollinated variety is judged, released and grown as itself, so selection there stops at the per se phenotype of Step 6’s first half. A hybrid parent is judged by a cross it will never be sold as, which is the entire reason general and specific combining ability exist as concepts. The quantity being estimated is the line’s general combining ability (GCA), the average performance of its crosses expressed as a deviation from the mean of all crosses (the concept is that of Sprague and Tatum (1942), whose paper the book does not quote; the wording and Equation 9.6 below are this chapter’s); what a particular cross does beyond the sum of its two parents’ GCAs is the specific combining ability (SCA). Reciprocal recurrent selection, as this chapter uses the term, ranks the lines of each pool on their testcrosses to the other pool: a line’s score is its GCA against that tester pool plus whatever SCA it has with the testers actually sampled. That is the book’s own description of the scheme (Section 5.11.1 works out what a tester-based mean carries); it is not a statement of what Comstock et al. (1949) report, which the book cites for the name and does not report beyond the title.
On the full factorial of Step 4 the GCA of every A line against pool B can be computed exactly, and under the model of Step 2 it has a closed form. With \(u_{ik}\) the line’s allele indicator, \(\bar G\) the factorial mean and \(g^A_i\) the GCA of pool-A line \(i\) against pool B (the notation of Appendix A),
\[g^A_i \;=\; \frac{1}{n_B}\sum_{j} G_{ij} - \bar G \;=\; \sum_k \alpha^{(B)}_k\,(u_{ik} - p_{Ak}),
\qquad \alpha^{(B)}_k = a_k + d_k\,(1 - 2\,p_{Bk}) \tag{9.6}\]
\(\alpha^{(B)}_k\) is the average effect of substituting the line’s allele into a pool-B background – the same \(\alpha = a + d(q - p)\) of Step 3, with the frequency of the tester pool, not the line’s own pool. That is the algebraic content of the sentence “combining ability is a property of a line against a tester”: change the tester pool and the weights change. Its dominance part, \(\sum_k d_k (1 - 2 p_{Bk})(u_{ik} - p_{Ak})\), is the gca_A of heterosis_gca_sca() (Section 5.11), and the interaction residual of the factorial is that function’s sca. Relative to Chapter 5, Equation 9.3, Equation 9.4 and Equation 9.6 are Equation 5.3, Equation 5.4 and Equation 5.15 written on AlphaSimR’s coding; but the \(g^A_i\) of Equation 9.6 is the whole GCA of line \(i\) (additive plus dominance), whereas the \(g^A_i\) of Equation 5.15 is the dominance part alone, which is what gca_A returns. The chunk asserts all three identities; Table 9.12 gives the two variances and the correlation between a line’s own genetic value and its GCA.


Show code
gca_true <- tapply(gv(fact)[, 1], fact@mother, mean)[A@id] - as.numeric(meanG(fact))
gca_formula <- drop(sweep(U, 2, pA) %*% (a + d * (1 - 2 * pB)))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(gca_true), as.numeric(gca_formula))))

hg <- heterosis_gca_sca(U, V, d)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(gca_true) - as.numeric(sweep(U, 2, pA) %*% a),
                           as.numeric(hg[["gca_A"]]))))

G_ij <- tapply(gv(fact)[, 1], list(fact@mother, fact@father), mean)[A@id, B@id]
sca  <- sweep(sweep(G_ij, 1, rowMeans(G_ij)), 2, colMeans(G_ij)) + mean(G_ij)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(unname(sca), unname(hg[["sca"]]))))

var_gca <- mean(gca_true^2)
var_sca <- mean(sca^2)
fmt(data.frame(var_GCA_A = var_gca, var_SCA = var_sca,
               cor_perse_gv_vs_GCA = stats::cor(gv(A)[, 1], gca_true)), 4)

The correlation cor_perse_gv_vs_GCA of Table 9.12 is the one to hold on to. Under Equation 9.6, the part of \(g^A_i\) that the line’s own genetic value does not carry is the dominance part, weighted at QTL \(k\) by \(d_k (1 - 2 p_{Bk})\), so what sets its size is how far the tester pool’s frequencies sit from one half. quickHaplo() samples every allele at frequency one half (Step 4), and here the mean of \(|1 - 2 p_{Bk}|\) over the 1000 QTL is 0.144, against a maximum of 1. The dominance part of the GCA has a variance that is 0.6 percent of the variance of the GCA, and a line’s own genetic value correlates with its GCA at 0.997. In this draw, then, the dominance weights are small and per se value ranks combining ability closely. That is a property of the founder frequencies, not of the two halves being undifferentiated: pools with no divergence but an allele-frequency spectrum away from one half have weights away from zero as well. Anything that moves \(p_{Bk}\) away from one half – the founders’ frequency spectrum, drift in the tester pool after a split, selection – gives the testcross information the line per se does not carry. Step 8 separates the two routes: its split = 0 row has a coalescent frequency spectrum and no divergence, and the sweep measures what divergence adds to that.


9.6.3 How many testers, how many locations
A programme cannot cross every candidate to every line of the other pool. It uses \(t\) testers and \(r\) locations (\(t\) is the \(k\) of the mating-design notation of Appendix A, renamed because \(k\) indexes QTL here; it is not the selfing generation of Equation 9.5 nor a Student \(t\)), and the estimate of \(g^A_i\) is the mean phenotype of the line’s \(t\) testcrosses, each an entry mean over \(r\) plots. Writing the testcross phenotype as \(\bar G + g^A_i +
g^B_j + s_{ij} + e_{ij}\) with \(e_{ij}\) the entry-mean error of variance \(\sigma^2_e / r\), and averaging over the \(t\) testers (whose own GCAs are common to every candidate and drop out of the ranking), the estimate is \(\hat g^A_i = g^A_i + \bar s_i + \bar e_i\), with \(\bar s_i\) the mean of the line’s SCA with its \(t\) testers and \(\bar e_i\) the mean error. The statistic the chunk computes is a sample correlation between \(\hat g^A_i\) and \(g^A_i\) over the \(n_A =\) 30 fixed candidate lines, with the \(t\) testers drawn without replacement from the \(n_B =\) 30 lines of pool B. To first order its expectation is
\[\rho(t, r) \;=\; \sqrt{\frac{v_g}{v_g + v_s + v_e}}, \qquad
v_g = \frac{1}{n_A - 1}\sum_{i=1}^{n_A} (g^A_i)^2, \quad
v_s = \frac{\sigma^2_{SCA}}{t}\cdot\frac{n_A}{n_A - 1}\cdot\frac{n_B - t}{n_B - 1}, \quad
v_e = \frac{\sigma^2_e}{t\,r} \tag{9.7}\]
where \(v_g\) is the sample variance (\(n_A - 1\) divisor) of the candidates’ true GCA, because the correlation is taken over exactly those \(n_A\) points; \(\sigma^2_{SCA} = \frac{1}{n_A n_B}\sum_{ij} s_{ij}^2\) is the SCA variance realised on this factorial (computed above; not the closed form of Appendix A for independent lines), \((n_B - t)/(n_B - 1)\) is the finite-population correction for \(t\) testers drawn without replacement from \(n_B\), \(n_A/(n_A - 1)\) turns the mean of the per-candidate variances of \(\bar s_i\) into the expected sample variance, and \(\sigma^2_e\) is SP$varE, the plot error of Step 2. The textbook form of Equation 9.7 replaces \(v_g\) by the population variance of GCA and \(v_s\) by \(\sigma^2_{SCA}/t\): it assumes an infinite tester pool and population variances. It is kept in Table 9.13 as predicted_infinite, so the two can be compared. Neither corrects the second-order term of a sample correlation (the Jensen term); it is measured directly, not assumed away, in Table 9.14, and left uncorrected because it is small at this \(n_A\). The simulation measures the thing itself: repeated draws of the tester set and of the field error, at every combination.
Chapter 5 and Chapter 18 hold the same expression and it is not repeated here. With no plot error (\(\sigma^2_e = 0\)) and the population variances, Equation 9.7 is the \(\rho_k\) of Equation 5.21 (Section 5.13.6) for heterosis, with that chapter’s \(k\) called \(t\) here, and as \(n_B \to \infty\) it is the least-squares \(\rho\) of Table 18.1 (Section 18.3), where \(c\) crosses per line and \(r\) plots per cross play the roles of \(t\) and \(r\). What this chapter adds is the finite-pool and sample-variance factors in \(v_s\), the plot error through locations, and the measured Jensen term below.


Show code
grid  <- expand.grid(testers = c(1, 2, 4, 8), reps = c(1, 4))
n_acc <- 20
acc   <- sapply(seq_len(n_acc), function(rep) {
  set.seed(300 + rep)
  testers <- B[sample(B@nInd, max(grid[["testers"]]))]
  tc <- hybridCross(A, testers, crossPlan = "testcross", simParam = SP)
  apply(grid, 1, function(g) {
    ph  <- setPheno(tc, reps = g[["reps"]], simParam = SP)@pheno[, 1]
    use <- tc@father %in% testers@id[seq_len(g[["testers"]])]
    est <- tapply(ph[use], tc@mother[use], mean)[A@id]
    stats::cor(est, gca_true)
  })
})
# The prediction, for the statistic actually computed above: a sample
# correlation over the n_A FIXED candidates, with t testers drawn WITHOUT
# replacement from the n_B lines of pool B.
#   est_i = GCA_i + sbar_i + ebar_i
#   v_g : the candidates' sample variance of GCA (n_A - 1 divisor), because
#         the correlation is taken over exactly these n_A points;
#   v_s : sbar_i is the mean of t values from row i of sca, whose n_B entries
#         average zero, so Var(sbar_i) = (s2_i / t) (n_B - t) / (n_B - 1) with
#         s2_i = mean_j sca_ij^2; the column means of sca are zero too, so the
#         sample mean of sbar over candidates is exactly zero and the expected
#         sample variance is mean_i Var(sbar_i) n_A / (n_A - 1)
#         = var_sca n_A / (n_A - 1) (n_B - t) / (n_B - 1) / t;
#   v_e : varE / (t r), independent of everything else.
# To first order E[cor] = sqrt(v_g / (v_g + v_s + v_e)). The second-order
# (Jensen) term of the sample correlation is not corrected here; it is
# measured by Gaussian Monte Carlo in the chunk below the accuracy grid and
# reported there (`jensen_max`) rather than asserted in advance.
# `predicted_infinite` is the textbook form -- population variances, infinite
# tester pool -- kept so the two can be compared at this replication.
n_A <- A@nInd; n_B <- B@nInd
var_gca_n1 <- stats::var(gca_true)
fpc <- (n_B - grid[["testers"]]) / (n_B - 1)
v_s <- var_sca * (n_A / (n_A - 1)) * fpc / grid[["testers"]]
v_e <- SP$varE / (grid[["testers"]] * grid[["reps"]])
grid[["predicted"]] <- sqrt(var_gca_n1 / (var_gca_n1 + v_s + v_e))
grid[["predicted_infinite"]] <- sqrt(var_gca / (var_gca + var_sca / grid[["testers"]] + v_e))
grid[["observed_mean"]] <- rowMeans(acc)
grid[["observed_sd"]]   <- apply(acc, 1, stats::sd)
grid[["z"]] <- (grid[["observed_mean"]] - grid[["predicted"]]) /
  (grid[["observed_sd"]] / sqrt(n_acc))
fmt(grid, 3)

Show code
# The second-order term the first-order prediction leaves out: the bias of a
# sample correlation over n_A points, by Gaussian Monte Carlo per cell,
# y = x + N(0, v_s + v_e), E[cor(x, y)] minus the first-order value. In the
# table above the candidates are the SAME 30 lines in every draw, so `jensen`
# holds x fixed at gca_true and draws only the noise -- the design actually
# measured. `jensen_random_x` redraws x ~ N(0, v_g) as well, the textbook
# small-sample bias of a correlation between two random variables, which is
# a different (larger) quantity and not the one the table is exposed to.
set.seed(600)
n_mc <- 4000
cor_cols <- function(x, y) {
  xc <- sweep(x, 2, colMeans(x)); yc <- sweep(y, 2, colMeans(y))
  colSums(xc * yc) / sqrt(colSums(xc^2) * colSums(yc^2))
}
jensen_mc <- function(x_of) vapply(seq_len(nrow(grid)), function(i) {
  x <- x_of()
  y <- x + matrix(stats::rnorm(n_A * n_mc, 0, sqrt(v_s[i] + v_e[i])), n_A)
  mean(cor_cols(x, y)) - grid[["predicted"]][i]
}, numeric(1))
jensen <- jensen_mc(function() matrix(gca_true, n_A, n_mc))
jensen_random_x <- jensen_mc(function()
  matrix(stats::rnorm(n_A * n_mc, 0, sqrt(var_gca_n1)), n_A))
names(jensen) <- names(jensen_random_x) <- paste0("t", grid[["testers"]], "_r", grid[["reps"]])
jensen_max <- max(abs(jensen))
# cells as rows: eight cells as columns would not fit the page

          random_x = c(jensen_random_x, max_abs = max(abs(jensen_random_x)))), 4)

The Jensen term for the design actually run (fixed_candidates, gca_true held fixed at the 30 candidates) is at most 0.003 in absolute value across the eight cells, i.e. 0.8 percent of the smallest accuracy (accuracies run from 0.39 to 0.92), which is what “left uncorrected” means quantitatively; random_x is the larger, textbook small-sample bias of a correlation between two random variables, shown only for contrast and not the quantity this chapter’s statistic carries.
Accuracy rises with both, and the two arguments buy different things. More locations shrink only the error term; more testers shrink the error term and the SCA term, because a line’s specific interactions with its testers average out. Table 9.13 is 20 draws of the tester set and of the field error per cell; the corrected and the textbook predictions differ by at most 0.007 here. z is the observed mean minus the corrected prediction in units of the standard error of that mean over the 20 draws; the largest |z| over the eight cells is 1.63 (it would be 1.91 against the textbook form). The two-sided 5 percent point of t with 19 degrees of freedom is 2.09 unadjusted and 3.07 for the 8 cells (Bonferroni, conservative: the cells share the same tester draws), so at this replication the largest |z| is within both points, and no cell is shown to differ from the prediction. Each observed_sd is across tester sets and error draws, on a fixed set of candidates: what a single testcross trial’s ranking is worth depends on which testers were drawn, not only on how many; with one tester at one location the spread across tester sets is 0.35 of the accuracy itself.
In the scheme of Step 8 the testers are 2 individuals of the opposite pool and the trials have one location, which puts it in the low-accuracy corner of Table 9.13. A real maize programme would use elite inbred testers and several locations; Hallauer et al. (2010) is the maize reference on the choice of tester (cited here without a page, the book not being available to check one).

9.7 Step 7 – Two traits, and an index on phenotypes
corA makes the traits genetically correlated, which is where selection stops being one-dimensional. This step uses an additive trait pair on its own founder draw: index theory is written on breeding values, and the point being made does not need dominance. Table 9.15 gives what the draw realised.


Show code
set.seed(202)
f2 <- quickHaplo(nInd = 80, nChr = 10, segSites = 100, inbred = TRUE)
SP2 <- SimParam$new(f2)
SP2$addTraitA(nQtlPerChr = 100, mean = c(10, 10), var = c(1, 4),
              corA = matrix(c(1, -0.4, -0.4, 1), 2, 2))
SP2$setVarE(h2 = c(0.6, 0.1))

mt <- newPop(f2, simParam = SP2)
varG_f2 <- diag(varG(mt))   # genetic variances of the founders, for the text
for (k in 1:3) mt <- randCross(mt, nCrosses = 1000, simParam = SP2)
mt <- setPheno(mt, simParam = SP2)

G <- varG(mt); P <- varP(mt); a2 <- c(1, 1)
fmt(data.frame(cor_genetic = stats::cov2cor(G)[2, 1],
               cor_pheno   = stats::cov2cor(P)[2, 1],
               h2_trait1   = as.numeric(diag(G)[1] / diag(P)[1]),
               h2_trait2   = as.numeric(diag(G)[2] / diag(P)[2])), 3)

G and P in the code are the genetic and phenotypic covariance matrices of the traits, the \(\boldsymbol\Sigma_G\), \(\boldsymbol\Sigma_P\) of Appendix A, not the relationship matrix \(\mathbf{G}\).

The realised genetic correlation is -0.42 against the requested -0.4; the phenotypic one is -0.08, much weaker, because the environmental components were left uncorrelated (SP$setCorE() is where that would change). The realised heritabilities are 0.47 and 0.07, not the requested 0.6 and 0.1: setVarE(h2 = ) sets the error variance from the founders’ genetic variance (1 and 4 for the two traits), and after three rounds of random mating the genetic variances of the population measured are 0.62 and 2.82, so the realised ratio is lower (the same loss as the varA of Step 3). The two traits differ in variance and, sharply, in heritability – the ordinary situation.
What the pipeline default is, and what this step is not. stage2_select() defaults to weights = NULL, equal weight on every trait after build_ctx() standardises each criterion, so the default is the economic weights \(a_j = 1/\operatorname{sd}(\text{criterion}_j)\). Chapter 4 (section “What weights = NULL is assuming”) shows that when the criteria are multi-trait best linear unbiased prediction (BLUP) predictions of the genetic values that index is the optimum, so the Smith-Hazel gap is a property of an index on phenotypic records and not a defect of the default. Step 7 is the phenotypic case, and it is not the default: P is the phenotypic covariance matrix, and the weights a2 = c(1, 1) are on the raw trait units of two traits whose genetic variances are 1 and 4, which are not \(1/\operatorname{sd}\) weights. The comparisons below (the trait-1 gain and the loss of attainable correlation) are therefore statements about indices on phenotypes, not about weights = NULL. Two reasons the step still belongs here. First, the AlphaSimR bridge hands stage2_select() phenotypes: alphasimr_to_stage1() passes hybrid_pop@pheno, one plot per hybrid, as the trait columns, so the final subsection of Step 8 runs the default on standardised testcross phenotypes – the phenotypic-criteria case that Chapter 4 does not treat, and whose gap to the Smith-Hazel index is not measured here. Second, the step adds to Chapter 4 a covariance pair realised from a simulated population (corA, setVarE()) rather than an invented one, and a numerical check that Smith-Hazel is the maximiser, which Chapter 4 does not give. The index functions are those of Chapter 4 (Table 9.16):


Show code
cor_with_H <- function(w)
  drop(crossprod(w, G %*% a2)) /
    sqrt(drop(crossprod(w, P %*% w)) * drop(crossprod(a2, G %*% a2)))

Bw <- rbind(equal       = a2,
            smith_hazel = index_smith_hazel(P, G, a2),
            restricted  = index_restricted(P, G, a2, R = cbind(c(0, 1))))
# expected response per unit selection intensity on the index I = b'x:
# the vector of phenotypic differentials is S = i P b / sqrt(b'Pb), and the
# multi-trait breeder's equation R = G P^-1 S gives R = i G b / sqrt(b'Pb)
dG <- t(apply(Bw, 1, function(w) drop(G %*% w) / sqrt(drop(crossprod(w, P %*% w)))))
colnames(dG) <- c("gain_trait1", "gain_trait2")
idx_tab <- cbind(Bw, dG, aggregate = rowSums(dG),
                 cor_with_H = apply(Bw, 1, cor_with_H))
fmt(idx_tab)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(idx_tab[, "aggregate"],
                           idx_tab[, "cor_with_H"] * sqrt(drop(crossprod(a2, G %*% a2))),
                           check.attributes = FALSE)),
          abs(idx_tab["restricted", "gain_trait2"]) < 1e-10 * max(abs(dG)))

Trait1, Trait2: index weights; gain_trait1, gain_trait2: expected genetic change per unit selection intensity on the index, in trait units; aggregate: their sum; cor_with_H: correlation of the index with the aggregate genotype. restricted: the index holding trait 2 at zero expected gain.

gain_trait1 and gain_trait2 are the expected genetic change in each trait per unit of selection intensity on the index, G b / sqrt(b' P b), and aggregate is their a-weighted sum – which equals cor_with_H times the standard deviation of the aggregate genotype, asserted. Three readings, in the order they matter:

Equal weights are not the Smith-Hazel solution. Smith-Hazel puts 0.75 units of weight on trait 2 for every unit on trait 1, not 1.00. The index is \(\mathbf{b} = \boldsymbol\Sigma_P^{-1}\boldsymbol\Sigma_G\mathbf{a}\) (Equation 4.5, with its conditions for \(\mathbf{b} \propto \mathbf{a}\), in Chapter 4; b = P^-1 G a here), attributed there to Smith (1936) and Hazel (1943), whose papers neither that chapter nor this one read. Here the heritabilities are 0.47 and 0.07 and the genetic and phenotypic correlations -0.42 and -0.08, so G is nowhere near a multiple of P, and the table shows that (1, 1) is not an eigenvector of P^-1 G.
The cost on the objective is modest here; the composition of the gain is not. Equal weighting loses 0.2 percent of the attainable correlation with the aggregate genotype. But it moves trait 1 by 0.011 per unit intensity where Smith-Hazel moves it by 0.044, 4.1 times as much; both indices put most of the aggregate into trait 2, whose genetic variance is 4.6 times larger, and the weights decide how much trait 1 moves at all. An index that is nearly as good on the objective can still land the gain somewhere else.
The restricted index holds the expected gain in trait 2 at zero: it is \(6.6 \times 10^{-17}\) in the table, zero to rounding, at a cost of 15 percent of the aggregate. This is a model expectation, G b / sqrt(b' P b) computed from this population’s sample matrices (Equation 4.6), not a realised change in a selected sample. The form is the restricted index that Chapter 4 reports from Kempthorne and Nordskog (1959), a paper that chapter did not read and whose matrix form it gives as the book’s own; this chapter adds no reading of it. Chapter 4 also lists the four ways an equality restriction on a trait differs from the alpha inequality on diversity, and that restricting a group coancestry while maximising gain is the lineage of Meuwissen et al. (2020), not of this index.

Smith-Hazel is defined as the weight vector maximising that correlation, so the claim is checkable against a numerical optimum rather than taken on faith (this check is this chapter’s own addition to Chapter 4):


Show code
opt <- stats::optim(c(1, 1), function(w) -cor_with_H(w), method = "BFGS")
d_opt <- abs(-opt$value - cor_with_H(Bw["smith_hazel", ]))
stopifnot(d_opt < 1e-6)           # BFGS tolerance, not machine precision
c(numerical = -opt$value, smith_hazel = cor_with_H(Bw["smith_hazel", ])) |> fmt(10)
#>   numerical smith_hazel 
#>   0.2438417   0.2438417
cat("absolute difference:", format(d_opt, digits = 2), "(asserted < 1e-6)\n")
#> absolute difference: 1.1e-15 (asserted < 1e-6)


Multi-trait genomic selection in wheat, balancing yield against protein content and quality, is the standing plant example (Michel et al. 2019). In the hybrid scheme below only trait 1 enters the ranking; the second trait rides along in the contract so that stage2_select() has an index to build.

section: 9.8 Step 8 – The parts assembled: reciprocal recurrent selection
text:
9.8 Step 8 – The parts assembled: reciprocal recurrent selection
Everything above was one operation at a time. A breeding scheme is those operations in a loop, and the loop for two heterotic pools is reciprocal recurrent selection: each pool is improved using the other pool as tester. Doubled-haploid lines are drawn from pool A, testcrossed to pool B (and vice versa), the testcross hybrids are phenotyped, and the lines with the best mean testcross performance – the testcross-mean estimate of Step 6 – are recombined to found the next cycle’s pool. Elite lines from both pools, at the end, are crossed directly to produce the commercial hybrids. It is exactly the asymmetry Chapter 23 argues for: selection happens on the hybrid, recycling happens within pool.

9.8.1 Founding two pools with a real coalescent history
This is the one place the chapter pays for runMacs2() rather than quickHaplo(). AlphaSimR::runMacs2(..., split = ) draws founder haplotypes from a population-split coalescent history: one ancestral population, then two demes of equal size that stopped exchanging migrants split generations ago, with the first half of the sampled individuals from one deme and the second half from the other. That is the realistic analogue of simulate_lines()’s Balding-Nichols draw in Chapter 6, and between-pool divergence is the entire subject of Chapter 3, so a stylised substitute would not do. Table 9.17 summarises one draw at the bridge’s default settings.


Show code
fp <- alphasimr_founder_pools(rrs_cfg)
founder_geno <- pullSegSiteGeno(c(fp[["pop_A"]], fp[["pop_B"]]), simParam = fp[["SP"]])
fmt(data.frame(pool_A = fp[["pop_A"]]@nInd, pool_B = fp[["pop_B"]]@nInd,
               markers = ncol(founder_geno),
               heterozygous_fraction = mean(founder_geno == 1),
               gd_A = alphasimr_gd(fp[["pop_A"]], fp[["SP"]]),
               gd_B = alphasimr_gd(fp[["pop_B"]], fp[["SP"]])), 3)
