Reading alphasimr_founder_pools() against Steps 1 and 2, it is runMacs2(nInd = , nChr = , segSites = , split = ) followed by SP$addTraitAD(nQtlPerChr = seg_sites, meanDD = 0.4, varDD = 0.1) – the same dominance model as Step 2 – and SP$setVarE(h2 = 0.4). Two things about it must be said before any number is read. The founders are outbred: runMacs2() is called without inbred = TRUE, so each pool is a sample of a random-mating population, heterozygous at the fraction of sites given in Table 9.17 (heterozygous_fraction), as an open-pollinated maize population would be; the inbred lines of the scheme are made from them by makeDH() inside each cycle. And there is no separate marker panel: every one of the 150 segregating sites per chromosome is a QTL, so the sites that carry the trait are the ones pullSegSiteGeno() reads for X, f and fL throughout. alphasimr_gd() is 1 - mean(f), the exact definition gene_diversity() uses, computed from that pull, so the two pools are already on the same scale as every diversity number in the rest of the book.
These founders come from runMacs2(), and Step 1 did not establish whether they repeat from the seed (it measured one pair of runMacs() calls and never called runMacs2()). Everything below is computed from them, so the chapter does not rely on the founders repeating: it replicates every Step 8 measurement over independent founder draws, reports the spread, and writes any verdict that rests on a t near its critical value as the render’s.
What split does. The bridge’s default is split_gen = 100. The sweep of Table 9.18 draws 20 independent founder sets at each of four split times and measures three things on each: the partition of Caballero and Toro (2002) over the two pools (ct_partition(), the general form of gd_partition()). The partition is the one defined in Equation 3.9 of Chapter 3 and is not re-derived here: with the two pools as the subpopulations, \(GD_T = 1 - \bar f\) is the total gene diversity (\(\bar f\) the census-weighted mean molecular coancestry over all pairs of the founder individuals of the two pools, the notation of Section 3.1, computed by ct_partition() from the individual genotypes pulled by pullSegSiteGeno(); no hybrid enters) and \(GD_T = GD_{WI} + GD_{BI} + GD_{BS}\), where \(GD_{WI}\) is the component within individuals (half the observed heterozygosity of a plant), \(GD_{BI}\) the component between individuals within a pool, and \(GD_{BS}\) the component between the two pools (Table 3.2). \(F_{ST} = GD_{BS} / GD_T\) is the identity of Equation 3.10, with \(F_{ST}\) the statistic of Equation 3.7 and not the one referenced to the between-population coancestry that Chapter 3 also records. The share of expected heterosis that the divergence term carries (heterosis_partition(), Chapter 5), and – the Step 6 question with divergence – how much of a DH line’s exact GCA against the other pool’s DH lines its own genetic value can see. For that last one, 10 DH lines are drawn from every founder, the full factorial between the two DH sets is made, and the GCA of each pool-A line is split into its additive and dominance parts with heterosis_gca_sca(); the identity behind that split was asserted in Step 6. The chunk also records, per draw, an ascertainment bookkeeping that the reading of GD_T will need: the fraction of sites monomorphic within each pool, the fraction fixed for opposite alleles in the two pools, and the part of GD_T those sites carry. Table 9.19 then tests the two GCA statistics between the extreme split times.


Show code
split_draw <- function(split, seed) {
  cfg <- utils::modifyList(rrs_cfg, list(split_gen = split, seed = seed))
  fp_s <- alphasimr_founder_pools(cfg)
  SP_s <- fp_s[["SP"]]
  pool <- rep(c("A", "B"), c(cfg[["n_pool_A"]], cfg[["n_pool_B"]]))
  geno <- pullSegSiteGeno(c(fp_s[["pop_A"]], fp_s[["pop_B"]]), simParam = SP_s)
  ct   <- ct_partition(geno, pool)
  pA_s <- colMeans(geno[pool == "A", ]) / 2
  pB_s <- colMeans(geno[pool == "B", ]) / 2
  d_s  <- SP_s$traits[[1]]@domEff
  a_s  <- SP_s$traits[[1]]@addEff
  hp   <- heterosis_partition(pA_s, pB_s, d_s)
  # Ascertainment: runMacs2() returns sites that segregate in the POOLED
  # sample, so a site fixed for different alleles in the two pools is kept
  # and, with equal pool sizes, sits at pooled frequency 1/2 -- the maximum
  # of 2 p q. GD_T = mean 2 pbar qbar exactly (census weights, equal sizes),
  # so it splits into the part those fixed differences carry and the rest.
  mono_A <- pA_s %in% c(0, 1)
  mono_B <- pB_s %in% c(0, 1)
  fixed  <- mono_A & mono_B & (pA_s != pB_s)
  pbar_s <- (pA_s + pB_s) / 2
  h_s    <- 2 * pbar_s * (1 - pbar_s)
  stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(ct[["diversity"]][["GD_T"]],
                             ct[["diversity"]][["GD_WI"]] + ct[["diversity"]][["GD_BI"]] +
                               ct[["diversity"]][["GD_BS"]])),
            isTRUE(all.equal(ct[["diversity"]][["GD_T"]], mean(h_s))),
            isTRUE(all.equal(ct[["global"]][["F_ST"]],
                             ct[["diversity"]][["GD_BS"]] / ct[["diversity"]][["GD_T"]])))
  set.seed(seed)
  dh_A <- makeDH(fp_s[["pop_A"]], nDH = n_dh_gca, simParam = SP_s)
  dh_B <- makeDH(fp_s[["pop_B"]], nDH = n_dh_gca, simParam = SP_s)
  hyb  <- hybridCross(dh_A, dh_B, crossPlan = "testcross", simParam = SP_s)
  gca  <- tapply(gv(hyb)[, 1], hyb@mother, mean)[dh_A@id] - as.numeric(meanG(hyb))[1]
  U_s  <- pullQtlGeno(dh_A, simParam = SP_s) / 2
  hg   <- heterosis_gca_sca(U_s, pullQtlGeno(dh_B, simParam = SP_s) / 2, d_s)
  # GCA = additive part + dominance part (the Step 6 identity), so its
  # variance is var(add) + var(dom) + 2 cov(add, dom): three terms, not two.
  gca_add <- as.numeric(sweep(U_s, 2, colMeans(U_s)) %*% a_s)
  gca_dom <- as.numeric(hg[["gca_A"]])
  stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(gca), gca_add + gca_dom)))
  data.frame(split = split, seed = seed,
             F_ST  = ct[["global"]][["F_ST"]],
             GD_T  = ct[["diversity"]][["GD_T"]],
             GD_BS = ct[["diversity"]][["GD_BS"]],
             mono_A = mean(mono_A), mono_B = mean(mono_B),
             fixed_diff = mean(fixed),
             GD_T_fixed = sum(h_s[fixed]) / length(h_s),
             GD_T_other = sum(h_s[!fixed]) / length(h_s),
             maf_pooled = mean(pmin(pbar_s, 1 - pbar_s)),
             heterosis_divergence_share = hp[["divergence"]] / hp[["total"]],
             GCA_var = stats::var(gca),
             GCA_var_add = stats::var(gca_add),
             GCA_var_dom = stats::var(gca_dom),
             GCA_cov2 = 2 * stats::cov(gca_add, gca_dom),
             GCA_dominance_share = stats::var(gca_dom) / stats::var(gca),
             cor_perse_GCA = stats::cor(gv(dh_A)[, 1], gca))
}
splits <- c(0, 10, 100, 1000)
sw <- do.call(rbind, lapply(splits, function(s)
  do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(n_split_draws), function(r)

Read Table 9.18 (a) and Table 9.18 (b) together: the first is the mean over the 20 draws, the second their standard deviation. What was measured: F_ST rises from 0.023 at split = 0 to 0.572 at split = 1000, and GD_BS from 0.007 to 0.191, each step many standard deviations wide; the divergence share of expected heterosis rises from 0.022 to 0.366. GD_T does not stay flat: it is 0.314 at split = 0, 0.299 at split = 100 and 0.334 at split = 1000, and the rise from split = 100 to split = 1000, 0.035, is 17 standard errors at this replication. Table 9.18 (c) is the bookkeeping behind that rise. Across the same range the fraction of sites monomorphic within pool A goes from 0.065 to 0.562 (pool B: 0.067 to 0.564), the fraction of sites fixed for opposite alleles in the two pools from 0 to 0.189, the part of GD_T those sites carry (GD_T_fixed) from 0 to 0.094, and the part carried by every other site (GD_T_other) falls from 0.314 to 0.239.
What is inferred from Table 9.18 (a) to Table 9.18 (c): runMacs2() returns the sites that segregate in the pooled sample of the two demes, so a site fixed for opposite alleles in the two pools is kept and, with equal pool sizes, sits at pooled frequency one half – the maximum of \(2\bar p \bar q\), which is exactly what GD_T averages over sites (asserted in the chunk). The rise in GD_T therefore comes entirely from sites fixed for opposite alleles, an ascertainment effect of how the founder sites are sampled, while diversity at every other site falls with divergence. At those other sites the direction is the one Chapter 5 gives for drift: diversity within pools falls, the between-pool component rises, and the total does not rise (GD_T_other falls in Table 9.18 (c)). How much of GD_T a marker panel shows under divergence therefore depends on how its sites were ascertained, which is a property of the panel and not of the pools.
Table 9.18 (d) and Table 9.18 (e) are the combining-ability side, mean and standard deviation, and Table 9.19 is the contrast between the two extreme split times, unpaired because the draws are independent. GCA is the sum of its additive and dominance parts (asserted in the chunk), so its variance is \(\mathrm{var}(\mathrm{add}) + \mathrm{var}(\mathrm{dom}) + 2\,\mathrm{cov}(\mathrm{add}, \mathrm{dom})\), three terms. What was measured, from split = 0 to split = 1000: GCA_var goes from 0.574 to 0.414, GCA_var_add from 0.504 to 0.345, GCA_var_dom from 0.059 to 0.07, and GCA_cov2 (\(2\,\mathrm{cov}\)) from 0.011 to -0.002, the last with between-draw standard deviations of 0.041 and 0.072; its largest \(|\text{mean}|/\text{s.e.}\) across splits is 1.19, against the two-sided 5 percent point \(t_{0.975,\,19} =\) 2.09. The ratio GCA_dominance_share \(= \mathrm{var}(\mathrm{dom}) / \mathrm{var}(\mathrm{GCA})\) rises from 0.102 to 0.187 (t = 4.3). Which part drives it: holding the dominance part at its split = 0 value and moving only the additive part to its split = 1000 value gives a ratio of 0.142; holding the additive part and moving only the dominance part gives 0.12. And the per se-versus-GCA correlation falls from 0.948 to 0.906 (t = -3.9). Both correlations are below the 0.997 of Step 6’s undifferentiated halves, but that comparison crosses a change of founders, trait draw and line number, so the within-sweep contrast is the one that isolates split. The split = 0 row is the frequency-spectrum route of Step 6 without divergence: its pooled minor-allele frequency is 0.233, so the mean of \(|1 - 2\bar p_k|\) over sites, which equals \(1 - 2\,\)maf_pooled exactly, is 0.534, against 0.098 for Step 6’s two halves.
Multiplicity of the sweep. The statistics decided against a critical value in this section are the two contrasts of Table 9.19, the GCA_var_dom contrast and the covariance term at each of the 4 split times: 7 tests, a number fixed by this paragraph and not by the data. The point \(t_{0.975,\,19} =\) 2.09 used above is unadjusted for them: it is the permissive end for a verdict of a difference (it ignores the number of tests) and the strict end for a verdict of “not distinguishable from zero”. The Bonferroni point for 7 tests is 3.01. Against it, in this render, 2 of the 7 statistics are beyond it (2 are beyond the unadjusted point); the tests are not independent (the statistics are computed on the same draws and the covariance term enters the ratio); Bonferroni holds the family-wise level at or below 5 percent whatever the dependence, and is not its exact value. The F_ST, GD_BS and GD_T movements, the ascertainment bookkeeping of Table 9.18 (c) and the one-part-at-a-time decomposition (gca_only()) are descriptive: no test is attached to them and none is adjusted, and they are exploratory.
What is inferred: in this render the fall of the additive part of the GCA variance accounts for more of the rise in the ratio than the growth of the dominance part; an additive part that falls with divergence does so because the sites that fix within a pool stop contributing to it (at linkage equilibrium its variance over DH lines is \(\sum_k a_k^2\, p_{Ak} q_{Ak}\)), so the ratio can rise without the dominance part growing at all. The ratio is a partition of \(\mathrm{var}(\mathrm{GCA})\) only insofar as the covariance term is negligible. In this render that term is within the two-sided 5 percent point at every split; with 20 draws, a term within that point is not shown to differ from zero, which is not a bound on its size. If the founders differ between the executions that produce the HTML and the PDF (see “Founders from MaCS”), a term whose \(|t|\) lies near the unadjusted point (2.09) and below the Bonferroni point (3.01) could fall on either side in the two formats; no inference drawn in this paragraph depends on which side it falls, but the render’s own wording above and the counts in it do. In magnitude, at split = 0 \(|2\,\mathrm{cov}|\) is 0.19 times GCA_var_dom, and dropping it changes the ratio of the split = 0 means from 0.103 to \(\mathrm{var}(\mathrm{dom}) / [\mathrm{var}(\mathrm{add}) + \mathrm{var}(\mathrm{dom})] =\) 0.105. “Share” is used only in that qualified sense, and each founder draw calls runMacs2(), whose repeatability from set.seed() was not established (Step 1), so that verdict is this render’s and may change with the next. Whether the dominance part itself grows with divergence is a separate question, and the algebra does not fix its sign: at linkage equilibrium its variance over DH lines is \(\sum_k d_k^2 (1 - 2 p_{Bk})^2\, p_{Ak} q_{Ak}\), and divergence pushes the weight \((1 - 2 p_{Bk})^2\) up at the same loci where it pushes \(p_{Ak} q_{Ak}\) down. Measured, GCA_var_dom changes by 0.011 from split = 0 to split = 1000 (t = 0.9, against the unadjusted point \(t_{0.975,\,19} =\) 2.09), so in this render that change is not distinguishable from zero; being computed from runMacs2() founders over 20 draws, it is this render’s verdict and not a property of the scheme. The ratio’s own contrast is beyond the same point in this render; where it is beyond it and positive, what it supports is that a larger share, in the qualified sense above, of \(\mathrm{var}(\mathrm{GCA})\) is invisible to a line’s own genetic value after the split, through whichever part the decomposition above identifies, and nothing here separates how much of the between-draw spread is the trait drawn with each founder set and how much is the DH sampling. The limit of the inference is the scale: 12 individuals per pool, 750 sites, 20 draws per split, and a split in coalescent generations that is not calibrated to any named heterotic-pool pair. No other scale was simulated, so whether any of these directions holds at another one is not claimed.

alphasimr_rrs_cycle() runs the same six steps for each pool, symmetrically (pool A tested on B, pool B tested on A), and every one is a primitive from above:

Double haploids (Step 5). makeDH() draws 3 fully homozygous lines from each individual in the current pool – at this chapter’s Step 8 configuration, 12 parents x 3 DH each = 36 DH lines per pool, per cycle. Because the pool is outbred, the DH lines from one parent differ from each other: this is the lottery of Step 4, drawn one generation earlier than in a line programme.
Pick reciprocal testers. The first 2 individuals of the current opposite pool are used as testers – an arbitrary slice by index, not a random or merit-based draw, outbred individuals rather than inbred lines, and a different set each cycle because step 6 recreates the pool. This is the RRS-defining move: a line’s value is judged by its cross onto the other heterotic pool, not by itself.
Testcross and phenotype (Step 6). hybridCross() forms the full factorial between every DH line and every tester – 36 DH x 2 testers = 72 testcross hybrids per pool – and setPheno() adds phenotyping error sized to the heritability set by SP$setVarE(h2 = ), at one location.
GCA estimate (Step 6). Testcross phenotypes are grouped by DH-line parent (tapply(pheno[, 1], mother, mean)) and averaged across the 2 testers each line was crossed to. This is the estimator of Step 6, but the quantity it estimates is the line’s value against outbred testers from the current pool, not the GCA of Equation 9.6, which is defined against inbred pool-B lines. Only trait 1 is used for this ranking even though this chapter’s config simulates 2 traits per line; the second trait rides along in X/hybrids but plays no role in selection here. Step 7 is what it would take to use both.
Keep the elites (Step 6). The 6 DH lines per pool with the highest mean testcross phenotype are kept as elite_A/elite_B.
Recombine (Step 5). randCross() random-mates the elites back up to 12 individuals, founding the next cycle’s pool A (symmetrically for B).

elite_A/elite_B are what step 6 mates – and, in the last cycle, what the final commercial cross uses instead of being recombined again. The cycle’s summary mixes two different populations on purpose: mean_tc_A/mean_tc_B average over all DH lines tested that cycle (the population’s testcross performance before selection), while gd_A/gd_B are gene diversity of only the 6 surviving elites (the population after selection). That asymmetry is exactly what Figure 9.1 plots – response measured pre-selection, diversity measured post-selection.


9.8.3 The trajectory across cycles, replicated, against a paired control
alphasimr_pipeline() runs alphasimr_rrs_cycle() in a loop for 4 cycles, carrying pop_A/pop_B forward from one cycle’s output to the next’s input. Only the last cycle’s elite_A/elite_B go on to found the commercial hybrid pool; every earlier cycle’s elites are spent entirely on randCross()ing the next cycle’s pool.
One run of that loop is an anecdote, and it would be an anecdote about one founder draw. The loop is written out here instead, so that three things can be added to it: a paired no-selection control (random_elite = TRUE, which draws the elites at random and leaves every other operation – the DH lines, the testcrosses, the recombination – the same operations, so the two arms differ by selection in expectation; because the random pick calls sample() and the selected pick does not, the arms’ random streams part at the cycle-1 elite pick, and from there on their Mendelian sampling and phenotyping errors are independent realisations, which the paired t below counts as noise), the between-pool partition of the recombined pools each cycle, and the genetic value of the actual product, the elite factorial.


Show code
run_rrs <- function(fp, cfg, random_elite = FALSE, seed = 1) {
  set.seed(seed)
  SP_r  <- fp[["SP"]]
  pop_A <- fp[["pop_A"]]; pop_B <- fp[["pop_B"]]
  pool  <- rep(c("A", "B"), c(cfg[["n_pool_A"]], cfg[["n_pool_B"]]))
  pools_row <- function(pop_A, pop_B) {
    ct <- ct_partition(pullSegSiteGeno(c(pop_A, pop_B), simParam = SP_r), pool)
    data.frame(gd_pool_A = alphasimr_gd(pop_A, SP_r),
               gd_pool_B = alphasimr_gd(pop_B, SP_r),
               GD_BS = ct[["diversity"]][["GD_BS"]],
               F_ST  = ct[["global"]][["F_ST"]])
  }
  rows <- list(cbind(cycle = 0, mean_tc_A = NA, mean_tc_B = NA, gd_A = NA, gd_B = NA,
                     hybrid_meanG = NA, pools_row(pop_A, pop_B)))
  for (i in seq_len(cfg[["n_cycles"]])) {
    cy <- alphasimr_rrs_cycle(pop_A, pop_B, SP_r, cfg, random_elite = random_elite)
    pop_A <- cy[["pop_A"]]; pop_B <- cy[["pop_B"]]
    prod  <- hybridCross(cy[["elite_A"]], cy[["elite_B"]], crossPlan = "testcross",
                         simParam = SP_r)
    rows[[i + 1]] <- cbind(cycle = i, cy[["summary"]],
                           hybrid_meanG = as.numeric(meanG(prod))[1],   # trait 1
                           pools_row(pop_A, pop_B))
  }
  do.call(rbind, rows)
}

arms <- lapply(seq_len(n_rep), function(s) {
  fp_s <- alphasimr_founder_pools(utils::modifyList(rrs_cfg, list(seed = s)))
  list(sel = run_rrs(fp_s, rrs_cfg, random_elite = FALSE, seed = s),
       ctl = run_rrs(fp_s, rrs_cfg, random_elite = TRUE,  seed = s))
})

What was measured (Figure 9.1, Table 9.22 and Table 9.23): over 48 paired replicates, the selected arm’s mean testcross phenotype at cycle 4 differs from the control’s by +2.46 (mean_tc_A, pool-A lines on pool-B testers) and +2.42 (mean_tc_B, pool-B lines on pool-A testers) trait units, with paired standard deviations of 1.13 and 1.16; the elite factorial’s genetic value – the product – differs by +2.99 (t = 16.2). Gene diversity of the elite lines, averaged over the two pools, differs by -0.011 (paired s.d. 0.018, t = -4.5), and that of the recombined pools by -0.011 (t = -4.2). Between the pools, GD_BS differs by +0.012 (t = 6.5) and F_ST by +0.048 (t = 5.3). The two-sided 5 percent point of t with 47 degrees of freedom is 2.01. Against it, in this render, the response – both testcross means and the product – is beyond it; the pooled elite-line gene-diversity difference is beyond it; the pooled recombined-pool difference is beyond it; the GD_BS difference is beyond it; the F_ST difference is beyond it.
Multiplicity. Table 9.22 (a) tests 11 statistics, each against the unadjusted point just given. They are not independent: the pooled means are averages of the per-pool rows, and the elite-line and recombined-pool gene diversities are computed on the same elites. The Bonferroni two-sided 5 percent point for 11 comparisons is 2.98, the correction reported here; it is conservative given the dependence and is not the exact family-wise level. Against it, in this render, the response statistics (both testcross means and the product) are all beyond it (smallest \(|t|\) 14.4); the pooled elite-line gene-diversity difference is beyond it (t = -4.5); the pooled recombined-pool difference is beyond it (t = -4.2); GD_BS is beyond it and F_ST is beyond it. The two pooled gene-diversity means (gd_elite_mean, gd_pool_mean) are constructions made to reduce the noise of the per-pool rows, not a test declared before the data were looked at, so every conclusion about diversity in this section is exploratory. The response statistics are what the scheme is built to move, and their correction is the one stated above.
Pooling the two pools’ differences is not free noise reduction, and Table 9.22 (b) (pool_tab) measures what it buys. Averaging halves the variance only if the two pools’ paired differences are independent across founder draws. For the elite-line gene diversity they are correlated at 0, and the pooled standard deviation, 0.018, is close to the 0.018 it would be if they were independent: pooling does what it should there. For the testcross mean they are correlated at 0.89, and the pooled standard deviation is 1.11 against 0.81 if independent: pooling does not reduce that noise. The construction of the two statistics accounts for the correlation without any appeal to the founder draw: mean_tc_A is the mean of pool-A lines on testers from the current pool B and mean_tc_B the mean of pool-B lines on testers from the current pool A, so both are estimates of the same A x B hybrid level, and progress in either pool raises both (better lines in one statistic, better testers in the other). How much of the correlation is that and how much is the founder draw is not separated here. The gd_A/gd_B and gd_pool_A/gd_pool_B rows are per pool and show the asymmetry between two exchangeable pools that any one set of 48 draws produces; the mean_tc_A/mean_tc_B rows are not per-pool responses, for the reason just given. Table 9.23 says how much of the pools’ loss is selection: the control loses gene diversity too – 6 elites recombined into 12 individuals is a bottleneck whether or not the elites were chosen – and the selected arm’s mean loss exceeds the control’s, with the pooled t just stated as the evidence.
What is inferred: with real meiosis and a dominance trait behind it, the A x B hybrid level responds to reciprocal recurrent selection – both testcross means and the elite factorial’s genetic value measure it – and at this replication that response is beyond t_crit. How much of it each pool contributes is not identified by these statistics: each testcross mean carries the progress of both pools, so a response in pool A alone would raise mean_tc_A and mean_tc_B together. Whether it spends within-pool diversity faster than the same bottleneck under drift alone is an exploratory question (multiplicity above). In this render the pooled gene-diversity t is beyond the unadjusted point for the elite lines and beyond it for the recombined pools, and at least one of them is also beyond the Bonferroni point; the supported reading is therefore that selection spends more within-pool diversity than the bottleneck alone, with the correction. Per founder draw, the ratio of the mean elite-line selection component to its paired standard deviation is 0.6, so a single draw does not settle its sign; the 48-draw t of -4.5 against t_crit = 2.01 is what decides it. Where the sign holds, the control separates the selection component of the loss from the bottleneck (drift) component, within this design. It is not a replication of another chapter’s control: Chapter 23 follows diversity across cycles under a budget alpha against the frozen founding base and has no random-selection arm, and Chapter 22 measures its loss against the programme’s own starting point “rather than against a random-selection baseline of the same size”, as it says there. Chapter 24 has another paired no-selection design, built on the same founder wrapper and measuring a different quantity, the gap between varA and genicVarA. The between-pool rows: the GD_BS difference is beyond t_crit; where it is, and positive, RRS has moved the pools further apart than the control did. Whether that raises heterosis is not tested here. Chapter 5 infers, and says it has not shown, that selection on cross performance is the only process considered there that can move frequencies according to where the dominance is, and that the alignment of divergence with dominance, \(\operatorname{cov}(d, y^2)\) of Section 5.9, is built or eroded cycle by cycle; this chapter computes neither that alignment nor the divergence share of expected heterosis across cycles (the share is computed only across founder split times, in Table 9.18 (a)), so that inference stays untested. F_ST \(= GD_{BS} / GD_T\) moves with its denominator as well, and GD_T of the recombined pools is not recorded in Table 9.22 (a), so GD_BS is the row read for divergence. What limits the inference is the scale – 12 founders per pool, 4 cycles, 2 testers at one location, 48 draws – and, if runMacs2() founders do not repeat from the seed (not established, Step 1), the numbers in this paragraph and any verdict that rests on a t near t_crit may differ between renders.


9.8.4 The final hybrid pool through stage2_select(), unchanged
alphasimr_pipeline() is the loop above without the instrumentation: founders, 4 cycles, then alphasimr_make_hybrids() testcrosses the final cycle’s elites directly against each other – a full factorial between the 6 pool-A elites and 6 pool-B elites, so 36 commercial hybrids – and phenotypes them the same way every testcross in this chapter was phenotyped. alphasimr_to_stage1() then does the bookkeeping that makes this look like any other stage-1 output: it remaps AlphaSimR’s internal line ids into the 1..n_A, n_A+1..n_A+n_B convention hybrids$line_A/line_B and fL use elsewhere in the book, and builds fL by stacking the elite lines from both pools’ genotypes into one matrix and computing a single joint coancestry matrix over all of them – not two separate per-pool matrices – which is what lets theta_pools() and the rest of the pipeline index into pool A and pool B lines with one consistent numbering. Table 9.24 shows both stages.

st1 <- res[["stage1"]]
# the contract holds one row per elite A x B hybrid

sel <- stage2_select(st1[["X"]], st1[["f"]], st1[["hybrids"]], n_sel = n_hyb_sel, fL = st1[["fL"]],
                     verbose = FALSE)
fmt(sel[["metrics"]][, c("scenario", "alpha", "GD", "GD_BS", "F_ST", "index")], 4)

Read as a divergence statistic, not as a measure of heterosis.

title: 9  Simulating a hybrid breeding programme: AlphaSimR from the ground up
section: 9.9 Assumptions, and what this adds over Chapter 6
text:
9.9 Assumptions, and what this adds over Chapter 6
What is more realistic here. Actual recombination and linkage (a genetic map per chromosome, not independent markers), a trait with directional dominance so that testcross selection has something real to select on and heterosis and inbreeding depression have a value, outbred founder pools with a coalescent split behind them, and multi-generation recurrent selection with a paired control rather than one static pool.
What is declared, and where. Steps 2–6 use inbred founders from quickHaplo() with every site a QTL and dominance degrees drawn at meanDD = 0.4, varDD = 0.1; the “pools” of Steps 4 and 6 are two undifferentiated halves of one founder set. Step 7 uses a separate additive founder draw. Step 8 uses outbred founders from runMacs2(split = ), again with every site a QTL; its DH lines are fully inbred, its testers are outbred individuals, and every loss of diversity is measured against the same run’s founders (cycle 0) and against the paired no-selection control – not against a random-subset null of the same size, which is the reference Chapter 16’s alpha uses. Against the labels A1–A8 (listed in Chapter 1; Chapter 8 maps all eight), Step 8 keeps A1 (two heterotic pools), A3 (recycling within pool), A4 (discrete cycles) and, for the trajectory, A6 (measured against the founders of cycle 0); it relaxes A2 for the founders (outbred; the DH lines are fully inbred), A5 (linked sites, every site a QTL) and A7 (directional dominance); A8 does not apply, the chapter runs its own configuration.
What is still simplified. Testers are the first 2 individuals of the current opposite pool, an arbitrary slice by index – not chosen at random or by merit, and not the elite inbred tester a real programme would use; because randCross() recreates each pool every cycle, the testers change from cycle to cycle, so successive cycles’ testcross means are not on a common tester and are comparable only through the pools’ genetic level; there is one phenotyping environment (setPheno()’s error variance, no genotype-by-environment term – Chapter 22 adds one); the population-split coalescent history is a stylised divergence process, not calibrated to a named heterotic-pool pair; doubled-haploid production is instantaneous, skipping the field seasons Step 5 counted; and selection acts on trait 1 only – the 2 traits this chapter’s config simulates are all carried through X/hybrids, but only the first ever enters the GCA ranking. The accuracy prediction of Step 6 is first order in the sample correlation – its finite-tester-pool and sample-variance corrections are applied, its second-order term is not – and the selfing trajectory of Step 5 follows 400 parallel lineages from one cross, checked at seven generations.
Scale. Step 8 runs live at a scale of its own (12 + 12 founders, 750 markers, 4 cycles, 48 paired founder draws). It is not the teaching scale book_cfg of the rest of the book (25 + 25 lines, 2000 markers), nor the default of rrs_config (20 + 20 founders, 500 sites); Steps 2 to 6 use 60 founders and 1000 QTL and Step 7 80 founders. AlphaSimR is fast enough at this size that no caching is needed, unlike the marker-assisted backcrossing (MABC) scans in Chapter 8. Step 8’s numbers may change on re-execution if its founders do (Step 1 does not establish whether runMacs2() founders repeat from the seed); a mean over draws moves by the order of its standard error (the between-draw standard deviation above over the square root of the number of draws), and so may a conclusion that rests on a t near t_crit, which is why the chapter writes each such inference conditionally on the render’s own t. A heavier, production-scale run is inst/scripts/run_alphasimr.R:
Rscript inst/scripts/run_alphasimr.R --test          # smoke run
Rscript inst/scripts/run_alphasimr.R --out=DIR        # full run
It runs alphasimr_pipeline() at a larger configuration, feeds the resulting hybrid pool through stage2_select(), and writes the cycle trajectory and selection metrics as CSVs.

title: 9  Simulating a hybrid breeding programme: AlphaSimR from the ground up
text:
9.10 Where this connects
Chapter 6 and Step 8 build the same three-object contract from two different generative models – the fast one and the realistic one – which is the point of drawing that seam where the book does: everything past it, build_ctx() through stage2_select(), cannot tell which one it is looking at. Chapter 5 is the algebra Steps 3, 4 and 6 verify against AlphaSimR: inbreeding depression against genParam(), expected heterosis against a full factorial, and the GCA/SCA decomposition against the exact combining abilities. Chapter 4 supplies the breeder’s equation Step 6 checks and the index theory Step 7 uses; Chapter 24 is where Step 3’s varA-against-genicVarA gap becomes the subject rather than a diagnostic. Chapter 3 supplies the partition Step 8 measures across split and across cycles. Chapter 23 follows gene diversity across cycles under a diversity budget alpha with the package’s own faster simulator. Step 8 has no such budget (its control is random elites, not a constraint), so it does not cross-check that chapter’s alpha result; it measures the same quantity, gene diversity of the pools across cycles, under unconstrained selection on a simulator with real meiosis. Chapter 24 builds its linked arm on the alphasimr_founder_pools() wrapper of this step, and takes the varA against genicVarA gap of Step 3 as the quantity it then measures across cycles.
Chapter 22, in the Evidence and practice part, is the other half of the method: the same primitives assembled into an inbred-line programme with staged yield trials, where the question is not which hybrids to sell but how fast a variety pipeline can run and what it spends to run faster.
This closes the Simulation part. The Metrics and prediction part that follows turns from generating populations to measuring their diversity, starting with Chapter 10.

title: 10  Diversity metrics in the genomic era
text:
10.1 The programme this chapter is written for
A diversity metric can only be judged against a population whose drift and inbreeding are known independently of the metric. The live examples of this chapter use two things from the Simulation part, the lines and hybrids of simulate_lines() and simulate_data() (Chapter 6), which are the candidate set of every selection in this chapter, and one frequency-level drift model, pool_traj() of Section 10.7.4, written here. The F4 panels of Chapter 7, the backcross populations of Chapter 8 and the AlphaSimR cycles of Chapter 9 are not measured in this chapter: they depart from assumptions A2 and A5 of Section 10.1, and A1-A8 are this chapter’s list, not a list the Simulation part uses (Chapter 7 and Chapter 8 map their departures onto it; Chapter 6 and Chapter 9 do not).
In classical theory, inbreeding measured as loss of heterozygosity and inbreeding measured as drift of allele frequencies are the same thing. Meuwissen et al. (2020) show that inside genomic optimal-contribution schemes they stop being the same thing, and can diverge badly, whenever diversity is controlled through identity by state (IBS) on a marker panel. Only when control is through identity by descent (IBD) is the classical equivalence restored.
The practical consequence is uncomfortable:
If you constrain \(\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{c}'\mathbf{G}\mathbf{c}\) using a VanRaden \(\mathbf{G}\) (VanRaden 2008), you are constraining drift. The loss of heterozygosity in your germplasm may be running at a different rate, in either direction, from the one you believe you are controlling.
This chapter is written for one kind of programme, stated in full in Section 10.1: an allogamous, maize-type hybrid programme running reciprocal recurrent selection over two heterotic pools. The first half defines the metrics; the second half is the sequence of steps that puts them into a cycle report, with the check and the failure mode of each step.
Every number in this chapter is computed under these assumptions. They are declared here because several of the results are false outside them. Chapter 1 describes the programme itself, stage by stage; this section states only what every number in this chapter assumes about it.
A1. The species is allogamous and the product is an F1 hybrid. Maize-type: two heterotic pools, A and B, crossed to produce single-cross hybrids. The commercial product carries the heterozygosity; the parents do not. Nothing here is addressed to a self-pollinated crop whose product is a line, and nothing here is addressed to a programme whose commercial unit is a synthetic or a population cross – both change which quantity is the product and therefore which loss matters.
A2. Parent lines are fully inbred, by doubled-haploid (DH) induction or by selfing to fixation. This is a property of the programme, not of the mating system: an allogamous crop bred for hybrids still delivers inbred parents. In this simulation the lines are homozygous at every locus, which the coancestry kernel reports exactly (Table 10.1):
Show code
inb <- c(het_fraction_lines   = mean(L / 2 == 0.5),
         self_coancestry_min  = min(diag(molecular_coancestry(L / 2))),
         het_fraction_F1      = mean(ctx$X == 0.5),
         twice_GD_WI_hyb      = 2 * gd_partition(seq_len(ctx$N), ctx)[["GD_WI_hyb"]])
stopifnot(inb[["het_fraction_lines"]] == 0, inb[["self_coancestry_min"]] == 1,
          isTRUE(all.equal(inb[["het_fraction_F1"]], inb[["twice_GD_WI_hyb"]])))
fmt(as.data.frame(t(inb)), 6)

The first two are asserted equal to 0 and 1 and the last two equal to each other. Dimensionless, six decimals.

Line heterozygosity is zero and every line’s self-coancestry is 1, so individual-level inbreeding coefficients are 1 by construction and carry no management information. The F1s carry 0.362 of their loci heterozygous, and that fraction is exactly twice GD_WI_hyb – the identity Section 5.5 derives (Equation 5.7). The manageable quantity is therefore an allele frequency in a pool, never a homozygosity within an individual. Every later section is computed on frequencies.
A3. Germplasm is recycled within pool; only information crosses the pool boundary. Lines are chosen on hybrid performance against the opposite pool and recycled inside their own pool, the loop Section 1.1 describes stage by stage. (Comstock et al. (1949) is the paper the book cites for the tester-based scheme; this chapter takes nothing from it beyond its existence and title, “A breeding procedure designed to make maximum use of both general and specific combining ability”, as Section 5.11 does.) A DH taken from an \(A \times B\) F1 would be a blend of both pools and would destroy the heterotic pattern, so it never happens. run_cycles() in Chapter 23 implements this loop in reduced form: recycling is driven by line usage in the selected hybrids, with no trials and no S3, and the index known without error (its assumptions C7 and C8 in Chapter 23, which Section 1.1 also states).
A4. Cycles are discrete. Pool sizes are constant across cycles and no generation overlap is modelled. Real programmes overlap cycles and reuse the same line for years, which makes a cycle index a poor clock for any \(\Delta F\) read off it. This book neither models nor measures that bias, and no later chapter treats it; it is a limit of every rate reported here, not a result.
A5. Markers are biallelic, coded \(0/0.5/1\) as the frequency of the reference allele within the individual. Whether they are neutral depends on which simulator produced them and on which row of a table reads them; the statement “markers are neutral” is not made without that qualification, and it is not true of this chapter’s own data in general. Three cases:
A consequence stated as a limit of this chapter: wherever simulate_data() is the source, the marker panel and the set of causal loci are the same set. The gap between a marker panel and the causal loci it samples (the marker-versus-QTL gap) is not modelled and not measured here; the only treatment of it in this chapter is the report of the four panels of Meuwissen et al. (2020) (their Methods), none of which is reproduced.
Markers are in linkage equilibrium within pool in the founding draw, because each line’s genotype is drawn independently per locus (simulate_lines()); lines recycled under A3 share ancestors, and that independence no longer describes them. Linkage equilibrium makes the audit step of Section 10.7.5 a best case, and that is said again where the number is reported.
A6. The frequency base \(p_0\) is frozen at the founding cycle and never recomputed. This is ctx$p0, computed by build_ctx() at the founding cycle and stored. Section 10.7.1 is that step and measures what happens without it.
A7. No dominance enters any metric in this chapter. \(\theta\), gene diversity \(GD = 1 - \theta\) and \(\alpha\) are functions of allele frequencies alone. The dominance side of the same germplasm – what the divergence between pools is worth in heterosis – is Chapter 5, and the two must not be mixed inside one constraint.
A8. The scale is the book’s teaching scale: 25 + 25 lines, 2000 markers, 625 hybrids in the full factorial. Two other scales are named in this book and no chunk of this chapter runs either: the programme size the package declares as production (71 + 71 lines, 25000 markers; R/00_data.R), and the sim_config default that inst/scripts/ run (50 + 50 lines, 5000 markers), which several chapters also call the production scale. Where a result is scale-dependent, it says so.

text:
Frequency-level toys (pool_traj() of Section 10.7.4, the minor-allele-frequency (MAF) weight rule of Table 10.11): no trait exists, so nothing is selected on one. Neutral by construction.
Selections on ctx <- simulate_data(book_cfg): that simulator draws a marker effect on each of three traits at every marker (Chapter 6). The truncation, balanced (w = 1), capped and index-weighted selections select on an index of those traits, so the markers their metrics read are themselves under selection. The max-diversity plan (w = 0) never reads the index, but its metrics are still read on markers that carry trait effects.
run_cycles() of Chapter 23 does not use simulate_data(): it draws simulate_pools() with a finite number of quantitative trait loci (QTL; n_qtl = 300 by default).

title: 10  Diversity metrics in the genomic era
section: 10.3 The metrics, one at a time
text:
10.3 The metrics, one at a time

10.3.1 Rate of inbreeding and effective size
What you manage is not \(F\) but its rate of accumulation, Equation 10.1. \(F\) is a stock; \(\Delta F\) is a flow.
\[\Delta F = \frac{F_t - F_{t-1}}{1 - F_{t-1}}, \qquad N_e = \frac{1}{2\Delta F} \tag{10.1}\]
with \(F_t \in (-\infty, 1]\) the inbreeding coefficient of cycle \(t\) against the frozen base (negative values are possible for \(F_{hom}\), see Section 10.3.2), \(\Delta F\) the per-cycle rate and \(N_e\) the effective size it implies (Falconer and Mackay 1996, Ch. 3-4).
Since \(1 - F_t = (1 - \Delta F)^t\), a regression of \(\log(1 - F_t)\) on \(t\) has slope \(\log(1 - \Delta F)\), so \(\Delta F = 1 - e^{\text{slope}}\) and \(-\text{slope}\) is only its first-order approximation. The linearity of that regression is itself a diagnostic: in Meuwissen et al. (2020), \(\log(1 - F_{drift})\) was approximately linear under every scheme, while \(\log(1 - F_{hom})\) showed marked curvature under some, notably the one based on runs of homozygosity (ROH). Curvature means a non-constant rate – your \(N_e\) target is not being met steadily.
A tropical maize recurrent programme targeting \(N_e = 50\) per cycle needs \(\Delta F = 0.01\). Measuring \(F\) only at cycle 8 and dividing by 8 hides the possibility that cycles 1-3 were conservative and cycles 6-8 collapsed the base. Section 10.7.4 fits the regression on a case where the answer is known in advance, and then on one where the diagnostic has to fire.


10.3.2 F_hom, homozygosity-based
The inbreeding coefficient \(F\) (Wright 1922) is, in its classical definition, the correlation between uniting gametes (the standard wording; it was not checked against Wright (1922), which this book has not read: UNVERIFIED). Under random drift in a closed population its consequence is \(H_t = H_0(1 - F_t)\), so \(F\) is the proportional loss of heterozygosity relative to the base (Falconer and Mackay 1996, Ch. 3). The homozygosity lens takes that consequence as its definition – the fraction of heterozygosity already lost relative to the base, Equation 10.2:
\[F_{hom} = 1 - \frac{1}{m}\sum_k \frac{2p_{t,k}(1 - p_{t,k})}{2p_{0,k}(1 - p_{0,k})}
          = 1 - \frac{1}{m}\sum_k \frac{H_{t,k}}{H_{0,k}} \tag{10.2}\]
with \(p_{t,k} \in [0,1]\) the frequency of the reference allele at marker \(k\) in the population being scored, \(p_{0,k} \in (0,1)\) the same frequency in the frozen base, \(H = 2p(1-p)\) the expected heterozygosity under random mating, and \(m\) the number of markers (written \(N_{SNP}\) in Meuwissen et al. (2020), their Eq. 1A, where it is the total marker count; the book’s \(m\) is used throughout). This book restricts the sum to markers polymorphic in the base, because \(H_{0,k} = 0\) makes the ratio undefined otherwise – freq_metrics() does that with keep <- ctx$p0 > eps & ctx$p0 < 1 - eps, so \(m\) then counts the markers kept – and the restriction changes nothing against their result, since their own panels were random samples of loci already segregating in the base population.
It can be negative. If management pushes frequencies toward 0.5, heterozygosity rises above the base and the “inbreeding coefficient” goes below zero. That is not a numerical error: it is the expected behaviour of any scheme that maximises heterozygosity on the monitored panel.
It protects against inbreeding depression and the expression of deleterious recessives in homozygosis. It is the right lens when the dominant risk is vigour – in this programme, the vigour of the segregating crossing block and not of the fixed lines, which is a narrower claim than it looks and is qualified at the end of this section.

10.3.2.1 What this lens is computed on, and what it is not
\(F_{hom}\) as freq_metrics() computes it takes \(p_t\) from colMeans(X[idx, ]): the reference-allele frequency of the merged hybrid set. With inbred parents that merged frequency is \(\bar p = (\tilde p_A + \tilde p_B)/2\), with \(\tilde p_A\) and \(\tilde p_B\) the two pools’ frequencies weighted by the line usage the selection induces. So the \(He\) column of the same call is \(\overline{2\bar p(1 - \bar p)}\), which is \(GD_T = 1 - \bar f\) of the Caballero & Toro partition (Caballero and Toro 2002) (Chapter 3, Equation 3.9) identically, not approximately: \(\bar f = (\theta_A + 2\theta_{AB} +
\theta_B)/4 = \overline{\bar p^2 + (1 - \bar p)^2}\) under A2.
That is gene diversity of the notional merged pool, and it is not the heterozygosity of the product. The realised F1 heterozygosity is \(2\,GD_{WI\text{-}hyb}\) – exactly, by the self-coancestry identity of assumption A2 – and on the full factorial it equals \(GD_T + GD_{BS}\), the between-pool component counted twice (Equation 5.7 of Section 5.5, which also states its limit on selected subsets). The difference between the two quantities is therefore \(GD_{BS}\), which the \(F_{hom}\) lens does not carry, and which moves with the selection (Table 10.3 for the merged-pool quantities, Table 10.4 for the hybrid-level ones):

Two identities hold to machine precision in Table 10.3 and Table 10.4, and the stopifnot() enforces both on every render: \(He = GD_T\), and the realised F1 heterozygosity equals \(2\,GD_{WI\text{-}hyb}\). The third comparison is not an identity on a selected subset: \(GD_T + GD_{BS}\) departs from the realised heterozygosity by at most 0.0043 across these four rows, because \(GD_T\) and \(GD_{BS}\) are computed from line-usage weights – what a random re-pairing of the selected parents would give – while \(GD_{WI\text{-}hyb}\) scores the pairs actually chosen (Chapter 5 states the same limit from the other side).
Now read the ranking. The table has three distinct plans, not four: balanced (w = 1) returns exactly the truncation set, as Section 10.7.2 shows, so the two rows are identical in every column of both tables. On this candidate set (data seed 1) truncation has the highest \(F_{hom}\) of the three, 0.0426, which is 9.4 null s.d. above the resampled mean of 0.0069 and on the usual reading is “most heterozygosity lost”. Its realised F1 heterozygosity is 0.3646 against a null mean of 0.3617, z = 2.51, reached or exceeded by 0.3% of the 1000 resampled subsets. That is one founder draw, and the unit of replication of this simulation is the founder draw, so the sign of that z is tested on twenty of them in Table 10.6 before anything is inferred from it.

Result. Over the twenty draws the z of the truncation selection’s realised F1 heterozygosity ranges from -4.47 to 3.9; it is negative in 7 of 20, above 2 in 4 and below \(-2\) in 2. Data seed 1, the draw used everywhere else in this chapter, is one of the positive ones. The \(F_{hom}\) z of truncation is above 0 on 20 of 20 draws (smallest 3.7), and the z of the max-diversity plan’s realised F1 heterozygosity is above 0 on 20 of 20 (smallest 5.8).
Interpretation. The measurements support two statements and no third. (i) \(F_{hom}\) and realised F1 heterozygosity are different quantities and can disagree strongly: on data seed 1 the max-diversity plan has \(F_{hom}\) at z = -4.8 and F1 heterozygosity at z = 7.8, and truncation has a high \(F_{hom}\) z on every draw while its F1 heterozygosity z changes sign across draws. (ii) Whether truncation on the index leaves the hybrids more or less heterozygous than random subsets has no consistent sign at this scale: it depends on the founder draw, split as the counts of Table 10.6 show. The statement that truncation hybrids are more heterozygous than random ones, and the mechanism that would explain it (the \(A \times B\) pairs kept being more heterozygous than random pairs), are therefore not claimed. The random row, a single subset, sits at z = -0.88 on the same column and is no control either. What limits these inferences is the number of draws (20), the scale (25 + 25 lines, 2000 markers) and the single subset size of 60; none was varied. \(GD_{BS}\) is not evidence on the pairs actually kept: it is computed from line-usage weights, not from the pairs (Section 10.3.2). On data seed 1 it ranks truncation and the max-diversity plan in the opposite order to F1 heterozygosity – truncation \(GD_{BS}\) at z = 27.4 against F1 heterozygosity at z = 2.51, the max-diversity plan \(GD_{BS}\) at z = 0.47 against z = 7.85 – and the rise of \(GD_{BS}\) under truncation is the usage-concentration effect Section 10.7.6 derives, measured there on this one draw only.
Within a heterotic pool under reciprocal recurrent selection, \(F_{hom}\) on the pool’s own frequencies is still the right lens for one thing, and that one thing is narrower than it is usually stated to be. It is the segregating crossing block, which is not inbred and in which inbreeding depression is therefore expressed: \(ID = 2F\sum_k d_k p_k q_k\) (Falconer and Mackay 1996, Ch. 14), with \(d_k\) the dominance effect at locus \(k\), \(p_k\) and \(q_k = 1 - p_k\) the pool’s current frequencies, and \(F \in [0,1]\) the block’s inbreeding coefficient relative to random mating at those same current frequencies – which is not the \(F_t\) of this chapter’s two lenses, measured against the frozen base \(p_0\), and the two must not be substituted for one another. Section 5.6 verifies that quantity against heterosis_partition()’s shared term. It is built from the same per-locus product \(p_k q_k\) that \(F_{hom}\) aggregates – but weighted by \(d_k\), which \(F_{hom}\) does not carry, so \(F_{hom}\) locates the erosion and does not price it.
It does not anticipate the per-se value of the inbred lines themselves. Under A2 a line has no heterozygous locus, so its dominance contribution is exactly zero whatever the pool’s frequencies are – Section 5.6 measures that exact zero – and a fully homozygous genotype’s value is therefore the additive sum \(\sum_k a_k (2x_{ik} - 1)\) alone, the genotypic-value model of Chapter 5 with \(x_{ik} \in \{0, 1\}\) at every locus and \(a_k\) the per-locus additive effect. Its pool mean moves with the frequencies in whichever direction they move, so there is no directional decline there for \(F_{hom}\) to anticipate. It also says nothing about between-pool divergence (Chapter 5). Computed instead on the homozygosity of individual inbred parents it is 1 by construction – assumption A2 – and is useless for management. The mating system of the species does not rescue that: an inbred maize line is as fixed as an inbred wheat line. What distinguishes the hybrid programme is that the pool of lines can be intermated, so the pool has a frequency vector worth managing even though none of its members does.



10.3.3 F_drift, drift-based
\[F_{drift} = \frac{1}{m}\sum_k \frac{(p_{t,k} - p_{0,k})^2}{p_{0,k}(1 - p_{0,k})} \tag{10.3}\]
with the same symbols as Equation 10.2.
Never negative. It has the algebraic form of the standardised-variance definition of \(F_{ST}\) – a variance of allele frequencies divided by \(p_0(1-p_0)\) – which is how Meuwissen et al. (2020) relate it (“similar to the definition of \(F_{ST}\)”, their text after Eq. 1B, citing Holsinger and Weir (2009), who separate that definition from the several other quantities carrying the same name). The priority of that form is not claimed here, and no paper of Wright’s is cited for it. \(F_{drift}\) differs from it in what is partitioned, not in the form: here the variance is of one population’s frequencies through time around the frozen base \(p_0\), in the other it is of a set of populations in space around their mean. The \(F_{ST}\) column of this chapter is the spatial one; it is defined once, and distinguished from \(F_{BN}\) and from Fst_Wright, in Section 10.7.6 (Table 10.30). \(F_{drift}\) is exactly the quantity constrained when G_VR2 goes into the optimiser.
It protects against random change in phenotypic value for traits outside the selection objective, against rare deleterious recessives rising to dangerous frequencies, and against irreversible loss of rare alleles.
It must not be read as a measure of this programme’s selection intensity, even though Meuwissen et al. (2020) offer exactly that reading for a locus under directional selection. They call \(\delta p^2/[p_0(1-p_0)]\) “an approximation to the squared total intensity (\(i^2\)) applied to the marker” (citing Liu and Woolliams (2010) for the underlying non-linearity), and where the only thing moving frequencies is truncation selection on a trait, that reading is theirs to make. But \(F_{drift}\) is accumulated over every source of displacement a scheme has – selection, pure drift, and a diversity constraint that pushes frequencies on its own – and the three are not separable from the statistic alone. Section 10.7.4 runs a crossing block with no selection of any kind and \(F_{drift}\) climbs across the cycles to a value the step reports, which under an unconditional intensity reading would be a large intensity applied by nothing; Section 10.7.2’s max_div plan moves \(F_{drift}\) by minimising coancestry, not by selecting on any trait. Even where selection is the only driver, the displacement is not a function of frequency alone: it depends on the average effect of a gene substitution at that locus, \(a + d\,(q - p)\) (Falconer and Mackay 1996, Ch. 7) – classically written \(\alpha\), which in this book is the diversity-loss statistic instead (Chapter 5 says the same) – and on the phenotypic standard deviation of the trait under selection, neither of which appears anywhere in \(F_{drift}\). So an intensity read off F_drift alone, with no independent knowledge of what moved it, cannot be trusted, and this chapter does not attempt one. What constraining F_drift does constrain is the squared displacement of the genome from its base, whatever moved it.
A programme running six cycles of genomic selection with a VanRaden \(\mathbf{G}\) and reporting \(\Delta F \approx 1\%\) has reported \(\Delta F_{drift}\) on the training panel. Quantitative disease-resistance loci not yet prioritised may have hitch-hiked to extreme frequencies alongside yield QTL, and none of that appears in the reported metric.

text:
10.4 The classical equivalence, and the covariance that destroys it
Under purely random drift, with \(E[\delta p_t \mid p_0] = 0\) for every \(p_0\),
\[\frac{\mathrm{var}(p_{t,k})}{p_0(1-p_0)} = 1 - \frac{H_t}{H_0}
  \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; F_{drift} = F_{hom}.\]
The paper’s central result, Equation 10.4, quantifies the departure:
\[F_{hom} - F_{drift} \;=\; 2\,\mathrm{cov}\!\left(
  \frac{\delta p_{t,k}}{\sqrt{p_{0,k}(1-p_{0,k})}},\;
  \frac{p_{0,k} - 1/2}{\sqrt{p_{0,k}(1-p_{0,k})}}\right) \tag{10.4}\]
(Meuwissen et al. 2020, their Eq. 3), where \(\delta p_{t,k} = p_{t,k} - p_{0,k}\) and the covariance is taken over markers with divisor \(m\) – which is why freq_metrics() computes it as 2 * mean(x * y) and not with cov(). The two differ for two independent reasons: stats::cov() divides by \(m - 1\), and \(\overline{xy} = \mathrm{cov}_{N}(x, y) + \bar x\,\bar y\), so the product term vanishes only if one of the two means is zero – either will do, and neither is zero here.
In words: if the direction of frequency change is correlated with the starting frequency, the two measures diverge. The non-obvious part is that this covariance is induced by the diversity management itself, not by directional selection – Meuwissen et al. (2020) demonstrate this by running the scheme with random genomic estimated breeding values (GEBVs), and the divergence persists.

10.4.1 Verifying the identity
freq_metrics() returns all three quantities – Equation 10.2, Equation 10.3 and Equation 10.4 – in one marker sweep. The identity is asserted in tests/testthat/test-lenses.R; here it is on live data (Table 10.7, Table 10.8):

set.seed(31)
idx <- sample.int(ctx$N, 60)
fm <- freq_metrics(idx, ctx)
fmt(as.data.frame(t(fm[c("F_hom", "F_drift", "cov_diag")])), 6)

WarningYour minor-allele-frequency (MAF) spectrum decides how bad this is



Meuwissen et al. (2020) state this as an expectation rather than as a measured comparison: “the covariance generated is expected to be larger for WGS [whole-genome sequence] data where allele frequencies are extreme with typical MAF close to 0, than for SNP [single-nucleotide polymorphism] (chip) panels where allele frequencies are generally closer to 1/2” (their second Conclusion bullet), having observed that the strength of the covariance “depends on the distribution of \((p_0 - \tfrac12)\)” (their Discussion). Their own simulation used four panels, all random samples of the same WGS data (a SNP panel for best linear unbiased prediction (SNP-BLUP), a neutral panel, a QTL panel and a second management panel) – none a SNP chip – so the comparison across a WGS panel and a chip panel is an inference from the algebra of Equation 10.4 and not a result of their experiment either.
The algebra can be made a number, which is worth doing because it decides whether G_VR2 is usable. Apply one deterministic management rule – move every frequency 5% of the way toward 0.5, the caricature of a heterozygosity-maximising constraint used again in Section 10.7.4 – to a sequence-like panel whose folded site-frequency spectrum has density proportional to \(1/[p(1-p)]\), and then to MAF-filtered subsets of the same draw (Table 10.11):


Show code
set.seed(21)
# Folded site-frequency spectrum with density proportional to 1/[p(1-p)] on
# [1e-3, 1 - 1e-3]: the logit of p is uniform. One draw, filtered four ways.
p_seq <- plogis(runif(2e5, qlogis(1e-3), qlogis(1 - 1e-3)))
maf_row <- function(floor, pull = 0.05) {
  p0 <- p_seq[pmin(p_seq, 1 - p_seq) >= floor]
  p1 <- p0 + pull * (0.5 - p0)                 # the rule, applied exactly
  s2 <- p0 * (1 - p0)
  c(maf_floor = floor, markers = length(p0),
    kappa = mean((p0 - 0.5)^2 / s2),           # the panel's own weight
    F_hom = 1 - mean(p1 * (1 - p1) / s2),
    F_drift = mean((p1 - p0)^2 / s2),
    cov_diag = 2 * mean((p0 - 0.5) * (p1 - p0) / s2))
}
mafw <- as.data.frame(t(sapply(c(0.001, 0.01, 0.05, 0.20), maf_row)))
# Under this rule all three lenses are multiples of one panel statistic, kappa.
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(mafw$F_drift, 0.05^2 * mafw$kappa)),
          isTRUE(all.equal(mafw$cov_diag, -2 * 0.05 * mafw$kappa)))
keep0  <- ctx$p0 > 1e-6 & ctx$p0 < 1 - 1e-6        # as freq_metrics() drops them
kappa_book <- mean((ctx$p0[keep0] - 0.5)^2 / (ctx$p0[keep0] * (1 - ctx$p0[keep0])))
# kappa of the ancestral U(0.05, 0.95) draw of simulate_lines(), by quadrature.
kappa_anc <- stats::integrate(function(p) (p - 0.5)^2 / (p * (1 - p)) / 0.9,
                              0.05, 0.95)$value
fmt(mafw, 4)

Under a rule of this form \(\delta p = c\,(0.5 - p_0)\) the algebra is exact: \(F_{drift} = c^2 \kappa\) and cov_diag \(= -2c\kappa\) with \(\kappa = \overline{(p_0 - 0.5)^2 / [p_0(1-p_0)]}\), the panel statistic the stopifnot() of Table 10.11 verifies. Everything about the panel enters through \(\kappa\), and \(\kappa\) is 32.4 times larger at a MAF floor of 0.001 than at 0.05 on the same draw: cov_diag moves from -3.577 to -0.111 for the same 5% pull. For reference, this book’s own hybrid panel has \(\kappa =\) 1.27 over the 1934 markers polymorphic in the base, which sits at the chip-like end of that table – the ancestral \(U(0.05, 0.95)\) draw of simulate_lines() alone gives \(\kappa =\) 0.64, about half of it, and the rest comes from the Balding-Nichols divergence at \(F_{BN}\) = 0.15 and the finite sample of lines per pool (not decomposed further here); none of it is biological.
Translated to plants, as a stated expectation and not as a measurement on real germplasm: genotyping-by-sequencing (GBS) or skim-seq retaining the full spectrum puts a programme at the high-\(\kappa\) end; a 20-50k chip filtered to MAF > 0.05 puts it at the low-\(\kappa\) end. The rule of Table 10.11 is a caricature, not an optimiser, so the ratio between panels is the transferable part and the absolute values are not.

10.5 The other matrices, briefly
F_IBD via G_LA. Instead of assuming a 50/50 transmission probability for each parental allele (as the pedigree matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) does), linkage analysis over the markers infers which parental haplotype was actually transmitted along the chromosome. It requires pedigree and markers. It measures IBD relative to a base explicitly defined as unrelated and non-inbred, so frequency change is determined by the base population rather than by linkage disequilibrium generated during selection – and the problematic covariance disappears. It was the only scheme tested that met both the \(\Delta F_{hom}\) and \(\Delta F_{drift}\) targets, on the managed panel and at unmonitored neutral loci. On gain it was not the highest in absolute terms; what Meuwissen et al. (2020) report is that at the same averaged inbreeding – interpolating each scheme’s gain to the mean of \(F_{hom}\) and \(F_{drift}\) – G_LA beat \(\mathbf{A}\) in 65 of 100 replicates and G_ROH in 62 of 100 (their Genetic Gain section).
For a hybrid programme this is the point of greatest friction, and also the one where the news is best. In biparental populations and backcross families G_LA is natural and cheap – phase is known and the number of meioses since the base is small. In a maize recurrent-selection population with a complete recycling pedigree – which a programme that records the F1 parents of every DH line has – it is feasible. In a germplasm panel without pedigree it is inapplicable, and the honest alternative is segment-based IBD.
F_ROH. A run of homozygosity is an uninterrupted stretch of homozygous markers; the logic is that many consecutive markers are unlikely to be IBS by chance, so the stretch is probably IBD. The fundamental ambiguity is that F_ROH is IBD when runs are long (recent inbreeding) and homozygosity when they are short (ancient inbreeding, accumulated IBS). The minimum-length threshold is therefore a knob that selects the age of inbreeding you are measuring, and there is no well-defined reference base.
Empirically, G_ROH behaved more like G_0.5 than like an IBD measure. It also is not guaranteed positive semi-definite – its elements are computed pairwise – and required substantial diagonal additions for inversion, which made it diagonally dominant and artificially inflated the number of parents selected.
In an inbred parent line the entire genome is one ROH and \(F_{ROH} \approx 1\): the metric saturates for exactly the reason assumption A2 makes every individual-level coefficient useless. Applied instead to the hybrids, or to the segregating crossing block from which DH lines are induced, it is useful for diagnosing erosion of an elite pool. For management inside an optimiser, check positive definiteness carefully – Section 10.7.7 shows the check.

Table 10.12 summarises how each of the seven matrices behaved in the optimiser of Meuwissen et al. (2020).

10.6 Reference results
Target \(\Delta F = 0.005\) per generation (\(N_e = 100\)). Values at the unmonitored neutral loci (their Panel N), generation 20, as reported by Meuwissen et al. (2020). Table 10.13 transcribes four columns and derives one:

dF_hom, dF_drift and gap are the three Panel N columns of their Table 2. gap is the level \(F_{hom} - F_{drift}\) reached in generation 20, not a rate and not a difference of the two rate columns; it is cov_diag of Equation 10.4 accumulated over the 20 generations. Their reported standard errors are \(< 2.5 \times 10^{-5}\) on the rates and \(< 2.2 \times 10^{-4}\) on gap.
gain is their Table 3: cumulative genetic gain after 20 generations, expressed in units of the initial genetic standard deviation, standard errors \(\le 0.004\).

(2020) use: their own interpolation (Genetic Gain section, their Figure 5) compares gains at a common generation-20 level of averaged inbreeding, \((F_{hom} + F_{drift})/2\) from their Table 3 – a stock – not at a common mean of the two rate columns used here. gain_per_dF is offered only as a same-chapter summary of Table 10.13, and reading 1 of this list states explicitly which ordering it does and does not support.

Four readings:

No IBS scheme met both targets; the IBD scheme G_LA met both, the targets being ceilings (Meuwissen et al. 2020, Conclusion). On Panel N its dF_drift is 2% under 0.005 (their Table 2 gives the same 0.0049 for Panel M, not transcribed here, and their text states “within 2% of the target for both Panels M and N”) and its dF_hom 14% under it (0.0043 against 0.005). At equal mean inbreeding, G_LA beat \(\mathbf{A}\) in 65 of 100 replicates and G_ROH in 62 of 100.

Those are animal-breeding numbers under the assumptions of Section 10.9, and none of them is reproduced here. What follows is.

10.7 The monitoring protocol
Seven steps, in the order a cycle report is assembled. Each one names the function to call, the quantity to check, and what a failure looks like.

10.7.1 Step 1 – Freeze \(p_0\) at the founding cycle
Both lenses are ratios to a base, so the base is the first thing a cycle report has to pin down. In this book it is ctx$p0, the allele frequencies of the candidate set, computed in build_ctx() at cycle 0 and overwritten, with ctx$maf_pop, by the stored cycle-0 values at every later cycle (run_cycles() does this in cycle_ctx(); see the Call of this step).
At the hybrid level the base is not a free choice: on the full factorial it is the average of the two pool bases, exactly (Table 10.14).


Show code
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(ctx$p0, as.vector((P0["A", ] + P0["B", ]) / 2))))
# Unequal pool sizes, still a complete factorial: each pool-A line appears in
# n_pool_B hybrids and each pool-B line in n_pool_A, so the internal weight
# stays uniform within each pool and the identity is untouched.
cfg_u <- utils::modifyList(book_cfg, list(n_pool_A = 10, n_pool_B = 40))
ctx_u <- simulate_data(cfg_u)
Pu    <- pool_freqs(simulate_lines(cfg_u) / 2,
                    rep(c("A", "B"), c(cfg_u$n_pool_A, cfg_u$n_pool_B)))
# A balanced INCOMPLETE factorial -- not the full n_A*n_B hybrids, but each
# line still used equally often within its own pool (a cyclic 1-to-3 design,
# the shape of a real NCII): the identity does not need completeness.
k <- 3
idx_bal <- unlist(lapply(seq_len(book_cfg$n_pool_A), function(a) {
  bpart <- ((a - 1 + 0:(k - 1)) %% book_cfg$n_pool_B) + 1
  which(ctx$ped$a == a & ctx$ped$b %in% (bpart + book_cfg$n_pool_A))
}))
p_bal <- colMeans(ctx$X[idx_bal, , drop = FALSE])
# "every line used exactly k times": the balance the identity needs
stopifnot(all(table(c(ctx$ped$a[idx_bal], ctx$ped$b[idx_bal])) == k))
# An UNbalanced candidate set with concentrated line usage: it is not.
p_sub <- colMeans(ctx$X[sel_truncation(ctx, 60), , drop = FALSE])
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(ctx_u$p0, as.vector((Pu["A", ] + Pu["B", ]) / 2))),
          isTRUE(all.equal(p_bal, as.vector((P0["A", ] + P0["B", ]) / 2))))
data.frame(max_abs_deviation = formatC(c(
  complete_balanced      = max(abs(ctx$p0 - (P0["A", ] + P0["B", ]) / 2)),
  complete_unequal_pools = max(abs(ctx_u$p0 - (Pu["A", ] + Pu["B", ]) / 2)),
  incomplete_balanced    = max(abs(p_bal - (P0["A", ] + P0["B", ]) / 2)),
  truncation_subset      = max(abs(p_sub - (P0["A", ] + P0["B", ]) / 2))), digits = 3, format = "g"))

Each pool-A line appears in 25 hybrids and each pool-B line in 25, so a column mean over the factorial is \((p_A + p_B)/2\) with no weighting left over. Two consequences a breeder should read off this identity. First, freezing \(p_0\) at the hybrid level freezes both pool bases jointly, so the hybrid-level lenses cannot attribute erosion to one pool – that is Section 10.7.6’s job. Second – and this is the part that is easy to state wrongly – what the identity requires is uniform line usage within each pool, not completeness of the factorial as such. With 10 lines in one pool against 40 in the other, still complete, the identity holds to \(1.1 \times 10^{-16}\). It holds just as exactly (\(1.1 \times 10^{-16}\)) on a balanced but incomplete factorial – 75 of the 625 possible hybrids, each line used exactly 3 times, the shape of a real North Carolina Design II (NCII) – because each pool’s lines are still used equally often within that pool. What re-weights the two pools inside the base is unequal line usage, which a balanced partial factorial does not have and a selected subset typically does: the column means of the 60-hybrid truncation set depart from \((p_A + p_B)/2\) by up to 0.313 on a single marker, because truncation concentrates hybrids on a few high-value lines in each pool. A base computed on a set with unequal line usage is therefore a different base – which is the failure mode of the truncation_subset row of Table 10.14, and not a property of the design being a factorial or not.
Now the failure mode. build_ctx() recomputes p0 <- colMeans(X) on every call, so rebuilding the context from the selected hybrids each cycle – which is what re-running a G-construction function per cycle amounts to – re-anchors the base on the population you were about to measure (Table 10.15):


Show code

Xs     <- ctx$X[i_md, , drop = FALSE]
rebase <- build_ctx(X = Xs, f = molecular_coancestry(Xs), G = NULL,
                    traits = ctx$traits[i_md, , drop = FALSE],
                    ped = ctx$ped[i_md, ], n_lines = ctx$n_lines,
                    pool = ctx$pool, fL = ctx$fL, cfg = NULL)
rb <- rbind(frozen_base = freq_metrics(i_md, ctx)[c("F_hom", "F_drift", "cov_diag")],
            rebased     = freq_metrics(seq_along(i_md), rebase)[c("F_hom", "F_drift", "cov_diag")])
stopifnot(all(abs(rb["rebased", ]) < 1e-12))
fmt(rb, 6)

The check has to be on the base itself, and it has to be the right check. If the base is stored per cycle, comparing each cycle’s vector with cycle 0’s catches the failure; collapsing the whole history into a range() does not, because range() discards the cycle dimension and returns the marker-wise spread of \(p_0\), the same number whether the base moved or not – here 1, the whole unit interval, because 66 of the 2000 markers are fixed in the candidate set (Table 10.16):

    all_identical_to_cycle0 = all(vapply(h, identical, logical(1), h[[1]])),
    max_abs_deviation       = max(vapply(h, function(p) max(abs(p - h[[1]])), 0)),
    collapsed_range         = diff(range(unlist(h))))
}

The first two columns separate the two histories; the third is the same number in both rows, which is the whole point.
Call. build_ctx() once at cycle 0 and store p0 <- colMeans(X) from it. build_ctx() has no p0 argument and recomputes colMeans(X) on every call, so at each later cycle build the context and then overwrite both ctx$p0 <- p0 and ctx$maf_pop <- pmin(p0, 1 - p0) (freq_metrics() reads maf_pop as well as p0). run_cycles() does exactly this in its internal cycle_ctx(). Check. identical(ctx$p0, p0_cycle0) at every cycle – one TRUE, with no tolerance. With a stored history, max(vapply(p0_history, function(p) max(abs(p - p0_history[[1]])), 0)), which must be exactly 0. Never a range() over the flattened history. Warning sign. \(F_{drift}\) near zero in a cycle where line usage was visibly concentrated, or an \(F_{drift}\) series that does not accumulate across cycles. Threshold. There is none to tune: the correct value of the base drift is exactly zero.


10.7.2 Step 2 – Compute both lenses in one marker sweep
freq_metrics() is the single sweep: it computes \(He\), alleles_lost, \(F_{hom}\), \(F_{drift}\), cov_diag, cor_dp_p0 and rare_retained from one colMeans(X[idx, ]). Anything else needing the selected frequencies belongs inside it, not in a second function with its own sweep.
The pure max-diversity greedy is the G_0.5 scheme in miniature: it constrains molecular coancestry and nothing else. Its signature has to be read against a resampled baseline rather than against one random draw, for the reason the Result of this step makes explicit. The baseline is the package’s own null_distribution() (built in Section 10.3.2, 1000 resampled subsets of the same size), and the z-scores come from discriminatory_power(), so the comparison is the same machinery every scenario in Chapter 25 is reported through (Table 10.17, Table 10.18):

# The linear pull toward 0.5 that a selection implies: slope, through the origin,
# of (p_selected - p0) on (0.5 - p0) over the markers polymorphic in the base.

Result. The max-diversity plan drives \(F_{hom}\) negative, -0.0113, which is 4.8 s.d. below a null mean of 0.0069: the selection is more heterozygous on the monitored panel than the frozen base. Its cov_diag is -0.0174, 4.9 s.d. below a null centred on -0.0001. Its \(F_{drift}\), however, is 0.006 against a null mean of 0.007: a z of -0.67, and 76% of the 1000 resampled subsets pay more drift than it does. Truncation is the row with the drift bill: \(F_{drift}\) = 0.0558, z = 35.1.
This is where one draw would have misled. The random row is a single subset, and its \(F_{drift}\) sits 1.3 s.d. below the resampled mean – further below it than max_div is – so a two-row random-versus-max_div comparison reports max-diversity as paying more drift than random, which the 1000-subset null says it does not. The failure is not the metric, it is the baseline: with a null s.d. of 0.0014 on a quantity whose value is 0.006, no single draw can serve as a control.

full_run <- function(cx, B = 300, seed = 7) {
  d_i <- sel_greedy(cx, 60, w = 0)
  set.seed(seed)
  rnd <- t(vapply(seq_len(B), function(b)
    freq_metrics(sample.int(cx$N, 60), cx)[c("F_hom", "F_drift")], numeric(2)))
  dm <- freq_metrics(d_i, cx)
  c(z_full_hom   = (dm[["F_hom"]]   - mean(rnd[, 1])) / stats::sd(rnd[, 1]),
    z_full_drift = (dm[["F_drift"]] - mean(rnd[, 2])) / stats::sd(rnd[, 2]))
}

Interpretation, and what it does not license. At this scale, on a single selection from a fixed candidate set, minimising molecular coancestry (the max_div plan, w = 0, which maximises gene diversity GD = 1 - theta) buys a measurable divergence between the two lenses – the negative covariance that the G_0.5 row of Table 10.10 predicts – and no measurable drift excess over random sampling when the plan is optimised and read on the same, full marker panel. The same plan optimised on half of the markers does show a drift excess against random subsets on both halves (Section 10.7.5), which this chapter does not explain; the statement here is not a general one about minimising coancestry. The drift excess Meuwissen et al. (2020) report for G_0.5 (\(\Delta F_{drift} =\) 0.0176 against a 0.005 target) is a 20-generation cumulative result under recurrent optimal contributions, where each cycle’s frequency change compounds on the last; one subset drawn once from one candidate set is not that experiment. Nor is the multi-cycle arm of Section 10.7.4: it stipulates a pull of 0.05 toward 0.5 and applies no selection, whereas the pull this plan implies (the slope of \(p_t - p_0\) on \(0.5 - p_0\), through the origin, over the markers polymorphic in the base) is 0.013, against -0.003 for the random draw, about 4 times smaller than the stipulated 0.05. The direction of what that arm shows is algebra (Equation 10.4); its size is not transferable to this plan. The book’s selections run across cycles are those of run_cycles() in Chapter 23, which reports both lenses there. What survives at one cycle is the covariance, and a report carrying only \(F_{hom}\) would not show it.
One thing Table 10.17 quietly says about the weight rather than the metric:
