At this scale w = 1 is not a compromise between index and coancestry – it returns the truncation set exactly, because the index is standardised to unit variance (sd(ctx$index) = 1) while the spread of \(\theta\) across candidate subsets of the same size is \(7.58 \times 10^{-4}\), the standard deviation of the theta column over the 2000 cheap-metric resamples of the same null. That is a ratio of 1319: three orders of magnitude, not two. A linear weight has to be calibrated to that ratio, which is why sel_greedy_budget() sweeps a logarithmic grid of w instead of trusting any single value.
Call. freq_metrics(idx, ctx) per cycle; metrics_cheap() if you also need the coancestry block, metrics_full() post-hoc for the expensive ones. Check. Both lenses present in the report, side by side, with the sign of \(F_{hom}\) preserved (never take an absolute value or clamp at zero). Warning sign. A single “inbreeding” column in the cycle report. If you cannot tell which lens it is, it is the one your constraint used, and the other one is unmeasured. Threshold. Not the \(\Delta F\) target. Both columns here are stocks accumulated against the frozen base, and a stock cannot be compared with a rate – Section 10.7.4 opens on exactly that point. Within one cycle the reference is the resampled null of Table 10.17, i.e. the z-scores of Table 10.18, read on both lenses separately and never on their average. The comparison with the programme’s \(\Delta F\) budget requires a trajectory and happens only through the regression of Section 10.7.4.


10.7.3 Step 3 – Report the covariance, not just the two lenses
cov_diag is the gap between the two lenses, and by Equation 10.4 it is not an approximation of the gap – it is the gap, which the stopifnot() of Table 10.8 enforces on every render. The operational point is that cov_diag is the only column that tells you why the two lenses disagree, and its sign identifies the mechanism from Table 10.10: negative means the management pushed frequencies toward 0.5, positive means it pushed them to the extremes.
Call. freq_metrics(idx, ctx)[["cov_diag"]], already computed by step 2 at no extra cost; cor_dp_p0 from the same call is the scale-free version. Check. cov_diag == F_hom - F_drift to machine precision. If it does not, the base and the frequencies were computed on different marker sets. Warning sign. \(|\)cov_diag\(|\) of the same order as the stock it is meant to explain. In the panel of Section 10.7.2 the max-diversity plan reports cov_diag = -0.0174 against an \(F_{drift}\) of 0.006: the discrepancy between the two lenses is 2.9 times the quantity being reported. Threshold. No absolute one, and not the \(\Delta F\) budget – cov_diag is a stock like the two lenses it separates. Compare it with \(F_{drift}\) in the same row, as just done, and with the resampled null: the null_sd row of Table 10.17 puts the max-diversity plan 4.9 s.d. out, which is the statement that the covariance was induced by the management rather than by the sampling.


10.7.4 Step 4 – Regress \(\log(1 - F)\) on cycle, and read \(R^2\)
A single cycle’s \(F\) is a stock and cannot be compared to a rate target. The rate comes from the trajectory. Before trusting the regression on a real programme, calibrate it on a case whose answer is known.
The known case is the drift model of Equation 1.4: with \(n_{gam}\) allele copies sampled per cycle, \(\Delta F = 1/n_{gam}\) and \(N_e = n_{gam}/2\), so a crossing block of \(n\) plants (\(n_{gam} = 2n\), \(N_e = n\)) and a pool re-derived as \(n\) doubled-haploid lines (\(n_{gam} = n\), \(N_e = n/2\)) differ by a factor of two. The DH regime is literally what next_pool() does in Chapter 23: one Bernoulli draw per locus per new line. What this step adds is the calibration of the \(\log(1 - F)\) regression against those two known rates; Table 10.19 gives the crossing-block trajectory.


Show code
# One heterotic pool, n_gam allele copies sampled per cycle, n_cyc cycles,
# `reps` independent replicates. `pull` first moves every frequency a fixed
# fraction toward 0.5: a caricature of a heterozygosity-maximising constraint,
# not an optimiser.
pool_traj <- function(n_gam, m, n_cyc, pull = 0, reps = 20, seed = 11) {
  out <- vector("list", reps)
  for (r in seq_len(reps)) {
    set.seed(seed + r)
    p0 <- runif(m, 0.05, 0.95)
    s2 <- p0 * (1 - p0)
    p  <- p0
    rows <- vector("list", n_cyc + 1L)
    for (t in 0:n_cyc) {
      rows[[t + 1L]] <- data.frame(
        rep = r, cycle = t,
        F_hom    = 1 - mean(p * (1 - p) / s2),
        F_drift  = mean((p - p0)^2 / s2),
        cov_diag = 2 * mean((p0 - 0.5) * (p - p0) / s2))
      p <- rbinom(m, n_gam, p + pull * (0.5 - p)) / n_gam
    }
    out[[r]] <- do.call(rbind, rows)
  }
  do.call(rbind, out)
}

per_cycle <- function(tr, n_gam) {
  a <- aggregate(cbind(F_hom, F_drift, cov_diag) ~ cycle, tr, mean)
  a$expected <- 1 - (1 - 1 / n_gam)^a$cycle
  # One s.d. per lens: the two lenses are not equally noisy across replicates,
  # so a deviation has to be compared with the s.d. of the lens it came from.
  a$sd_hom   <- aggregate(F_hom ~ cycle, tr, sd)$F_hom
  a$sd_drift <- aggregate(F_drift ~ cycle, tr, sd)$F_drift
  a
}

# dF from the slope, not from its first-order approximation.
dF_fit <- function(a, col) {
  d <- a[a$cycle > 0, ]                 # cycle 0 is identically zero by construction
  f <- lm(log(1 - d[[col]]) ~ cycle, d)
  b <- coef(f)[["cycle"]]
  c(dF = 1 - exp(b), Ne = 1 / (2 * (1 - exp(b))), R2 = summary(f)$r.squared)
}

For the crossing block the fitted rates are 0.00979 and 0.01007 against a target of 0.01, giving \(N_e\) of 51.1 and 49.7 against the true 50. For the DH-derived pool of the same 50 lines they are 0.01941 and 0.01987 against a target of 0.02, giving \(N_e \approx\) 25 against the true 25. In both regimes the largest deviation of either lens from the closed form (0.0032 and 0.0052) falls on the homozygosity lens; the drift lens deviates by at most 0.0005 and 0.0011. The yardstick for a deviation of a mean over 20 replicates is the standard error of that mean, the between-replicate s.d. divided by \(\sqrt{20}\), taken per cycle and per lens: scaled that way the largest deviation over the 24 comparisons (12 cycles, two lenses) is 2.13 standard errors for the crossing block and 2.06 for the DH pool, both below the two-sided 5% Bonferroni bound for 24 comparisons, \(z =\) 3.08. That is a description of this seed family, not a test: the bound is normal while each s.e. comes from only 20 replicates, and the comparisons are correlated (one trajectory per replicate feeds all cycles), so the bound is neither guaranteed conservative nor exact. Repeating the two calibrations over 20 seed families (seed = 11, 111, …, 1911), the larger of the two statistics exceeds 3.08 in 4 of them, so the chunk does not assert it. The smallest \(R^2\) of the four fits is 0.9993, and the chunk asserts \(R^2 \ge 0.999\) on all four (calibrated on this seed family at this scale).
Two things to carry out of that. The regression recovers \(N_e\) to within the sampling noise of 20 replicates of 2000 loci, which is what licenses the \(R^2\) threshold of this step’s Threshold – at this scale only: 20 replicates, 2000 loci, 12 cycles, one pool, one seed family. And a pool maintained as doubled-haploid lines drifts at twice the rate of a crossing block of the same count, so a programme that recycles 50 DH lines per pool per cycle is running at \(N_e \approx\) 25, not 50. That factor of two is structural, not a simulation artefact: it is the homozygosity of the DH itself.
A third thing, which is what the \(F_{drift}\) section (Section 10.3.3) needed and could not compute at that point in the chapter. At cycle 12 the unmanaged crossing block stands at \(F_{drift} =\) 0.1141 and the DH pool at 0.2142, with no selection applied in any cycle of either arm: pool_traj(pull = 0) is a binomial resampling of the previous cycle’s frequencies and nothing else. A statistic that reaches those values under pure drift is not an accumulated selection intensity, and reading it as one would attribute an intensity to a process that has none.

Figure 10.1: The two lenses on one heterotic pool over 12 cycles, averaged over 20 replicates of 2000 loci, against a base frozen at cycle 0. Points are replicate means, filled circles F_drift and triangles F_hom; no dispersion is drawn, the between-replicate standard deviations are in Table 10.19, Table 10.22 and Table 10.20. Left: a crossing block of 50 plants (100 allele copies per cycle). Centre: the same 50 lines re-derived as doubled haploids (50 allele copies per cycle), which drifts at twice the rate. In both, the closed form 1 - (1 - 1/n_gam)^t is the dashed line and the two lenses sit on it. Right: the crossing block with every frequency moved 5% toward 0.5 before each drift step, where the homozygosity lens reports a gain of heterozygosity against the frozen base while the drift lens ends at 2.02 times the unmanaged block’s value and rises at a non-constant rate; the dashed line is the same neutral closed form, here a reference both lenses leave. Nothing is selected in any panel; the divergence in the right-hand panel is produced by the management rule alone.





Figure 10.1 puts the three arms side by side. At cycle 12 the managed pool reports \(F_{hom} =\) -0.366 and \(F_{drift} =\) 0.231, a gap of -0.597 which is exactly cov_diag. The calibrated diagnostic of this step fires on both lenses. On \(\log(1 - F_{drift})\), \(R^2 =\) 0.9924, below the 0.995 threshold of this step’s Threshold, against 0.99996 in the unmanaged arm; the per-cycle increment of \(F_{drift}\) rises from 0.0122 in the first cycle to 0.0221 in the last, because the deterministic displacement toward 0.5 compounds on the drift. The rate is therefore not constant, and this chapter does not convert the slope (0.0228 per cycle, an average over 12 cycles and nothing more) into an \(N_e\). The comparison that needs no constant rate is the stock: at cycle 12 the managed pool’s \(F_{drift}\) is 2.02 times the unmanaged crossing block’s. The fit on \(\log(1 - F_{hom})\) returns a negative rate, -0.0233, and therefore a negative \(N_e\), which is the arithmetic telling you the series it was handed is not an inbreeding trajectory at all; \(R^2\) falls to 0.96 on that lens against 0.99935 in the unmanaged arm.
The inference, and its limits: a rule that pushes frequencies toward 0.5 generates exactly the negative covariance that the G_0.5 row of Table 10.10 predicts, and it does so with no selection whatsoever. Meuwissen et al. (2020) make the corresponding point with random GEBVs: their G_VR2(~,M) arm has no directional selection, although it still maximises an index (a random one), and the divergence persists. What this arm does not establish is the magnitude – pull = 0.05 is a stipulated caricature, not a fitted optimiser, and the stock ratio of 2.02 would move with pull, with \(n_{gam}\) and with the ancestral frequency distribution. The direction is algebra; the size is this parameterisation.
Call. lm(log(1 - F) ~ cycle) on cycles \(1..t\), separately for each lens; \(\Delta F = 1 - e^{\text{slope}}\), because \(1 - F_t = (1 - \Delta F)^t (1 - F_0)\) makes the slope \(\log(1 - \Delta F)\). The approximation \(\Delta F \approx -\text{slope}\) errs by \(O(\text{slope}^2)\), a relative error of about \(\Delta F / 2\) (1.01% at \(\Delta F = 0.02\)); Chapter 23 fits the same regression to run_cycles() output. Check. \(R^2\) on both fits, and the sign of \(\Delta F\). Warning sign. A negative fitted \(\Delta F\) (the series is not an inbreeding series), or an \(R^2\) that is high while the two lenses disagree in sign – a smooth curve through the wrong quantity. Threshold. Calibrated on one seed family (Table 10.21, Table 10.23): the four neutral fits give \(R^2 \ge\) 0.99935 (a margin of 0.00035 over the asserted 0.999) and the two managed fits \(R^2 \le\) 0.99243 (a margin of 0.00257 under 0.995). The \(R^2\) was not repeated over the seed families that fam_dev uses for the deviation statistic, and the thresholds were set from the same data they are read on; treat \(R^2 < 0.995\) on an averaged series as a non-constant rate at this scale only, and recalibrate at another number of replicates, loci or cycles. \(R^2\) says that the rate is not constant, not why: a decelerating, saturating series depresses it too, and Chapter 23 shows that case – there the diagnostic fires on the unconstrained run.


10.7.5 Step 5 – Audit on loci that did not enter the management
The constraint is met on the panel it is computed on. Whether it is met anywhere else is a separate measurement, and it needs loci that did not enter the management. Split the marker panel in two, manage on one half, and read the report on the other (Table 10.24, Table 10.25).
Which rows leave the audit half unseen depends on A5. The max-diversity plan (w = 0) never reads the index, so for it the audit half is unseen. The index-weighted plan (w = 1) selects on an index whose trait effects sit at every marker, the audit half included – the chunk asserts that the index of the management context is the full-panel index – so its audit-half reading is the response of a selection that did see those loci through the trait, and the row is reported as such, not as an off-panel reading.

Result. The plan that maximises diversity on the management half reports \(F_{hom} =\) -0.0300 there and \(F_{hom} =\) 0.0221 on the half it never saw: on this draw the sign reverses. Its drift readings are 0.0117 and 0.0124 – practically the same number on both halves, a gap of 0.0007 against 0.0521 on the homozygosity lens. That \(F_{hom}\) gap is 5.4 s.d. of the random-subset gap (s.d. 0.0098). Over the twenty draws, the managed-half \(F_{hom}\) is negative on 20 of 20 and the audit-half \(F_{hom}\) is positive on 16 of 20, so the sign reverses on the latter count and not on every draw; the \(F_{hom}\) gap is between 2.3 and 6.4 s.d. of the random-subset gap. The \(F_{drift}\) of this plan stands at z = 3.5 and 3.9 against the nulls of the management and audit halves, close to each other on every draw (largest absolute difference 1.1), but above zero. Over the twenty draws the managed-half z is above 0 on 19 of 20 and above 2 on 16 of 20 (smallest -0.77), and the audit-half z is above 0 on 19 of 20 and above 2 on 17 of 20 (smallest -0.26). The same plan optimised and read on the full panel, over the same twenty draws and the same null size (era-full-panel-20, Section 10.7.2), has an \(F_{drift}\) z between -1.6 and 1.5, above 2 on 0 of 20 (seed 1: -0.67). On half the markers, then, this plan pays a drift cost against random subsets on both halves that it does not pay on the full panel; why is not explained here, and no mechanism is claimed.
The index-weighted row is a different object. Its \(F_{hom}\) gap is small (-0.0051), but its \(F_{drift}\) on the audit half is z = 33.4 against the audit-half null (between 23 and 34.3 over the twenty draws): directional selection on a trait with effects at the audit loci moves those loci’s frequencies, as it must.
Interpretation. For the max-diversity plan, the only row whose audit half is unseen, the homozygosity lens does not generalise off the panel it was maximised on: its \(F_{hom}\) gap exceeds the sampling noise of the split on every draw. The drift lens gives the same reading on both halves. For the index-weighted plan, the small \(F_{hom}\) gap says nothing about the design of the audit, because that row is a selection response on the audit loci; it is not a noise reference for the split, and nothing about the max-diversity result was inferred from it. Two limits. First, in this simulation loci are in linkage equilibrium within pool (assumption A5), so the two halves are as independent as a split panel can be. With real linkage disequilibrium the audit half is correlated with the management half, the measured gap shrinks, and the audit becomes less sensitive: the gap measured here is close to an upper bound on what a real split panel would report, not a typical value. In addition, both halves of this simulated panel carry trait effects (A5), so the audit separates an unmonitored marker from a monitored one and cannot separate a marker from a causal locus: the marker-versus-QTL gap is outside what this step measures. Second, this is a one-cycle measurement at the teaching scale on twenty founder draws; no cycle-by-cycle version of this audit is run anywhere in this book.
Call. Two contexts over disjoint marker sets, both anchored on slices of the same frozen \(p_0\); freq_metrics() on each. Check. The \(F_{hom}\) and \(F_{drift}\) gaps between managed and audit halves, read against random-subset nulls on each half. Warning sign. A sign reversal in \(F_{hom}\), as in Table 10.26. Also a large gap in \(F_{drift}\), which would mean the management is not even controlling drift off its own panel. Threshold. The gap should be compared with the sampling noise of the split: the s.d. of the audit-minus-management gap over random subsets (here 0.0098 for \(F_{hom}\), data seed 1), not with the gap of a selection that used the index, which is a selection response, as Table 10.26 shows.


10.7.6 Step 6 – Read the two pools separately, and never \(F_{ST}\) alone
Everything so far is a single-population reading. A hybrid programme has two, and they must be constrained in opposite directions: within pool, limit \(\Delta F\); between pools, preserve divergence, because that is the heterosis engine (Chapter 5 proves the identity, Chapter 13 Trap 3 states the prescription). A single global \(\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{c}'\mathbf{G}\mathbf{c}\) cannot express that. Table 10.27 reads the two pools separately for four selections, and Table 10.28 gives the line usage behind them.

Two gene-diversity columns sit in Table 10.27 and they are the same quantity reached by two routes, which the stopifnot() in the chunk enforces on every render: GD is \(1 - \theta\) from \(\mathbf{f}\) over the selected hybrids (Chapter 11), GD_T is \(1 - \bar f\) from the line-usage weights of the Caballero & Toro partition, and both reduce to \(\overline{\bar p_k^2 + (1 - \bar p_k)^2}\) with \(\bar p\) the usage-weighted merged frequency, because under A2 a hybrid’s marker row is the average of its two parents’. It is the same identity as \(He = GD_T\) in Section 10.3.2, and GD, GD_T and Nei’s \(He\) (Nei 1973) are one number on this germplasm. The columns that are a different quantity are \(GD_{BS}\) and \(F_{ST}\): both are built from \(\tilde f = (\theta_A + \theta_B)/2\), which no hybrid-level average can reproduce, and both are read in Table 10.27 and Table 10.30.
Result. Truncation on the index costs 4.1% of gene diversity against the random baseline – the \(\alpha\) of Chapter 11, here against gd_ref = 0.3259, the mean gene diversity of the 2000 resampled random subsets of Section 10.3.2 (Section 11.9), and not against the single random row of the table – and 5.4% against the max-diversity ceiling. Meanwhile \(\theta_A\) rises to 0.7581 against \(\theta_B =\) 0.7219, and the effective number of lines used falls to 4.49 in pool A against 11.84 in pool B. One line appears in 23 of the 60 hybrids.
The dangerous column is \(F_{ST}\). It rises from 0.1095 to 0.1678 under truncation, and so does \(GD_{BS}\). Read as divergence, that looks like a gain in heterosis potential. It is not: by the Caballero & Toro definitions gd_partition() implements (Caballero and Toro 2002), \(GD_{BS} = \tilde f - \bar f\) with \(\tilde f = (\theta_A + \theta_B)/2\) and \(\bar f = (\theta_A + 2\theta_{AB} + \theta_B)/4\), so concentrating usage inside one pool raises \(\tilde f\) about twice as fast as it raises \(\bar f\) (exactly so at fixed \(\theta_{AB}\), which also moves) and therefore raises the between-pool component – even though the two pools’ lines are unchanged and their coancestry matrix \(\mathbf{f}^L\) is fixed. All that moved is the weight the selection puts on each line. \(F_{ST}\) then divides by a \(GD_T\) that fell at the same time – the GD_T column of Table 10.27, from 0.3302 to 0.3124 – which amplifies the artefact: the numerator rises by 45% while the denominator falls by 5%. A within-pool collapse and a genuine divergence are indistinguishable in \(F_{ST}\), and only the separate \(\theta_A\), \(\theta_B\) columns tell them apart.
The limitation to state here rather than hide: freq_metrics() computes its two lenses on ctx$X against ctx$p0, and Section 10.7.1 showed that hybrid base to be \((p_A + p_B)/2\). So \(F_{hom}\) and \(F_{drift}\) as this package computes them are pooled over the two pools and cannot, on their own, tell you which pool eroded. The pool-level attribution comes from three other places: \(\theta_A\) and \(\theta_B\) (theta_pools()), the effective number of lines used per pool (ne_lines_pool()), and the pool-level panel s1_monitor() returns from the line matrix (Table 10.29):

Note which two agree. gd_partition()’s F_ST is \(GD_{BS}/GD_T\), the Nei \(G_{ST}\) form and the standardised-variance form of Chapter 3 (Equation 3.7), and it equals s1_monitor()’s Gst_Nei to machine precision, and also the ratio of marker means \(\overline{\Delta p^2/4}\,/\,\overline{\bar p\bar q}\) (asserted in the chunk of Table 10.30). Fst_Wright, in the code’s name, is the between-referenced statistic \((\theta_w - \theta_B)/(1 - \theta_B)\) of R/05_pipeline_metrics.R; Chapter 3 records that the book cites no external source for it, and the label “Wright” is the code’s, not a claim about a paper. It is 1.81 times larger than Gst_Nei on the same germplasm. Three quantities are therefore in play and must not be confused: the \(F_{ST}\) of this chapter (\(GD_{BS}/GD_T\), the Nei \(G_{ST}\) form, a statistic computed on the pools as they stand), Fst_Wright (between-referenced), and the Balding-Nichols parameter \(F_{BN}\) (fst of sim_config, the divergence by which the founder pools were generated, not a statistic of the sampled lines). That is Chapter 13 Trap 2, and it is the reason to name the definition in the report rather than the symbol.
Call. theta_pools(), gd_partition(), ne_lines_pool(), max_line_use(), ne_parents() on the selection; s1_monitor() on the line matrix of each cycle. Check. \(\theta_A\) and \(\theta_B\) separately; \(GD_{BS}\) held in a band, not maximised; the number of distinct lines used per pool. Warning sign. \(F_{ST}\) rising while \(GD_T\) falls – by the algebra of this step the signature of a one-pool collapse, as in the truncation row of Table 10.27 (one selection on one draw; how often this holds across germplasm is not measured here), not evidence of divergence. An Ne_lines asymmetry between pools of the size in the truncation row of Table 10.28 (4.5 against 11.8). Threshold. A per-line usage cap is the direct instrument: the capped row is sel_greedy(ctx, 60, w = 1, max_use = 4), which holds \(|\theta_A - \theta_B|\) at 0.0056 and both pools above 15.5 effective lines, against an index of 0.82 where truncation reached 1.99. That index difference is the price, and Chapter 23 is where it is paid back or not. max_use defaults to NULL everywhere in this package, so the cap is opt-in.






TipThe diagnostic nobody runs



Schemes based on IBD selected many parents in Meuwissen et al. (2020); VanRaden-style schemes selected few. If your optimal-contribution run is delivering high gain with a suspiciously small number of parents and \(\Delta F\) on target, compute \(F_{hom}\) and \(F_{drift}\) separately on a panel not used in the management (Section 10.7.5). The difference between them is your hidden bill. This book’s implementation is ne_parents(), which Chapter 25 reports alongside the two lenses for every scenario. Table 10.27 and Table 10.28 are the small version of the same diagnostic: between the random and truncation rows gene diversity falls by 4.1% (against the single random draw, the baseline Section 10.7.2 shows is no control, so read the comparison that follows as an order of magnitude) while the effective number of parents falls from 39.3 to 13.0, which is 67% – the two relative drops differ by a factor of 16. A budget written on gene diversity alone is therefore a weak constraint on the parent count, and the capped row – the same greedy with max_use = 4 – is what holding the parent count directly costs: 31.0 effective parents at an index of 0.82 where truncation reached 1.99. Measured on one candidate set at the teaching scale, with a single random draw as the random row.




10.7.7 Step 7 – Check the matrix you are about to invert






NoteAn implementation note that is routinely ignored



G_VR1, G_VR2, G_0.5 and G_i(p) are all only semi-definite positive, so every one of them needs a ridge \(\varepsilon\) added to the diagonal (\(\varepsilon = 0.01\) in Meuwissen et al. (2020), their Methods, where it is written \(\alpha\); renamed here because \(\alpha\) is the diversity loss in this book) before it can be inverted and before the optimal-contribution algorithm will run. \(\mathbf{A}\) and G_LA are positive definite by construction.
The mechanism is not the same for all four, and the difference matters here. Meuwissen et al. (2020) (their Methods) attribute the zero eigenvalue of all four to the centring of the genotypes; for G_0.5 this chapter departs from that, and Table 10.31 shows why. For the centred VanRaden forms it is the centring: in this book’s vanraden_G(), \(\mathbf{Z}\) is centred on the scored population’s own allele frequencies, so its columns sum to zero over individuals, the constant vector lies in the null space and one degree of freedom is gone by construction. That centring is this book’s construction, not claimed to be VanRaden (2008)’s, who is cited for the form of \(\mathbf{G}\) only (the paper’s abstract speaks of base-population frequencies, and Meuwissen et al. (2020) write \(\mathbf{Z}\) with \(p_0\)); centred on base frequencies the columns would not sum to zero exactly, and the exact argument of this step would not apply as stated. For G_0.5 \(= 4\mathbf{f} - 2\mathbf{J}\) – an affine map of the molecular coancestry this book calls \(\mathbf{f}\), with \(\mathbf{J}\) the \(N \times N\) matrix of ones – it is not the centring: \(\mathbf{f}\) is not centred on anything and stays in \([0, 1]\) by design (Chapter 2), and G_0.5 inherits non-zero row sums from it. Their deficiency has a different cause, derived at Equation 10.5. Both statements are checkable:


Show code
Zh  <- ctx$X - 0.5
G05 <- 4 * ctx[["f"]] - 2                       # G_0.5 = 4f - 2J
rkf <- qr(ctx[["f"]])$rank
rkG <- qr(ctx[["G"]])$rank
rk05 <- qr(G05)$rank
# Identities: f is half plus a Gram matrix; VanRaden G sums to zero (centring).
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(ctx[["f"]], 2 * tcrossprod(Zh) / ctx$m + 0.5)),
          isTRUE(all.equal(G05, 8 * tcrossprod(Zh) / ctx$m)),
          abs(sum(ctx[["G"]])) < 1e-8,
          min(rowSums(G05)) > 0)
# Measured on this data set, not theorems: rank(G) = rank(f) - 1 and
# rank(G_0.5) = rank(f) (G_0.5 = 4 f - 2 J is affine in f, not equal to it).
stopifnot(rkG == rkf - 1, rk05 == rkf)
data.frame(value = formatC(c(
  f_equals_half_plus_gram = max(abs(ctx[["f"]] -
                                      (2 * tcrossprod(Zh) / ctx$m + 0.5))),
  f_rowsum_min            = min(rowSums(ctx[["f"]])),
  f_rowsum_max            = max(rowSums(ctx[["f"]])),
  G05_rowsum_min          = min(rowSums(G05)),
  G_sum                   = sum(ctx[["G"]]),
  G_rowsum_max_abs        = max(abs(rowSums(ctx[["G"]]))),
  rank_f = rkf, rank_G05 = rk05, rank_G = rkG, n_lines = ctx$n_lines, N = ctx$N), digits = 4, format = "g"))

\(\mathbf{f} = 0.5 + \tfrac{2}{m}\mathbf{Z}_h\mathbf{Z}_h'\) with \(\mathbf{Z}_h = \mathbf{X} - \tfrac12\mathbf{J}_{N \times m}\) (the hybrid marker matrix centred at 0.5, with \(\mathbf{J}_{N \times m}\) the \(N \times m\) matrix of ones), to machine precision – a Gram matrix plus the positive rank-one term \(0.5\,\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}'\), hence positive semi-definite, and with row sums nowhere near zero (f_rowsum_min of Table 10.31), so neither \(\mathbf{1}\) nor any other constant vector is in its null space. The same holds for G_0.5 \(= \tfrac{8}{m}\mathbf{Z}_h\mathbf{Z}_h'\) (the \(0.5\,\mathbf{J}\) term cancels in \(4\mathbf{f} - 2\mathbf{J}\)): its row sums are positive (G05_rowsum_min), and its rank, 49, equals that of \(\mathbf{f}\) on this data set, so every rank statement of this step about \(\mathbf{f}\) applies to G_0.5 as measured here. VanRaden’s \(\mathbf{G}\) on the same hybrids has sum(G) and every row sum at numerical zero, which is the centring, and its rank comes out exactly one below \(\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{f})\) on this data set: one dimension is what centring costs, and it is the only part of either deficiency that centring explains. The other 576 missing dimensions have a different cause entirely, and the rest of this step is that cause.


In a hybrid programme the deficiency is far worse than one zero eigenvalue, and it is structural rather than numerical. A hybrid’s marker row is the average of its two parents’ rows, so \(\mathbf{X} = \tfrac12 \mathbf{B}\mathbf{G}^L\) with \(\mathbf{B}\) the \(N \times L\) parent-usage incidence matrix (a 1 in the two columns of its parents) and \(\mathbf{G}^L\) the \(L \times m\) line genotype matrix coded 0/1 of Appendix A (the L / 2 object of simulate_lines(); the superscript keeps it apart from the \(\mathbf{G}_\bullet\) relationship matrices of this chapter). With \(\mathbf{J}_{r \times c}\) the \(r \times c\) matrix of ones, the hybrid coancestry matrix is a Gram matrix, \(\mathbf{f} = [\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{J}_{N \times m} - \mathbf{X}]\,
[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{J}_{N \times m} - \mathbf{X}]'/m\), so its column space is that of \([\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{J}_{N \times m} - \mathbf{X}]\). Every row of \(\mathbf{B}\) has exactly two 1s, so \(\mathbf{B}\mathbf{1}_L = 2\,\mathbf{1}_N\): the constant vector already lies in the column space of \(\mathbf{B}\). Hence \(\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{B}\mathbf{G}^L/2\) and \(\mathbf{J}_{N \times m} - \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{B}(\mathbf{J}_{L \times m} - \mathbf{G}^L)/2\) both have their columns in that space, and so does \(\mathbf{f}\). That is a theorem, Equation 10.5, for any selection and any line genotypes: \[\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{f}) \le \mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{B}) \tag{10.5}\] however many hybrids there are (and also \(\le m + 1\), because every column of \(\mathbf{J} - \mathbf{X}\) is \(\mathbf{1}_N\) minus a column of \(\mathbf{X}\); that second bound is not binding at this scale). The same argument covers G_0.5 \(= \tfrac{8}{m}\mathbf{Z}_h\mathbf{Z}_h'\), since \(\mathbf{Z}_h = \mathbf{B}(\mathbf{G}^L - 0.5\,\mathbf{J}_{L \times m})/2\). Whether the bound is attained depends on \(\mathbf{G}^L\) and is a measurement. Measured in Table 10.32 and Table 10.33:


Show code
incidence <- function(idx, ctx) {
  B <- matrix(0, length(idx), ctx$n_lines)
  B[cbind(seq_along(idx), ctx$ped$a[idx])] <- 1
  B[cbind(seq_along(idx), ctx$ped$b[idx])] <- 1
  B
}
# A separate set from the `sels` of @sec-era-fhom: these vary n_sel, which is

rk$deficiency <- rk$n_sel - rk$rank_f

Result. In all five selections the rank of \(\mathbf{f}\) equals the rank of the parent-usage incidence matrix exactly. On the full factorial that is 49 \(= L - 1\) for 50 lines, against 625 hybrids: a deficiency of 576, with a smallest eigenvalue at \(-4.3 \times 10^{-13}\) (a numerical zero; its digits depend on the BLAS). The random_20 draw, which uses 27 lines, is full rank. That is generic, not guaranteed: over 1000 independent random 20-hybrid draws (seed 33) 90.4% are full rank, the smallest rank is 18, and \(\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{f}) = \mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{B})\) in 100% of them.
Interpretation. The deficiency is not a rounding artefact and does not shrink with more markers; it is the factorial structure. \(N\) hybrids built from \(L\) lines live in an at most \(L\)-dimensional space, so any hybrid-level optimiser that needs \(\mathbf{f}^{-1}\) must regularise, and the amount of regularisation required is predictable before any eigendecomposition: compute \(\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{B})\), which costs one qr() on an \(N \times L\) 0/1 matrix. Two statements are asserted in the chunk and they have different standing. \(\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{f}) \le \mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{B})\) is the theorem of Equation 10.5, so \(\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{B})\) is a guaranteed upper bound on what the inversion has to work with. The equality rank_f == rank_incidence is a measurement – five selections plus 1000 random draws, at one scale and on one draw of line genotypes – and a set of lines whose genotypes are linearly dependent would break it without breaking the theorem. The rank deficiency is also the reason this book’s selection machinery never inverts \(\mathbf{f}\): metrics_cheap() and the differential-evolution (DE) fitness only ever evaluate the quadratic form \(\mathbf{c}'\mathbf{f}\mathbf{c}\), which needs no inverse. The quadratic-programming routes do need a definite matrix, and both optimal_contributions() and ocs_quadprog() add diag(1e-8, n) for exactly this reason – about 4 orders of magnitude above the numerical zero reported in Table 10.33 (the figure moves with the BLAS), and its effect on the optimum is not measured here. See Chapter 15 and Section 14.3.2.
Call. qr() on the usage incidence matrix, or on \(\mathbf{f}\) restricted to the candidate set; eigen(..., only.values = TRUE) for the spectrum if you want the size of the numerical zero. Check. rank(f) < n_sel, and how far below. Warning sign. A quadratic-programming solver that returns without error but with contributions concentrated on a handful of hybrids: a singular matrix makes the objective flat along \(N - \mathrm{rank}\) directions, and the solver will pick a vertex. Threshold. The added diagonal \(\varepsilon\) must exceed the largest magnitude of the numerically-zero eigenvalues, here about \(4 \times 10^{-13}\), by several orders of magnitude; \(\varepsilon = 0.01\) on a matrix whose diagonal averages 0.82 is a perturbation of about 1.2% and must be documented as such, because it changes the optimum.

title: 10  Diversity metrics in the genomic era
text:
10.8 What not to do
Four recommendations that do not need their own step. Each one is labelled with what backs it, because they are not backed equally: one is measured in this chapter, three are positions taken by Meuwissen et al. (2020) and carried forward here as their argument, and none of the three has been tested on plant germplasm anywhere in this book.
Do not maximise marker heterozygosity as an objective. Measured here: raising heterozygosity on the monitored panel raises it far less at unmonitored loci – Section 10.7.5 measures a reversal of sign on 16 of 20 founder draws and a gap above the noise of the split on all 20, under linkage equilibrium, which makes it a best case. Their argument, not measured here: doing so also raises IBD-based inbreeding, because “changes in allele frequency result from multiple copies of a subset of base generation alleles, so increasing frequency is promoting IBD based inbreeding” (Meuwissen et al. 2020, Discussion, Management of Diversity). No relationship matrix this book puts into an optimiser is IBD-based – every one of them is identity-by-state – so that half is a reason to distrust the objective, not a result reproduced here.
Region-specific diversity targets rarely earn their complexity. Their argument. Meuwissen et al. (2020) give two grounds in the same paragraph: that causative alleles of quantitative traits are quite evenly distributed across the genome (their Discussion, citing Wood et al. (2014) on human stature – an observation about one species and one trait, not about maize), and that “what happens in a sample of loci does not necessarily predict what happens at loci outside that subset”, which is the claim Section 10.7.5 does test, at the marker level. They name the major histocompatibility complex as the case that does earn a constraint of its own; the plant analogue offered here is R-gene-type resistance loci, where allelic diversity has direct and known value. That analogy is offered as such, and nothing in this book measures it.
Deleterious recessives are a load problem, not a diversity problem. Their judgement: for regions carrying known recessive defects, “direct inclusion of the known defects in the breeding goal seems more effective in controlling their frequencies” than prioritising the region for diversity management (Meuwissen et al. 2020, Discussion). Neither they nor this book compare the two routes quantitatively, so read it as the expectation of the authors of the scheme, not as a measured efficiency. In a hybrid programme there is a second and independent reason, which follows from A1 and A2 rather than from anyone’s judgement: a recessive carried at low frequency in pool A is masked in every \(A \times B\) hybrid unless pool B carries it too, so the load is expressed in the crossing block and in the DH induction, not in the product.
In a pure conservation scheme the problem is expected to be worse, not better. Their expectation, stated as one: “the potential covariance between the change in allele frequency and the initial frequency is expected to increase, since the inbreeding management term is more important in pure conservation schemes” (Meuwissen et al. 2020, Discussion), which is why they argue the IBD recommendation is stronger there. Their only arm without directional selection, G_VR2(~,M) with random GEBVs, still maximises an index, so no pure conservation scheme was run to test it; the sign of the mechanism is nevertheless the same algebra as the rest of this chapter – a constraint that is the only thing moving frequencies is a constraint that generates the whole covariance.

10.9 Limits of the animal-to-plant transposition
Table 10.34 sets each assumption of the simulation of Meuwissen et al. (2020) against the situation in a hybrid crop programme.




Table 10.34: Assumptions of the simulation of Meuwissen et al. (2020) (left) and the corresponding situation in a two-pool hybrid crop programme (right). The Ne_parents values in the fourth row are computed in Section 10.7.6 (Table 10.28) at the book’s teaching scale.










Assumption in the paper
Situation in a hybrid crop programme




discrete generations, two sexes, one contribution per individual
same line reused for years, cloning of parents through DH maintenance, overlapping cycles, one line used in dozens of crosses

None of this invalidates the central conclusion. It is an algebraic property of the optimiser, not a biological property of the species. What it changes is which matrix is practicable, and – for a two-pool programme – that one global constraint is never enough.

title: 11  A catalogue of diversity metrics
text:
11.1 Group coancestry, and the off-diagonal problem
Chapter 10 separated two lenses on one selection, \(F_{hom}\) and \(F_{drift}\), and read both against a resampled null of random subsets before that null had been defined. This chapter is where the catalogue of metrics is defined once, where the baseline of that null is derived (Section 11.9), and where every metric, those two lenses included, is read against it (Section 11.10). It also settles what “no loss” means, which turns out to be less obvious than it sounds.
Every metric in the catalogue has the same signature, f(idx, ctx) -> scalar. That uniformity is what makes metrics interchangeable inside an optimiser and what lets Chapter 12 benchmark them against each other on equal terms. It does not mean that they read the same object, and this chapter keeps four inputs apart (Chapter 2 gives the convention):
Only the first group reads the hybrid-level matrix \(\mathbf{f}\), and a centred matrix stored in its place would reach only that group (Chapter 2).
The group coancestry (Cockerham 1967) of a set \(S\) of \(n\) individuals is the mean of all \(n^2\) elements, diagonal included. Caballero and Toro (2002, 290) average over all pairs of individuals and cite Cockerham (1967) for it (Cockerham’s own text was not checked here):
\[\theta_S \;=\; \frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{i \in S}\sum_{j \in S} f_{ij}
            \;=\; \frac{1}{n^2}\,\mathbf{1}'\mathbf{f}_S\mathbf{1}. \tag{11.1}\]
It is the probability that two alleles sampled at random from the whole set are identical – including the possibility that both come from the same individual. That is why the diagonal enters: it is the chance of sampling the same individual twice, which is entirely real when the set is used as a crossing pool.
Splitting the diagonal mean \(\bar f_d\) from the off-diagonal mean \(\bar f_o\) of Equation 11.1,
\[\theta_S \;=\; \frac{\bar f_d}{n} \;+\; \frac{n-1}{n}\,\bar f_o . \tag{11.2}\]
So the off-diagonal mean – the metric many programmes already report – is one of two terms. When \(\bar f_d\) varies little across individuals, which is the case in an all-F1 population, the two rank almost identically (Table 11.1).

section: 11.2 Gene diversity: \(\theta\) and \(H_e\) are the same quantity
text:
11.2 Gene diversity: \(\theta\) and \(H_e\) are the same quantity
This is the result that simplifies everything downstream. Write \(x_{ik} \in \{0, 0.5, 1\}\) for the marker value of individual \(i\) at marker \(k\), one of \(m\) markers. Starting from Equation 11.1, insert \(f_{ij} = m^{-1}\sum_k[x_{ik}x_{jk} +
(1-x_{ik})(1-x_{jk})]\) (Equation 2.5) and swap the order of summation. Each marker contributes two double sums, and each factors:
\[\frac{1}{n^2}\sum_i\sum_j x_{ik}x_{jk}
  = \Big(\frac{1}{n}\sum_i x_{ik}\Big)^2 = \bar p_k^2,
  \qquad
  \frac{1}{n^2}\sum_i\sum_j (1-x_{ik})(1-x_{jk}) = (1 - \bar p_k)^2 = \bar q_k^2,\]
with \(\bar p_k\) the group’s allele frequency and \(\bar q_k = 1 - \bar p_k\). Hence
\[\theta_S = \frac{1}{m}\sum_k \big(\bar p_k^2 + \bar q_k^2\big), \tag{11.3}\]
and \(GD_S = 1 - \theta_S = m^{-1}\sum_k 2\,\bar p_k \bar q_k \equiv H_e\), which is Equation 1.2: Nei’s gene diversity (Nei 1973) in its plug-in form, at the set’s own frequencies and without the \(2n/(2n-1)\) small-sample correction. Group coancestry and expected heterozygosity are not two independent checks. They are one quantity written two ways. Table 11.2 gives both pairs for one random subset.


Show code
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(theta_group(idx, ctx), theta_from_freq(idx, ctx))),
          isTRUE(all.equal(gene_diversity(idx, ctx), he_nei(idx, ctx))))

data.frame(quantity = c("theta, via_submatrix", "theta, via_frequency",
                        "difference", "GD", "He_Nei"),
           value = c(sprintf("%.6f", c(theta_group(idx, ctx), theta_from_freq(idx, ctx))),
                     sprintf("%.1e", d_theta),
                     sprintf("%.6f", c(gene_diversity(idx, ctx), he_nei(idx, ctx)))))

The chunk asserts both equalities with all.equal() at its default relative tolerance, \(1.5 \times 10^{-8}\); the size of the printed difference is exactly 0. This equality is the implementation’s strongest sanity check. If it fails, f is centered, rescaled, or built on the wrong marker coding.
Three practical consequences:

One fewer metric to justify to a technical committee.
“Losing 5 % of diversity” acquires an exact meaning: \(GD_S\) is 5 % below the expected heterozygosity of a random subset of the same size (Section 11.9), not 5 % of the set’s own.
Two computation routes with the same answer and very different costs. The matrix route is \(O(n^2)\); the frequency route is \(O(nm)\). For \(n = 200\) and \(m = 25000\) that is forty thousand operations against five million. Table 11.3 times both at this chapter’s scale.

    if (t > target || r > 2e6) return(1e6 * t / r)
    r <- r * 4L
  }
}

title: 11  A catalogue of diversity metrics
text:
11.3 Status number \(N_s\)
Lindgren et al. (1997) express group coancestry on the scale of individual counts:
\[N_s = \frac{1}{2\theta_S}. \tag{11.4}\]
\(N_s\) reads as a head count only on coancestry measured against a base population, in which unrelated non-inbred individuals have coancestry 0 with each other and \(1/2\) with themselves: a set of \(n\) of them has \(\theta_S = 1/(2n)\) and \(N_s = n\). Molecular \(\mathbf{f}\) is identity in state and is not measured against such a base: unrelated individuals sit at a floor set by the marker frequencies, not at 0 (Chapter 2, Equation 1.3). By Equation 11.3, \(\theta_S = m^{-1}\sum_k(\bar p_k^2 + \bar q_k^2)\), and \(\bar p_k^2 + \bar q_k^2 \ge 1/2\) at every biallelic locus, so on \(\mathbf{f}\) \(\theta_S \in [1/2, 1]\) and \(N_s \in [1/2, 1]\) for every set. Here \(N_s\) is a monotone decreasing rescaling of \(\theta_S\), not a number of individuals. The two edge cases are the two bounds (Table 11.4):


Show code
fake <- ctx
fake[["f"]] <- matrix(0.5, 5, 5)      # every group frequency 0.5: theta at its lower bound
lo <- c(theta = theta_group(1:5, fake), Ns = status_number(1:5, fake))
fake[["f"]] <- matrix(1, 5, 5)        # all identical and homozygous: theta at its upper bound
hi <- c(theta = theta_group(1:5, fake), Ns = status_number(1:5, fake))
data.frame(case = c("all f = 0.5", "all f = 1"), rbind(lo, hi), row.names = NULL)

Warning\(N_s\) is a descriptor, not a drift projection



Toro et al. (2020) report, in their abstract, that under optimal molecular management diversity increases in the early generations, so that the rate-based effective size \(N_e = 1/(2\Delta F)\) (Equation 10.1) takes negative values, and that in the long term it does not reach an asymptote and behaves unpredictably. Only the abstract was read for this chapter.
This does not invalidate \(N_s\). \(N_s\) is a monotonic reparametrisation of \(\theta\) – a static descriptor of a set – while \(N_e\) is a rate between generations. Use \(N_s\) to compare sets; do not extrapolate it to project future drift. For the same reason, do not substitute the linkage-disequilibrium \(N_e\) here: that estimates population history, not the composition of a selected sample.


And, from Chapter 10: \(\theta\) tracks homozygosity, not drift. \(GD\) and \(N_s\) describe the expected heterozygosity \(H_e\) of the merged set at its own frequencies (Equation 1.2). That is not the heterozygosity the F1s carry. For the complete factorial of the selected lines at their usage weights the expected F1 heterozygosity is \(GD_T + GD_{BS}\) (Equation 5.6, Chapter 1), and the heterozygosity of the pairs actually kept is \(2\,GD_{WI\text{-}hyb}\), which a selection can move against \(GD\). In Table 11.10, from the random subset of this chapter to truncation, \(GD\) goes from 0.3259 to 0.3124 while GD_WI_hyb goes from 0.1814 to 0.1823; this is one founder draw and one random subset. Chapter 10 measures the sign of the truncation selection’s realised F1 heterozygosity against a random-subset null on twenty founder draws and finds no consistent sign (Table 10.6). \(GD\) is therefore not a measure of next season’s hybrid vigour, which needs the F1s’ own heterozygosity and dominance at the loci that matter (Chapter 5), not the coancestry among candidates. \(GD\) and \(N_s\) also do not certify that allele frequencies are moving as unmanaged drift would have moved them, which matters more across multiple recurrent cycles than for a single round of hybrid selection.

11.4 Effective number of parents
A metric independent of \(\mathbf{f}\), computed purely from the pedigree. With \(p_i\) the frequency with which line \(i\) appears as a parent among the selected hybrids,
\[N_{e,\text{par}} = \frac{1}{\sum_i p_i^2}, \tag{11.5}\]
the reciprocal of Simpson’s concentration index \(\sum_i p_i^2\) (Simpson 1949); the founder equivalents of Lacy (1989) are attributed the same form over founder contributions (UNVERIFIED: the 1989 paper was not available, only the concept was confirmed from secondary sources). It captures what coancestry can blur: in a hypothetical set of 200 hybrids that draws on only 12 lines, \(\theta\) can be acceptable if those 12 happen to be genetically distant from each other. The case is constructed, not computed here. Table 11.5 gives it for the five selections. It is bounded above by the number of lines, 50, a bound reached only if every line is used equally often.

title: 11  A catalogue of diversity metrics
text:
11.5 Allelic richness
\(\theta\) and \(H_e\) are averages across markers and are dominated by intermediate-frequency alleles. A lost rare allele barely moves them, yet in a closed population, with no reintroduction from outside germplasm, the loss is irreversible. López-Cortegano et al. (2019) (pp. 1-2) relate expected heterozygosity to the short-term response to selection and allelic diversity, which is more sensitive to bottlenecks, to the long-term one. So count markers that were polymorphic in the population and became rare or fixed in the selection, with MAF the minor allele frequency in the selection \((S)\) or in the whole population (pop):
\[A_{\text{lost}} = \#\{k : \text{MAF}^{(S)}_k < 0.05 \;\wedge\;
                            \text{MAF}^{(\text{pop})}_k \ge 0.05\}. \tag{11.6}\]
Table 11.6 counts \(A_{\text{lost}}\) for the five selections.

  cor(red[["theta"]], red[[v]], method = "spearman"))

The redundancy analysis of Chapter 12 does not single alleles_lost out as non-redundant with \(\theta\). That analysis is cached external data: metric_redundancy.csv has no producer in this repository, is not regenerated by any script here, and nothing in this chapter reproduces it. Read from the file, the Spearman correlation with \(\theta\) over its 621 selections is 0.932 for alleles_lost_MAF, -0.925 for Ne_parents and -0.967 for eff_dim. Chapter 12 reports that the metrics keeping most rank variation after regressing on \(\theta\) are allelic richness (the count of alleles retained) and \(N_{e,\text{par}}\), not alleles_lost. On that analysis the rank correlation of alleles_lost with \(\theta\) is 0.932 (\(\rho^2 =\) 0.87), strong but short of a monotone relation, so the case for tracking it rests on the argument above, that a lost rare allele barely moves \(\theta\), and on the result of López-Cortegano et al. (2019) reported in Section 11.5. It does not rest on the redundancy analysis. That analysis does not include F_drift or F_hom, so it says nothing about them; of the metrics in Table 11.18, F_drift separates truncation from random subsets most strongly on this draw.
López-Cortegano et al. (2019) compared, in a subdivided simulated population, strategies maximising expected heterozygosity (\(H_T\), the same family as \(GD\)) against strategies maximising allelic diversity (\(A_T\)). Maximising \(A_T\) retained more alleles and controlled molecular inbreeding better than maximising \(H_T\), except when all the weight of the optimisation is placed on the within-subpopulation component, where maximising \(H_T\) controlled molecular inbreeding best while still retaining fewer alleles. Their markers are multiallelic haplotypes of single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNP), not the biallelic markers whose minor-allele-frequency threshold defines \(A_{\text{lost}}\), so the result is read here as direction, not as a number to transfer.
The explanation the paper gives depends on the structure of the population. For a single undivided population it cites Fernández et al. (2004), as reported there: maximising heterozygosity leads alleles toward intermediate frequencies, which reduces the chance that rare alleles are lost by drift, so that in undivided populations maximising \(H_T\) can serve both heterozygosity and allele number; in that undivided case the allele-count method kept some rare alleles at low frequencies, where they were more likely to be lost eventually. For subdivided populations it reports instead that maximising global heterozygosity comes at the cost of more homozygosity in each subpopulation, at least in the short term, and of a substantial loss of alleles. This chapter offers no mechanism beyond that report: the step from “frequencies pushed toward 0.5” to a later loss of alleles under heterozygosity management in the subdivided case is not in the paper and is not tested here.
Their recommendation for structured conservation programmes was to make \(A_T\), not \(H_T\), the primary target. In this pipeline’s terms: alleles_lost deserves a place next to \(\theta\) as a tracked outcome, not only as a post-hoc sanity check, whenever the selection feeds several future cycles rather than a single hybrid release.

title: 11  A catalogue of diversity metrics
text:
11.6 Distances: E-NE and A-NE
Odong et al. (2013) proposed, and Core Hunter 3 (De Beukelaer et al. 2018) implements, two measures, entry-to-nearest-entry (E-NE) and accession-to-nearest-entry (A-NE) distances, capturing opposite aspects that \(\theta\) alone cannot separate. Core Hunter 3 computes them on its own marker distances; this book uses \(\eta_{ij} = 1 - f_{ij}\):
\[\text{E-NE} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i \in S} \min_{j \in S,\, j \ne i} \eta_{ij},
  \qquad
  \text{A-NE} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \min_{j \in S} \eta_{ij}, \tag{11.7}\]
with \(N\) the number of candidates in the population.

E-NE measures non-redundancy within the selection. It distinguishes “200 individuals spread out” from “100 near-identical pairs spread out” – configurations that can share the same \(\theta\).
A-NE measures representativeness of the population. It detects a selection that optimises \(\theta\) by concentrating in one region of genetic space and ignoring the rest.

Table 11.7 gives both for the five selections of this chapter.


Show code
fmt(t(sapply(sels, function(s) c(ENE = ene(s, ctx), ANE = ane(s, ctx)))), 4)

# A-NE with the self-distance set to 0 (Odong et al. 2013), for comparison
ane_odong <- vapply(sels, function(s) {
  d <- 1 - ctx[["f"]][, s, drop = FALSE]
  d[cbind(s, seq_along(s))] <- 0
  mean(apply(d, 1, min))
}, numeric(1))
ane_pkg <- vapply(sels, ane, numeric(1), ctx = ctx)
ane_gap <- ane_pkg - ane_odong
stopifnot(all(ane_gap >= 0))

title: 11  A catalogue of diversity metrics
text:
11.7 Effective dimensionality
Over the eigenvalues \(\gamma_i\) of the double-centered submatrix,
\[D_{\text{eff}} = \frac{(\sum_i \gamma_i)^2}{\sum_i \gamma_i^2} \tag{11.8}\]
has the form of the participation ratio, a term from the physics of localised vibrational modes (the attribution to Bell and Dean (1970) is UNVERIFIED: the paper could not be opened) applied here to eigenvalues. It counts how many independent directions of genetic variation remain: 1 if all variation lies on a single axis, \(n - 1\) if spread evenly over the \(n - 1\) dimensions that double-centering leaves. Table 11.8 gives it for the five selections.


Show code
fmt(data.frame(D_eff = sapply(sels, eff_dim, ctx = ctx)), 2)

# leading eigenvalue of the raw submatrix against n * theta (Rayleigh bound)
lead_ratio <- sapply(sels, function(s)
  eigen(ctx[["f"]][s, s], symmetric = TRUE, only.values = TRUE)$values[1] /
    (length(s) * theta_group(s, ctx)))
stopifnot(all(lead_ratio >= 1 - 1e-12))

# the uncentered participation ratio of the random subset, against the package value
D_pkg <- eff_dim(sels[["random"]], ctx)
l_unc <- eigen(ctx[["f"]][sels[["random"]], sels[["random"]]],
               symmetric = TRUE, only.values = TRUE)$values
D_unc <- sum(l_unc)^2 / sum(l_unc^2)

The submatrix is double-centered before the eigendecomposition. On a raw all-positive f the leading eigenvalue is at least \(n\theta\), because the Rayleigh quotient of \(\mathbf{f}_S\) at \(\mathbf{1}/\sqrt{n}\) is \(\mathbf{1}'\mathbf{f}_S\mathbf{1}/n = n\theta_S\), and for the five selections here it exceeds \(n\theta_S\) by at most 0.017 %. An uncentered version of Equation 11.8 would only re-measure \(\theta\) under a more expensive name – a mistake worth naming because it is easy to make and produces a plausible-looking number.
The two forms are easy to tell apart. On the random subset of this chapter the package’s double-centered \(D_{\text{eff}}\) is 26.19 and the uncentered ratio is 1.47, a factor of 18 apart. The eff_dim column of the cached redundancy analysis (Chapter 12, external data, see above) has mean 1.49 and range 1.44 to 1.51, which is of the order of the uncentered ratio and not of the package value. That cache was built at 12000 markers (Chapter 12) and this chapter runs at 2000, so the comparison crosses scales, and without a producer script it cannot be confirmed which form the cache used. That the cached column is uncentered is therefore a reading of the numbers, not a verified fact, and settling it needs the producer script of that cache.

11.8 Decomposition by heterotic group
The diversity between the two heterotic pools and the diversity within each are different resources. With inbred parents, the complete factorial and flat dominance (\(d_k \equiv 1\)), the divergence term of expected heterosis is GD_BS itself (Chapter 5); with \(d_k\) varying across loci it is the \(d\)-weighted version, which GD_BS does not fix, so divergence is worth having where it lands on the dominance loci and worth nothing where it does not. The diversity within each pool is the fuel for future progress, which Chapter 23 demonstrates. The simulated index of this chapter has no dominance term, so GD_BS below is a component of a partition and not a heterosis measure. Following Caballero and Toro (2002), compute molecular coancestry between lines and weight it by each line’s usage among the selected hybrids:
\[\theta_A = \mathbf{w}_A' \mathbf{f}^{L} \mathbf{w}_A, \qquad
  \theta_B = \mathbf{w}_B' \mathbf{f}^{L} \mathbf{w}_B, \qquad
  \theta_{AB} = \mathbf{w}_A' \mathbf{f}^{L} \mathbf{w}_B, \tag{11.9}\]
with \(\mathbf{w}_A\) and \(\mathbf{w}_B\) the usage weights of the pool-A and pool-B lines, each rescaled to sum to 1 within its pool (line_weights(), Appendix A).

Two things to read in Table 11.10. GD_WI is zero to machine precision (largest absolute value across the five selections \(6.7 \times 10^{-16}\), asserted below \(10^{-12}\)): the parent lines are inbred, so there is no within-individual diversity at line level – the algebra of Chapter 3 predicted this, and it is why GD_WI_hyb, the heterozygosity actually carried inside the F1s, is reported separately. And GD_BS rises under truncation, from 0.0374 for the random set to 0.0524.
Table 11.11 compares the three sources. The rise is measured, and the index of this simulation is additive in the two parents (the chunk below asserts that a regression of the index on the parent lines has \(R^2 = 1\), Chapter 6), with no dominance term, so no pair of lines is complementary beyond the sum of its parents’ values and complementarity between lines cannot be the cause. Section 10.7.6 gives the algebra for the same effect on the same kind of selection: with \(\tilde f = (\theta_A + \theta_B)/2\) and \(\bar f = (\theta_A + 2\theta_{AB} + \theta_B)/4\), \(GD_{BS} = \tilde f - \bar f\) (Caballero and Toro (2002)), and concentrating usage inside one pool raises \(\tilde f\) about twice as fast as \(\bar f\) at fixed \(\mathbf{f}^L\), so \(GD_{BS}\) rises without any change in the lines. Truncation’s effective number of lines (ne_lines_pool()) is 4.5 in pool A and 11.8 in pool B, against 17.6 and 16.8 for the random set.

Result. The mean GD_BS of 300 random subsets of 60 hybrids is 0.0358; of 300 subsets of 60 hybrids drawn from 5 random pool-A lines crossed with 12 random pool-B lines, with no selection on the index, it is 0.0492 (standard error of the mean \(6.9 \times 10^{-5}\)); the truncation selection has 0.0524. Line concentration alone therefore reproduces 81 % of the rise from the random mean to truncation under the rule \(k_A \times k_B\) = 5 \(\times\) 12; with 7 \(\times\) 17 lines the share is 49 %, and with the 10 \(\times\) 23 distinct lines of the truncation selection it is 27 %. Interpretation. The share is not a property of the selection alone: it falls as the control arm uses more lines. Equal usage over the distinct lines of the truncation selection is far less concentrated than the truncation’s own usage (effective numbers of lines 4.5 and 11.8), so that rule is a less matched control, and the 27 % is read as the result of that mismatch, not as a counter-result; which of the three rules is the right control was not settled here. Under the matched rule most of the rise is the usage-concentration effect of the algebra of Section 10.7.6, and none of it needs a heterosis reading. What is not isolated is the remainder, which could be selection on the index favouring lines that are also more divergent, or the unequal usage of truncation against the equal usage here; this is one founder draw and one subset size, and the comparison was not run at another scale.

11.8.1 Where this could go next
\(\theta_A\), \(\theta_B\) and \(\theta_{AB}\) as computed here are diagnostic: reported, not fed back into the objective. The subdivided-population literature offers a ready-made way to promote them into a tunable target. Total gene diversity partitions as \(H_T = H_S + D_G\) (Nei 1973) (\(D_G\) is the symbol of López-Cortegano et al. (2019) for the between-subpopulation component, which they take from Nei; Nei’s own symbol was not checked, only his abstract was read), and Caballero and Rodríguez-Ramilo (2010) give the allelic analogue \(A_T = A_S + D_A\). López-Cortegano et al. (2019), managing a simulated population subdivided into five subpopulations, maximise the weighted forms
\[H_\lambda = D_G + \lambda H_S, \qquad A_\lambda = D_A + \lambda A_S, \tag{11.10}\]
where \(H_S\) and \(A_S\) are the within-subpopulation components, \(D_G\) and \(D_A\) the between-subpopulation components, and \(\lambda \in [0, \infty)\) is a weight chosen by the manager. The subscript \(\lambda\) marks this as the weighted objective, distinct from Nei’s unweighted total \(H_T = H_S + D_G\): the two are equal only at \(\lambda = 1\). Reading the two subpopulations as the two heterotic pools is this book’s analogy, not theirs. \(\lambda = 0\) optimises only between-pool divergence – protects the divergence term of heterosis, ignores each pool’s internal health. \(\lambda \to \infty\) optimises only within-pool diversity – protects each pool’s future options, ignores the cross.
That maps directly onto the two constraints a maize breeder already has in mind but applies only qualitatively: don’t blend the pools versus don’t paint either pool into a corner. Turning \(\lambda\) into a second explicit knob alongside \(\alpha_{\max}\) is the natural next step if pool erosion shows up in practice. The current implementation reports the ingredients and leaves the weighting to the analyst.
\(\lambda\) need not stay a matter of taste when the objective is expected heterosis. Take inbred parents, two pools with equal weight, which the A \(\times\) B complete factorial imposes, and per locus \(H_{S,k} = p_{Ak}q_{Ak} + p_{Bk}q_{Bk}\), \(H_{T,k} = 2\bar p_k(1 - \bar p_k)\) and \(D_{G,k} = H_{T,k} - H_{S,k} = y_k^2/2\), with \(\bar p_k\) and \(y_k\) as in Equation 5.5. Averaged over loci, \(H_S = m^{-1}\sum_k H_{S,k}\) and \(D_G = m^{-1}\sum_k D_{G,k}\), as in the partition of Chapter 3. By Equation 5.5 the expected heterozygosity of the A \(\times\) B crosses at locus \(k\) is \(H_{T,k} + D_{G,k}\), and since \(H_{T,k} = H_{S,k} + D_{G,k}\) it is also
\[p_{Ak} + p_{Bk} - 2p_{Ak}p_{Bk} \;=\; H_{T,k} + D_{G,k} \;=\; H_{S,k} + 2D_{G,k}. \tag{11.11}\]
The shared term of Equation 5.5 is \(H_{T,k}\), not \(H_{S,k}\): it already contains one \(D_{G,k}\). With \(d_k \equiv 1\) the expected heterosis, averaged over loci, is \(H_S + 2D_G = 2(D_G + H_S/2)\), twice \(H_\lambda\) of Equation 11.10 with \(\lambda = 1/2\) fixed by the algebra. With dominance effects \(d_k\) (Chapter 5), \(m^{-1}\sum_k d_k(H_{S,k} + 2D_{G,k}) = 2\bar d_D\,(D_G + \lambda_d H_S)\), where
\[\lambda_d = \frac{\bar d_H}{2\,\bar d_D}, \qquad
  \bar d_H = \frac{\sum_k d_k H_{S,k}}{\sum_k H_{S,k}}, \qquad
  \bar d_D = \frac{\sum_k d_k D_{G,k}}{\sum_k D_{G,k}} \tag{11.12}\]
are the \(H_S\)-weighted and \(D_G\)-weighted means of \(d\). Reading \(\lambda_d\) as a maximisation weight, \(\lambda_d \in [0, \infty)\), needs net directional dominance on the two weighted loci, \(\bar d_D > 0\) and \(\bar d_H \ge 0\): if \(\bar d_D \le 0\) the leading factor \(2\bar d_D\) reverses the objective (maximising expected heterosis would then minimise the bracket, or leave \(\lambda_d\) undefined at \(\bar d_D = 0\)), and \(\bar d_H \ge 0\) is what keeps \(\lambda_d\) non-negative. \(\lambda_d\) departs from \(1/2\) only when dominance lines up differently with within-pool heterozygosity than with between-pool divergence, and a frequency-only partition cannot see that because \(d\) does not appear in it. \(\lambda_d\) is computed from a plan’s own frequencies, so it is a local weight rather than a constant of the population, and it is the right weight only for expected heterosis as the objective: López-Cortegano et al. (2019) run \(\lambda = 1\) mainly and also \(\lambda = 0\), \(0.5\) and \(1000\) (p. 3); they take \(0.5\) from Bennewitz and Meuwissen (2006), as a value suggested to maximise the total genetic variance of a hypothetical quantitative trait (as reported there; that paper was not read here). The weight \(1/2\) is also the \(\lambda_d\) of flat dominance, in the same form \(D_G + \lambda H_S\), but the two arguments differ (the variance of a quantitative trait there, the expected heterozygosity of the F1 here) and whether they are related is not examined. In the partition of Chapter 3, \(H_T = GD_T\), \(D_G = GD_{BS}\) and \(H_S = GD_T - GD_{BS} = GD_{WI} + GD_{BI} = GD_{WS}\); Equation 11.11 is then \(1 - \theta_{AB} = GD_T + GD_{BS}\), Equation 5.6, which Chapter 5 checks on the full factorial and which the chunk below asserts on the five selections (Table 11.13), together with the per-locus algebra on random frequencies. \(1 - \theta_{AB}\) is the expected heterozygosity of the complete factorial of the selected lines at their usage weights. It is not the heterozygosity of the pairs actually kept, \(2\,GD_{WI\text{-}hyb}\) (the F1_het of Table 10.4), which the table gives in its last column.

  tp <- theta_pools(s, ctx); gp <- gd_partition(s, ctx)
  c(one_minus_theta_AB = 1 - tp[["theta_AB"]],
    HS_plus_2DG = (gp[["GD_T"]] - gp[["GD_BS"]]) + 2 * gp[["GD_BS"]],
    F1_realised = 2 * gp[["GD_WI_hyb"]])
}))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(het_check[, "one_minus_theta_AB"], het_check[, "HS_plus_2DG"])))

Equation 11.12 is an identity, not a definition, so the chunk below asserts it (Table 11.14). The pool frequencies are those of the selected lines at their usage weights (line_weights(), simulate_lines()), and the dominance effects \(d_k\) are drawn from a gamma law, so they vary across loci; with \(d_k \equiv 1\), \(\lambda_d = 1/2\) exactly. The identity also equals the closed form heterosis_expected() divided by \(m\).


Show code
Lh <- simulate_lines(book_cfg) / 2           # lines, 0/1; same draw as ctx
lambda_d_check <- function(s, d) {
  w <- line_weights(s, ctx)
  pA_ <- drop(w$A %*% Lh); pB_ <- drop(w$B %*% Lh)
  HS_ <- pA_ * (1 - pA_) + pB_ * (1 - pB_); DG_ <- (pA_ - pB_)^2 / 2
  dH <- sum(d * HS_) / sum(HS_); dD <- sum(d * DG_) / sum(DG_)
  lam <- dH / (2 * dD)
  lhs <- mean(d * (HS_ + 2 * DG_))
  rhs <- 2 * dD * (mean(DG_) + lam * mean(HS_))
  stopifnot(dD > 0, dH >= 0,                 # the conditions stated above
            isTRUE(all.equal(lhs, rhs, tolerance = 1e-12)),
            isTRUE(all.equal(lhs, heterosis_expected(pA_, pB_, d) / length(d),
                             tolerance = 1e-12)))
  c(lambda_d = lam, relative_error = abs(lhs - rhs) / lhs)
}
set.seed(8)
d_k <- stats::rgamma(ctx[["m"]], shape = 2, rate = 4)
lam_flat <- t(sapply(sels, lambda_d_check, d = rep(1, ctx[["m"]])))
stopifnot(all(abs(lam_flat[, "lambda_d"] - 1/2) < 1e-12))
lam_var <- t(sapply(sels, lambda_d_check, d = d_k))
fmt(cbind(lambda_d_flat = lam_flat[, "lambda_d"], lambda_d_gamma = lam_var[, "lambda_d"],
          relative_error = lam_var[, "relative_error"]), 4)

text:
11.9 The correct baseline

11.9.1 Why not compare against the whole population
The natural comparison – coancestry of the selected set against that of the whole population – is biased by construction. Applying Equation 11.2 to both:
\[\mathbb{E}[\theta_S] - \theta_N
  = \left(\frac{1}{n} - \frac{1}{N}\right)\left(\bar f_d - \bar f_o\right) > 0, \tag{11.13}\]
where \(\theta_N\) is Equation 11.1 with \(S\) the whole population of \(N\) candidates, the expectation is over random subsets \(S\) of size \(n\) drawn without replacement, and \(\bar f_d\), \(\bar f_o\) are the population’s diagonal and off-diagonal means; the inequality holds since \(\bar f_d > \bar f_o\) whenever individuals are not clones. For a given, non-random \(S\) the means of Equation 11.2 are the set’s own and the difference can take either sign: the max-diversity greedy of this chapter has \(\theta_S =\) 0.66976 against \(\theta_N =\) 0.67191. A random sample already looks less diverse than the population it came from, with no selection whatsoever. The bias is pure sampling and grows as the sample shrinks. Table 11.15 compares the prediction with the mean of 400 random subsets.


Show code
fd <- mean(diag(ctx[["f"]])); fo <- mean(ctx[["f"]][upper.tri(ctx[["f"]])])

Note also that the off-diagonal mean of a random subset is an unbiased estimator of the population’s off-diagonal mean. So the metric many programmes already use is free of this particular bias – but it is not \(\theta_S\). By Equation 11.2 it omits the term \(\bar f_d/n\), the part of the set’s coancestry that depends on \(n\) and is real when the set is used as a crossing pool, so \(1/(2\bar f_o)\) is not the \(N_s\) of the set and the gap between the two grows as \(n\) shrinks.


11.9.2 Operational definition of loss
The “0 % loss” reference is the distribution of random subsets of the same size:
\[\alpha \;=\; \frac{GD_{\text{ref}} - GD_S}{GD_{\text{ref}}}. \tag{11.14}\]
Here \(GD_{\text{ref}}\) (gd_ref in the code) is the mean \(GD\) of random subsets of size \(n\). \(\alpha = 0\) means “as diverse as a random sample of the same size”; \(\alpha < 0\) means more diverse than chance. Resampling also delivers the standard deviation, and hence a z-score for any strategy. Table 11.16 gives the baseline of this chapter’s pool.

11.9.3 How to set the \(\alpha\) limit
The acceptable limit should not be chosen a priori. Pure truncation – the unconstrained optimum of the index – gives the \(\alpha\) (Equation 11.14) at which the constraint stops binding. This is not the largest \(\alpha\) over all subsets, which a minimum-diversity selection would reach; it is the largest \(\alpha\) a gain-maximising selection ever needs. If it is below your intended limit, the constraint restricts nothing and you have bought a false sense of control.


Show code

At this book’s teaching scale (25 + 25 lines, 2000 markers, \(n =\) 60) truncation reaches \(\alpha =\) 4.13 %, so a 5 % limit would be inoperative. The value at the package’s production scale (71 + 71 lines, 25000 markers, as in A8 of Section 10.1) and at the sim_config default (50 + 50 lines, 5000 markers) is not computed in this chapter, and this one does not transfer to either. The correct procedure is to trace the \(\alpha\)-versus-gain frontier and choose its knee: Chapter 15 shows the frontier of the greedy over the merit weight and Chapter 16 gives the recipe.

title: 12  Choosing metrics: collapse, cost, redundancy
text:
12.1 Finding 1: the hybrid coancestry matrix is never needed
Chapter 11 built a catalogue. This chapter asks which of it to keep, and answers with two questions the catalogue could not: what does each metric cost per evaluation, and how much of what it reports is already in \(\theta\).
The recommendation is two metrics inside the optimiser and three at validation.
Three findings drive this, and each is derived and verified below rather than asserted.
crumbs: 12  Choosing metrics: collapse, cost, redundancy

title: 12  Choosing metrics: collapse, cost, redundancy
text:
12.1.1 Derivation
Let lines \(a, b, \dots\) be homozygous, with \(\mathbf{f}^L\) their molecular coancestry matrix. The hybrid \((ab)\) carries one genome from each parent. Molecular coancestry is the probability that two alleles, one drawn at random from each individual, are identical in state. Drawing at random from hybrid \((ab)\) selects parental genome \(a\) or \(b\) with probability \(\tfrac12\) each, and likewise for \((cd)\), so
\[f_{(ab),(cd)} \;=\; \tfrac14\left(f^L_{ac} + f^L_{ad} + f^L_{bc} + f^L_{bd}\right).\]
Now let a selection of \(n\) hybrids use line \(a\) exactly \(k_a\) times across all its parental slots, \(\sum_a k_a = 2n\), and write \(w_a = k_a/(2n)\). Group coancestry of the selected hybrids is the mean of \(f\) over all ordered pairs; substituting the identity above and collecting terms by line gives
\[\theta_S \;=\; \mathbf{w}^{\top}\, \mathbf{f}^L \,\mathbf{w},\]
with the selection allele frequencies following the same collapse, \(\bar{\mathbf{p}} = \mathbf{w}^{\top}\mathbf{G}^L\).


12.1.2 Four consequences
The \(N \times N\) hybrid matrix is never required. Memory drops from \(O(N^2)\) to \(O(L^2)\). At \(L = 300\) lines and \(N = 22{,}500\) hybrids that matrix would occupy 3.77 GB; in the benchmark below it was deliberately never formed, and every metric that needs it simply has no timing entry at that scale.
The vector \(\mathbf{w}\) is a sufficient statistic. Group coancestry, gene diversity, status number, effective number of parents, selection allele frequencies and the heterotic-pool decomposition are all functions of \(\mathbf{w}\) alone. One \(O(L)\) tabulation per evaluation serves all of them.
Swapping one hybrid is a rank-2 update. Exchanging hybrid \(h\) for \(h'\) changes at most four entries of \(\mathbf{w}\), so \(\theta\) updates in \(O(L)\) rather than \(O(L^2)\).
The discrete hybrid problem is exactly optimal-contribution selection on lines, restricted to the lattice \(w_a \in \{0, 1/(2n), 2/(2n), \dots\}\). That connects it directly to the OCS literature of Chapter 15, with the caveat that the lattice restriction makes it combinatorial rather than the continuous quadratic programme OCS usually solves.

WarningTwo implementation traps found while building this



R’s $ performs partial matching on lists, so ctx$f silently returns ctx$fL when the hybrid matrix is absent – a wrong answer with no error. Every accessor in the package uses ctx[["f"]]. Any pipeline carrying both matrices in one list is exposed to this.
R integers are signed 32-bit, so bitwShiftL(1L, 31L) is NA and the usual multiply-based popcount overflows. The bitset in pack_lines() packs 31 bits per word, and popcount32() counts them with a branch-free SWAR routine.

Three thresholds matter:

The genotype-scan route is disqualified. Computing \(\theta\) from selection allele frequencies costs 14.2 hours per million evaluations. The line route costs 106 us – a 482x reduction for an algebraically identical number.
The incremental swap is effectively free at 5 us, or 1.4 seconds per million evaluations. \(N_{e,\text{par}}\) at 7 us shares the same state vector and is free in practice once \(\theta\) has been computed.
Allelic richness cannot go inside the loop, and need not. The bitset implementation is 5.7x faster than the floating-point version, but still 178x the cost of the line-route \(\theta\). It belongs at validation.

title: 12  Choosing metrics: collapse, cost, redundancy
section: 12.3 Finding 3: the metric space is nearly one-dimensional
text:
12.3 Finding 3: the metric space is nearly one-dimensional
621 selections were generated across four strategy families – random, truncation at varying intensity, greedy construction over a grid of diversity weights, and restricted line pools – and all 17 metrics computed on each.





Metric redundancy. A: Spearman correlations. B: PCA of rank-transformed metrics. C: the discriminating case, inside a narrow coancestry band.




PC1 absorbs 88% of the rank variance; PC2 adds 7%. Rank correlations with \(\theta\) are \(|\rho| \ge 0.93\) for status number, \(H_e\), effective dimensionality, \(N_{e,\text{par}}\) and MAF-threshold allele loss. Reporting these alongside \(\theta\) adds cost and length, not information.
But the marginal correlation is the wrong test. The question is whether a metric varies at fixed \(\theta\) – because \(\theta\) is the constraint, and any metric that is a deterministic function of it cannot discriminate among plans the optimiser treats as equivalent. Two analyses agree:

After regressing each metric’s ranks on \(\theta\) (quadratic), allelic richness retains 52% of its rank standard deviation and \(N_{e,\text{par}}\) retains 36%. Effective dimensionality retains 25% – close to a restatement of \(\theta\).
Inside a band \(\theta \in [0.666, 0.670]\) containing 399 selections, alleles retained still spans 171 markers (11,680 to 11,851 of 12,000) and \(N_{e,\text{par}}\) spans 30.1 to 55.8.

Plans the constraint cannot distinguish differ materially in how much allelic variation they carry forward. That is the empirical justification for the two-metric recommendation.

12.3.1 Reproducing the argument at book scale


Show code
set.seed(77)
grid <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq(0, 4, length.out = 30), function(w) {
  s <- sel_greedy(ctx, 60, w = w)
  data.frame(w = w, theta = theta_group(s, ctx), Ne_par = ne_parents(s, ctx),
             lost = alleles_lost(s, ctx))
}))
rnd <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:60, function(i) {
  s <- sample.int(ctx$N, 60)
  data.frame(w = NA, theta = theta_group(s, ctx), Ne_par = ne_parents(s, ctx),
             lost = alleles_lost(s, ctx))
}))
all <- rbind(grid, rnd)

plot(all$theta, all$Ne_par, pch = 19, col = ifelse(is.na(all$w), "grey60", "#b2182b"),
     xlab = expression(theta), ylab = expression(N[e]~"parents"))
legend("topright", c("greedy sweep", "random"), pch = 19,
       col = c("#b2182b", "grey60"), bty = "n")
grid()





At fixed theta, the effective number of parents still varies by a factor of two. The constraint cannot see the difference; the second metric can.

c(n_in_band = nrow(band),
  theta_span = diff(range(band$theta)),
  Ne_par_min = min(band$Ne_par), Ne_par_max = max(band$Ne_par),
  alleles_lost_span = diff(range(band$lost)))

These numbers come from a two-pool simulation at \(F_{ST} = 0.15\). The qualitative conclusion – near one-dimensionality, with allelic richness as the exception – is robust in direction, but the exact residual fractions shift with pool divergence and marker density. Re-running the redundancy analysis on real genotypes is a half-hour job and worth doing before treating the recommendation as final.

12.4 Finding 4: the encoding, not the constraint handler, decides whether DE works
The optimiser was run under four simultaneous restrictions: diversity loss \(\le 0.5\%\), \(N_{e,\text{par}} \ge 50\), at most 6 uses per line, and heterotic-pool balance within 5%. Budget fixed at 60,000 evaluations for every configuration, three seeds each.





Differential evolution under four simultaneous restrictions at equal evaluation budget.







Mean over 3 seeds. All configurations returned feasible plans.
