The anchor numbers are as follows.

Maize (Li et al. 2026). Mean accuracy was 0.418 under full overlap and 0.479 to 0.504 under every other allocation. Returns diminish beyond about 50 % coverage: going from 50 % to 67 % cost 33 % more phenotyping and returned 3.5 to 5.4 % accuracy. Top-50 % coincidence was above 61.9 % in all 25 strategies.
Wheat (Atanda et al. 2022). Going from 0 to 50 % common lines raised predictive ability by 42 % to 989 %, depending on the environment. Plot \(h^2\) was 0.18 in the worst environment. Genetic correlations between environments in the same year ranged from \(-0.04\) to \(0.67\).
Cassava (Lubanga et al. 2025). With 20 % of records per environment, predictive ability was moderate (maxima of 0.53 for dry matter and 0.47 for fresh root yield). Phenotyping cost could be cut by up to 80 %.
Potato (Hild Aono and Chawade 2026). For pairs of environments at 50 % completeness, \(r^2\) was 0.995 to 0.997 with an image-derived environment kernel, against 0.612 to 0.798 with the genomic kernel. Section Section 19.10 covers the caveat.

The common denominator is the genetic correlation between environments, and the size and diversity of the training set. Together they explain most of the spread. In Atanda et al. (2022), the environment with low heritability and weak correlations stayed poorly predicted under every design. In Li et al. (2026), plant height was the trait with the strongest between-environment correlations (0.36 to 0.67) and the best predicted. Grain yield had no strong correlations and was predicted worst. Modelling G x E explicitly helped in every study that tested it (Lubanga et al. 2025; Li et al. 2026). Cutting phenotyping by 50 to 80 % without losing accuracy is feasible. The exact cut depends on the programme’s own between-environment correlations, and does not transfer between programmes.

19.6 The minimum-overlap controversy
The literature disagrees openly on how much overlap is needed:

Atanda et al. (2022) conclude that “a substantial overlap of lines between environments” is needed.
Crespo-Herrera et al. (2021) suggest 30 to 50 common lines.
Persa et al. (2023) report a gain with as few as 10.
Lubanga et al. (2025) find that more overlap made prediction worse: predictive ability fell and MSE rose monotonically with the number of overlapping genotypes, and the fully non-overlapping design was the best.
Li et al. (2026) sit in between. Full overlap was the worst design, and the four partial or non-overlapping designs tied.
Werner, Covarrubias-Pazaran, et al. (2025) and González-Diéguez et al. (2026) do without overlap altogether. All of their connectivity comes from relationships.

A proposed reconciliation, offered here as a hypothesis. The designs are not comparable because they confound overlap with the size and diversity of the training set:

In Lubanga et al. (2025) the training set per environment is fixed in size. More overlap therefore means fewer distinct genotypes observed.
In Atanda et al. (2022) more overlap means a larger calibration set per environment, growing from 46-47 lines to as many as 165.

A second factor is family structure. Families of 1 to 9 individuals (Atanda et al. 2022) give the relationship matrix little to work with, so physical overlap has to carry the connection. Families of 20 to 50 (Werner, Covarrubias-Pazaran, et al. 2025; González-Diéguez et al. 2026) let the relationship matrix carry all of it.
The first half of the hypothesis is testable directly with the package. The experiment uses four locations and a training set fixed at 80 hybrids per location out of 400. A fraction of the 80 is a core common to all four locations, and the rest are unique to each location. Family size runs from unrelated lines to half-sib families of 10 (regenerate.R sparse, part c; 30 replicates per point; known components; plot \(h^2 = 0.4\)).


Show code
ov <- subset(core, part == "overlap")
fs <- sort(unique(ov$family_size))
cols <- c("grey40", "#1b9e77", "#d95f02")[seq_along(fs)]
op <- par(mar = c(4.2, 4.2, 3.2, 1))
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = range(ov$acc_all - 2 * ov$acc_all_se, ov$acc_all + 2 * ov$acc_all_se),
     xlab = "Overlap: fraction of each location's plots in the common core",
     ylab = "Accuracy, all hybrids")
for (i in seq_along(fs)) {
  d <- ov[ov$family_size == fs[i], ]; d <- d[order(d$overlap), ]
  lines(d$overlap, d$acc_all, type = "b", pch = 19, col = cols[i])
  arrows(d$overlap, d$acc_all - 2 * d$acc_all_se, d$overlap, d$acc_all + 2 * d$acc_all_se,
         angle = 90, code = 3, length = 0.03, col = cols[i])
}
d0 <- ov[ov$family_size == fs[1], ]; d0 <- d0[order(d0$overlap), ]
axis(3, at = d0$overlap, labels = d0$n_distinct, cex.axis = 0.8)
mtext("distinct hybrids observed", 3, line = 2, cex = 0.8)
legend("bottomleft", bty = "n", lwd = 2, col = cols,
       legend = ifelse(fs == 1, "unrelated lines", paste("half-sib families of", fs)))
par(op)








Figure 19.5: Accuracy over all 400 hybrids against the fraction of each location’s 80 plots taken by a core common to all four locations, by half-sib family size. The training size is held fixed, so more overlap means fewer distinct hybrids observed (top axis). Bars are two standard errors over 30 replicates. In-repo sweep, known variance components.





With the training size held fixed, accuracy falls as overlap rises: it is 0.023 to 0.059 lower under full overlap than under none, 1.6 to 4.7 standard errors of the difference depending on family size. The drop is resolved for unrelated lines and for families of 10, and not for families of 4 (1.6 standard errors), whose curve has the same direction. The cause is the confound, not overlap as such. Every hybrid moved into the common core is one fewer distinct hybrid observed (top axis). This is the Lubanga et al. (2025) pattern, reproduced with the mechanism exposed.
The second half of the hypothesis is not supported at this scale. The family-size curves cross, and they differ by at most 2.2 standard errors at any one overlap: of the 15 pairs compared (every pair of family sizes at every overlap, with no correction for multiple comparisons), 1 exceeded two standard errors and 0 exceeded three. In hindsight the reason is structural. In a female x male factorial every line is already the parent of 20 hybrids, so the factorial carries much of the connectivity before any relationship among lines is added. Half-sib families add relatively little on top of that. In a line-breeding programme like Atanda et al. (2022), each entry is its own genotype and no parent links them, so family structure should matter far more. This experiment cannot test that case. The experiment also holds the training size fixed, so it does not reproduce Atanda et al. (2022)’s design, in which more overlap also meant a larger calibration set and the two effects pull in opposite directions.
What to do with this. The right question is not “how many common genotypes?”. It is “how much effective connectivity does the design have, counting both physical overlap and relationships?”. The experiment above suggests that physical overlap and relationships between the lines of different environments are partial substitutes, and Atanda et al. (2022) found both the genetic correlation between environments and the genomic relationship of lines across them among the drivers of sparse-testing accuracy. In a hybrid factorial, shared parents already supply much of the relationship side.

text:
19.7 Connectivity and checks
Connectivity is not the same as overlap. Two designs with the same number of common genotypes can be connected very differently, depending on how those genotypes are distributed. Hybrids add a dimension. There is female x male connectivity, the subject of Section 18.2.3. There is genotype x location connectivity. And there is female x male x location, for which no metric is agreed (Section 19.13); Section 20.4 gives a necessary screen and a counter-example to sufficiency, and leaves the metric open. The available tools are:

the rank of the incidence matrix;
the PEV of pairwise contrasts, and the reliability derived from it;
the connected components of the genotype-environment graph.

Checks do three jobs:

anchor connectivity;
estimate within-environment error in unreplicated trials, as in the augmented design of Li et al. (2026);
control spatial trend (Cullis et al. 2006; Williams et al. 2011).

Restricted randomisation is a cheap connectivity tool. Werner, Covarrubias-Pazaran, et al. (2025) kept full-sibs apart within a location, but did not measure the restriction against unrestricted randomisation. Section 19.11.3 does measure a structured layout against unrestricted randomisation.
Connectivity can be checked before planting. Compute it at the planning stage, rather than finding out from a model that does not converge.






TipBox 4 – Computing the connectivity of a design before planting it




Build the genotype x environment incidence matrix.
Check the connected components of the bipartite graph. Every location should share hybrids, or at least parents, with every other.
Compute the mean PEV of the target values under the intended model, with provisional variance components.
Convert it to reliability, \(1 - \overline{\mathrm{PEV}}/\sigma^2_G\).
Compare candidate designs on the same metric.



Show code
set.seed(8)
nF <- 20; nM <- 20; L <- 6
Af <- relmat_halfsib(nF, 5); Am <- relmat_halfsib(nM, 5)
vc <- sparse_vc(0.3)
recipe <- function(M) {
  cn  <- sparse_connectivity(M, nF, nM)                       # steps 1-2
  # PEV does not depend on y, so any phenotype vector will do (steps 3-4).
  cells <- which(M == 1L, arr.ind = TRUE)
  ph  <- data.frame(y = 0, hyb = cells[, 1], loc = cells[, 2])
  pev <- sparse_blup(ph, nF, nM, L, vc, Af, Am)$pev
  c(plots = sum(M), fem_cover = cn$fem_cover, disconnected_pairs = cn$frac_disconn,
    reliability = 1 - mean(pev) / vc$Vg)
}
fmt(rbind(complete_2loc = recipe(sparse_alloc(nF, nM, 2, strategy = "complete")),
          random_k2     = recipe(sparse_alloc(nF, nM, L, 2, "random")),
          parentage_k2  = recipe(sparse_alloc(nF, nM, L, 2, "parentage"))), 3)

section: 19.8 Sparse testcrossing and the number of testers
text:
19.8 Sparse testcrossing and the number of testers
The central idea of González-Diéguez et al. (2026) is to treat the tester as an “environment”. Each line is crossed to one tester, but full-sibs go to different testers. What gets evaluated against several testers is therefore the haplotype, not the genotype. This removes a real logistical constraint. The more accurate alternative, an incomplete factorial among candidates (Section 18.4), needs hand pollination at scale and synchronised flowering between pools.








Figure 19.6: Sparse testcrossing. A biparental cross yields 20 DH lines; each line is crossed to one of four testers, so the family – not the line – meets every tester. The relationship matrix connects the full-sibs, and through them the four testers.








Table 19.3: Sparse testcrossing in González-Diéguez et al. (2026): accuracy and gain against a single tester at an equal number of testcrosses. Every sparse layout beat the single tester, and gains plateau at 5 to 10 testers; 3 to 5 is the practical recommendation.

The advantage is largest in early cycles, while the pools are still close. That does not confine the method to emerging programmes. Real commercial pools sit at a minimum Nei distance of 0.17 (Legarra et al. 2023) and an \(F_{ST}\) of 0.223 (Kadoumi et al. 2025), which corresponds to cycles 2 to 4 of the simulation.
A useful side effect is that sparse testcrossing slowed the erosion of within-pool variance. It stops selection from piling onto closely related lines that happen to nick with one tester. The authors recommend combining it with optimum contribution selection (Chapter 15; Santantonio and Robbins (2020)).
The deterministic tradition reaches the same order of magnitude by another route (C. Longin et al. 2006). The advocates of incomplete factorials (Seye et al. 2020; Lorenzi et al. 2022; Lorenzi et al. 2024; Melchinger and Frisch 2023) reach a different conclusion. In González-Diéguez et al. (2026), an approximate incomplete factorial matched 3 to 5 testers, with much heavier logistics. Two costs were not modelled. Five testers need ten isolation blocks. And in many public programmes hand pollination is already routine, which lowers the extra cost of the factorial.






TipBox 5 – Choosing testers: theory against practice



The classical recommendation is a low-performing tester, or one carrying recessive alleles at the loci of interest. Such a tester discriminates among candidates best (Hull 1945; Rawlings and Thompson 1962). Commercial practice uses elite testers, chosen for seed production and per se performance, because the testcross may itself become a product. The consequence follows from Section 5.11: GCA is measured against the tester’s allele frequencies. An elite tester carries the favourable allele at many loci and shrinks the visible differences there, so a few elite testers sample the opposite pool’s frequencies poorly. Several testers spread across the pool, the sparse-testcross recipe, sample them better (C. Longin et al. 2006; Jong et al. 2023).

section: 19.9 What sparsity does to variance components and to the BLUP
text:
19.9 What sparsity does to variance components and to the BLUP
Two questions are often merged in the literature, and they should be kept separate:

Do the predictions stay accurate?
Do the variance-component estimates stay unbiased?

The second is barely covered. None of the six primary studies reports bias in \(\sigma^2_{GCA}\), \(\sigma^2_{SCA}\) or \(\sigma^2_{GE}\) under sparsity. The indirect evidence is thin:

In Hild Aono and Chawade (2026) the G x E term degraded prediction under high sparsity, because there were too few individuals to estimate it. The authors recommend dropping it in that regime.
In Li et al. (2026) propagating prediction uncertainty barely changed the GCA estimates (correlation 0.9974 to 0.9998 with the point estimates). That is a sensitivity of GCA, not of the variance components.

Two diagnostics separate the questions.

The dispersion slope \(b_1\), from regressing truth on prediction. \(b_1 = 1\) means no scale bias. \(b_1 < 1\) means the predictions are too spread out, and \(b_1 > 1\) means they are over-shrunk.
PEV and reliability. These can be computed before any data exist (Box 4), so they serve as design tools.

Accuracy and estimation quality do not degrade at the same rate. A design can rank candidates well and still estimate the SCA and G x E variances badly (Cullis et al. 2006; Piepho and Mohring 2007; Smith and Cullis 2018; Tolhurst et al. 2019). The simulation of Section 19.11.3 measures this directly. That is the gap in the primary literature it was designed to fill.

title: 19  Sparse testing: which hybrids go to which locations
text:
19.10 Sparse testing with phenomics
Phenomic data pose a specific problem. Markers can be read from a seedling whatever happens in the field. Sensor data exist only for plots that were actually grown, so they cannot serve as a covariate for an individual that was never observed. There are three ways out:

multi-trait models with image indices as secondary traits;
kernel regression on the indices;
the proposal of Hild Aono and Chawade (2026): use the images to build an environment kernel.

The environment kernel is built in three steps. A PCA of the image traits is run within each environment. The first-component eigenvector of each environment is extracted. The kernel entries are the correlations between those eigenvectors.
The image kernel matched or beat the genomic kernel from about 30 to 33 % completeness, reaching \(r^2 = 0.997\) on pairs of environments. Below about 20 % the genomic kernel was preferable again. The authors warn of possible information leakage, because the kernel came from the same trial that supplied training and validation. The result should be reported with that caveat.








Figure 19.7: Building an environment kernel from images, after Hild Aono and Chawade (2026). The dashed box marks where training and validation share information – the leakage the authors flag.





The approach is attractive for programmes without routine genotyping. It is also promising for maize, where sensor phenotyping exists but has not been tested in this arrangement with hybrids. It connects to envirotyping. When locations are close together, coarse-grid weather covariates discriminate poorly, and images capture differences that the weather data miss (Costa-Neto et al. 2020; Crossa et al. 2021; Rincent et al. 2017). NIRS-based phenomic prediction in maize points the same way, in a non-sparse setting (DeSalvio et al. 2024).
Sensor data enter sparse testing as descriptors of environments, not of genotypes. This inversion solves the availability problem. In programmes that genotype little, it can partly replace the genomic matrix.

text:
19.11 Simulation as a sizing tool

19.11.1 Why simulate before designing
None of the published numbers transfers directly to another programme. Each one depends on the between-environment correlations, the family structure, the \(\sigma^2_{SCA}/\sigma^2_{GCA}\) ratio and the heritability of the programme that produced it, and the authors say so themselves (Werner, Covarrubias-Pazaran, et al. 2025; González-Diéguez et al. 2026). A simulation can do three things an experiment cannot:

it knows the true values;
it can rerun the programme a hundred times;
it can isolate one factor at a time.

The tools exist. AlphaSimR covers the genetics , Chapter 9, FieldSimR covers plots and G x E (Werner et al. 2024), and sommer or BGLR fit the models (Covarrubias-Pazaran 2016). Staged-allocation theory provides the deterministic cross-check (Mi et al. 2014; C. F. H. Longin et al. 2006). Simulation does not replace the experiment. It replaces guessing at the design of the experiment.


19.11.2 Realistic parameters: what the literature supplies

Two features of real data a simulation must respect:

Environmental variance exceeds genetic variance by an order of magnitude. For maize grain yield, \(\sigma^2_{env}/\sigma^2_g \approx 8.1\) (Li et al. 2026).
Between-environment correlations for yield are often weak. Scenarios should be anchored on measured parameters, not chosen for numerical convenience.



19.11.3 What the simulation finds
The model. The study simulated a female x male factorial of single crosses, tested with one plot per hybrid x location cell. The phenotype is
\[
y = \mu + \text{loc} + \mathrm{GCA}^f + \mathrm{GCA}^m + \mathrm{SCA}
  + \mathrm{GCA}^f{\times}\text{loc} + \mathrm{GCA}^m{\times}\text{loc}
  + \mathrm{SCA}{\times}\text{loc} + e .
\]
The target is the value in the TPE, \(\mathrm{GCA}^f + \mathrm{GCA}^m +
\mathrm{SCA}\). In every replicate, 20 % of the hybrids get no plot at all. These are the CV1 hybrids, predicted only through relationships.
The calibration is sparse_vc():

\(\sigma^2_f = \sigma^2_m = 1\) and \(\sigma^2_{SCA} = 0.25\);
every interaction with location is half its main effect;
plot \(h^2\) of 0.20 or 0.40.

In sparse_vc() the components are s2f, s2m, s2s (\(\sigma^2_{SCA}\)), s2fl, s2ml (the two GCA x location variances), s2sl (\(\sigma^2_{SCA\times L}\), written \(\sigma^2_{s\ell}\) in Section 20.2) and s2e.
These choices imply a genetic correlation between locations of \(V_G/(V_G+V_{GE}) = 0.667\). That sits inside the 0.36 to 0.67 measured in maize (Li et al. 2026) and close to the 0.60 of Werner, Covarrubias-Pazaran, et al. (2025). The SCA:GCA ratio of 0.25 lies among the values in González-Diéguez et al. (2026), and the two heritabilities bracket Werner, Covarrubias-Pazaran, et al. (2025)’s 0.10 and the 0.30 of González-Diéguez et al. (2026).
The four strategies, all at the same cost of \(k\) locations per hybrid out of \(L\) in the trial (\(k\) is not the testers per pool of Chapter 18):

complete;
random: each hybrid goes to \(k\) locations drawn at random;
optimised blocks: an exchange algorithm on the mixed-model coefficient matrix, with replicated checks;
parentage: the factorial is cut into cyclic groups, each holding every female and every male, and groups are dealt to locations so that every location receives both whole pools.

The last is sparse_alloc(strategy = "parentage").
Validation of the estimator. Before any comparison, the estimator was checked on the complete design, where REML must recover the true components (Table 19.5).


Show code

19.11.3.2 2. At fixed cost, spreading plots over locations beats concentrating them
This is the most actionable result (Figure 19.8, right). Each planted hybrid keeps two plots (the 80 % of the factorial that is planted, so 640 plots in every design of the panel), the cost of a two-location trial of those hybrids. At \(h^2 = 0.4\), accuracy rises from 0.831 with both plots in the same two locations to 0.860, 0.883 and 0.892 as those plots are spread across 4, 6 and 10 locations. At \(h^2 = 0.2\) it rises from 0.733 to 0.819. Not one extra plot is spent, and no planted hybrid gains a location: each is still in two. What grows is the number of environments the trial samples, and with it the number of locations over which each parent’s crosses, and so its GCA, are spread. The gain saturates between six and ten locations. This slice never varied the locations per hybrid and never traded a location against a replicate, so it measures only the value of sampling more trial sites at a fixed number of plots – the “broader sampling of trial sites” of Werner, Covarrubias-Pazaran, et al. (2025) – not a trade against replication.

19.11.3.4 4. Parent coverage, not shared hybrids, carries the connectivity
Consider ten locations with two per hybrid at \(h^2 = 0.4\). The best design there is the parentage design, with accuracy 0.897. Its harmonic-mean concurrence, the number of hybrids a pair of locations shares, is 0.000: some pairs of locations share no hybrid at all. This is structural. Twenty groups at two locations each touch at most 20 of the 45 location pairs. Random allocation shares hybrids between almost every pair (harmonic mean 5.466) and is less accurate. What the parentage design keeps is parent coverage. The mean fraction of females present per location is 0.999, against 0.965 for random allocation.
Once a relationship matrix is in the model, what carries connectivity is representing both pools in every location, not repeating the same hybrids across locations. Put this together with Section 19.6 and it reads as one account of the Atanda et al. (2022) versus Lubanga et al. (2025) disagreement. Shared hybrids are one way to connect environments. Shared parents are another, cheaper one, and in a hybrid factorial the shared parents come for free.


19.11.3.5 5. Dispersion is small where REML converges; the SCA variance is not recoverable

     xlab = "Locations per hybrid, k", ylab = "Dispersion slope b1", ylim = c(0.5, 1.5))

Figure 19.10: Left: median relative bias of REML components and of plot h2 by locations per hybrid k, over all cached scenarios. Right: the dispersion slope b1 (truth on BLUP), one point per scenario; the dashed line is no dispersion bias. Scenarios with k = 1 and incomplete REML convergence produce the outliers (axis clipped at 0.5-1.5).





Prediction holds up where the components are estimable. In the scenarios where every REML fit converged – all with \(k \ge 2\) – the dispersion slope lies between 0.845 and 1.076, on both sides of 1 (median 1.005). With \(k \ge 4\) it lies between 0.942 and 1.057. At \(k = 1\) no scenario had every fit converge; the median slope there is 0.968, with outliers far from 1 (Figure 19.10, right). Sparsity therefore costs accuracy without a systematic dispersion bias at \(k \ge 2\), with individual scenarios off by up to 15 %; at \(k = 1\) the REML evidence does not settle the question, and the known-component sweep of 1, whose slopes sit near 1 at \(k = 1\), shows only that the estimator is undispersed when the components are right. The GCA variance, the GCA x location variance and plot \(h^2\) have median biases near zero at every \(k\).
\(\sigma^2_{SCA}\) is the exception. Its median relative bias is +12 % at \(k = 4\), +30 % at \(k = 2\), and +220 % at \(k = 1\). Much of this is present in the complete design too (Table 19.5), so it is mainly a problem of identifying a small component, and sparsity makes it worse. A programme that needs a reliable SCA is in product development, not population improvement. It cannot fix the problem by adding coverage to a stage-1 trial.
The hidden cost is convergence. REML converged in 100.0 % of fits with four locations per hybrid, 97.0 % with three, 88.5 % with two, and only 42.6 % with one. That is 411 non-convergences in 2630 fits.






ImportantBox – Why REML does not converge when each hybrid sees one location



With \(k = 1\) each hybrid contributes a single plot in a single location. The data then carry no within-hybrid information to separate a hybrid’s GCA from its GCA x location deviation. The likelihood is flat along that ridge. The algorithm walks to the boundary of the parameter space and stops without meeting its criterion. The BLUPs from those fits are still usable. They come from solving the mixed-model equations at the current components, which is exactly what sparse_blup() does with known ones. The variance estimates are not usable, and should not be reported. Predicting well and estimating well are different achievements. At \(k = 1\) a trial can still do the first.




19.11.3.6 6. Two stages: test every candidate sparsely rather than a subset densely
The two-stage scenario works as follows:

A pool of 400 candidate hybrids is available.
Stage 1 tests \(N_1\) of them sparsely and keeps the top \(q\) by BLUP.
Stage 2 tests the survivors densely in new locations.
The final analysis is joint.

The metric is the realised gain: the mean true value of the ten hybrids finally chosen, in genetic standard deviations. Under 700 total plots, the gain is 1.358 when stage 1 tests 100 candidates, 1.778 for 200, and 2.148 for all 400. Across all budgets, efficiency relative to an oracle that selects on the truth rises from 0.585 to 0.935. The share of the true top 5 % captured rises from 19.8 % to 72.1 %.

     xlab = "Total plots (log scale)", ylab = "Realised gain (genetic SD)")

lines(o$plots_total, o$gain_max_sd_units, col = "grey60", lwd = 3)
for (n in names(cl)) {
  e <- a[a$N1 == as.numeric(n), ]; e <- e[order(e$plots_total), ]
  lines(e$plots_total, e$gain_sd_units, type = "b", pch = 19, col = cl[n])
}

With a fixed budget, stage 1 should cover every candidate with few plots each, not a subset with many. The best combinations among the cached settings used four stage-1 locations at 50 % sparsity, eight stage-2 locations, and kept the top 10 to 20 %.


19.11.3.7 Limitations of the simulation
The simulation has six limitations.

One plot per cell. SCA x location then has the same incidence as plot error, and the analysis model absorbs it into an i.i.d. residual that estimates \(\sigma^2_{SCA\times L} + \sigma^2_e\). Equal incidence alone does not make the two inseparable: drawn with the kernel \(\mathbf A_f \otimes \mathbf A_m\), as sparse_simulate() draws it, SCA x location is correlated between related crosses in one location and could be carried as a structured term; Section 20.2 measures what that buys in one configuration. Within-location replication was not simulated.
G x E is full-rank and symmetric in the fast layer, and rank one in the genomic layer. Neither layer has the factor-analytic structure of real trials or a crossover/non-crossover split (Burgueño et al. 2012; Werner, Covarrubias-Pazaran, et al. 2025).
The pools are symmetric and unselected. There are no cycles of reciprocal recurrent selection, so the simulation says nothing about long-run pool trajectories (Chapter 23) or about unbalanced pools.
Cost is counted in plots, not money. Opening a location costs more than adding plots to an existing one. The advice to spread plots assumes the marginal location is moderately priced (Section 18.7 has the cost structure).
The grid is reduced. It has at most 15 replicates per cell, no 200-hybrid level, and the high-SCA block run separately. The two-stage layer has 4 replicates and the genomic layer 8.
Components are checked by mean bias only. No per-replicate confidence intervals were computed.

title: 19  Sparse testing: which hybrids go to which locations
text:
19.12 Practical recommendations by stage
Stage 1 (first agronomic testcross trial).

Give priority to the number of candidates and the number of locations in the trial. At fixed plots per hybrid, spread them over more locations, up to about six (result 2).
Use 3 to 5 testers in sparse testcrossing, with full-sibs spread across testers.
Use low partial replication (p-rep of 0.1 to 0.2), with checks replicated in every block.
When plots per hybrid fall to one or two, use a layout that puts both pools in every location (results 3 and 4).
The estimation target is GCA. Do not expect a reliable SCA at this stage (result 5).

Stage 2 (pre-commercial hybrids).

Test fewer candidates, and raise replication and environmental coverage.
Keep a common core large enough to estimate the between-environment genetic correlations.
The estimation target is now specific performance and stability, so SCA and G x E matter.

Decisions that span both stages.

Genotype the parents, not the hybrids.
Check connectivity before planting (Box 4).
Match the between-environment covariance to the amount of data. Do not force an unstructured matrix on a very sparse design.
Advance on GBLUP rather than BLUE when heritability is low to moderate and locations are few (Atanda et al. 2022; Endelman et al. 2014).

What not to do.

Put everything in one location, however many candidates that allows. It gave the most variable gain in Werner, Covarrubias-Pazaran, et al. (2025), with replicates of negative gain.
Use one tester at stage 1 when there is infrastructure for three.
Transfer a sparsity percentage from another crop or programme without your own simulation.
Fit a G x E term under extreme sparsity (Hild Aono and Chawade 2026).

The right sparse design changes from stage to stage because the parameter of interest changes: GCA in stage 1, specific performance and stability in stage 2.






TipBox 6 – A checklist for designing a sparse trial




Define the TPE and the market segment.
Estimate the genetic correlations between candidate locations from historical data.
Fix the budget in plots.
Choose the axis of sparsity: environments, testers, or both.
Fix the number of testers.
Fix the partial-replication rate.
Choose the checks and how often they appear.
Generate the allocation by restricted randomisation or a formal criterion. Where plots per hybrid are fewest, keep both pools in every location.
Compute connectivity and the expected PEV before planting (Box 4).
Simulate the design with the programme’s own parameters (sparse_vc(), sparse_simulate(), sparse_blup()).
Fix the analysis model and the covariance structure a priori.
Fix the decision metric and the cut-off a priori.

section: 19.13 Limitations of the evidence, and perspectives
text:
19.13 Limitations of the evidence, and perspectives
The authors of the primary studies declare their own limitations:

Li et al. (2026): a narrow genetic base and a single year.
Atanda et al. (2022): no way to identify the optimal overlap, and families of 1 to 9.
Werner, Covarrubias-Pazaran, et al. (2025): no cost model, and no hybrid structure.
Lubanga et al. (2025): a training set that was not optimised.
González-Diéguez et al. (2026): no G x E, no epistasis, no diversity management, and the logistic cost ignored.
Hild Aono and Chawade (2026): possible information leakage, and very similar environments.

As a research agenda, the open gaps are these.

SCA estimation, and prediction of specific hybrids, under sparsity. This chapter’s simulation shows the variance component is not recoverable at stage

The accuracy of specific unseen crosses is still unmeasured.

A three-dimensional connectivity metric, female x male x location. It would join Section 18.2.3 to Box 4. Section 20.4 defines a pair of counts for it.
The long-run effect on pool divergence and within-pool variance, in interaction with optimum contribution selection (Chapter 23; Chapter 15; Santantonio and Robbins (2020)).
Phenomics-assisted sparse testing in maize hybrids.
Pools unequal in size and breeding level, which is the usual commercial case.
Cost-accuracy frontiers in money, including isolation blocks and hand pollination.
The rate of wrongly discarded candidates as the evaluation metric, in place of the correlation.
Prospective empirical validation. Almost all the evidence for sparse testing comes from resampling complete data or from simulation, not from trials designed sparse from the start (Alemu et al. 2024; Crossa et al. 2017).

Sparse testing changes the stage-1 question. It is no longer “which genotypes can I evaluate well?”. It becomes “which haplotypes can I evaluate well, and against what sample of the opposite pool?”. The evidence is sufficient to adopt sparse designs at stage 1 with confidence. It is not sufficient to prescribe a universal sparsity level. That decision remains specific to each programme, and should be sized by the programme’s own simulation.

19.14 Reproducibility and assumptions
regenerate.R sparse reruns the phenotypic core of the cached study with R/17_sparse_testing.R. The scale and calibration are the same: 20 x 20 hybrids, half-sib families of four, and 20 % of hybrids untested. There are two differences:

the variance components are known, not estimated by REML;
the parentage allocation’s exchange search minimises the number of disconnected location pairs before the harmonic concurrence. The cached study’s criterion returned \(-\infty\) for any disconnected start, which left its search no gradient.



Show code
cr <- subset(core, part %in% c("spread", "k1"))
cr$cached <- mapply(function(L, k, s, h) {
  x <- s4$acc_all_mean[s4$nLoc == L & s4$k == k & s4$strategy == s & s4$h2_plot == h]

title: 19  Sparse testing: which hybrids go to which locations
text:
19.15 Where this connects

Chapter 18 chose which crosses to make. This chapter chose where to plant them, mostly with the whole factorial taken as given. Result 6 traded locations per candidate against a smaller stage-1 factorial at equal plots; what it leaves is the version in which every line stays in the data and the unmade crosses are predicted, so that an extra location per hybrid costs a cross rather than a parent. Result 2 never varied the locations per hybrid; it held two plots per hybrid and widened the trial. The joint problem, Section 18.9’s second gap, is Chapter 20.
The GCA/SCA decomposition and the tester-frequency argument behind Box 5 are derived in Section 5.11.
The relationship matrices that make sparse designs analysable are those of



The staged-trial trade-off of Chapter 22 is the line-breeding version of result 6.
Spreading testers and parents to slow within-pool erosion is the same concern as Chapter 15 and Chapter 23. Sparse testcrossing does by design what a diversity constraint does by optimisation.

title: 20  Which crosses, at which locations? Joint sparse allocation
text:
20.1 Why the two decisions are one
Chapter 18 chose which crosses to make from two pools, with the field design held fixed. Chapter 19 chose which locations each hybrid goes to, with the whole factorial taken as given. A programme makes both decisions out of one budget, in the same season, and each changes what the other can do: a cross that is not made cannot be planted anywhere, and a cross planted in one location says nothing about the others except through its parents. This chapter treats the two as one decision.
The search reported in Section 20.3 found strong methods for each half but none that chooses the crosses and their locations together for a two-pool hybrid programme – an absence of evidence from one search, not a proof of absence. The nearest treatments optimise the crosses and leave the environments to the trial manager (Heslot and Feoktistov 2020; Kadam et al. 2021), or optimise the environments for a fixed entry list (Cullis et al. 2020; Montesinos-López et al. 2022). This is the second gap of Section 18.9, and it needs the female x male x location connectivity metric Section 19.13 asked for.
The results this chapter defends:
Write \(n_F\) and \(n_M\) for the female and male lines – the pool-A and pool-B candidates, \(n_A\) and \(n_B\), of Chapter 18 – \(n_c\) for the number of distinct crosses made, \(L\) for the locations, \(k\) for the number of locations each cross is planted in (as in Chapter 19; not the testers per pool of Chapter 18, which appear in this chapter only in the label tester k=2 of Figure 20.1), and \(r\) for plots per cross per location. The field budget is
\[
B = n_c \, k \, r .
\tag{20.1}\]
Chapter 18 varied \(n_c\) (through the crosses per line \(c\), \(n_c = c\,n_F\) for a circulant plan) at fixed \(k\); Chapter 19 varied \(k\) and the layout at fixed \(n_c = n_F n_M\). At \(r = 1\), which is the stage-1 norm, fixing \(B\) ties the two together: halving the crosses doubles the locations each one can see. The nearest earlier look at this trade is result 6 of Section 19.11.3, which at equal plots compared testing every candidate at few locations against a smaller factorial at more, and found the first better. There the excluded candidates are a smaller factorial, so their parents leave the data, and a second stage with selection follows. Here every line stays in the data, the unmade crosses are predicted from it, and the comparison is of stage-1 accuracy alone. Result 1 (Section 20.5.1) points the same way as result 6.
The two terms buy different things. More crosses sample more of the factorial (in the circulant plans every line is in the data at every split; in the random sparse plans of Section 20.5 it is not, Section 20.4), which is what predicts the crosses never made (Section 18.6; Melchinger et al. (2023)). More locations per cross average that cross’s genotype x location deviations, \((g^f\ell)\), \((g^m\ell)\) and \((s\ell)\) in Equation 20.2, over more environments, which is what sharpens the estimate of a cross that was made. That is the expectation under the model of Section 20.2, not a result of Chapter 19: its result 2 held the locations per hybrid fixed while widening the trial (the difference from raising \(k\) is drawn in Section 20.5), and its result 6 measured selection after two stages, not the estimate of each made cross. A parent’s GCA is averaged over the locations of all its crosses, which an allocation can widen without adding locations per cross. Which term matters more depends on the SCA:GCA variance ratio, the genotype x location share of the genetic variance and how well the relationship matrix links lines across families – the quantities a programme knows least about at stage 1.

text:
20.2 The joint model
The model is Chapter 19’s, unchanged:
\[
y_{ijl} = \mu + \ell_l + g^f_i + g^m_j + s_{ij}
        + (g^f\ell)_{il} + (g^m\ell)_{jl} + (s\ell)_{ijl} + e_{ijl},
\tag{20.2}\]
where \(g^f_i\), \(g^m_j\) and \(s_{ij}\) are the \(\mathrm{GCA}^f_i\), \(\mathrm{GCA}^m_j\) and \(\mathrm{SCA}_{ij}\) of Section 19.2 (the \(g^A_i\), \(g^B_j\) and \(s_{ij}\) of Chapter 18, with the female pool as A; Appendix A), \(\ell_l\) is the fixed effect of location \(l\), \(g^f \sim N(\mathbf 0, \mathbf A_f\sigma^2_f)\), \(g^m \sim N(\mathbf 0, \mathbf A_m\sigma^2_m)\), \(s \sim N(\mathbf 0, (\mathbf A_f \otimes \mathbf A_m)\sigma^2_s)\), and the three interactions with location carry the same kernels crossed with the identity \(\mathbf I_L\) over locations: \((g^f\ell) \sim N(\mathbf 0, (\mathbf A_f \otimes \mathbf I_L)\sigma^2_{f\ell})\), \((g^m\ell) \sim N(\mathbf 0, (\mathbf A_m \otimes \mathbf I_L)\sigma^2_{m\ell})\), \((s\ell) \sim N(\mathbf 0, (\mathbf A_f \otimes \mathbf A_m \otimes \mathbf I_L)\sigma^2_{s\ell})\), and \(e_{ijl} \sim N(0, \sigma^2_e)\) i.i.d. In sparse_vc() these are s2f, s2m, s2s, s2fl, s2ml, s2sl and s2e. The target is the value in the target population of environments, \(g^f_i + g^m_j + s_{ij}\).
One simplification is inherited from Chapter 19. With one plot per cross per location, \((s\ell)_{ijl}\) and \(e_{ijl}\) have the same incidence, but the simulator draws \((s\ell)\) with the kernel of Equation 20.2, correlated between related crosses in one location, so a model could carry it as a structured term. The analysis model does not: it absorbs it into an i.i.d. residual of variance \(\sigma^2_{s\ell} + \sigma^2_e\) (vc$s2res). The best linear unbiased prediction (BLUP) and every PEV below are therefore exact for the analysis model, not for the generating one. With known components the cost is measured directly, by a literal generalised least squares (GLS) solve that carries the structured kernel, in the configuration of Table 20.5 (Table 20.1).


Show code
# Literal GLS BLUP of the target g^f + g^m + s, with (s l) given the kernel
# Ksl over the hybrids within a location: A_f x A_m as simulated, or I as
# analysed. Circulant c = 4, 20 x 20 half-sib pools, 8 locations, k = 2,
# plot h2 = 0.4; 30 paired replicates per SCA level.
ms <- local({
  n <- 20; nLoc <- 8; A <- relmat_halfsib(n, 5); AA <- kronecker(A, A)
  pf <- rep(seq_len(n), each = n); pm <- rep(seq_len(n), n)    # male fastest
  set.seed(41)
  M <- joint_alloc(design_circulant(n, n, c = 4), n, n, nLoc, k = 2,
                   strategy = "coverage")
  gls <- function(ph, vc, Ksl) {
    f <- pf[ph$hyb]; m <- pm[ph$hyb]; h <- ph$hyb
    same <- outer(ph$loc, ph$loc, "==")
    V <- vc$s2f * A[f, f] + vc$s2m * A[m, m] + vc$s2s * AA[h, h] +
      same * (vc$s2fl * A[f, f] + vc$s2ml * A[m, m] + vc$s2sl * Ksl[h, h]) +
      diag(vc$s2e, nrow(ph))
    X <- model.matrix(~ factor(ph$loc)); Vi <- solve(V)
    b <- solve(crossprod(X, Vi %*% X), crossprod(X, Vi %*% ph$y))
    C <- vc$s2f * A[pf, f] + vc$s2m * A[pm, m] + vc$s2s * AA[, h]
    drop(C %*% Vi %*% (ph$y - X %*% b))
  }
  vapply(c(low = "low", high = "high"), function(sca) {
    vc <- sparse_vc(0.4, sca)
    set.seed(42)
    d <- vapply(seq_len(30), function(r) {
      s <- sparse_simulate(M, n, n, vc, A, A)
      mis <- gls(s$pheno, vc, diag(n * n))
      # The I-kernel GLS is the analysis model: it must equal sparse_blup().
      if (r == 1) stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(mis,
        sparse_blup(s$pheno, n, n, nLoc, vc, A, A)$blup, tolerance = 1e-8)))
      cor(gls(s$pheno, vc, AA), s$g_target) - cor(mis, s$g_target)
    }, 0)
    c(diff = mean(d), se = sd(d) / sqrt(length(d)))
  }, c(diff = 0, se = 0))
})
knitr::kable(data.frame(SCA = colnames(ms), fmt(t(ms), 6), row.names = NULL),
             col.names = c("SCA level", "Mean difference", "SE"))

Carrying the structured kernel changes accuracy over all hybrids by -0.00002 (SE 0.00002) at low SCA and -0.00006 (SE 0.00005) at high SCA: nothing detectable, because \(\sigma^2_{s\ell}\) is a small share of the residual (5 % and 14 %) and half-sib relationships of 0.25 give the kernel off-diagonals of at most 0.25. The check covers one plan at \(h^2 = 0.4\); stronger relationships or a larger \(\sigma^2_{s\ell}\) would need it repeated.
What is new is only the incidence. A crossing plan \(P \subset \{1..n_F\} \times
\{1..n_M\}\) and an allocation give a 0/1 matrix \(M\) of size \(n_F n_M \times L\) whose row is zero when \((i, j) \notin P\) and sums to \(k\) otherwise. The R/17 functions take such an \(M\) directly; unmade crosses are predicted through \(\mathbf A_f\), \(\mathbf A_m\) and the GCA they share with made crosses – the CV1 prediction of Section 19.4 (T2 of Section 18.6 when both parents are in made crosses), produced by the plan rather than by a mask.


Show code

set.seed(21)
M <- joint_alloc(p, 6, 6, nLoc = 3, k = 1, strategy = "coverage")
stopifnot(sum(M) == nrow(p) * 1, all(rowSums(M) %in% c(0, 1)))  # N_P = n_c k
c(crosses_made = sum(rowSums(M) > 0), plots = sum(M), per_location = colSums(M))

#>            12            12             4             4             4

20.3 What the literature offers
Two searches were run: in October 2026 the Consensus index (Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, PubMed), Crossref and a general web search, reaching bioRxiv and the Crop Science / Plant Genome literature; on 20 October 2026, PubMed directly. Terms combined sparse testing, multi-environment trial, allocation of genotypes / hybrids to environments, incomplete factorial, mating design, training set optimisation, CDmean, A-optimality and genetic relatedness, with and without hybrid and maize, then genotype-based allocation (stratified or representative allocation, population structure in training-set and trial design, anticlustering). Nine families emerge (Table 20.2); none was built for the joint problem and each supplies a piece. The training-set optimisation tools of Akdemir et al. (2021) and Isidro y Sanchez and Akdemir (2021) could in principle select genotype-environment pairs, but none of the papers found does so for a crossing plan.

Optimising the field for a given entry list (rows 1, 2, 5, 6) supplies the criterion. Butler et al. (2014) and Cullis et al. (2020) optimise the A-optimality of the predicted genetic effects under the mixed model that will analyse the trial, relationship matrix included, and beat designs built for unrelated entries in silico; Lisle et al. (2021) diagnose whether a multi-environment design can estimate its variance parameters at all; Rio et al. (2022) extend CDmean, the mean coefficient of determination (Rincent et al. 2012), to genotype x environment (G x E) models, so reliability can be forecast before planting. The criterion of this chapter is that framework restricted to GCA. Incomplete-block allocation of lines to locations beat random allocation by 1.4 to 26.5 % in mean squared error (Montesinos-López et al. 2022) and was best with random close behind (Osval A. Montesinos-López et al. 2023); two of four allocation methods were slightly better, with accuracy barely lower at a 15:85 training-testing split (O. A. Montesinos-López et al. 2023); and at equal environments per line incomplete blocks performed better than random and were less variable (Montesinos-López et al. 2024) – the second a worst-case property a mean accuracy does not show. Lell et al. (2021) (1,604 wheat hybrids) found equal subgroups in overlapping subsets of environments one promising design, with high accuracy and low variability; Mothukuri et al. (2025) guided the split by relatedness to fully tested maize lines, with a weak correlation (0.20 to 0.31) between relatedness and accuracy. The overlap question is Section 19.6’s (Jarquin et al. 2020; Crespo-Herrera et al. 2021; Lubanga et al. 2025; Atanda et al. 2022). Which environments to sample is a further choice: sets chosen with a crop-growth-model criterion estimated wheat phenology parameters better than random sets twice as large (Rincent et al. 2017), a moderate mega-environmental allocation could potentially raise selection response by up to 43 % for the same resources (González-Barrios et al. 2019), and Hoefler and Gutierrez (2026) optimise its replication and sparsity by simulation. The locations here are exchangeable, which a real target population of environments is not.
Choosing entries and crosses for given environments (rows 3, 4, 7) supplies the search and the coverage logic. Kadam et al. (2021) report that optimising PEV or CDmean over all possible single crosses, not only those made, raised the expected prediction accuracy of the training set (a model forecast, not a realised accuracy) and conclude that it may be worthwhile; Heslot and Feoktistov (2020), the closest methodological precedent, choose which maize hybrids to create and phenotype by mixed binary-integer differential evolution, extended to designing a connected population before crossing; Guo et al. (2019) chose maize, wheat and rice hybrid training sets from the parents’ genotypes, beating random and PEV- or CD-optimised sets with 2 to 13 % of the hybrids. Endelman et al. (2014) asked the budget question within fixed biparental barley and maize families, choosing no cross: an unbalanced design over several locations predicted better than every entry in one, and up to 250 yield-plot equivalents per family the optimum did not genotype more progeny than were phenotyped (its relation to result 1 is in Section 20.5.1). Sparse factorials train hybrid prediction at least as well as tester designs, and fewer crosses per line favours the lines never crossed (Seye et al. 2020; Lorenzi et al. 2022; Melchinger et al. 2023). González-Diéguez et al. (2026) instead spread three to five testers sparsely among full-sibs (sparse testcrossing), which beat a single tester at an equal number of testcrosses and was matched, not beaten, by an approximate incomplete factorial (Section 19.8). Thomsen et al. (2026) is observational: sparse, unreplicated multi-environment data from a commercial winter oilseed rape hybrid programme, covering 1.67 % of mother x father combinations, which a GCA + SCA model still predicted (Section 18.4). Schoemaker et al. (2024), trading testers against environments in maize, found three to five well-chosen environments match ten random ones – the closest empirical look at one corner of the joint budget.
Representing genetic structure (rows 8, 9) supplies the balancing objective. For training sets, stratified sampling suited strong structure (rice) and CDmean, or CDmean within subpopulations, mild structure [wheat, all traits but test weight and heading date; Isidro et al. (2015)]; uniform sampling of the genetic space beat stratified and random sampling and matched maximising CD in maize and wheat, with all methods alike in strongly structured rice (Bustos-Korts et al. 2016); and stratified sampling with a marker-effect-weighted relationship matrix was best for forward prediction (Berro et al. 2019). Ou and Liao (2019) derived a new optimality criterion from Pearson’s correlation between the genomic estimated breeding values and the phenotypic values of a test set, under a ridge-regression whole-genome model, applicable to data with varying degrees of population structure; they illustrate it on rice (strong structure) and wheat (mild structure), implement it in the R package TSDFGS, and report it advantageous over existing methods. Akdemir and Isidro-Sánchez (2019) compared targeted training sets, optimised using the genotypes of the test set, with untargeted ones, and found the targeted sets gave the highest accuracies. Core Hunter (De Beukelaer et al. 2018) selects subsets on allele-frequency and distance criteria. All of these choose which candidates to phenotype.
Representation per environment has one precedent. Atanda et al. (2021) chose by CDmean which members of each full-sib family go to each environment, so that every biparental population is represented everywhere (their CV2), against predicting new populations tested in some environments only (CV1). Accuracy was similar. Their case for CV2 is about the data (every family phenotyped everywhere, a complete historical record), and their gain from grouping environments by growing and management conditions is a finding about the environments. Nor is CV1 against CV2 a controlled test of representation: the two differ in what is predicted (new populations against the unphenotyped half of phenotyped families) as well as in how families are spread. The formal object behind balancing is k-means anticlustering (Papenberg and Klau 2021), partitioning a set into groups of prescribed size that are as alike as possible.
Why balance at all is therefore this chapter’s own inference, with no direct empirical test in either direction. Genomic prediction across a maize hybrid diversity panel came mostly from differences in mean between breeding populations [predicting each from the others gave 0.12 for grain yield; Windhausen et al. (2012)], so subgroup means are much of what is predicted. Under the model of Section 20.2, with fixed location effects and a connected design, concentrating one subgroup’s crosses in a few locations does not bias the BLUP of its mean; it inflates the PEV of contrasts between subgroups, which pass through the effects of locations they do not share. Bias needs a systematic subgroup x location interaction the analysis model does not carry: the GCA x location terms, correlated within a family through \(A_f\), carry a random family x location interaction with mean zero, not a systematic one. Against the presumption, Fernandez-Gonzalez et al. (2023) found in a benchmark of training-set optimisers that a diverse training set made prediction robust to structure and clustering information was less effective. None of these papers allocates a crossing plan.
The gap is therefore precise. The criteria (PEV and CD with relatedness) and the search methods (exchange algorithms, differential evolution) exist, and each half has been optimised separately. Missing is the object that holds the crossing plan and the allocation under one budget, and evidence on how to split it.

title: 20  Which crosses, at which locations? Joint sparse allocation
text:
20.4 Design criteria computable before planting
Two quantities can be read off \(M\) before a seed is sown.
The mean PEV of GCA. The left-hand side of the mixed-model equations depends on the design alone, so the prediction error variance of every GCA effect is known before any phenotype exists. joint_pev() returns its mean over the \(n_F + n_M\) GCA effects, the trace of the GCA block of the inverted coefficient matrix divided by its order, exact for the analysis model of Section 20.2 with known components. It is an A-type criterion on the effects themselves, not the mean PEV of pairwise differences between effects used as the A-value in model-based design (Butler et al. 2014); the two differ by the covariance terms and need not rank designs identically. Table 20.4 shows it ranking allocations of one plan. It is blind to SCA and to the difference between predicting made and unmade crosses.
Two component counts. A single graph with females, males and locations as nodes is the obvious female x male x location metric, and it is wrong: a location node joins every parent planted there, so at one location it reports one component for any plan, two disconnected North Carolina design II (NC II) blocks included. A shared location links only sums of GCA. joint_connectivity() therefore returns two counts alongside the R/17 diagnostics:

n_comp_cross, the components of the female x male graph of the crosses that receive a plot, pooled over locations. At one location it is exactly the bipartite count of Section 18.2.3.
n_comp_loc, the components of the location graph in which two locations are joined when they share a parent.

Both equal to 1 is necessary for GCA and location contrasts to be linked by data, and the pair is not two independent conditions: if every location receives a plot, n_comp_cross = 1 implies n_comp_loc = 1. Locations split into two sets sharing no parent would put each planted cross wholly in one set, disconnecting the cross graph. So n_comp_loc adds information only when n_comp_cross > 1 or a location is empty. Neither count is sufficient, and the pair does not detect confounding of GCA with location. With 2 x 2 pools, two locations and \(k = 1\), the crosses (1,1) and (1,2) at location 1 and (2,1) and (2,2) at location 2 give n_comp_cross = 1 and n_comp_loc = 1, yet the female contrast is the location contrast: the fixed-effects matrix of location, female and male is rank-deficient by one (Table 20.3). A check that would detect this is the rank of that matrix over the planted plots; joint_connectivity() does not compute it. The two counts are therefore a screen, not the female x male x location metric Section 19.13 asked for, which remains open.


Show code
pix <- list(f = rep(1:2, each = 2), m = rep(1:2, 2))  # male fastest, as in R/17
Ma <- cbind(loc1 = as.integer(pix$f == 1), loc2 = as.integer(pix$f == 2))
cn <- joint_connectivity(Ma, 2, 2)
cells <- which(Ma == 1L, arr.ind = TRUE)
Xa <- model.matrix(~ loc + f + m,
                   data.frame(loc = factor(cells[, 2]), f = factor(pix$f[cells[, 1]]),
                              m = factor(pix$m[cells[, 1]])))
rk <- qr(Xa)$rank
stopifnot(cn[["n_comp_cross"]] == 1, cn[["n_comp_loc"]] == 1, rk == ncol(Xa) - 1)

             col.names = c("Female", "Male", "Location 1", "Location 2"))

Show code
# Share of random sparse plans (20 x 20) with at least one uncrossed line.
uncrossed <- function(p, n) {
  any(tabulate(p[["parent1"]], n) == 0 | tabulate(p[["parent2"]], n) == 0)
}
n_unc <- 20000
unc <- c(c4 = NA, c8 = NA)
set.seed(21)
unc[["c4"]] <- mean(replicate(n_unc, uncrossed(design_random_sparse(20, 20, c = 4), 20)))
set.seed(22)
unc[["c8"]] <- mean(replicate(n_unc, uncrossed(design_random_sparse(20, 20, c = 8), 20)))
# A c = 4 plan with an uncrossed line passes both counts.
set.seed(23)
repeat {
  pu <- design_random_sparse(20, 20, c = 4)
  du <- design_diagnostics(pu, 20, 20)
  if (uncrossed(pu, 20) && du[["components"]] == 1) break
}
cn_u <- joint_connectivity(joint_alloc(pu, 20, 20, nLoc = 8, k = 2, strategy = "coverage"),
                           20, 20)
stopifnot(cn_u[["n_comp_cross"]] == 1, cn_u[["n_comp_loc"]] == 1, !du[["connected"]])


Neither count sees a line that receives no cross. design_random_sparse() draws \(\mathrm{round}(c\,n_F)\) cells of the factorial without a per-line guarantee, so a line can go uncrossed; design_components() labels it unused and both counts are taken over the lines in use. In 2^{4} random sparse plans on the 20 x 20 pools of Section 20.5, the share with at least one uncrossed line was 0.348 at 4 crosses per line and 0.001 at 8. One c = 4 plan with an uncrossed line, allocated by coverage to eight locations at two per cross, returns n_comp_cross = 1 and n_comp_loc = 1. design_diagnostics() flags it (connected is FALSE because lines_A or lines_B falls short of the pool). Within the random family, therefore, moving from 8 to 4 crosses per line changes the number of lines in the data as well as the split, and the two random configurations of Section 20.5 do not isolate the split; the circulant plans, which cross every line \(c\) times, do.

set.seed(11)
vc <- sparse_vc(0.3); A <- relmat_halfsib(10, 2)
p <- design_circulant(10, 10, c = 3)

  M <- joint_alloc(p, 10, 10, nLoc = 4, k = 2, strategy = s, vc = vc,
                   Af = A, Am = A, n_iter = 100)
  cn <- joint_connectivity(M, 10, 10)
  data.frame(strategy = s, plots = sum(M), pev_gca = joint_pev(M, 10, 10, vc, A, A),
             fem_cover = cn$fem_cover, male_cover = cn$male_cover,

}))

20.4.1 Allele frequencies per location
Neither criterion of Section 20.4 reads a genotype. A plan can be connected and low in PEV and still send most crosses of one subgroup to a few locations, which costs precision in subgroup contrasts, or bias under a subgroup x location interaction the model omits (Section 20.3 gives the argument and the evidence on both sides). The quantity that sees the imbalance is computed from the hybrids’ marker genotypes, and its algebra is exact.
The decomposition. Let \(\mathbf X_P\) be the hybrid marker matrix of the planted plots: one row \(\mathbf x_u\) per plot \(u\) (a cross planted at \(k\) locations appears \(k\) times) and \(N_{SNP}\) markers coded 0/0.5/1 as everywhere in this book (the symbol of Section 10.3.2, since \(m\) marks the male pool). It has \(N_P = n_c k r\) rows, the budget in plots. Write \(n_l\) for the plots at location \(l\), \(\bar{\mathbf p}_l\) for their allele frequencies (column means) and \(\bar{\mathbf p}\) for those of all planted plots. Summing the one-way analysis-of-variance identity over markers,
\[
\sum_u \lVert \mathbf x_u - \bar{\mathbf p} \rVert^2
= \sum_l \sum_{u \in l} \lVert \mathbf x_u - \bar{\mathbf p}_l \rVert^2
+ SS_B,
\qquad
SS_B = \sum_l n_l \lVert \bar{\mathbf p}_l - \bar{\mathbf p} \rVert^2 ,
\tag{20.3}\]
with \(SS_B\) the between-location sum of squares, summed over markers.
The plan and \(k\) fix the rows of \(\mathbf X_P\), hence the left-hand side; an allocation only decides which location each row goes to. Minimising \(SS_B\) is therefore maximising the within-location sum, the k-means objective, which is what Papenberg and Klau (2021) call k-means anticlustering: groups of prescribed size (which carries the loads \(n_l\)) made as alike as possible. What their formulation does not carry is the item structure: here each cross enters as exactly \(k\) copies that must go to \(k\) different locations, whereas anticlustering assigns every item once and independently.
On \(\mathbf X_P\), \(SS_B/(N_P N_{SNP})\) is the plot-weighted mean squared deviation of a location’s allele frequencies from the pooled ones. On a 0/1 matrix \(\mathbf Z\) with one column per subgroup (a family, a heterotic subgroup, a female-family x male-family class) the column means are subgroup shares, and minimising \(SS_B\) equalises them. The two objectives differ; Table 20.5 measures both.
The diversity lens. The gene diversity of location \(l\)’s plots, \(GD_l = 1 - \theta_l\) over the molecular coancestry of Section 2.3, is \(\frac{1}{N_{SNP}} \sum_v 2\bar p_{lv}(1 - \bar p_{lv})\) over markers \(v\), Nei’s gene diversity at the location’s frequencies (Section 11.2; Nei (1973)). Because \(2p(1-p)\) is quadratic in \(p\), the decomposition carries over exactly:
\[
\sum_l \frac{n_l}{N_P}\, GD_l \;=\; GD_P - \frac{2\,SS_B}{N_P\, N_{SNP}},
\tag{20.4}\]
with \(GD_P\) the gene diversity of all planted plots. Take the locations as the subpopulations of Chapter 3 and weight them, as that chapter weights the subpopulations of Caballero and Toro (2002), by their share \(N_i/N_T = n_l/N_P\) of the plots. Then \(GD_P\) is \(GD_T = 1 - \bar f\), the left-hand side is \(GD_{WS} = 1 - \tilde f\), and
\[
\frac{2\,SS_B}{N_P\, N_{SNP}} = GD_{BS} = \tilde f - \bar f
\tag{20.5}\]
exactly, for any loads; it is also the \(\bar D\) in Chapter 3’s \(F_{ST}\), and Nei’s \(D_{ST} = H_T - H_S\) (Nei 1973) with \(H_S\) the plot-weighted mean of the location diversities (the plain mean under equal loads). \(SS_B\) differs from all of these only by the factor \(N_P N_{SNP}/2\). Between heterotic pools this component is the heterosis engine, to be preserved; between the locations of one trial it is a nuisance, to be minimised.
The base. \(SS_B\) is centred on \(\bar{\mathbf p}\), the planted set’s own frequencies, not on a frozen base \(\mathbf p_0\) (Section 10.7.1). Against \(\mathbf p_0\) – here the frequencies of the complete factorial of candidate lines –
\[
\sum_l n_l \lVert \bar{\mathbf p}_l - \mathbf p_0 \rVert^2
= SS_B + N_P \lVert \bar{\mathbf p} - \mathbf p_0 \rVert^2 ,
\tag{20.6}\]
and the second term is fixed by the crossing plan, so with the plan fixed the two bases rank allocations identically. That term is the plan’s departure from the pool in the drift lens: \(\lVert \bar{\mathbf p} - \mathbf p_0 \rVert^2\) is the numerator of \(F_{drift}\) (Section 10.7.2; Meuwissen et al. (2020)) before each marker is standardised by \(p_{0}(1 - p_{0})\), with the planted set in the place of cycle \(t\). It is not a loss of gene diversity, which the book keeps in the other lens: per marker \(GD(p_0) - GD(\bar p) = 2(p_0 - \bar p)(1 - p_0 - \bar p)\), whose sign depends on which side of \(1/2\) the two frequencies sit. \(SS_B\) belongs to the allocation, the drift term to the crossing plan (Section 18.11).
Table 20.5 computes all of this for one plan at the scale of the sweep of Section 20.5, under four allocations: random; coverage; an exchange search that swaps two plots between locations when \(SS_B\) falls (loads and \(k\) unchanged); and the same search on \([\mathbf X_P,\; w\mathbf Z]\), the markers with the female-family x male-family indicators appended and \(w\) set so that both blocks carry the same total sum of squares over the planted plots. Rows: between_pct, \(100\,SS_B\) over the marker sum of squares; rms_dp, \(\sqrt{SS_B/(N_P N_{SNP})}\); gd_short_pct, the shortfall of the plot-weighted mean \(GD_l\) from \(GD_P\), in % of \(GD_P\); groups_between_pct, between_pct on \(\mathbf Z\); families and family_pairs, the share of each pool’s parent families, and of the plan’s family classes, present per location; fem_cover and pev_gca as in Table 20.4. The chunk asserts the decomposition (Equation 20.3), the \(GD\) identity (Equation 20.4) on \(\mathbf f\) and \(GD_{BS} = 2\,SS_B/(N_P N_{SNP})\) (Equation 20.5) for every allocation, and the change of base (Equation 20.6), which has power only on the random sparse plan checked after the table (a circulant plan uses every line equally often, so its drift term is zero). No accuracy is computed.


Show code
nF <- 20; nM <- 20; nLoc <- 8; nfam <- 5; n_snp <- 500
fam <- rep(seq_len(nfam), each = nF / nfam)
# A DH line carries its family's common parent at each marker with probability
# 1/2, else an unrelated gamete; a hybrid is the mean of its two parents (0/0.5/1).
dh_pool <- function(q) {
  par <- matrix(rbinom(nfam * n_snp, 1, rep(q, each = nfam)), nfam)
  ifelse(matrix(runif(nF * n_snp) < 0.5, nF), par[fam, ],
         matrix(rbinom(nF * n_snp, 1, rep(q, each = nF)), nF))
}
set.seed(31)
U <- dh_pool(runif(n_snp, 0.1, 0.9)); V <- dh_pool(runif(n_snp, 0.1, 0.9))
pix <- list(f = rep(seq_len(nF), each = nM), m = rep(seq_len(nM), nF))  # male fastest
Xh <- (U[pix$f, ] + V[pix$m, ]) / 2
p0 <- colMeans(Xh)                      # frozen base: the complete factorial
pl <- design_circulant(nF, nM, c = 4)
A <- relmat_halfsib(nF, nfam); vc <- sparse_vc(0.3)
ss <- function(Z) sum(sweep(Z, 2, colMeans(Z))^2)
between <- function(Z, g) {             # SS_B for the rows of Z grouped by location g
  n <- tabulate(g, nLoc)
  sum(n * rowSums(sweep(rowsum(Z, g) / n, 2, colMeans(Z))^2))
}
freq_terms <- function(M) {
  cl <- which(M == 1L, arr.ind = TRUE); X <- Xh[cl[, 1], ]; g <- cl[, 2]
  n <- tabulate(g, nLoc); NP <- nrow(X); SSB <- between(X, g)
  W <- sum(vapply(split(seq_len(NP), g), function(r) ss(X[r, , drop = FALSE]), 0))
  stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(ss(X), W + SSB, tolerance = 1e-12)))
  # Plot-weighted mean GD_l = GD_P - 2 SS_B / (N_P N_SNP), computed on f itself.
  f <- molecular_coancestry(X)
  fll <- vapply(seq_len(nLoc), function(l) vapply(seq_len(nLoc), function(j)
    mean(f[g == l, g == j]), 0), numeric(nLoc))   # mean coancestry between locations
  gd_l <- 1 - diag(fll); gd_P <- 1 - mean(f); w <- n / NP
  stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(sum(w * gd_l), gd_P - 2 * SSB / (NP * n_snp))))
  # Caballero & Toro (2002) with weights N_i / N_T = n_l / N_P: GD_BS = f_til -
  # f_bar = D_bar (mean Nei distance) = 2 SS_B / (N_P N_SNP), for any loads.
  Dij <- outer(diag(fll), diag(fll), "+") / 2 - fll
  stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(sum(w * diag(fll)) - mean(f), 2 * SSB / (NP * n_snp))),
            isTRUE(all.equal(drop(w %*% Dij %*% w), 2 * SSB / (NP * n_snp))))
  # Change of base to p0: the extra term depends on the plan, not the allocation.
  SSB0 <- sum(n * rowSums(sweep(rowsum(X, g) / n, 2, p0)^2))
  stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(SSB0, SSB + NP * sum((colMeans(X) - p0)^2))))
  gp <- paste(fam[pix$f[cl[, 1]]], fam[pix$m[cl[, 1]]])
  nu <- function(z) mean(tapply(z, g, function(v) length(unique(v))))
  c(between_pct = 100 * SSB / ss(X), rms_dp = sqrt(SSB / (NP * n_snp)),
    gd_short_pct = 100 * 2 * SSB / (NP * n_snp) / gd_P,
    groups_between_pct = 100 * between(model.matrix(~ gp - 1), g) /
      ss(model.matrix(~ gp - 1)),
    families = (nu(fam[pix$f[cl[, 1]]]) + nu(fam[pix$m[cl[, 1]]])) / (2 * nfam),
    family_pairs = nu(gp) / length(unique(gp)),
    fem_cover = joint_connectivity(M, nF, nM)$fem_cover,
    pev_gca = joint_pev(M, nF, nM, vc, A, A))
}
# Swap the locations of two plots when SS_B of Y falls: loads and k fixed.
# Y has one row per hybrid, as Xh; Y = Xh balances marker frequencies.
freq_balance <- function(M, Y, n_iter = 5000) {
  cl <- which(M == 1L, arr.ind = TRUE)
  S <- rowsum(Y[cl[, 1], , drop = FALSE], cl[, 2]); n <- colSums(M)
  for (it in seq_len(n_iter)) {
    i <- sample.int(nrow(cl), 2); x <- cl[i[1], 1]; y <- cl[i[2], 1]
    a <- cl[i[1], 2]; b <- cl[i[2], 2]
    if (a == b || M[x, b] == 1L || M[y, a] == 1L) next
    d <- Y[y, ] - Y[x, ]
    if (sum((S[a, ] + d)^2 - S[a, ]^2) / n[a] + sum((S[b, ] - d)^2 - S[b, ]^2) / n[b] < 0) {
      S[a, ] <- S[a, ] + d; S[b, ] <- S[b, ] - d
      M[x, c(a, b)] <- c(0L, 1L); M[y, c(b, a)] <- c(0L, 1L)
      cl[i, 2] <- c(b, a)
    }
  }
  M
}
# Family-class indicators Z (one column per female-family x male-family class),
# weighted so that Z and the markers carry the same total SS over the planted
# plots (fixed by the plan and k, whatever the allocation).
Zh <- model.matrix(~ factor(paste(fam[pix$f], fam[pix$m])) - 1)
rP <- rep((pl$parent1 - 1) * nM + pl$parent2, 2)        # planted rows, k = 2
wZ <- sqrt(ss(Xh[rP, ]) / ss(Zh[rP, ]))
set.seed(32)
fr_a <- replicate(5, {
  Mc <- joint_alloc(pl, nF, nM, nLoc, k = 2, strategy = "coverage")
  stopifnot(sum(Mc) == 2 * nrow(pl))                 # N_P = n_c k, used as NP below
  sapply(list(random = joint_alloc(pl, nF, nM, nLoc, k = 2, strategy = "random"),
              coverage = Mc, freq_balanced = freq_balance(Mc, Xh),
              freq_family_balanced = freq_balance(Mc, cbind(Xh, wZ * Zh))),
         freq_terms)
})
fr <- data.frame(strategy = dimnames(fr_a)[[2]], t(apply(fr_a, 1:2, mean)), row.names = NULL)
knitr::kable(fmt(apply(fr_a, 1:2, mean), 4))   # = t(fr): metrics as rows

Result. Over five allocations of the same plan, the between-location share of the marker sum of squares is 3.97 % (SD 0.30) under random placement, 1.08 % (SD 0.10) under the coverage rule, 0.55 % (SD 0.04) after the exchange search on markers and 1.26 % after the search on markers and family classes (\(w =\) 6.86); a random partition of the same plots into eight locations, ignoring that the copies of a cross must be apart, gives \((L-1)/(N_P-1) =\) 4.40 % in expectation. The mean location falls short of \(GD_P\) by 1.66 %, 0.45 %, 0.23 % and 0.53 %. The share of each pool’s parent families present per location is 0.985 to 1.000 under every strategy. Female-family x male-family classes are present at 0.57 to 0.60 per location under the first three strategies, with a between-location share (groups_between_pct) of 3.6 to 4.1 %, and at 0.79, share 0.9 %, under the fourth, against a ceiling of 0.80 (20 plots per location for 25 classes). Female coverage is 0.891 under the coverage rule and 0.860 under the fourth strategy; mean PEV of GCA is 0.504, 0.494, 0.492 and 0.495. On a random sparse plan with the same mean of four crosses per line, whose lines enter 1 to 8 crosses, the drift term \(N_P \lVert \bar{\mathbf p} - \mathbf
p_0 \rVert^2\) is 23.6 % of the \(\mathbf p_0\)-centred sum, \(F_{drift}\) of the planted set is 0.0043, the change of base holds, and the planted set’s gene diversity is above that of \(\mathbf p_0\) at 42 % of markers and below it at the rest.
Interpretation. Balancing parents per location balances their alleles: the coverage rule removes most of the frequency imbalance, and the marker search a further 49 % of what remains, at no cost in PEV of GCA here. Marker balance harmonises allele frequencies but not subgroup shares: under it the family classes stay at the level of random placement. Putting the class indicators into the criterion raises class presence from 0.60 at its coverage start to 0.79, close to the 0.80 ceiling, and pays for it in the marker term (1.26 % against 0.55 % for the marker-only search), in female coverage and a little in PEV – a trade-off set by \(w\), which was fixed by the equal-sum-of-squares rule, not tuned. Family presence barely separates the strategies, because half-sib families reach nearly every location under any of them. The limits, which hold wherever this section is used later: the search is first-improvement over 5,000 random pair swaps with no convergence test, so its rows bound what 5,000 proposals buy, not the minimum of \(SS_B\); one plan at one scale was examined; and no accuracy was computed, so whether a smaller \(SS_B\) on either block improves prediction, or protects subgroup contrasts against a subgroup x location interaction, is untested (Section 20.7).
The share needs no package function. For a 0/1 plan M (one row per hybrid, one column per location, as joint_alloc() returns) and a hybrid marker matrix X in the same row order it is three lines of base R; with X replaced by 0/1 subgroup indicators it gives groups_between_pct. On the random sparse plan above, checked against the chunk’s own between():

SSB <- sum(table(g) * rowSums(sweep(rowsum(XP, g) / c(table(g)), 2, colMeans(XP))^2))
100 * SSB / sum(sweep(XP, 2, colMeans(XP))^2)   # between-location share, %

text:
20.5 What the simulation finds
The sweep crosses six configurations that all spend 160 plots (the tester design 152) – circulant plans with 8, 4 and 2 crosses per line at 1, 2 and 4 locations per cross, random sparse plans with 8 and 4, and a two-tester design at two locations – with the allocation strategies, two plot heritabilities and two SCA levels (sparse_vc(): SCA a quarter of, or equal to, a GCA variance; genotype x location half of each main effect, so a genetic correlation of 2/3 between locations). Pools are 20 x 20 in half-sib families of four; eight locations; 30 replicates per cell (Figure 20.1).
Comparisons between strategies are paired; those between configurations are not. Within one configuration and scenario each replicate draws one plan, random and coverage allocate it, and both are simulated from the same seed, so they share the true genetic values (sparse_simulate() draws every effect before it looks at the allocation). Each configuration draws its own seeds, so the budget-split comparisons of result 1 are between independent cells, with both cells’ standard errors combined. The exchange search is too slow to repeat per replicate: per cell one plan gets a coverage allocation (start) and a search from it, and those two fixed designs are simulated in every replicate with the same seed, pairing optimised with its own start.
The evidence bar. A difference is detected past two standard errors of the difference. Chapter 18 calls a difference resolved only past three; a quantity between two and three is flagged where it appears.

20.5.1 1. The budget split: crosses against locations


Show code
lev <- c("circulant c=8, 1 loc", "circulant c=4, 2 loc", "circulant c=2, 4 loc",
         "random c=8, 1 loc", "random c=4, 2 loc", "tester k=2, 2 loc")
op <- par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(7.5, 4, 2, 0.5), mgp = c(2.4, 0.7, 0))
for (sc in c("low", "high")) for (h in c(0.2, 0.4)) {
  d <- js[js$sca == sc & js$h2_plot == h, ]
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0.5, length(lev) + 0.5),
       ylim = range(js$acc_all - 2 * js$acc_all_se, js$acc_all + 2 * js$acc_all_se),
       xaxt = "n", xlab = "", ylab = "Accuracy, all hybrids",
       main = bquote(italic(h)^2 == .(h) * ", " * .(sc) ~ "SCA"), cex.main = 0.95,
       font.main = 1)
  axis(1, at = seq_along(lev), labels = lev, las = 2, cex.axis = 0.75)
  title(xlab = "Configuration", line = 6.3)
  for (j in seq_along(strat_col)) {
    e <- d[d$strategy == names(strat_col)[j], ]
    x <- match(e$label, lev) + (j - 2) * 0.2
    arrows(x, e$acc_all - 2 * e$acc_all_se, x, e$acc_all + 2 * e$acc_all_se,
           angle = 90, code = 3, length = 0.02, col = strat_col[j])
    points(x, e$acc_all, pch = 19, col = strat_col[j])
  }
  if (sc == "high" && h == 0.2)
    legend("topright", legend = names(strat_col), col = strat_col, pch = 19,
           bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
}

Figure 20.1: Accuracy (correlation between predicted and true genetic value) over all 400 possible hybrids at a budget of 160 plots (tester design 152), by configuration (plan, crosses per line \(c\), locations per cross) and allocation strategy; one panel per plot heritability \(h^2\) and SCA level. Points are cell means over 30 replicates, error bars span plus or minus two standard errors. optimised is one fixed design per cell. 20 x 20 pools in half-sib families of four, eight locations, known variance components; in-repo sweep (regenerate.R joint).





Figure 20.1 reads left to right along the budget identity (Equation 20.1). Within the circulant family, with the coverage allocation, 160 crosses at one location each reach 0.787 at \(h^2 = 0.4\) and low SCA, 80 crosses at two locations 0.767, and 40 at four 0.700. With high SCA the steps are larger – 0.682, 0.636, 0.535. The order holds in all four scenarios, unevenly: the step from 80 to 160 crosses is 0.5 to 3.4 standard errors of the difference, the step from 40 to 80 0.5 to 4.4. Of the 8 steps, 4 – 160 versus 80 at \(h^2 = 0.2\), low SCA; 160 versus 80 at \(h^2 = 0.4\), low SCA; 80 versus 40 at \(h^2 = 0.2\), low SCA; 80 versus 40 at \(h^2 = 0.2\), high SCA – are under two standard errors, and 160 versus 80 at \(h^2 = 0.4\), high SCA, at 2.14, is under Chapter 18’s three; only their direction agrees with the rest. The two-tester design, with 76 crosses at two locations, sits below the circulant plan with 80 crosses at two locations in every scenario and strategy, at nearly the same budget (152 against 160 plots).
For the crosses that were made the comparison reverses (Table 20.6). Forty crosses at four locations estimate those crosses at 0.845, against 0.807 for 160 crosses at one location (\(h^2 = 0.4\), low SCA; z = 2.67, under Chapter 18’s three), because each is seen in four locations rather than one. Across scenarios this difference is 1.2 to 6.0 standard errors; the smallest, 1.2 at \(h^2 = 0.2\) and low SCA, is not resolved. Nor is the reversal visibly monotone: at \(h^2 = 0.2\) and high SCA, 80 crosses at two locations reach 0.610 against 0.618 for 160 at one (z = -0.32, not resolved). A programme that picks parents on GCA, or will choose among all possible single crosses with a prediction model, should spend the budget on distinct crosses. One that will advance only crosses it has made estimates them better from more locations, but then chooses among 40 candidates instead of 160, and the response to selection depends on that intensity as well as on accuracy, which this chapter does not model.
