title: Appendix C — Verification
text:
C.1 The method: slow oracles
A derivation the reader cannot re-run against a naive implementation is a claim, not a verification. This appendix says how each result in the book was checked, and how to re-run the checks.
Every fast route in the package has a deliberately slow, literal counterpart in R/09_reference.R that transcribes the definition with no algebraic shortcut. The fast route must match it to machine precision.
Show code
ref_theta
#> function (idx, ctx) 
#> mean(ctx[["f"]][idx, idx])
#> <bytecode: 0x77c7af52a0>
#> <environment: namespace:hybdiv>
theta_group
#> function (idx, ctx) 
#> {
#>     f <- ctx[["f"]]
#>     if (!is.matrix(f)) 
#>         stop("ctx[[\"f\"]] (hybrid coancestry) is missing")
#>     mean(f[idx, idx])
#> }
#> <bytecode: 0x77c7b2e778>
#> <environment: namespace:hybdiv>
fast_theta
#> function (idx, ctx) 
#> {
#>     cnt <- line_counts(idx, ctx)
#>     u <- which(cnt > 0L)
#>     cu <- cnt[u]
#>     s <- sum(cu)
#>     as.numeric(crossprod(cu, ctx$fL[u, u, drop = FALSE] %*% cu))/(s * 
#>         s)
#> }
#> <bytecode: 0x77c7b65d90>
#> <environment: namespace:hybdiv>
Three implementations of one quantity: a literal mean over the submatrix, the packaged version, and the line-route collapse that never forms the submatrix at all. They must agree.
Show code
sim  <- simulate_pools(n_A = 20, n_B = 20, m = 1500, seed = 7)
ctxp <- ctx_from_pools(sim)
set.seed(3); sel <- sample.int(ctxp$N, 50)

c(oracle     = ref_theta(sel, ctxp),
  packaged   = theta_group(sel, ctxp),
  line_route = fast_theta(sel, ctxp),
  max_dev    = max(abs(c(theta_group(sel, ctxp), fast_theta(sel, ctxp)) -
                       ref_theta(sel, ctxp))))
#>       oracle     packaged   line_route      max_dev 
#> 6.708316e-01 6.708316e-01 6.708316e-01 1.110223e-16
The oracles exist so that this comparison is possible for a reader who does not trust the derivation – which is the correct posture.

title: Appendix C — Verification
section: C.7 Known limitations of the verification
text:
C.7 Known limitations of the verification
Stated so they are not mistaken for oversights.
The oracles share the author’s understanding. They check that the fast route computes what the slow route computes. They cannot check that the slow route implements the right definition. That is what the reproduction of the published Caballero & Toro tables in Chapter 3 is for – an external check against numbers this project did not produce.
Monte Carlo checks have Monte Carlo error. Where a test asserts agreement with a simulated expectation rather than an algebraic identity, the tolerance is loose by necessity, and a genuinely small bias would pass.
Everything is verified on simulated data. The identities are algebraic and will hold on real genotypes. The empirical results – which metrics are redundant, how much index a constraint costs – were derived at \(F_{ST} = 0.15\) with simulated markers, and Chapter 12 says explicitly that they should be re-derived on real genotypes before being treated as settled.
One chapter’s headline results come from outside this repository. The mating-design sweep of Chapter 18 (mating_scenarios_summary.csv and its siblings) was produced by an external study whose code needs AlphaSimR and sommer; it shipped with its own 37-check validation report, summarised in that chapter, but it is not re-run by anything here. What is re-run is its phenotypic core (regenerate.R mating), and Section 18.10 compares the two.
The sparse-testing chapter (Chapter 19) has the same structure. Its REML grid, two-stage scenario and genomic layer are cached from an external study, which validated its own estimator on the complete design (Table 19.5). The in-repo regenerate.R sparse re-runs the known-component core, and Section 19.14 compares the two.

title: Appendix D — The bibliographic corpora
text:
D.6 Limitations
These are abstract screens. Relevance and the metric annotations were scored from titles and abstracts, not from full texts. A paper that computes a metric without naming it in the abstract is invisible to this table – which almost certainly understates how often coancestry is computed as an intermediate step.
The queries shaped the answer. 29 plant-breeding queries were run; a different query set would return a different landscape. The strong maize skew is by design, and the counts for other crops are too small to support a claim about those crops.
“Not established in the retrieved set” means exactly that. Every such statement in Chapter 21 is a claim about this corpus, not about the literature as a whole. It is a prompt to look further before assuming novelty, not a proof of it.
Citation counts are a snapshot at screening time and are already stale.

Reproduce this chapter
All the code of this chapter, in order and with the explanation kept as comments, is one script: 93-corpora.R. Download it, install hybdiv, and run it top to bottom in an empty directory; cached results are fetched on first use.
